title: Money Laundering (Placement, Layering, Integration)
one_screen: Criminals attempt to disguise illicit proceeds by processing funds through multiple steps (often called placement, layering, integration) to make them appear legitimate. In practice these steps can overlap or repeat rather than being strictly sequential.
bodyText: Money laundering is the process of making illegally-gained money appear legal. In common terms, it involves introducing criminal proceeds into the financial system (placement), moving them through complex transactions to obscure origins (layering), and finally using them in legitimate markets (integration). For example, a drug trafficker may deposit cash into a front-company’s bank account (placement), rapidly move funds between accounts or countries (layering), and then use the cleansed funds to buy real estate (integration). The FATF emphasizes that authorities should consider money laundering risks at all stages – placement, layering and integration – even though in reality these can overlap. Placement – physically putting illicit cash into the financial system (e.g. cash deposits, buying chips at a casino) – is very risky for criminals. Layering – transferring funds through multiple accounts, instruments or entities to hide trails – creates complexity but can arouse bank suspicions through unusual patterns. Integration – investing laundered money into legitimate businesses or assets (real estate, luxury goods) – lets criminals enjoy their proceeds. Importantly, real-world laundering seldom follows a neat one-way flow; criminals may cycle funds or intermingle legitimate and illicit transactions to muddy the trail. A bank’s AML program must detect signs of these stages. For instance, sudden large cash deposits by a new customer (suggesting placement) or a string of rapid transfers through offshore accounts (suggesting layering) should trigger scrutiny. Because money laundering is defined by its intent rather than just specific steps, banks use broad Suspicious Transaction Report (STR) criteria – any transaction “indicating proceeds of crime” – rather than looking only for textbook P-L-I patterns. Initial ML Concept Flow +-------------+ | Illicit Cash | +-------------+ | v +-------------+ <--- Bank deposit, purchase of chips, etc. (Placement) | Financial | | System | +-------------+ | v +-------------+ <--- Many transfers, conversions, foreign wires (Layering) | Complex | | Transactions| +-------------+ | v +-------------+ <--- Purchase of assets or businesses (Integration) | Legitimate | | Economy | +-------------+ Banks must monitor for unusual deposits, rapid transfers, and sudden asset purchases by new or high-risk customers, as these may indicate placement, layering or integration of illicit funds. Assuming all money laundering neatly follows “placement → layering → integration” can blind analysts to schemes where funds re-enter or loop through the system in non-linear ways. **Money laundering** — processing criminal proceeds to hide their origin. --- **Proceeds-based financing (e.g. fraud)** — using illicit or legitimate funds to finance any activity. The confusion arises when a loan might be secured with dirty money; laundering focuses on hiding sources, whereas the loan per se is a financial crime enabled by those hidden funds. **No delta.** The core concept of money laundering (concealing criminal funds) is universal, though each country’s law (e.g. India’s PMLA, US BSA, UK POCA) defines specific offences.

title: Terrorist Financing
one_screen: Terrorist financing is collecting or providing funds to support terrorism. Unlike money laundering, it may involve funds from lawful sources and focuses on concealing the destination and purpose of money, not necessarily its origin.
bodyText: Terrorist financing (TF) involves raising or moving money to fund terrorist activities. Crucially, TF funds can come from both illegal and completely legitimate sources (donations, charities). For example, a charity donation may be diverted to extremist groups; the donor’s money wasn’t criminally obtained, so “fund placement” isn’t needed, only disguise of the destination. FATF and the Egmont Group stress that terrorists typically aren’t as concerned with hiding *where* money came from, but they do hide where it’s going and what it will buy. For banks, this means focusing on transaction patterns that suggest support for terrorism: e.g. frequent small payments to charities or NGOs based in conflict zones, purchases of military gear or specific supplies, or international transfers to entities with extremist ties. Unlike money laundering, the key risk factors include connections to known extremist groups, donations to shell charities, or unexplained funding of persons on watchlists. Financial institutions must report any transaction suspected to finance terrorism via Suspicious Activity Reports (SARs/STRs) just as for laundering. Apply enhanced scrutiny to cross-border transfers, new high-risk charities, or foreign nationals sending money to known conflict regions. If funds flow towards suspects of terrorism, report immediately. Ignoring a transaction just because the money source seems legitimate (e.g. a salary or donation), forgetting that TF risk is about *destination and use*, not origin. **Terrorist financing** — providing funds (legal or illegal) to support terrorism. --- **Money laundering** — disguising illicit origins of criminal proceeds. They get mixed up because both are predicate offences requiring detection, but TF can involve fully legal funds, while ML always involves criminal proceeds. — PMLA covers TF financing; banks must report suspicious TF under FIU-IND guidelines (as STR). — Terrorism financing is criminal under Terrorism Act 2000; UK firms file SARs to NCA for TF-related activity. — EU AMLD obliges Member States to criminalize terrorist financing (including from lawful sources); STRs must include TF suspicions. — Under U.S. law (18 U.S.C. § 2339A/B), giving material support or funds to terrorists (even from legal sources) is illegal; banks file SARs for TF (covering both domestic and foreign terrorists).

title: Proliferation Financing
one_screen: Proliferation financing is the provision of funds or financial services for the creation or spread of weapons of mass destruction. It is illegal under UN sanctions and FATF standards, and financial institutions must screen against WMD sanctions lists.
bodyText: Proliferation financing means supplying money, goods or services to help manufacture nuclear, chemical or biological weapons or their delivery systems, contrary to UN regulations. It covers funds used by state or non-state actors to buy missile parts, nuclear materials, or related know-how. FATF has issued guidance that PF is a high-risk area tied to UN sanctions programs. For example, funding an international buyer to ship missile components into a sanctioned country would be PF. Unlike typical ML or TF, proliferation finance is usually done by governments or front companies acting for rogue states. Sanctions lists (UN, EU, US) explicitly target individuals and entities involved in WMD programs. Banks must therefore do special screening: check customers and transactions against UN Security Council lists for proliferation (e.g. North Korea, Iran sanctions) and flag any matches. Because PF involves evasion of sanctions, detecting it relies on sanctions compliance rather than pattern analysis. Block or reject any transaction involving a person or entity on a WMD-related sanctions list. Implement payment filters specifically for proliferation-related products or entities. Treating PF just like terrorism financing. PF usually involves state actors and strict UN lists; it often requires additional government licenses, so do not ignore sanctions compliance. **Proliferation financing** — funding the spread of WMD capabilities (subject to strict UN sanctions). --- **Terrorism financing** — funding terrorism (often banned by domestic/UN rules but not limited to WMD). They are mixed up because both involve “illicit finance,” but PF is specifically WMD-related and always illegal under international law. **No delta.** All jurisdictions implement UN sanctions on proliferation the same way: by requiring EDD for any customer or payment linked to WMD-sensitive activities and mandatory blocking of UN-listed individuals/entities.

title: FATF and Global Standards
one_screen: The Financial Action Task Force (FATF) is an international body that sets AML/CFT standards (40+9 Recommendations). Its rules aren’t laws, but countries adopt them locally. FATF conducts mutual evaluations and classifies jurisdictions into “grey” (monitored) and “black” (high-risk) lists.
bodyText: The FATF issues non-binding recommendations that form the global standard for anti-money laundering (AML) and countering the financing of terrorism (CFT). It has 40+9 Recommendations, covering CDD, reporting, supervision, international cooperation, etc. According to FATF, these “set an international standard, which countries should implement through measures adapted to their circumstances”. In practice, each country enacts its own laws (e.g. the UK’s MLR, India’s PMLA/KYC Regulations, US BSA) to meet FATF standards. FATF also evaluates jurisdictions’ AML/CFT regimes. Every few years, member and key countries undergo peer review (“mutual evaluation”) to check compliance. The FATF maintains two important lists: (1) **High-Risk Jurisdictions (Call for Action, “black list”)** – these have serious strategic deficiencies and require countermeasures (e.g. a ban on new correspondent accounts). (2) **Jurisdictions under Increased Monitoring (“grey list”)** – these have deficiencies but are working with FATF to improve. For example, being grey-listed signals a need for enhanced due diligence on customers from that country. FATF Mutual Evaluation Cycle +------------------------+ | National AML/CFT Regime| +------------------------+ | v +------------------------+ | FATF Peer Review | (Mutual Evaluation) +------------------------+ | +---------+---------+ | | v v +--------+ +--------+ | Improved |<------ |Action | | Compliance | |Plan | +--------+ +--------+ | v +------------------------+ | Grey/Black List Outcome| +------------------------+ Always check the FATF list statuses of jurisdictions. If a country is grey- or black-listed, apply enhanced due diligence to counterparties from that country. Assuming FATF recommendations are law. They are **not legally binding**; instead each country implements its own legal framework based on them. Confusing grey list with black list (they imply different urgency) is a common error. **Grey List (increased monitoring)** — jurisdictions with strategic AML gaps, under FATF follow-up. --- **Black List (high-risk)** — jurisdictions with serious AML deficiencies requiring sanctions or countermeasures. (Newcomers often misunderstand grey-list countries as “black.”) **No delta.** The FATF standards and lists apply globally. Every member/territory is subject to the same evaluation methodology and must heed the same grey/black list status.

title: Banks as AML Gatekeepers
one_screen: Banks act as the financial system’s “first line of defense.” They are legally required to verify customers (KYC), monitor transactions, and report suspicious activity. Regulators rely on banks to enforce AML rules because banks handle the cash flows criminals need.
bodyText: Under the gatekeeper model, banks (and other regulated firms) have primary responsibility for spotting and reporting financial crime. Laws typically mandate that banks implement AML programs – including KYC checks, transaction monitoring, and reporting – so that the private sector polices the system. For example, RBI’s AML guidelines explicitly instruct banks to establish AML policies (KYC, STR reporting, etc.) with Board approval. This means if a terrorist or money launderer tries to move money, the bank’s controls should catch it first. Criminals must insert illicit money into banks to spend it, so banks are critical checkpoints. If suspicious, banks escalate by filing SARs/STRs with authorities (see Atom 15). Senior management appoints a Money Laundering Reporting Officer (MLRO) or compliance officer who ensures internal policies match regulations. Regulators (like RBI, FCA, FinCEN) then audit and examine banks’ AML controls for adequacy. Non-bank institutions (casinos, real estate, fintech) also play gatekeeper roles where they handle large transactions. Always assume customers are subject to AML rules. No matter how lucrative, a customer or transaction that fails KYC or looks unusual must be vetted or reported. Banks *must* file an STR/SAR if money laundering is suspected. Thinking AML is optional or “just a paperwork exercise.” In reality, failing AML duties (like ignoring a big cash deposit warning sign) can lead to penalties and even criminal charges for the bank and its officers. **Gatekeeper role (banks)** — duty to enforce AML by monitoring and reporting. --- **Regulator/Supervisor** — government agencies (RBI, FinCEN, FCA) that write rules and enforce them. Banks are *enforcers*, not regulators. — Under India’s PMLA, banks are explicitly required to follow RBI’s AML Master Directions (CIP, STRs, MLRO). — The Money Laundering Regulations impose KYC/AML duties on “regulated institutions” (including banks); the FCA supervises banks’ AML programs. — Each Member State’s law (per AML Directives) tasks banks/financial institutions with CDD and STR reporting. The EBA provides joint guidance, but local regulators enforce compliance. — US banks must comply with BSA (e.g. CIP Rule, CTR/SAR filing) under FinCEN oversight. Bank regulators (OCC, Fed, FDIC) examine AML controls, and FinCEN has broad enforcement powers.

title: KYC and Customer Identification (CIP)
one_screen: “Know Your Customer” (KYC) is the process of verifying a customer’s identity before opening an account. In the US this is called the Customer Identification Program (CIP). Banks must collect official ID, confirm it is valid, and record it.
bodyText: Customer Identification is the front-line of AML. Under law, banks cannot open a new account without verifying who the customer is. For example, India’s RBI KYC guidelines require banks to follow strict customer identification procedures when establishing relationships. In the US, the BSA’s CIP Rule mandates collecting at least name, date of birth, address and government ID number for each new customer. Common documents used include passports, government IDs (like PAN in India), and for companies – incorporation papers. The KYC process typically involves: customer provides identity documents; bank checks authenticity (e.g. original ID); and records a copy. For non-residents or politically exposed persons, additional checks may apply (see Atom 8 on PEP). If identity cannot be verified, the bank must refuse the account or transaction. All this information is documented. For example, RBI explicitly mandates that banks verify identity and maintain copies of proof-of-identity and address for every customer before business is undertaken. New Customer Onboarding | v +------------------+ | Customer | | Documents | +------------------+ | (ID, Address) v +------------------+ | Identify | | Customer (KYC) | +------------------+ | (Check documents) v +------------------+ | Verify Identity | +------------------+ | (Match info) v +------------+ +-------------+ | Approved | | Reject | | Account | | Account/ | | Opened | | Transaction | +------------+ +-------------+ Collect at minimum name, address, date of birth, and official ID when opening any account. Always record this information and keep it updated. Relying solely on customer-supplied documents without independent verification. Always compare the presented ID to official records or via KYC registries (like India’s CKYCR) to avoid forgeries. **KYC/CIP (Customer ID)** — initial verification step using IDs and documents. --- **Customer Due Diligence (CDD)** — broader process including ongoing risk assessment and monitoring (not just initial ID). Novices often think KYC and CDD are identical, but CDD encompasses the whole relationship lifecycle. — RBI’s Master Direction: banks must complete Customer Identification Procedure (CIP) and KYC before any transaction. Uses Aadhaar or documents. — MLR 2017 requires regulated firms to verify customer identities (CIP) at account opening and to identify BOs. — AML Directives mandate customer identification for all new accounts and significant transactions. — The BSA’s CIP rule requires US banks to collect name, DOB, address and TIN/ID number for each new account holder.

title: Beneficial Ownership
one_screen: Beneficial owner (BO) means the natural person(s) who ultimately owns or controls a customer (especially a company), even if not listed on official records. Laws typically use ownership thresholds (e.g. >10% in India, >25% in US) to identify BOs.
bodyText: Beneficial ownership refers to the real human owners behind legal entities. For corporate customers, “boilerplate” documents show only legal title (e.g. Board of Directors). AML rules therefore require banks to identify the individual(s) who ultimately own or control the company. For example, RBI’s KYC guidelines define a BO as someone holding >10% of shares or exercising control. US law (via FinCEN) similarly defines BOs as individuals with substantial control or ≥25% ownership. UK/EU AML rules use a 25% threshold or “significant control.” Finding BOs is often hard: the listed directors may not be the true owners (there may be nominee shareholders). Banks must obtain documentation or declarations to trace chain of ownership. This can involve checking public registries (like the UK PSC register) or trusting legal opinions. The BO requirement ensures banks see through shell companies and trust structures. Always obtain BO information for any corporate customer. Verify it with documents or public registries. If uncertain, treat the account as high-risk (issue EDD). In India, banks must collect IDs of all BOs (person with >10% or who controls the company). Accepting a single shareholder’s statement that “there are no other BOs.” In reality, multiple people can share ownership. Overlooking indirect ownership (e.g. via trusts or chains of companies) is also a common error. **Nominee** — person who is listed as owner on paper but holds assets on someone else’s behalf. --- **Beneficial owner** — the real person who ultimately owns or controls the asset or entity. They get mixed up because a nominee’s name is on the legal title, but the BO is the one with real power or benefit. — RBI KYC rules define BO as individuals holding ≥10% equity or control; banks must collect KYC of each such person. — MLR/Companies Act: BO/PSC is anyone with >25% shares or votes, or significant control. FCA guidance emphasizes verifying via the UK PSC register. — AML Directives: BO usually >25% ownership, must be identified and ID-verified. — The Corporate Transparency Act (FinCEN) defines BO as person with ≥25% ownership or exercising substantial control. U.S. firms must report BO info to FinCEN.

title: Politically Exposed Persons (PEPs)
one_screen: A PEP is someone entrusted with a prominent public function (e.g. senior politician, military officer). Because of corruption risk, PEPs (and their family/close associates) require enhanced due diligence.
bodyText: Politically Exposed Persons (PEPs) are individuals who hold or have held important government or international positions (e.g. heads of state, ministers, senior military or judiciary). The FATF warns that such positions carry a higher risk of bribery or corruption, as PEPs could abuse power for personal gain. Therefore banks must apply additional scrutiny to PEPs. This includes not only the PEP, but also close family members and known associates (they can be vehicles for laundering). For example, banks usually collect detailed information and source-of-funds for PEPs. Enhanced due diligence (EDD) means higher risk ratings, senior approval for maintaining the account, and more frequent transaction monitoring. Many rulebooks (e.g. UK, India, EU) require annual reviews of PEP accounts. Overlooking a customer’s PEP status is a common compliance mistake. FATF Recommendation 12 explicitly calls for risk-based measures for all foreign PEPs (with many countries extending it to domestic PEPs). Identify all customers who are PEPs (domestic or foreign as required by law) and require senior management approval to onboard them. Apply EDD: verify source of wealth, increase monitoring frequency, and record approvals. Ignoring *former* officials or relatives. PEP status often persists after leaving office, and close family can be just as risky. Never assume “just because a PEP is friendly, he’s low risk.” **PEP (Politically Exposed Person)** — someone currently or formerly holding a high government/party position. --- **Important public figure** — e.g. a celebrity or top banker. They are not PEPs unless they have held public office. People often erroneously think any prominent person is a PEP. — PEPs are defined under FIU-IND guidelines (aligned with PMLA Rule 9(13)) and include domestic officials and judiciary. Banks in India treat both Indian and foreign PEPs as high-risk. — The Money Laundering Regulations define PEP to include all domestic and foreign PEPs and their families. EDD is mandatory for all PEP relationships under Reg 12. — 4AMLD/5AMLD cover domestic, foreign, and international PEPs, including relatives; firms must apply EDD as per FATF guidance. — Under FinCEN, only *foreign* PEPs (and their relatives/associates) are explicitly defined for mandatory EDD. (Domestic politicians aren’t separately covered by CIP, though banks may still flag them internally.)

title: Risk-Based Approach (RBA)
one_screen: The risk-based approach means allocating AML resources according to the risk posed by each customer or transaction. Banks must assess risk factors (customer type, geography, product) and adjust due diligence intensity accordingly.
bodyText: Under FATF’s standards, banks are expected to tailor their AML controls to the level of risk. This means identifying each customer’s risk level (high, medium, low) based on factors like customer profile (e.g. PEP vs retail), country of origin (sanctioned vs safe), industry (cash-intensive vs usual), and product (complex instruments vs basic deposits). The FATF states that firms should “identify, assess and understand ML/TF risk… and take AML measures commensurate to the risk level”. For example, a high-risk client may have quarterly KYC reviews, while a low-risk retail saver may only need basic onboarding checks. A customer risk rating typically combines factors: a PEP from a high-risk country doing large wire transfers might be “high risk,” requiring enhanced due diligence. Conversely, a local salaried employee with small deposits is “low risk,” possibly even eligible for simplified due diligence. The product or transaction risk is also considered: certain services (like private banking or crypto trading) raise risk. The key is that higher-risk relationships have more rigorous checks (EDD) while very low-risk customers may get reduced scrutiny (SDD) if regulations allow. Always document a customer’s risk rating and apply the corresponding level of due diligence. Higher risk customers require senior review and more frequent monitoring, as per FATF’s guidance. Treating all customers identically (one-size-fits-all compliance). Also, misjudging risk: e.g. calling a high-net-worth business owner “low risk” just because they’re polite and have an account manager. **Customer risk** — the inherent ML/TF risk of the customer’s profile (PEP status, business type, location). --- **Transaction/product risk** — risk associated with a particular product or transaction (cash deposit, trade finance, etc.). They are often conflated; in fact, a high-risk customer can have safe transactions, and vice versa. **No delta.** All AML regimes (US BSA, UK MLR, RBI, EU AMLD) require a risk-based approach. The FATF standard (Rec.1) is implemented universally, though exact categories (what is “high risk”) may differ by country’s assessment.

title: Simplified vs Enhanced Due Diligence (SDD vs EDD)
one_screen: Due diligence intensity is matched to risk. Enhanced Due Diligence (EDD) means extra checks (for high-risk clients, e.g. PEPs, high-risk countries). Simplified Due Diligence (SDD) allows reduced checks for very low-risk customers.
bodyText: Enhanced Due Diligence (EDD) is required when a customer or situation is high-risk. FATF and most regulations demand EDD for PEPs, cross-border correspondent banking, and customers from FATF “gray/black” jurisdictions. For example, RBI directs banks to apply EDD measures (e.g. senior management approval, detailed source-of-funds analysis) for relationships with persons from high-risk countries flagged by the FATF. Other triggers include private banking services, complex corporate ownership, or any red flags. Simplified Due Diligence (SDD) is the opposite: lower-risk scenarios. For instance, stable salaried individuals in low-risk areas might only need standard ID verification. Many rules (UK MLR, EU AMLD) allow SDD in limited cases, but usually not in the US. RBI and FATF permit SDD only when risk is demonstrably minimal (e.g. listed companies with public financials). SDD might waive certain documentation if risk is very low, but it must still comply with basic KYC. Apply EDD whenever a customer, product, or country is assessed as high-risk (PEPs, shell companies, high-risk jurisdictions). Use SDD only when explicitly allowed by law and documented as low-risk. Maintain clear policies on what conditions allow simplifications. Mistakenly assuming simplified due diligence can apply just to expedite onboarding. (SDD is the exception, not the norm.) On the flip side, applying EDD inconsistently or without justification, which can delay business and annoy customers. **Simplified Due Diligence (SDD)** — reduced compliance measures for *low*-risk customers, permitted by law in narrow cases. It is not a way to cut corners unlawfully. --- **Inadequate due diligence** — poor or missing checks. Some confuse SDD with simply not doing enough. Proper SDD is documented as permitted by policy, not negligence. — RBI permits SDD for low-risk customers (e.g. salary accounts with salary credits) and mandates EDD for high-risk ones, including foreign entities from FATF-specified countries. — MLR 2017 allows SDD in limited categories (e.g. listed companies) and requires EDD for PEPs, TF, or high-risk scenarios. — EU AML law permits optional SDD if national authorities designate low-risk situations, and mandates EDD for PEPs and TF by virtue of FATF Rec 10/12. — The US does not formally recognize “SDD.” Banks are expected to use at least standard CIP for all customers. However, FinCEN allows some exceptions (e.g. certain trusted accounts). EDD for foreign PEPs was formerly required under FinCEN guidance, but overall US approach is risk-based without a labeled “SDD.”

title: Ongoing Due Diligence and Periodic Review
one_screen: Ongoing due diligence means continuously monitoring a customer and updating their profile as circumstances change. Periodic reviews (refreshing KYC at set intervals) must be done in line with risk level. Regulators expect banks to treat KYC as a “living” process, not a one-time task.
bodyText: Banks must monitor customers and transactions throughout the relationship. FATF Recommendation 10 requires “ongoing due diligence” – monitoring transactions against the customer’s known profile and keeping CDD information up-to-date. In practice this means reviewing accounts at regular intervals (e.g. annually for PEPs, every 2–5 years for normal accounts, with shorter intervals for higher risk). Periodic KYC refresh ensures information (such as employment, address or BO structure) hasn’t changed. For example, if a private company customer suddenly has a new director who is a PEP, the bank should detect this in a review. Ongoing checks also include watching for unusual activity via transaction monitoring (Atom 13). If alerts trigger, analysts re-assess the customer. Regulatory guidance (UK MLR, EU AMLD) explicitly mandates systems to flag when customer risk increases (winning elections, media scandals, sanctions hits). Essentially, one-time KYC is insufficient; institutions should treat compliance like continuous management of customer risk. ACAMS even coins “perpetual KYC” to describe updating client data in near-real time as events occur. Establish a schedule to review each customer’s risk and KYC at least annually for higher-risk and every few years for others. Immediately update any material change (address, BO, adverse media, sanction status). Document reviews. “Set and forget” KYC. Believing that a customer’s risk profile never changes. Failing to catch that an ordinary account became a PEP or involved a sanctioned country months after onboarding leads to regulatory failure. **Ongoing due diligence** — the continuous program of monitoring and updating customer information and risk rating. --- **Transaction monitoring** — the automated system scanning transactions for anomalies. Ongoing due diligence includes transaction monitoring but also periodic KYC refresh and watchlist rescreening, which some mistakenly equate only to transaction monitoring. **No delta.** Global AML standards (FATF Rec.10) demand ongoing monitoring. Local rules differ only in specifics: UK MLR 2017 requires periodic reviews (Reg 35) and immediate action on any red flags; RBI mandates yearly KYC updates for high-risk customers and EDD refresh; US FinCEN similarly expects risk-based ongoing monitoring though not prescriptive on frequency.

title: Perpetual KYC (Continuous Updating)
one_screen: Perpetual KYC is the practice of continuously updating customer profiles rather than relying solely on periodic refreshes. It means automatically re-verifying identity, sanctions, and risk as soon as new data appears (via screening and open sources).
bodyText: “Perpetual” or continuous KYC takes ongoing diligence further: banks strive to have real-time or event-driven updates of customer data. Instead of waiting a year for the next review, the bank’s systems continuously screen for changes. For example, automated processes may re-run name screening daily or alert staff if a customer appears in news or sanctions feeds. The goal is to “maintain a living view” of each client. ACAMS describes this as “perpetual KYC,” where client data is kept current through near-real-time monitoring of risk indicators. This trend away from calendar-based KYC means banks invest in technology: integrated data sources (legal registries, watchlists, media monitors) and trigger-based workflows. For instance, India’s CKYCR (central KYC registry) facilitates sharing updates across banks, reducing redundant KYC. Video KYC or e-KYC (Aadhaar-based) allow faster identity checks. The result is that if a customer’s situation changes (new BO, sanction hit, etc.), compliance is updated immediately, not at the annual review. Implement systems that alert compliance staff to material changes (sanctions, adverse news, ownership changes) so KYC can be updated immediately. Use centralized KYC registries (like India’s CKYCR) and re-screen customers periodically (or continuously for high risk). Relying purely on periodic checks and treating KYC reviews as routine paperwork. In today’s dynamic world, waiting six months for the next review can miss emerging risks. **Periodic Review** — scheduled KYC refresh (e.g. annual). --- **Perpetual KYC** — continuous, event-triggered updates. The confusion arises as both aim to keep KYC current; the difference is periodic is fixed schedule while perpetual is on change-driven alerts. — RBI’s CKYCR allows banks to update a central record; it mandates updates on PAN/Aadhaar info changes. E-KYC (Aadhaar) and Video KYC are accepted for quick onboarding and re-verification. — The FCA expects firms to have “systems to identify PEP status changes throughout the relationship”. The trend is to more frequent reviews beyond the regulatory minimum. — Anti-Money Laundering Package (2024) pushes for digitisation of KYC data and envisages an EU KYC “data house” for continuous updates. — No centralized KYC, but banks re-run watchlist screening at least daily/weekly. Regulatory focus is on whether changes (like home ownership or employment) should prompt updates under the RBA principle.

title: Transaction Monitoring
one_screen: Transaction monitoring is the automated process of screening payments and account activity for unusual patterns (based on rules, thresholds and typologies). It compares transactions against customer profiles and known risk indicators.
bodyText: Transaction Monitoring is the core tool for detecting suspicious activity. Banks set up rules (often via software) that flag transactions breaching certain thresholds or patterns. Common scenarios include: large cash deposits just under reporting limits, rapid movement of funds between unrelated accounts, or sudden spikes inconsistent with a customer’s profile. For example, a $50k transfer for a student-saver could trigger an alert, as it doesn’t match their expected behavior. The flagged alerts are then reviewed by analysts. To build these systems, banks use AML typologies – known money laundering patterns. This can include structuring (multiple small transfers to avoid limits), circular trades between affiliates, or payments to high-risk industries. Rules can be as simple as “cash > $10,000” or complex “transfer to a high-risk country followed by immediate account withdrawal.” Many institutions also incorporate machine learning to detect deviations from normal behavior. The output of transaction monitoring is a continuous stream of alerts for further triage. Maintain robust transaction monitoring systems that align with business profiles. Regularly update rules and thresholds (based on risk and past alert outcomes) so genuine criminal patterns are captured while routine transactions are mostly ignored. Overloading on alerts (setting too many rules) without tuning them leads to hundreds of false positives. Focus on the highest-risk triggers and calibrate thresholds to actual customer behavior, or important alerts get buried. **Transaction monitoring** — active scanning of transactions to find red flags. --- **Sanctions screening** — separate process of matching transaction parties against blacklist names. Both involve “screening,” but transaction monitoring looks at money flows/patterns, whereas sanctions screening only checks names against watchlists. **No delta.** The concept of automated transaction monitoring is a universal banking practice. Specific rules (e.g. reportable cash amount) vary: India requires CTR for cash > ₹10L monthly, US requires reports over $10,000. But all banks must monitor activity per local regulations.

title: False Positives and Alert Triage
one_screen: Modern AML monitoring flags far more legitimate transactions than criminal ones. Industry data show ~90–95% of alerts are false positives. The challenge is efficiently triaging each alert (reviewing context) to determine if it truly indicates suspicious activity.
bodyText: False positives (alerts that turn out to be benign) are the biggest operational burden in AML. Because systems err on the side of caution, routine transactions often trigger alerts. For example, a salary payment just over $10,000 or a loan repayment might look suspicious to untrained rules. Industry studies report that roughly 95% of AML alerts at banks are false positives. This means compliance teams spend most of their time confirming that alerted transactions were in fact normal. The triage process has multiple steps: (1) **Initial Triage:** Automated filters may re-check alerts for trivial causes (e.g. internal transfers). (2) **Investigation:** Analysts pull additional data (account statements, KYC info) and contact relationship managers. (3) **Escalation:** If no legitimate explanation is found, the case is escalated to file a Suspicious Activity Report (SAR/STR). Efficient triage is crucial: if analysts are swamped by false alerts, they may miss real crimes. Continuously optimize monitoring: recalibrate rules and thresholds using actual SAR outcomes. Keep records justifying each rule so examiners see due diligence. Use customer risk profiles to suppress unnecessary alerts (e.g. raise threshold for regular high-volume customers). Overlooking real suspicious activity because of alert fatigue. When teams see thousands of alerts a week, they may rubber-stamp many as false. Always assume any unresolved alert merits a thorough check. **False positive alert** — a flagged transaction that, after review, is determined to be legitimate. --- **True suspicious transaction** — actual illicit activity that should lead to a SAR. Many analysts term every alert “suspicious,” but only those confirmed after review qualify. Mixing them up leads to either over-reporting trivial cases or under-reporting real risks. **No delta.** All countries face the same false-positive problem with rule-based monitoring. However, regulators differ in expectations: some (like FinCEN) explicitly examine banks’ alert rates and tuning process, while others (UK FCA) emphasize the quality of SARs over quantity.

title: Suspicious Activity Reporting and Tipping Off
one_screen: Suspicious activity reports (SARs/STRs) are formal filings to authorities when a financial institution suspects money laundering or terrorist financing. The naming and exact process vary by country (e.g. SAR in US/UK, STR in India). Tipping off (informing the client they’re being reported) is strictly prohibited.
bodyText: Once an alert survives triage and the bank decides a transaction is suspicious, it must file a report to the FIU/regulator. In the US, banks file **SARs** to FinCEN under 31 CFR 1020; in India, they file **STRs** to FIU-IND within 7 working days of detection. The UK and EU also use the term **SAR** (or Suspicious Transaction Report in EU parlance) reported to the local FIU (NCA in the UK, FIUs in EU). Banks must include details of the transaction, customer, and why it’s suspicious. Meeting deadlines is critical (e.g. 30 days in US after suspicion). Importantly, the customer must **not** be told a report is filed. FATF and all AML laws forbid “tipping off.” For example, UK law (POCA) imposes up to 5 years jail for tipping off or prejudicing an investigation. The bank’s duty is to report in secret. No employee may hint to the customer or third parties that the transaction is under scrutiny. File a comprehensive SAR/STR to the designated authority whenever you know or suspect money laundering or terrorism financing, regardless of the transaction amount. Keep all SAR/STR filings confidential. Accidentally revealing an investigation. For instance, sending a collection notice to a client or closing their account without explanation can be construed as tipping off. Always refuse or delay suspicious transactions without explanation, rather than alerting the customer. **SAR/STR** — formal report to authorities of *suspected* illicit activity. --- **Currency Transaction Report (CTR)** — an automatic report of large cash transactions (e.g. $10K+ in US). Not every big transaction is suspicious; CTRs are just monitoring filings, not judgment calls. Newcomers sometimes think a CTR is the same as an STR (it is not). — Banks submit Suspicious Transaction Reports (STRs) to FIU-IND (via the FINnet portal) within 7 working days of detecting suspicion. In addition, Cash Transaction Reports (CTRs) are required for any cash above ₹10 lakh in a month (even if not suspicious). — Regulated firms file SARs to the UKFIU/NCA. They have 2 working days from the date of suspicion to report (usually via the SAR Online portal). Tipping off and prejudicing investigations are criminal offences under POCA (up to 5 years prison). — EU AML law requires filing a Suspicious Transaction Report to the national FIU. Member states also mandate large transaction reports (e.g. €10,000 cash threshold). — US banks file SARs to FinCEN if they detect funds derived from illegal activities or intended for illicit purposes. The CTR (Currency Transaction Report) is filed for cash over $10,000 (whether suspicious or not). SARs in the US do not have a tipping-off prohibition, but bank employees must not notify customers.

title: Sanctions Screening
one_screen: Sanctions screening involves checking customer names and transactions against global watchlists (UN, OFAC, etc.). This uses name-matching algorithms (often fuzzy matching) to catch known terrorists, criminals, or sanctioned entities. Screening is distinct from transaction monitoring because it matches specific identities rather than patterns.
bodyText: Sanctions screening is a separate discipline from general transaction monitoring. Banks must screen customers at onboarding and periodically re-screen accounts against sanctions lists: UN Security Council, US Treasury’s OFAC, EU, UK, etc. For transactions (especially cross-border payments), the payment’s beneficiary and originator names are also screened in real time to block any transfer involving a sanctioned party. Fuzzy or “approximate” matching is used to account for misspellings or transliterations. For example, a wire transfer to “Mohammed Salim” would be checked against “Mohammed Suleiman” using phonetic match logic. Sanctions screening is mandated by law. In the US, OFAC requires blocking any transaction involving a person on the Specially Designated Nationals (SDN) list. Similar rules exist globally. Unlike AML alerts, a sanctions match has no ambiguity – if the payee is on a list, the payment must be rejected or frozen. Thus, sanctions screening focuses on lists and name-matching, whereas transaction monitoring focuses on behavioral patterns. Maintain up-to-date sanctions and PEP lists (daily at least). Screen all new customers and every transaction against these lists using reliable matching software. Do not rely solely on exact spellings – use fuzzy logic to catch variants. Assuming exact name match is enough. Criminals often use aliases or misspellings; failing to catch those will let them slip by. Also, treating sanctions screening as part of AML monitoring – it’s a distinct process legally and technically. **Sanctions screening** — matching names against official sanctions/terrorism lists. --- **Transaction monitoring** — looking for suspicious activity patterns. The two are often conflated but sanctions screening simply verifies if transaction parties are blacklisted, whereas monitoring checks transaction *behavior*. **No delta.** Sanctions regimes are country-specific in content (different lists), but all jurisdictions require compliance with UN sanction lists. In practice: **IN** follows UN and domestic (e.g. ISIS list) sanctions via RBI circulars; **UK** implements UN/EU/UK lists via HM Treasury; **EU** has Union lists; **US** has its own OFAC list (e.g. North Korea, Iran). Screening processes are similar globally but lists differ.

title: Fraud and its Relationship to AML
one_screen: Fraud involves criminal deception for financial gain, whereas AML deals with concealing illicit funds. They overlap (e.g. fraud proceeds need laundering) and banks increasingly combine fraud and AML monitoring. Key terms: first-party vs third-party fraud, application fraud, mule accounts.
bodyText: Fraud and money laundering intersect but are distinct. Fraud is illegally obtaining funds (e.g. a customer lying on a loan form, identity theft, credit card scams). Money laundering is hiding the origin of criminal funds, which can include fraud proceeds. For example, funds stolen by fraud may need laundering through the banking system. **First-party fraud** is when the actual account holder deceives the bank (e.g. a borrower deliberately omits liabilities on a loan application). **Third-party fraud** (identity theft) is when someone else uses a customer’s identity or card without permission. These often trigger AML controls because stolen funds often pass through multiple accounts (see mule accounts below). **Application fraud** and **synthetic identity fraud** occur at onboarding: criminals submit fake or stolen IDs to open accounts. These then can be used to commit further fraud or laundering. **Mule accounts** are legitimate-looking accounts controlled by criminals. A mule (often an unwitting person) funnels stolen/fraudulent funds on behalf of others, thus blending fraud and money laundering. Given these overlaps, many banks now integrate Fraud and AML teams (“FRAML”). They share data and alerts, since unusual patterns might indicate either fraud or laundering. For instance, many small deposits followed by a large withdrawal could be either structured cash deposits (ML) or a fraudulent funding scheme. Combining teams improves efficiency and leverages common analytics (customer risk scoring, etc.). Treat fraud risk similarly to AML risk in high-end banking. Verify identities at application (to catch synthetic IDs) and monitor for typical fraud indicators (stolen card usage, unusual loan applications). Set up communication channels between fraud and AML units for suspicious cases. Assuming fraud is only the customer’s problem. In fact, fraud can generate illicit proceeds that must be reported if laundered. Also, ignoring small-value fraud patterns because they aren’t “money laundering” – these can aggregate to significant AML issues. **First-party fraud** — committed by the genuine account holder (e.g. lying on an application). --- **Third-party fraud (Identity theft)** — committed by someone else using stolen or synthetic credentials. These are often mixed up because both involve deception; the key is who controls the account. **No delta.** The definitions of fraud vs AML are consistent globally. However, specifics differ: India’s RBI KYC rules expressly cover application fraud; UK’s JMLSG includes guidance on fraud as an AML risk. The requirement to report fraud or co-operate with law enforcement is universal, even though definitions of fraud types derive from general criminal law, not AML regulation.

title: AML Governance and Oversight
one_screen: Governance sets up the AML framework: a designated compliance officer (MLRO/Principal Officer) ensures policy, training and reporting. Transaction monitoring and screening models count as regulated models subject to validation (MRM principles). Regulators typically enforce AML by penalizing failures (e.g. missing STRs, inadequate controls).
bodyText: An effective AML program requires strong governance. A bank’s board must approve AML policy and appoint a senior officer (MLRO or principal officer) to oversee compliance. For example, RBI mandates a Principal Officer in each reporting entity to file STRs and coordinate with FIU. The MLRO is responsible for ensuring controls are implemented, suspicious reports filed, and staff trained on AML. Other governance elements include an independent audit of AML processes, periodic compliance reviews, and clear escalation paths. Model Risk is a key oversight area now. Transaction monitoring systems are considered AML “models” and must be validated like other financial models. Regulators expect documented model risk management (see Warren CCR pack). This includes testing detection rules, reviewing backtesting results, and calibrating thresholds. Over-reliance on a black-box system without validation is a vulnerability. Regulators penalize banks for AML failures. Common triggers for enforcement include: failing to file STRs, ignoring AML exam findings, or having a compliance culture that downplays AML. UK authorities can prosecute failing-to-disclose offences (up to five years jail). In India, non-compliance with PMLA can incur fines (₹10k–₹100k per violation). US banks have faced massive fines for BSA breaches (e.g. inadequate CIP or SAR programs). FATF evals also put pressure on regulators; poor ratings can lead to tougher oversight. Ensure top management commitment. The MLRO/Principal Officer must be qualified, independent, and empowered. All AML models and tools (transaction monitoring, screening) should be validated and audited regularly. Letting AML governance lapse: e.g. MLRO role unfilled, outdated policies, or “tick-box” training with no real emphasis. Remember that complacency on governance itself triggers regulator action. **MLRO (Money Laundering Reporting Officer)** — the compliance officer in a bank responsible for AML reports and policies. --- **Internal Audit or Compliance Department** — separate functions. The MLRO is an operational officer (front-line AML), whereas internal audit reviews AML as part of broader risk audits. Mixing these roles violates four-eye principles. — RBI requires every reporting entity to appoint a Principal Officer (PO) to file STRs and comply with PMLA regulations. AML compliance is overseen by entities like RBI and FIU. — MLRO appointment is mandatory under MLRs; regulators (FCA/PRA) can sanction banks for weak AML controls. The JMLSG guidance is followed but not law. — National competent authorities enforce AML (and soon the EU AML Authority, AMLA, will centralize some supervision). Banks follow EBA guidelines but adapt to local laws. — Banks must designate a compliance officer (often called BSA Officer) to handle AML. Regulators (Fed, OCC, FinCEN) conduct examinations; enforcement actions (fines, orders) typically arise from regulatory audits or after breaches (e.g. fines by FinCEN/OCC for BSA violations).

title: Role of the Business Analyst (vs Product/Project Manager)
one_screen: A BA in a bank translates business needs into requirements, focusing on *what* and *why*, unlike a product manager (who defines product strategy and features) or a project manager (who plans the *how* and *when* of delivery).
bodyText: Business Analysts (BAs) gather business requirements and ensure that solutions address true business needs. They act as the liaison between business stakeholders and technical teams. BAs **do not** own product strategy or delivery schedules. A *Product Manager* (or Product Owner) is outward-facing – they define the product vision, customer needs, and high-level features. A *Project Manager* is responsible for planning, coordinating, and tracking the project timeline, budget, and resources. In contrast, the BA identifies *what* must be done (the requirements) and *why* (the business objective), but generally not *how* to build it or *when* to schedule tasks. For example, if a regulator mandates a new report, the Product Manager ensures the business values it and fits into the roadmap, the Project Manager schedules the implementation, and the BA defines the report’s data requirements and rules. The BA does **not** decide how the report is coded or which team builds it, nor do they own the release date – those are the project manager’s concerns. +-----------------+ +----------------------+ +----------------+ | Product Owner | -----> | Business Analyst | -----> | Development Team| +-----------------+ vision | (defines requirements) | spec +----------------+ +----------------------+ A BA defines *what* needs to be done and *why*, but does **not** dictate the *how* (that’s the domain of solution architects or developers) or *when* (that’s the project manager’s schedule). Confusing the BA role with the project or product manager role. For instance, asking the BA to manage the project budget or delivery schedule, or to own product strategy, leads to failure. The BA must resist the urge to become a mini–project manager. **Product Manager** — owns the product vision, market needs, and feature roadmap (external focus). --- **Project Manager** — owns the project plan, schedule, and budget (execution focus). ### No delta This distinction holds across jurisdictions: BAs globally focus on requirements gathering, whereas product/project management roles are organizational, not regulatory, differences.

title: Change Landscape: Regulatory vs Strategic vs Remediation
one_screen: Banks undertake strategic initiatives (growth or efficiency) and remediation (fixing defects), but *regulatory-driven* change is mandatory, with fixed deadlines and external oversight, requiring full compliance and auditability.
bodyText: Bank change programs fall into categories: **Strategic** (business-driven goals like new services or cost reduction), **Remediation** (fixing problems found by audit), and **Regulatory** (mandated by laws or regulators). Regulatory changes are unique: their deadlines are *unmovable* and non-negotiable, and failure to comply can incur penalties and license risk. These projects carry high visibility, involve many functions, and have huge impact. Because regulators require proof of compliance, regulatory programs demand rigorous documentation, traceability, and audit trails. For example, a compliance program like IFRS 9 transition is closely monitored by supervisors; banks often run parallel regimes to validate results before the fixed effective date. Strategic initiatives, by contrast, prioritize internal business value and have more flexible timelines. Remediation projects respond to issues (e.g. a control failure) and may have urgency but usually less external scrutiny. Regulatory projects behave differently: teams often use waterfall governance and stage gates to meet the firm deadlines. Cutting corners or missing details is dangerous; regulators expect complete traceability from each regulatory requirement to the implemented solution. Audit findings often arise when banks discover a gap between knowing the rule and effectively applying it. Treat regulatory change as mandatory, with fixed deadlines and senior oversight. Plan for full documentation and testing of compliance. Never assume you can shift a regulatory date to accommodate project delays. Treating a regulatory deadline like a usual internal deadline (i.e. deferring it or deprioritizing compliance tasks). Missing that fixed deadline invites exam findings and fines. **Strategic Change** — voluntary, business-driven initiatives (may adjust scope/deadlines based on ROI). --- **Regulatory Change** — mandatory compliance projects, externally imposed with firm deadlines and audit requirements. ### No delta Across jurisdictions, the nature of regulatory projects is the same: non-negotiable effective dates and mandatory compliance. Each regulator may set different dates, but the principle of fixed deadline and required audit evidence does not change.

title: Stakeholders in Bank Change Programs
one_screen: Successful change requires early and ongoing involvement of all impacted groups: business owners (front-line and process managers), risk and compliance, finance, IT/operations, data/model owners, internal audit and (where needed) the regulator.
bodyText: A bank change program involves many stakeholders. **Business owners** (line-of-business managers, product owners) define requirements. **Risk management** teams (credit, market, operational risk) must approve changes affecting risk profile. **Finance** stakeholders (finance, accounting) need to assess cost, budget impact, and reporting changes. **Technology/IT** teams design and build the solution. **Data owners** or **model owners** must be involved when data or risk models change, to align logic and validation. **Internal Audit** should be aware early – auditors will later review that controls and procedures were properly implemented. Finally, the **Regulator** (or compliance team, if working with external regulators) often signs off on regulatory changes or reviews evidence to ensure requirements are met. A BA bridges all these groups, collecting input and keeping them aligned. For example, a new risk-reporting requirement needs review by business (for accuracy), risk (for methodology), finance (for impact on reports), IT (for system changes), and model validation (for calculations). Missing a key stakeholder can derail a project; for instance, if IT or audit are not included until late, critical requirements (like data lineage or evidence logs) might be missed. Include all relevant stakeholders early and often. Document each group’s inputs and approvals. If a group (e.g. internal audit, model validation) is required to sign off on compliance, involve them from the start to avoid rework. Assuming one person can “speak for” multiple stakeholder groups or ignoring a group’s needs. A common mistake is treating the business as the only stakeholder and failing to involve risk or audit until late in the project. **Internal Audit** — the bank’s own independent check on controls and procedures (internal governance function). --- **Regulator** — the external authority enforcing compliance. Both review the project, but Internal Audit is part of the bank’s governance, whereas the Regulator is an external enforcer. ### No delta Stakeholder categories are universal in banking. All regulators expect a bank’s project to involve line management, risk/compliance, IT, finance, audit, etc. The names of groups may vary (e.g. FCA vs SEC), but the roles are similar.

title: Requirements Elicitation Techniques
one_screen: Elicitation is gathering information on what stakeholders need.  Techniques include structured interviews, workshops, observation, document analysis, surveys, and prototyping, chosen based on context and participant availability.
bodyText: Requirements elicitation is the process of discovering and collecting requirements from stakeholders. Common techniques: - **Interviews:** One-on-one meetings with SMEs or users to dig into specific needs. Structured interviews (with a prepared agenda and questions) are most common for detailed requirements. - **Workshops/JAD sessions:** Facilitated group sessions where stakeholders discuss processes or brainstorm solutions. Good for aligning different groups. - **Observation:** Watch users perform their real tasks (e.g. via screen-share or on-site). This uncovers implicit knowledge (like workarounds) that users might not mention. - **Document analysis:** Review existing documents, process flows, reports or contracts. This can elicit requirements without taking too much stakeholder time. - **Surveys/questionnaires:** Useful when many stakeholders are involved or geographically distributed. A survey can quickly gather input (quantitative or qualitative) from a broad group. - **Prototyping or demos:** Using mock-ups or existing systems to elicit feedback. Stakeholders react to a design, refining requirements. Each technique suits different situations. For example, if requirements are unclear and stakeholders are decentralized, a workshop may help align everyone. If SMEs are few but busy, thorough interviews with prepared questions are best. Observing users can catch missing steps in processes. The BA should mix and match techniques as needed, rather than relying on one method. Select elicitation methods that fit the situation. Always prepare thoroughly (set agendas, define questions). Use multiple techniques for cross-checking: e.g. interview a user and verify by process observation. Relying on a single method in isolation. For example, skipping document review and inundating busy stakeholders with questions they already answered in existing documentation, or doing only interviews and missing contradictory data in systems. **Interview** vs **Workshop**: An *Interview* is a one-on-one or small-group discussion for in-depth detail; a *Workshop* is a facilitated group meeting to reach consensus or brainstorm. They both gather input but are different formats and scopes. ### No delta Elicitation techniques are the same globally; only local languages or frameworks vary, not the methods themselves.

title: Interviewing Time-Pressed Subject Matter Experts
one_screen: SMEs are often busy and short on time.  Always prepare an agenda and pre-reads, ask targeted questions, and build credibility so even a short meeting is productive.
bodyText: When interviewing an SME who “does not have time,” preparation is key. Before the meeting, research the topic, study any existing documentation, and send a concise agenda or questionnaire in advance. Start by explaining the project’s purpose and how their input will be used; this shows respect and gains their cooperation. In the meeting, ask clear, focused questions. Prioritize questions so the most critical ones get asked first. If possible, schedule short, focused sessions (e.g. 30 minutes) and stick to that time. Always come with an agenda and demonstrate that you’ve “done your homework” — SMEs should not hear questions that could have been answered by your own prep. Use techniques like the *5 Whys* or scenario walkthroughs to get deep insight quickly. If an SME can’t meet face-to-face, consider email questions or quick confirmations to capture their knowledge. Treat every SME meeting as valuable and limited. Go in prepared and respectful of their time. Always document answers immediately, and confirm understanding before ending. Entering an SME meeting without preparation, or hoping to get detailed answers by casually catching them off guard. Another mistake is not validating their time constraints; for example, scheduling an hour when only 15 minutes is feasible. **Project Sponsor** vs **Subject Matter Expert (SME)**: A *Sponsor* is the executive or business champion who funds the project. An *SME* is a technical or functional expert providing detailed knowledge. A sponsor’s role is strategic; an SME’s is informational. They are often mixed up by new BAs. ### No delta These interpersonal techniques are universal. Bank SMEs in any country have limited time, so the approach to interviewing them is the same.

title: Process Mapping (As-Is vs To-Be)
one_screen: Process mapping diagrams the workflow of a process.  Mapping the current “as-is” process clarifies existing steps and bottlenecks; the “to-be” map lays out the improved future workflow.  Visualizing both highlights where changes are needed.
bodyText: A **process map** is a visual diagram of the steps in a business process. Common forms include flowcharts or swimlane diagrams. To create one, identify all activities, decisions, and participants. An *As-Is* map documents how things currently work; it may reveal inefficiencies, handoffs or delays. For example, an As-Is map of loan approval might show multiple manual checks. A *To-Be* map sketches the proposed future process, reflecting improvements (automation, parallel steps, elimination of waste). For instance, automating checks in the loan process would be shown as a direct flow to approval. +-----------+ +------------+ +-----------+ | Customer | ---> | Check | ---> | End | | Request | | manually | | | +-----------+ +------------+ +-----------+ +-----------+ +------------+ +-----------+ | Customer | ---> | Auto- | ---> | End | | Request | | check | | | +-----------+ +------------+ +-----------+ In practice, start with an As-Is map to ensure everyone agrees on the current process. Then discuss the To-Be process: ask how tasks can be done more efficiently or with fewer steps. Document both maps and annotate issues. The difference between As-Is and To-Be shows exactly what will change. Always create an accurate As-Is process map first, then derive the To-Be. The As-Is baseline is needed to measure improvement and avoid missing steps. Jumping straight to designing the new process without fully mapping the As-Is. This often leads to overlooking current constraints or hidden steps, resulting in gaps in the solution. **As-Is Process** — the current state workflow (often flawed or manual). --- **To-Be Process** — the future, improved workflow. They are frequently mixed up if one tries to innovate without understanding the current process. ### No delta Process mapping methodology is the same everywhere. Tools or notation (BPMN vs simple flowchart) may vary, but the concept of As-Is vs To-Be does not.

title: Root Cause Analysis
one_screen: Root Cause Analysis (RCA) is a method to find the underlying cause of a problem or error, not just its symptoms.  Techniques like “5 Whys” and fishbone diagrams are used to dig down to the true source of an issue.
bodyText: When a process fails or a requirement isn’t met, RCA helps prevent recurrence by fixing the core issue. The BA collects data about the problem, then uses a structured approach: for example, the **5 Whys** technique simply asks “Why?” repeatedly until the fundamental cause is found. Or use a **Fishbone (Ishikawa) diagram**, where the team brainstorms possible causes in categories (People, Process, Systems, etc.) and traces them back to root factors. For instance, if a loan payment is missed, an RCA might reveal that data mismatches caused a calculation error (one of many possible answers). The BA should lead the team through questioning until the real cause (e.g. a misconfigured data field) is identified. Document findings in an action plan to resolve the root issue and not just the symptom. Always go deeper: fix the root cause, not just the immediate error. Use structured RCA (5 Whys, fishbone, flow analysis) to uncover underlying factors. Stopping the analysis when a temporary fix is found. For example, just patching a software bug (symptom) without discovering that it was caused by a flawed business rule mapping. **Symptom** vs **Root Cause**: A *Symptom* is the visible error (e.g. a broken report). The *Root Cause* is the underlying reason (e.g. a missing data mapping rule). They are often mistakenly treated as the same. ### No delta RCA techniques apply in all industries. The concept of probing “why” multiple times or using a fishbone diagram is universal.

title: Requirements Traceability (Matrix)
one_screen: A traceability matrix links each requirement through design, code and testing.  It ensures every requirement (especially regulatory ones) is accounted for and verified.  This audit trail of requirements-to-tests is vital for regulators and audits.
bodyText: A **Requirements Traceability Matrix (RTM)** is usually a table or tool output mapping each requirement to its related artifacts (design specifications, code modules, test cases, test results). The BA or project manager creates/maintains the RTM. It guarantees that each requirement was implemented and tested. In banking, this is critical: regulators or auditors will want proof that every regulation-driven requirement has been satisfied. For example, if a requirement says “calculate capital ratio per Basel rules,” the RTM will show the design document section that implements it, the code module or report name, and the test cases that verify it. At audit time, the RTM provides a single view showing “Basel Cap Ratio req ➔ System Design ➔ Code ➔ Test Passed”. Traceability enforces discipline: if a requirement lacks test coverage, the matrix shows it. Banks often use the RTM to prove compliance. A comprehensive RTM helps avoid scope leakage and missed requirements. Requirement ID → Design Doc → Code Module → Test Case → Status R1: Basel Cap. → Design Sec 2.1 → Mod_Capital → TC01, TC02 → All passed Maintain full end-to-end traceability of every requirement, especially regulatory ones. The RTM must be started early and updated continuously. Each requirement should map to at least one test case that passes. Trying to build traceability after the fact or only partially tracing requirements. For example, failing to link a regulatory requirement to a specific test, then being unable to show auditors how it was verified. **Requirements Traceability Matrix** vs **Test Plan**: The *Traceability Matrix* maps requirements to tests and design. A *Test Plan* outlines the overall testing approach and schedule. They are different documents: the RTM is evidence, the test plan is strategy. ### No delta Banks in every jurisdiction must provide evidence of testing against requirements. The RTM concept is universal; differences lie only in which regulations’ requirements are in scope.

title: Business Requirements Document (BRD)
one_screen: The BRD captures *what* the business wants and *why*, including objectives, scope, stakeholders, and high-level requirements. It **must not** include solution design or technical details. Each requirement should have acceptance criteria.
bodyText: A **Business Requirements Document (BRD)** is the formal specification of business needs. It typically contains an executive summary, background, business objectives (e.g. compliance goals), scope, assumptions, and a list of requirements from the business perspective. Requirements in a BRD may include functional needs (e.g. “system shall generate monthly reports by day 5”) and non-functional needs (e.g. performance, audit trails). Importantly, the BRD states *what* is needed, not *how* to build it. It avoids technical solution detail (that belongs in a functional spec). Each requirement in the BRD should be clear and include acceptance criteria (conditions for success). For instance, instead of saying “system should be fast,” a BRD requirement would say “System must respond to user queries within 2 seconds” (with that criterion). This precision avoids ambiguity and ensures testability. Also include references to regulatory rules if applicable, and note any impacts (e.g. compliance reporting). Sample BRD section: Objective: Improve AML screening efficiency. Requirement: System should screen 100% of new accounts for PEP status within 1 hour of creation (Acceptance: Demonstrate 1-hour turnaround in test). A BRD defines *business needs and constraints*. It must not prescribe the solution. Document each requirement with its own acceptance criteria to make it verifiable. Mixing requirements with design. For example, writing “the system shall use rule X to calculate fee” (that’s a design decision) instead of “calculate fee per business rule.” Also avoid low-level detail or UI mockups in the BRD. **Business Requirements** vs **Functional Specification**: A *Business Requirement* describes what the business must have (high-level need or rule). A *Functional Specification* details how the system will fulfill those needs. They are different deliverables; the BRD should not become a development spec. ### No delta What goes into a business requirements document (objectives, scope, requirements with criteria) is the same everywhere. Regulators may want documentation, but the BRD itself is a project artifact, not jurisdiction-specific.

title: Functional Specifications vs Business Requirements
one_screen: **Business requirements** state *what* is needed, while **functional specifications** describe *how* the system will meet those needs.  A business requirement is high-level (e.g. “produce regulatory report X”), whereas a functional spec details the software logic, screens, or data elements to implement it. The BRD avoids technical detail.
bodyText: Once the business requirements are agreed, the next step is often a detailed functional specification (or functional requirements document). In the functional spec, analysts or developers spell out how each business need will be met technically: database fields, algorithms, screen designs, API calls, etc. For example, a business requirement might be “notify managers of high-risk trades.” The functional spec would describe the notification module, threshold parameters, and user interface. In practice, keep these separate: the BA focuses on business needs, while solution designers write the functional spec. The BRD should remain at a business level “without excessive technical detail”. Any technical content needed for implementation goes into the functional specification. Business requirements (in the BRD) and functional specifications are distinct. The BRD should capture *what and why*. Details of *how* to meet those requirements (logic, UIs, data formats) belong in the functional spec after the BRD is approved. Allowing design to creep into the BRD or holding back needed functional detail. For instance, adding a database table definition to the BRD is mixing layers. **Business Requirement** — a high-level need or rule that the solution must satisfy (e.g., “report X must include all customers over 60 days delinquent”). --- **Functional Specification** — the technical design documenting how the system will achieve that requirement (e.g., database queries, user interface fields, business logic). They get mixed up if a BA starts writing implementation detail in the BRD. ### No delta This separation of concerns is standard practice everywhere. Every bank’s BA should follow the principle regardless of jurisdiction.

title: Data Mapping Specification
one_screen: A data mapping spec is a field-by-field table linking each source field to a target field, including data type and the transformation rule.  It documents exactly how data moves or is converted from the old system to the new.
bodyText: For data migrations or integration, a **Data Mapping Specification** lists every data element to be transferred. Each row typically has: source table/field, source data type, target table/field, target data type, and *Transformation Logic/Business Rules*. For example, a mapping might say `SRC.CUST_ID (VARCHAR)` maps to `CUST.ACCOUNT_NUMBER (String)` with rule “pad with leading zeros to length 15”. Or “DOB (YYYYMMDD) → Birthdate (YYYY-MM-DD)” to reformat dates. This document serves as the *golden source* for developers and testers to implement and verify data flow. In banking, precise mapping is critical (e.g. for customer data, transactions). Missing a transformation can lead to errors or compliance issues. Document every data element and its transformation explicitly. Include data types and any business rule (e.g. code-to-description mapping) for each field. Assuming simple copy (source to target) for all fields. Some fields require non-trivial transformation (format changes, code mappings) which must be written down, or testers cannot verify correctness. **Source Field** vs **Target Field** in mapping: A *Source Field* is the field in the existing (origin) system. A *Target Field* is where it goes in the new system. Keep straight which is which when writing the spec. ### No delta Data mapping documentation is the same process in any country or system. The need for clear source-to-target definitions is universal.

title: Non-Functional Requirements (Performance, Retention, Auditability)
one_screen: Non-functional requirements define *how* the system performs: its quality attributes like speed, security, data retention, and audit capabilities. In banking, **auditability** (e.g. full logging and data retention) is often mandated for compliance.
bodyText: Non-functional requirements (NFRs) cover attributes not captured by functional specs. Key NFRs in banking projects include: - **Performance:** e.g. “System must handle 1000 concurrent users with response <2s.” - **Security & Compliance:** data encryption, access controls, KYC/AML checks, GDPR or similar data privacy. - **Availability:** e.g. “99.9% uptime required.” - **Data Retention:** how long data (or logs) must be kept (often 5–7 years or more). - **Auditability:** ability to trace actions – full logging of transactions and changes. Regulators explicitly require audit trails on changes. For example, a BA noted for a bank onboarding project that auditability (full action logs retained 7+ years) was a key NFR. Non-functional requirements are critical: even if the functionality is correct, failure in security or audit logging can invalidate a project. In regulated change, treat NFRs like compliance: put them in the requirement list and test for them. Always capture NFRs explicitly (security, performance, reliability, legal/policy requirements). In banking, *auditability* (e.g. detailed logs and retention policies) is first-class: include it as a requirement early. Assuming NFRs will be “obvious” or handled later. A common error is neglecting to require sufficient audit logging or forgetting to enforce retention, only to fail compliance checks later. **Functional Requirement** vs **Non-Functional Requirement**: A *Functional Requirement* describes what the system does (specific features). A *Non-Functional Requirement* describes constraints or qualities (like speed, security). For example, “generate monthly report” is functional; “report generation shall complete within 5 minutes” is non-functional. ### No delta The categories of performance, security, retention and audit requirements are the same across banks worldwide. Regulatory laws differ (e.g. GDPR vs CCPA), but the concept of NFRs is universal.

title: Testable Acceptance Criteria
one_screen: Acceptance criteria are the specific, testable conditions that define when a requirement is met.  Well-crafted criteria are clear, concise, and objectively verifiable.
bodyText: Each requirement (or user story) needs acceptance criteria that describe exactly what “done” means. They are written from the user’s perspective: e.g. “The search function returns results that match 100% or partially matching the query” (as in one example). According to Atlassian, acceptance criteria are “clear, concise, and testable statements” that define what success looks like. They should be measurable: instead of vague terms (“fast”, “user-friendly”), use objective thresholds (e.g. “90% of transactions processed within 2 seconds”). Each criterion should map to one or more executable tests. Good acceptance criteria eliminate ambiguity. They align development and QA teams and allow stakeholders to verify requirements. As one guide puts it, they define *“what success looks like”* and “translate the purpose into explicit, verifiable requirements”. For regulators, acceptance criteria often double as test cases to demonstrate compliance. Write acceptance criteria that are specific and measurable. Each criterion must be objectively verifiable (e.g. through a test or demo). If you can’t define a pass/fail condition, refine the requirement. Vague criteria. For example, “The system must be user-friendly” or “Reports should load quickly” are not testable. Also avoid combining multiple conditions into one criterion. Each criterion should stand alone (independent). **Acceptance Criteria** vs **Test Case**: *Acceptance Criteria* are the high-level conditions to meet for a requirement to be accepted. A *Test Case* is a detailed script with steps to verify those criteria. They serve related purposes (criteria shape tests) but are not the same thing. ### No delta The practice of defining testable acceptance criteria is universal across methodologies and jurisdictions.

title: User Stories and Acceptance in a Regulated Context
one_screen: In agile development, user stories (“As a user, I want…”) drive increments.  In a regulated project, each story’s acceptance criteria must tie back to formal requirements and evidence.  You may still use stories, but supplement them with thorough documentation and approvals for audit purposes.
bodyText: User stories are a popular agile format to describe functionality. However, in regulated banking change, “just” having user stories is not enough for audit evidence. For example, a story like “As an accountant I want to generate report X” must be backed by a formal requirement in the BRD or similar doc for traceability. The acceptance criteria for each story should explicitly cover any regulatory rule or business rule involved.
