In practice, BAs in banks often write user stories for the development team, but also maintain a requirements traceability matrix linking each story to the original business requirement or regulation. All acceptance criteria must be documented and tested; regulators may request proof that each story’s scope was approved by risk/compliance. If agile ceremonies (like demos) are used, capture their sign-off too. In short, use user stories for agile development, but never skip the required artifacts (requirements docs, trace matrix, approvals) needed in the regulated context. When using agile user stories in a regulated project, ensure each story and criterion has formal backing. Treat each as “level 1” requirements in the traceability matrix, and secure formal approval on them. Assuming “agile = no documentation.” In regulated change, you cannot omit documentation. Don’t rely solely on Jira tickets or casual “demo approval”; record story acceptance formally. **User Story** vs **Regulatory Requirement**: A *User Story* is a short description of a feature from an end-user’s perspective (agile format). A *Regulatory Requirement* is an explicit compliance mandate that must be met. User stories may implement a regulatory requirement, but the regulator cares about proof of the requirement being met, not just the story text. ### No delta This principle applies everywhere. Whether in India, US, or EU, using agile in regulation-heavy projects requires additional documentation.

title: Testing Lifecycle (Unit, System, Integration, UAT)
one_screen: A typical banking IT change goes through multiple test phases: Unit testing (by developers), Integration/System testing (by QA/IT), and User Acceptance Testing (by business).  Each phase has different owners and objectives.
bodyText: The testing process is layered: - **Unit Testing:** done by developers on individual code modules. Ensures each component works as intended. - **Integration Testing:** QA or IT tests combined modules or subsystems. Checks interfaces between components. - **System Testing:** QA tests the complete system against requirements (functional and non-functional). - **User Acceptance Testing (UAT):** Business users test end-to-end business scenarios in a production-like environment. UAT is led by the business (operations, product, compliance teams). UAT ensures the system meets real business needs before go-live. Each test type requires different participants: developers own unit tests, QA owns system/integration tests, and business stakeholders perform UAT. Testing each phase is critical: skipping system test and jumping to UAT, for instance, risks missing defects that developers should have caught. +-------------+ | Unit Test | +-------------+ v +-------------+ | Integration | | Test | +-------------+ v +-------------+ | System Test | +-------------+ v +------------------+ | User Acceptance | | Test (UAT) | +------------------+ Follow all test phases in order and involve the right people. Use unit and system tests to catch defects early, and let end users validate the solution in UAT. Treating UAT as the first time the business sees the solution. If unit/integration tests are inadequate, UAT will be overwhelmed with obvious issues. **System Test** vs **User Acceptance Test (UAT)**: *System Test* is executed by QA/IT to verify the software meets the specified requirements. *UAT* is done by business users to verify the system meets their needs in real-world scenarios. ### No delta These test phases and roles are standard in all banking projects globally.

title: Test Planning and Test Packs
one_screen: A test plan defines the scope, approach, resources, and schedule of testing. Test packs (test cases and data) list the specific scenarios with expected outcomes.  For each requirement, predefined test cases and datasets must be prepared before testing begins.
bodyText: Before execution, the BA (often with QA) creates a **Test Plan**: it includes test objectives, types of testing, environment details, schedule, and responsibilities. The plan ensures everyone knows what will be tested and when. Key to this is preparing **test packs**: collections of test cases and test data with expected results. For example, a pack for a regulatory report change might include sample transactions (input data) and the exact numbers expected in the output. In regulated projects, predefined test data is especially important: you must demonstrate that for each scenario, you know the “right answer” in advance. This way, testers (or auditors reviewing UAT) can verify correctness efficiently. The BA’s role is to help identify all required scenarios and define the expected results (often consulting SMEs or model owners for calculations). Testers then use this pack during UAT to systematically execute tests. Develop detailed test cases and data (test packs) for all requirements. Each test should have the input data and the precise expected result documented. Assuming testers will figure out expected outcomes on the fly. Without a predefined expected result, testers cannot conclusively pass/fail a case, and auditors will challenge the validity of the test. **Test Plan** vs **Test Case/Test Pack**: A *Test Plan* is the high-level strategy and timeline for testing. A *Test Case* (in a pack) is a specific scenario with steps and expected result. The plan is “what/when”, test cases are “how/results”. ### No delta The discipline of planning tests and defining expected results is a best practice everywhere.

title: UAT Coverage and Defect Management
one_screen: Ensure UAT covers all critical business and regulatory scenarios. Use metrics (e.g. scenario coverage %) to argue sufficiency.  Manage defects by classifying each by *severity* (technical impact) and *priority* (business urgency).
bodyText: **UAT Coverage:** The BA must confirm that UAT scenarios collectively cover all key requirements and risk areas. Typically, this is demonstrated by linking each requirement (and sub-case) to one or more UAT scenarios. In practice, teams track *scenario coverage percentage*. For example, Yethi’s core banking UAT practice uses end-to-end business scenarios (account opening, loan origination, payments) to ensure coverage. They measure how many of those planned scenarios have been executed successfully. To argue coverage is sufficient, present traceability: “Requirement X is covered by test cases TC1, TC2.” Focus on risk: prioritize testing of critical flows first. **Defect Management:** Each defect discovered in testing is logged with details. Importantly, classify it by **Severity** (the technical impact: *Critical* = system-blocker, *Major*, etc.) and **Priority** (how urgent the fix is to the business: high=must-fix, low=can wait). For example, a calculation error in a capital ratio (high severity) might also be high priority. Lowering defect list by severity/priority and reaching “0 critical open” is usually a go-live criterion. Track defects transparently: who fixes them, retest after fixes, and ensure no showstoppers remain before sign-off. Build UAT scenarios that cover *every* business requirement, especially regulatory ones. Use traceability and coverage metrics to justify adequacy. Classify and fix defects based on agreed severity/priority rules. Overconfidence that “we tested enough” without proof. Always use coverage measures or sign-offs on critical scenarios. Also, don’t mix up severity and priority – a minor typo may be low severity but could be high priority if it affects reporting. **Severity** vs **Priority**: *Severity* gauges the impact of a defect on system functionality. *Priority* indicates how quickly the defect should be fixed (a business decision). They are separate measures, not synonyms. ### No delta The need for clear UAT coverage and defect triage is the same in all banks. Regulatory or not, rigorous UAT and defect classification prevent missed issues.

title: Parallel Running & Go-Live Planning
one_screen: *Parallel running* means operating the old and new systems side-by-side for a period to compare outputs. *Go-live planning* (cutover) details how to switch to the new system, including rollback steps if needed.  Both are critical in regulated transitions.
bodyText: Before decommissioning legacy processes, banks often run *both* systems in parallel to ensure the new one works correctly. For example, a bank might process a day’s transactions in both the old system and the new IFRS-compliant system and compare the results. This parallel run period (sometimes months) builds confidence and provides audit evidence that the new outputs are accurate. It also allows real data to exercise the system without immediate risk. The *go-live plan* (cutover plan) is executed once parallel runs are complete. It is a detailed schedule: which data migration steps to perform, which systems to shut down/start up, and who is responsible for each action. The plan must include *rollback procedures*: if a critical issue occurs, how to revert to the old system to prevent business impact. For example, ensure backups and change logs are ready. Roles (executive sponsor, IT lead, BA, etc.) must be assigned for go/no-go decisions and communication to stakeholders. Include parallel running and dual-reporting as part of implementation. Plan go-live steps meticulously and always have a tested rollback strategy. Confirm decision criteria (e.g. “all parallel outputs match 99%”) before full cutover. Assuming go-live will succeed without rehearsal. A frequent mistake is not planning for failures – e.g. no rollback or contingency plan. Also failing to run both systems long enough to catch issues. **Parallel Run** vs **Dual Reporting**: A *Parallel Run* is running old and new systems at the same time to validate output. *Dual Reporting* is submitting reports in both old and new regimes (e.g. old accounting vs new) to regulators. They both involve duplication but serve different verification purposes. ### No delta These deployment practices are standard in banking globally, especially for compliance transitions.

title: Post-Implementation Review and Benefits Realisation
one_screen: After go-live, conduct a formal review comparing actual outcomes to planned objectives. Capture lessons learned and track whether expected benefits (cost savings, efficiency gains, compliance) are realized.
bodyText: Once the system is live and stable, a **Post-Implementation Review (PIR)** evaluates success. The BA should gather the project team and business stakeholders to review metrics and outcomes. Did the system meet the business objectives outlined in the BRD? For example, if the goal was a 50% reduction in report prep time, measure the actual improvement. Regulatory objectives (e.g. no compliance violations) must also be confirmed. Part of the PIR is **Benefits Realisation**: compare the business case predictions (e.g. lower costs, better risk metrics) to reality. If benefits fall short, identify why. Lessons from the review should feed back into process improvements for future changes. A formal PIR also provides closure: documenting success and issues demonstrates to auditors and leadership that the project delivered as intended (or what corrective actions are taken). Always schedule a post-launch review. It should include all key stakeholders, revisit requirements and scope, and check actual performance and risk metrics against targets. Skipping the review or only doing technical validation. Don’t forget to measure business impact. For example, installing a new compliance module but never checking if compliance reporting is actually more accurate counts as incomplete implementation. **Post-Implementation Review** vs **Project Closure**: A *PIR* examines project outcomes and lessons. *Project Closure* is the administrative final step (sign-offs, documentation archive). Both are needed, but PIR focuses on evaluation and benefits tracking. ### No delta Reviewing outcomes and realising benefits is a recommended practice worldwide, not specific to one jurisdiction.

title: Waterfall vs Agile in Banking
one_screen: Waterfall (stage-gate) and Agile (iterative) are both used in banks.  Regulatory changes often lean waterfall: fixed scope and deadlines drive sequential phases (requirements→design→build→test). Agile is better for evolving requirements, but must be adapted for compliance needs.
bodyText: Many banks use waterfall for compliance projects because regulators expect detailed plans and sign-offs. As one analyst notes, banks “generally set up regulatory projects in a sequential manner—finalize requirements, then design, then build, then test”. This ensures all regulatory criteria are identified and reviewed upfront. However, waterfall can struggle if requirements change mid-project (which happens frequently). Agile frameworks allow incremental development and frequent feedback, which can help manage changes. In reality, banks often use hybrids: they may scope and plan a regulatory change in detail (waterfall style) but develop components iteratively, or run multiple agile sprints for low-risk modules. If using Agile, the BA still needs to document and get approval for requirements. Sprints will produce user stories, but the overall scope cannot drift beyond what’s compliant. Regulators may allow iterative delivery internally, but they expect evidence that all parts of the regulation were handled. For a fixed regulatory date, waterfall gating provides clear go/no-go points (though it risks corner-cutting under pressure). Agile’s visibility (working demos) can reassure stakeholders, but BAs must reconcile it with the formal change control needed. Choose methodology based on project nature. Regulatory changes usually require upfront planning and documentation, so use waterfall or a controlled hybrid. If adopting Agile elements, ensure deliverables and approvals still meet compliance scrutiny. Attempting a pure agile approach for a fixed-scope regulatory program without adapting (e.g. without documentation or formal sign-off). Conversely, ignoring agile techniques entirely can lead to last-minute rework. **Waterfall** vs **Agile**: *Waterfall* is sequential, with completed phases (requirements→design→build→test). *Agile* is iterative and incremental, allowing requirements to evolve. They both aim to deliver systems, but differ in process: Agile values working software over docs, whereas Waterfall emphasizes planning and documentation. In banking, the line blurs, but they remain distinct approaches. ### No delta The trade-offs of waterfall vs agile are the same worldwide. Choice depends on project uncertainty and constraints, not jurisdiction. However, strict regulators may influence banks to favour waterfall-like controls.

title: Prioritisation & Estimation in Banking Projects
one_screen: Prioritize work using clear criteria (business value, risk, regulatory urgency) and defend choices with data.  Estimate tasks realistically using ranges or past data, accounting for optimism bias.
bodyText: BAs often help decide what to do first in a change program. Common prioritisation methods include *weighted scoring* (scoring features by value, cost, risk), *MoSCoW* (Must/Should/Could/Won’t), or simple *risk-first* (fix highest compliance risk first). For regulatory projects, items explicitly tied to required dates are usually top priority. Always document how you prioritized: for example, “Requirement A scored 9/10 on impact because it directly addresses a mandatory regulation” provides rationale. This transparency makes prioritisation defensible to management and auditors. For estimation, acknowledge that BAs and teams are naturally optimistic (the “planning fallacy”). Use historical data or three-point estimates (best/likely/worst) to capture uncertainty. Include a buffer for testing and integration complexities. For instance, if developing a new report took 10 days in a past project, plan 15 days for similar complexity. Clear estimation methods (e.g. story points, function points, or t-shirt sizes) help set realistic schedules and avoid last-minute scope cuts. Use objective criteria (value to business, compliance risk, regulatory deadline) in a documented prioritisation model. When estimating, always allow contingencies – it’s normal to be optimistic, so plan for known unknowns. Letting “priority” be decided by the loudest stakeholder or an incorrect assumption that all items are equally urgent. Also, giving point estimates (e.g. “5 days”) without ranges ignores uncertainty; this often leads to schedule overrun. **Urgency** vs **Importance**: An *Urgent* task has a tight deadline (often regulatory or external). An *Important* task has high business value or impact. They can differ (e.g. a bug might be urgent but low importance). Prioritisation should consider both, not mistake one for the other. ### No delta Banks use the same prioritisation logic everywhere. CFOs and regulators expect clear rationale for why one feature was delayed and another accelerated.

title: Managing Scope Change with Fixed Deadlines
one_screen: In projects with immovable regulatory deadlines, handle scope changes through a formal change control process.  Assess each new requirement’s impact on timeline and scope. If the deadline cannot move, negotiate resources or de-scope non-critical items rather than slipping the date.
bodyText: Scope changes are inevitable, but on a regulatory program the deadline is set by law. Every requested change must go through a structured change request process. The BA must document the change, analyze its impact on schedule and cost, and present to the Change Control Board. If adding new requirements, either find efficiency elsewhere or request additional resources (often hard to get). The key is *trade-offs*: for example, if a late rule change is issued, you might push some non-essential enhancements to the next phase. All approved changes and their rationales should be logged in a change control log. No unapproved scope creep should occur: formal approval (by business, risk, audit) is required for anything beyond original scope. In practice, regulators expect that the project was baselined and any changes are traceable. A formal change control ensures auditors see an audit trail of decisions (who approved a change and why). Always process scope changes formally. Do not slip regulatory deadlines. If new items arise late, escalate them to executives and re-prioritize or delay less-critical work. Allowing uncontrolled additions to scope (scope creep) because of “just this one change.” Each change must consider the fixed deadline. Avoid informal side agreements to implement extra features without updating the project plan. **Scope Change** vs **Scope Creep**: *Scope Change* is a formally approved modification with documented impact analysis. *Scope Creep* is uncontrolled expansion of scope. A regulated project should only have intentional scope changes through proper channels. ### No delta Change control discipline is standard in every banking regulation project. What varies by jurisdiction is the regulatory author, not how change is managed.

title: Why Regulatory Capital Exists
one_screen: Expected loss is the recurring, statistically anticipated cost of taking risk; unexpected loss is the adverse tail beyond that expectation. Provisions and pricing address expected loss, while capital exists principally to keep the bank solvent when realised losses exceed what was expected.
bodyText: A credit portfolio does not have one future loss number. It has a **loss distribution**: many possible outcomes, ranging from benign to severe. The mean or central estimate is expected loss. The distance from that expected amount to a sufficiently adverse loss level is unexpected loss. Basel’s IRB framework deliberately distinguishes the two: the risk-weight functions generate capital requirements for unexpected loss, while expected loss is separately compared with eligible provisions. That distinction explains why provisions and capital are complementary rather than interchangeable. A bank that expects a recurring amount of credit loss should recognise that economics through pricing, income and the applicable provisioning framework. Capital is a residual shock absorber: when losses are larger than the amount already recognised or economically anticipated, the loss reduces retained earnings and therefore Common Equity Tier 1 unless replenished. BIS research describes modern provisioning as addressing expected future losses while capital requirements provide resources against unexpected losses. The split is conceptual, not a claim that provisioning perfectly equals expected loss or that capital can never absorb an expected loss. Accounting provisions, regulatory expected-loss measures and economic estimates can differ because they use different horizons, parameters and objectives. Under the IRB framework, a shortfall of eligible provisions relative to regulatory expected loss affects regulatory capital; an excess may receive limited recognition subject to Basel rules. The practical capital question is therefore not “How much loss is expected?” but “After recognised loss allowances and earnings capacity, how much additional loss can the bank survive without becoming non-viable?” +----------------------+ | Credit loss outcomes | +----------------------+ | v +----------------------+ | Expected loss | | recurring / central | +----------------------+ | v +----------------------+ | Provisions + pricing | +----------------------+ | v +----------------------+ | Unexpected loss | | adverse tail | +----------------------+ | v +----------------------+ | Regulatory capital | | absorbs shock | +----------------------+ Provisioning and capital solve different loss-absorption problems: expected loss is not a reason to eliminate capital, and capital is not a substitute for timely recognition of expected loss. Treating “capital requirement” as the expected credit-loss number double-counts the centre of the loss distribution and misses the purpose of the prudential tail-loss cushion. **Expected loss** — the loss anticipated over a defined horizon under stated assumptions. --- **Unexpected loss** — adverse loss beyond the expected amount for which capital provides a solvency cushion. **No delta.** The expected-loss versus unexpected-loss distinction is an economic and prudential principle; accounting and provisioning rules differ by jurisdiction, but the loss-distribution logic does not.

title: Solvency and Liquidity in a Capital Context
one_screen: Solvency asks whether the value of the bank’s assets can absorb losses and still cover its liabilities; liquidity asks whether cash obligations can be met when due. Capital protects solvency, while liquidity resources protect payment capacity, and a bank can fail either test without initially failing the other.
bodyText: Capital is a balance-sheet loss absorber. If an asset worth 100 suffers a loss of 10, that loss must ultimately reduce some claim on the bank. Deposits and senior liabilities are not intended to take ordinary going-concern losses, so equity and qualifying regulatory capital stand between asset losses and creditor impairment. That is the solvency function of capital. Basel expresses risk-based requirements as qualifying capital relative to risk-weighted assets and separately maintains liquidity standards rather than treating liquidity as another form of capital. Liquidity is different. A solvent bank may own assets whose economic value exceeds its liabilities but be unable to turn those assets into cash quickly enough to meet withdrawals or maturing obligations. Conversely, a deeply insolvent bank can temporarily remain liquid if it still has cash or funding access. The two conditions interact because forced asset sales made to obtain liquidity may crystallise losses, and doubts about solvency can cause funding to disappear. Capital ratios therefore do not answer the question “Can tomorrow’s payment be made?” A large CET1 balance cannot itself settle a payment unless the bank has cash, central-bank reserves, marketable assets or funding capacity. Likewise, a stock of liquid assets does not repair a balance sheet whose losses have exhausted equity. The regulatory architecture reflects the distinction: risk-based capital and leverage requirements address loss-bearing capacity, while liquidity requirements sit in separate Basel framework modules. +----------------------+ | Bank under stress | +----------------------+ | | v v +-----------+ +-----------+ | Losses on | | Cash | | assets | | outflows | +-----------+ +-----------+ | | v v +-----------+ +-----------+ | Capital | | Liquidity | | absorbs | | meets | | losses | | payments | +-----------+ +-----------+ | | v v +-----------+ +-----------+ | Solvency | | Payment | | test | | capacity | +-----------+ +-----------+ Capital is not cash. A capital ratio is a solvency measure, not a statement that the bank possesses an equivalent amount of immediately spendable liquidity. Calling a liquidity shortfall a “capital shortfall” because both occur during stress leads to the wrong remedial action: raising equity and raising immediately available funding solve different immediate problems. **Solvency** — sufficient loss-absorbing net worth to withstand asset losses and remain viable. --- **Liquidity** — sufficient cash or reliably monetisable resources to meet obligations when they fall due. **No delta.** The distinction follows balance-sheet and cash-flow mechanics and does not depend on jurisdiction.

title: Going-Concern and Gone-Concern Capital
one_screen: Going-concern capital absorbs losses while the bank remains operating; gone-concern capital protects creditors and supports resolution once viability has been lost. Basel places CET1 and AT1 in Tier 1 going-concern capital and characterises Tier 2 as gone-concern capital.
bodyText: Loss absorption has a timing dimension. **Going concern** means the institution continues operating: deposits are serviced, lending continues and the legal entity has not crossed into resolution or failure. Capital that absorbs losses at this stage must be sufficiently permanent and subordinated that losses can be imposed without creating an ordinary payment default. Common Equity Tier 1 is the clearest example. Losses reduce retained earnings immediately, so CET1 bears deterioration continuously. Additional Tier 1 is also classified within Tier 1 and is designed for going-concern loss absorption, although its contractual and regulatory mechanisms differ from ordinary equity. Basel’s capital definition labels Tier 1 as going-concern capital and Tier 2 as gone-concern capital. **Gone concern** begins conceptually when ordinary private operation is no longer viable without resolution action or extraordinary support. Tier 2 is subordinated and designed to absorb losses before senior unsecured creditors and depositors in failure or resolution. The exact legal mechanism depends on national resolution law and instrument terms, so “gone concern” does not mean that every Tier 2 instrument automatically converts at the same accounting ratio. The distinction is about when and how reliably loss-bearing capacity is available. A funding instrument can be deeply subordinated yet still fail regulatory-capital eligibility if its maturity, redemption rights, incentives or contractual terms undermine the required permanence and loss absorption. Basel therefore uses detailed eligibility criteria rather than simply asking whether an instrument is called “equity” or “subordinated debt”. +-----------------------+ | Bank operating | | as going concern | +-----------------------+ | v +-----------------------+ | CET1 absorbs losses | | continuously | +-----------------------+ | v +-----------------------+ | AT1 provides further | | going-concern capacity| +-----------------------+ | v +-----------------------+ | Point of non-viability| +-----------------------+ | v +-----------------------+ | Tier 2 / resolution | | loss absorption | +-----------------------+ A capital instrument’s regulatory value comes from genuine loss-absorption capacity and permanence, not its accounting label or marketing name. Describing Tier 2 as a normal operating-loss buffer equivalent to CET1 ignores the reason regulators distinguish going-concern from gone-concern quality. **Going-concern capital** — capital capable of absorbing losses while the institution remains viable and operating. --- **Gone-concern capital** — loss-absorbing resources designed principally to protect creditors and support resolution after non-viability. **No delta.** Legal resolution mechanisms differ, but Basel’s conceptual distinction between Tier 1 going-concern capital and Tier 2 gone-concern capital is common.

title: The Regulatory Capital Stack
one_screen: Regulatory capital is a quality hierarchy: CET1 is the first and strongest loss absorber, AT1 supplements going-concern capital, and Tier 2 provides lower-ranking gone-concern capacity. Basel total regulatory capital is CET1 plus AT1 plus Tier 2, after applicable regulatory adjustments.
bodyText: **Common Equity Tier 1** is the highest-quality layer. It centres on ordinary common equity and retained earnings, subject to eligibility rules and deductions. Because accounting losses reduce retained earnings, CET1 responds directly to deterioration in the bank’s net asset value. **Additional Tier 1** consists of eligible instruments that are sufficiently permanent and loss absorbing to qualify as Tier 1 but do not meet all CET1 criteria. AT1 is therefore not “better debt”; it is a regulatory category whose instruments must satisfy restrictions concerning permanence, distributions, subordination and loss absorption. Basel treats CET1 plus AT1 as Tier 1 capital. **Tier 2** sits below Tier 1 in regulatory quality. It may include eligible subordinated instruments meeting Basel’s criteria and is principally gone-concern capital. Total capital is the sum of Tier 1 and Tier 2 after regulatory adjustments. Basel’s global minima are 4.5% CET1, 6% Tier 1 and 8% total capital as percentages of risk-weighted assets, before capital buffers and jurisdictional additions. Those Basel percentages are standards rather than universally binding statutory ratios: national authorities may impose higher minima or additional requirements. A crucial nesting rule follows from the hierarchy. CET1 can satisfy the CET1 minimum and, to the extent available beyond that need, higher-level Tier 1 or total-capital requirements. AT1 cannot satisfy CET1. Tier 2 cannot satisfy either CET1 or Tier 1. Quality therefore flows upward through the requirement stack; lower-quality capital cannot be substituted downward into a higher-quality requirement. +---------------------------+ | CET1 | | highest quality | +---------------------------+ | v +---------------------------+ | AT1 | | + CET1 = Tier 1 | +---------------------------+ | v +---------------------------+ | Tier 2 | | gone-concern layer | +---------------------------+ | v +---------------------------+ | Total regulatory capital | | CET1 + AT1 + Tier 2 | +---------------------------+ Capital categories are nested by quality: Tier 2 cannot cure a CET1 shortfall, and AT1 cannot cure a CET1 shortfall. Adding CET1, Tier 1 and total-capital percentages as though they were independent requirements triple-counts capital because the ratios are nested. **Tier 1 capital** — CET1 plus eligible AT1. --- **Total capital** — Tier 1 plus eligible Tier 2; it is not an additional layer equal to the sum of three minimum percentages. **No delta.** The CET1–AT1–Tier 2 hierarchy is the common Basel architecture; numerical national minima can differ.

title: Regulatory Adjustments and Deductions
one_screen: Accounting equity is not automatically regulatory capital. Prudential deductions and adjustments remove or limit balance-sheet items whose value may be unavailable, uncertain or double-counted precisely when the bank needs loss-absorbing capital most.
bodyText: The starting point for CET1 resembles accounting equity, but the prudential question is narrower: **can this amount genuinely absorb losses for the banking group under stress?** Regulatory adjustments convert accounting measures into the capital amounts recognised by the supervisor. A straightforward example is goodwill and certain other intangible assets. An accounting balance sheet may report them as assets, but their realisable value can be doubtful in distress and they do not provide cash or a claim against an external obligor that can absorb the bank’s losses. Basel therefore requires specified intangible amounts to be deducted from CET1, subject to the detailed framework. A second problem is **double counting**. Suppose one regulated financial institution holds capital issued by another and both count the same economic resources as loss-absorbing capital. Without consolidation or deduction, one unit of underlying equity could appear to support risks twice. Basel’s regulatory-adjustment framework therefore addresses significant investments in financial entities and related capital-recognition issues. Other adjustments can arise from deferred tax assets, own-credit effects, cash-flow hedge reserves, pension-related items and thresholds for specified investments. The exact treatment is technical and can change with local implementation; the permanent principle is that reported shareholders’ equity and regulatory CET1 are different quantities. Deductions also matter before ratios are calculated. A bank does not normally calculate CET1/RWA using gross accounting equity and then subtract the deduction from the ratio. It determines eligible regulatory capital after the prescribed adjustments and uses that amount as the numerator. +-------------------------+ | Accounting equity | +-------------------------+ | v +-------------------------+ | Apply prudential filters| | and deductions | +-------------------------+ | v +-------------------------+ | Remove / limit amounts | | not fully loss absorbing| +-------------------------+ | v +-------------------------+ | Regulatory CET1 | +-------------------------+ | v +-------------------------+ | CET1 / RWA ratio | +-------------------------+ Regulatory capital is an eligibility measure after prudential adjustments, not a synonym for book equity. Using the balance-sheet equity total as the CET1 numerator without applying regulatory adjustments can materially overstate prudential capital. **Accounting equity** — equity recognised under the applicable financial-reporting framework. --- **Regulatory CET1** — qualifying highest-quality capital after the prudential eligibility rules, filters and deductions have been applied. **No delta.** Specific deductions and thresholds differ in implementation, but every Basel-style framework distinguishes eligible regulatory capital from unadjusted accounting equity.

title: The Capital Buffer Stack
one_screen: Minimum capital is the line a bank must not normally cross; buffers are deliberately placed above that line so capital can absorb stress before minimum requirements are breached. Conservation, countercyclical and systemic buffers serve different purposes even when all are expressed as additional CET1 requirements.
bodyText: The **capital conservation buffer** creates a standing cushion above minimum capital. Under the Basel standard it is 2.5% of RWA and must be met with CET1. Its purpose is usability: a bank can enter the buffer during stress, but doing so increasingly constrains distributions so earnings are conserved and capital can be rebuilt. The **countercyclical capital buffer** is macroprudential rather than permanently fixed. Authorities can raise it when system-wide credit conditions indicate excessive risk build-up and release it when conditions deteriorate. Basel sets an international framework in which the bank-specific CCyB reflects relevant jurisdictional rates and cross-border exposures. **Systemic buffers or surcharges** address the additional damage that failure of a systemically important institution could cause. Their purpose is different from the conservation buffer: the added requirement reflects systemic externality rather than merely providing the same fixed cushion to every bank. This produces a layered target. Management should distinguish minimum requirements from buffers because the consequences of breaching them differ. Entering a buffer can trigger distribution restrictions while the institution remains above minimum capital; breaching a minimum is a more severe prudential condition. The exact stack is jurisdiction-specific. The United States, in particular, uses a stress capital buffer architecture for large firms rather than simply replicating the European combined-buffer structure. +-------------------------+ | Systemic / other buffer | +-------------------------+ | +-------------------------+ | Countercyclical buffer | +-------------------------+ | +-------------------------+ | Conservation buffer | +-------------------------+ | +-------------------------+ | Regulatory minimums | +-------------------------+ A buffer sits above a minimum because it is intended to be usable before the minimum is breached. Calling the conservation buffer an additional “minimum” obscures the graduated consequences that make a buffer usable in stress. **Minimum capital requirement** — the hard baseline prudential requirement. --- **Capital buffer** — additional loss-absorbing capacity above the minimum, normally coupled with consequences that intensify as the buffer is used. — RBI’s 2025 commercial-bank capital directions prescribe a 2.5% CET1 capital conservation buffer and a countercyclical framework above India’s higher domestic minima. [RBI Capital Adequacy Directions 2025, Table 1 and buffer provisions] — The PRA framework uses a combined-buffer architecture for firms in the ordinary regime; the separate SDDT regime taking effect on 1 January 2027 introduces a simplified capital-buffer structure. [PRA SS6/14 framework; PS4/26] — CRD-based combined-buffer requirements include conservation and applicable countercyclical/systemic components, with distribution restrictions linked to failure to meet the combined buffer. [CRD Article 141 / EBA Single Rulebook] — Large-bank requirements incorporate a firm-specific stress capital buffer informed by supervisory stress testing; this differs structurally from simply adding the European combined-buffer stack. [Federal Reserve Annual Report, Supervision and Regulation]

title: Distribution Constraints and Maximum Distributable Amount
one_screen: Buffers bite before minimums because entering the buffer restricts distributions while the bank can still remain legally capitalised above minimum requirements. The maximum distributable amount mechanism turns buffer depletion into progressively stronger limits on dividends, variable remuneration and other discretionary payouts.
bodyText: A usable capital buffer creates a design problem. If a bank can distribute capital freely after entering the buffer, shareholders or instrument holders may receive resources that supervisors intended to remain available to absorb losses. Conversely, if entering the buffer immediately creates the same consequences as breaching a minimum, management may avoid using the buffer even during legitimate stress. Basel solves this by imposing **capital conservation constraints** as CET1 falls through the conservation-buffer range. The deeper the bank moves into the buffer, the greater the share of earnings it must retain. Basel describes the buffer as usable while business continues, with automatic distribution restrictions increasing as capital approaches the minimum. In UK and EU terminology, the related calculation is commonly called the **maximum distributable amount**, or MDA. The MDA limits specified discretionary distributions when the combined buffer is not met. UK PRA materials identify affected distributions such as bonuses and AT1 coupons, while EU CRD Article 141 links failure to meet the combined-buffer requirement with restrictions on distributions. The important sequencing is therefore: first the bank uses excess management headroom; then it may enter regulatory buffers; distribution constraints intensify; only after further deterioration does it approach minimum capital requirements. A buffer is consequently neither “free capital” nor a second minimum. The US stress capital buffer reaches a similar objective through a different capital architecture, so European MDA terminology should not be mechanically imported into US requirements. +----------------------+ | Capital above buffers| +----------------------+ | v +----------------------+ | Buffer entered | +----------------------+ | v +----------------------+ | Distribution limits | | begin / intensify | +----------------------+ | v +----------------------+ | Minimum approached | +----------------------+ | v +----------------------+ | Severe prudential | | breach territory | +----------------------+ Distribution restrictions are a conservation mechanism triggered before capital minima are exhausted. Treating MDA as the amount of capital a bank is permitted to lose confuses a distribution limit with a capital stock. **MDA** — the maximum amount permitted for specified distributions under the applicable conservation regime. --- **Capital buffer** — the CET1 cushion whose depletion can cause the MDA restriction to apply. — RBI applies graduated capital-conservation ratios to earnings as CET1 enters the prescribed buffer bands. [RBI Capital Adequacy Directions 2025, capital conservation standards] — Ordinary-regime firms face MDA restrictions when they do not meet the combined buffer; the SDDT capital regime effective 1 January 2027 uses a simplified structure and removes the ordinary automatic-MDA architecture for SDDTs. [PRA CP9/24; PS4/26 and finalised Strong and Simple policy] — CRD Article 141 requires an MDA calculation and distribution restrictions when the combined-buffer requirement is not met. [CRD Article 141 / EBA] — The large-bank framework uses a stress capital buffer derived from supervisory stress testing rather than the EU-style combined-buffer/MDA architecture. [Federal Reserve Annual Report]

title: The Leverage Ratio Backstop
one_screen: The leverage ratio ignores most risk weights and compares Tier 1 capital with a broad exposure measure. It is a deliberately blunt backstop: risk-based models can change the measured riskiness of assets, but they cannot make the underlying exposure disappear.
bodyText: Risk-weighted capital requirements depend on judgements about relative risk. A low-risk exposure receives less RWA than a high-risk exposure, which improves risk sensitivity but creates dependence on classifications, parameters and models. The leverage ratio places a floor under how far that process can reduce required capital. Basel defines the leverage ratio as Tier 1 capital divided by the leverage-ratio exposure measure and establishes a 3% minimum in the global framework. The denominator is broader than accounting assets because it also captures specified off-balance-sheet and derivative exposures under prescribed measurement rules. The leverage ratio is **non-risk-sensitive** in the relevant sense: a unit of qualifying exposure generally enters the denominator without first being multiplied by its credit risk weight. That makes the measure crude, but the crudeness is intentional. It limits model risk, classification arbitrage and the possibility that a portfolio judged extremely safe under the RWA framework supports excessive balance-sheet leverage. The ratio is therefore a backstop, not a replacement for RWA. A bank can be constrained by either measure. A high-risk portfolio may be bound by risk-based capital while a very large portfolio of low-risk assets may be more constrained by leverage requirements. A practitioner should calculate both lenses rather than converting one into the other. “Low RWA density” does not imply “low leverage exposure”. +----------------------+ | Same bank exposures | +----------------------+ | | v v +-----------+ +-----------+ | Risk-based| | Leverage | | framework | | framework | +-----------+ +-----------+ | | v v +-----------+ +-----------+ | Apply risk| | Broad | | weights | | exposure | +-----------+ +-----------+ | | v v +-----------+ +-----------+ | RWA ratio | | Tier 1 / | | constraint| | exposure | +-----------+ +-----------+ The leverage ratio complements rather than substitutes for risk-weighted capital requirements. Using total accounting assets as an exact leverage-ratio denominator ignores regulatory treatment of derivatives and off-balance-sheet exposures. **Risk-based capital ratio** — qualifying capital divided by RWA. --- **Leverage ratio** — Tier 1 capital divided by a broadly measured exposure amount without ordinary credit risk weighting. — RBI prescribes a minimum leverage ratio of 4% for D-SIBs and 3.5% for other commercial banks. [RBI Capital Adequacy Directions 2025, para 262] — The UK applies its domestic leverage framework and leverage buffers to relevant firms; its design is not identical to the risk-based combined-buffer/MDA framework. [Bank of England, Financial Stability in Focus, December 2025] — The CRR leverage framework implements the leverage-ratio backstop alongside risk-based own-funds requirements; applicable overlays depend on institution type and current EU rules and must be checked in CRR. [Basel leverage principle; local CRR verification required] — US capital rules use leverage requirements alongside risk-based ratios, with additional leverage requirements applying to specified large organisations; the exact requirement depends on regulatory category. [Federal Reserve capital framework; institution-specific scope must be verified]

title: Risk Weights and Risk-Weighted Assets
one_screen: A risk weight converts an exposure amount into a regulatory risk measure: exposure × risk weight = RWA under the basic standardised credit-risk logic. The weight is a prudential calibration of relative risk, not a forecast that the stated percentage of the exposure will be lost.
bodyText: Suppose a qualifying exposure amount is 100 and the applicable standardised credit risk weight is 50%. Its credit RWA is 50. If a minimum total-capital ratio were applied to that RWA, the capital requirement would be calculated from 50, not directly from the 100 exposure. This two-stage structure separates the **risk measurement** step from the **capital ratio** step. Risk weights therefore act as regulatory scaling factors. Higher weights make a unit of exposure consume more capital; lower weights make it consume less. Under the standardised approach, weights are specified through exposure classes, counterparty characteristics, collateral treatment, external credit assessments where permitted, loan-to-value measures and other criteria. Basel’s revised standardised approach deliberately increases granularity and risk sensitivity while retaining supervisor-prescribed rules. A 100% risk weight does not mean a 100% probability of default or a 100% expected loss. It means one unit of exposure creates one unit of RWA before other applicable adjustments. Similarly, a 20% weight does not mean that 20% of the exposure is expected to disappear. **RWA density** is a useful derived intuition: RWA divided by a relevant exposure measure. A portfolio with 40 of credit RWA against 100 of exposure has 40% RWA density. But density is an output of regulatory measurement, not an independent risk parameter. Risk weights also differ from provisions. Provisions reduce the carrying value or recognise expected loss under the applicable framework; risk weights determine the capital denominator used to support unexpected risk. +----------------------+ | Exposure amount 100 | +----------------------+ | v +----------------------+ | Applicable RW = 50% | +----------------------+ | v +----------------------+ | Credit RWA = 50 | +----------------------+ | v +----------------------+ | Capital ratio applied| | to RWA | +----------------------+ A risk weight is a prudential scaling factor used to calculate RWA; it is not PD, LGD or expected loss. Reading a 150% risk weight as “the regulator expects to lose 150% of the loan” confuses a capital calibration with an economic loss forecast. **Risk weight** — the regulatory percentage or formula output applied to an exposure for RWA purposes. --- **Capital ratio** — qualifying capital divided by RWA; it is applied after RWA has been determined. **No delta.** Jurisdictions prescribe different detailed weights, but the standardised arithmetic of exposure amount multiplied by applicable risk weight is common.

title: Basel’s Three Pillars
one_screen: Pillar 1 supplies minimum quantitative capital rules, Pillar 2 adds bank-specific risk assessment and supervisory review, and Pillar 3 uses public disclosure to strengthen market discipline. A complete capital framework therefore asks not only “what does the formula require?” but also “what risks did the formula miss?” and “what must outsiders be told?”
bodyText: **Pillar 1** contains the prescribed methods for calculating minimum regulatory capital against defined risks. It creates comparability and a common quantitative baseline through rules governing eligible capital, RWA and minimum ratios. **Pillar 2** exists because no universal formula captures every material risk at every institution. The Basel supervisory review process requires banks to assess capital adequacy relative to their risk profile and strategy and requires supervisors to review that assessment and intervene where necessary. Pillar 2 is therefore not simply “extra Pillar 1”. It addresses risk coverage, governance, concentration, interest-rate risk and other vulnerabilities that may not be fully captured by the minimum formula, subject to the applicable local framework. **Pillar 3** promotes market discipline through regulatory disclosures. Basel describes it as complementing Pillars 1 and 2 by requiring information that allows market participants to assess regulatory capital, risk exposures and related prudential measures. The three pillars work together. A technically correct Pillar 1 ratio is not proof that the institution has adequate capital in every economic circumstance. Pillar 2 can identify additional needs. Pillar 3 makes material aspects of that risk and capital position observable to external stakeholders. The framework is thus formula, judgement and transparency rather than formula alone. +----------------------+ | Pillar 1 | | Minimum quantitative | | requirements | +----------------------+ | v +----------------------+ | Pillar 2 | | Internal assessment | | + supervisory review | +----------------------+ | v +----------------------+ | Pillar 3 | | Public disclosure | | + market discipline | +----------------------+ Pillar 1 is deliberately incomplete; Pillar 2 exists because material risk cannot be reduced to one universal minimum-capital formula. Calling every supervisory capital add-on “Pillar 1” loses the distinction between formulaic minimum requirements and institution-specific supervisory assessment. **Pillar 2** — internal capital assessment plus supervisory review of risks and capital adequacy. --- **Pillar 3** — disclosure and market discipline; it does not itself mean an additional capital charge. **No delta.** Terminology and legal implementation vary, but the Basel three-pillar architecture is the common conceptual structure.

title: The Four RWA Components
one_screen: Total RWA aggregates distinct prudential risk engines: credit risk, market risk, operational risk and credit valuation adjustment risk. They share the same capital denominator only after each component has been measured under its own rules.
bodyText: **Credit risk RWA** captures the risk that borrowers, counterparties or issuers fail to perform as required. It is usually the largest RWA category in a traditional banking book and can be calculated through standardised or, where permitted, internal-ratings-based methods. **Market risk RWA** addresses losses arising from movements in market risk factors for positions within the applicable trading-book and market-risk perimeter. Its measurement is not the same as simply risk-weighting a loan. **Operational risk RWA** addresses losses arising from inadequate or failed processes, people and systems or from external events under the applicable operational-risk framework. The Basel finalisation replaced prior multiple operational-risk approaches with a standardised approach in the global standard. **Credit valuation adjustment risk**, or CVA risk, concerns changes in the market value of counterparty-credit adjustments for covered derivatives and similar transactions. It is related to counterparty credit risk but is not identical to the default-loss capital charge: one concerns mark-to-market changes in credit valuation, the other the counterparty’s failure to perform. Basel contains a separate CVA capital framework. Basel’s minimum-capital calculation aggregates the prescribed RWA components to produce the denominator against which capital ratios are measured. The calculation should therefore be visualised as several risk engines feeding one capital ratio, not as one universal risk-weight formula. +------------------+ +------------------+ | Credit RWA | | Market RWA | +------------------+ +------------------+ \ / v v +------------------+ | Total RWA | +------------------+ ^ ^ / \ +------------------+ +------------------+ | Operational RWA | | CVA RWA | +------------------+ +------------------+ The four RWA components measure different risk types before being aggregated into the common risk-based capital denominator. Treating CVA risk as merely another name for counterparty default risk misses the mark-to-market credit-spread risk that the CVA framework is designed to capture. **Counterparty credit default risk** — risk of loss because the counterparty fails to perform. --- **CVA risk** — risk of loss from changes in the credit valuation adjustment before or without counterparty default. **No delta.** Detailed implementation dates and methods vary, but credit, market, operational and CVA risk are the core risk-based capital components in the Basel finalisation architecture.

title: The Standardised Approach to Credit Risk
one_screen: Under the standardised approach, the regulator prescribes the exposure classes, eligibility conditions and risk-weight rules instead of allowing the bank to generate the core credit-risk capital requirement from its own PD/LGD models. Revised Basel rules make this approach more granular and risk-sensitive while retaining external ratings only where the framework permits them.
bodyText: The first step is **exposure classification**. A banking-book exposure is assigned to the regulatory class that matches its counterparty and characteristics: for example sovereign, bank, corporate, retail or real-estate categories under the applicable framework. Classification matters because each class has its own rules. Next comes **risk-weight determination**. Depending on the exposure class and national implementation, the weight may depend on a permitted external credit assessment, loan-to-value measure, counterparty characteristics, repayment dependence or a prescribed fixed weight. Basel’s revised standardised approach does not simply map every loan to an external rating. Some classes use ratings, some use other risk drivers, and due-diligence requirements prevent blind mechanistic reliance where applicable. The **exposure amount** is then determined after relevant conversion and credit-risk-mitigation rules. Multiplying the adjusted exposure by its applicable weight produces credit RWA. The Basel finalisation strengthened the standardised approach partly because it also serves as the comparison basis for the output floor. A weak standardised approach would make that backstop ineffective. **Perishable — jurisdictional implementation dates below are current as at 27 August 2026. India’s revised standardised approach becomes effective on 1 April 2027; the UK Basel 3.1 rules become effective on 1 January 2027.** +----------------------+ | Banking-book exposure| +----------------------+ | v +----------------------+ | Exposure class | +----------------------+ | v +----------------------+ | Risk driver / rating | | where permitted | +----------------------+ | v +----------------------+ | CRM + exposure amount| +----------------------+ | v +----------------------+ | Risk weight | +----------------------+ | v +----------------------+ | Credit RWA | +----------------------+ Standardised does not mean uniform: the regulator standardises the methodology while allowing prescribed risk differentiation within it. Assuming every externally unrated exposure automatically receives the same risk weight ignores exposure-class-specific rules and non-rating risk drivers. **Standardised approach** — supervisor-prescribed methodology for exposure classification and risk weighting. --- **External credit rating** — one possible input to specified standardised risk weights; it is not the standardised approach itself. — RBI’s final 2026 Directions require the Standardised Approach for covered commercial-bank banking-book credit risk from **1 April 2027**; RWAs are exposure amount multiplied by prescribed standardised weights, using eligible ratings where the Directions specify. [RBI/DOR/2026-27/397, DOR.CRE.REC.5/21.06.201/2026-27] — PRA Basel 3.1 final rules revise the credit-risk standardised approach with effect from **1 January 2027**. [PRA PS1/26] — CRR3’s revised credit-risk framework has applied from **1 January 2025**, subject to CRR3 transitional provisions. [Regulation (EU) 2024/1623; European Commission banking-package Q&A] — The **19 March 2026** package proposes revisions to risk-based capital and standardised risk measurement; as at 27 August 2026 it remains a proposal, not a final rule. [Federal Reserve joint proposal; June 2026 Supervision and Regulation Report]

title: Foundation and Advanced IRB
one_screen: IRB allows approved banks to use internal estimates for specified credit-risk parameters, but the bank never owns the whole capital formula. Under Foundation IRB the supervisor supplies more of the loss parameters; under Advanced IRB the bank estimates more of them, subject to permission, constraints and validation.
bodyText: The **internal ratings-based approach**, or IRB, starts from borrower and facility risk estimates rather than a table of standardised risk weights. Basel then feeds those estimates into prescribed regulatory functions. The bank therefore models inputs; it does not freely choose the capital formula. For many corporate-type exposures under **Foundation IRB (F-IRB)**, an approved bank estimates probability of default while supervisory values govern specified other parameters such as loss given default and exposure at default, subject to the detailed Basel rules. Under **Advanced IRB (A-IRB)**, banks may estimate additional parameters where that approach remains permitted for the relevant exposure class. Permission is central. IRB is not an accounting method that a bank may elect simply because its internal models are sophisticated. Basel establishes minimum requirements covering rating systems, data, governance, validation and the use of internal ratings in risk management. Supervisors can restrict model scope, impose conditions or withdraw approval. Basel finalisation also narrows the areas in which advanced modelling may be used and applies input floors and an output floor. Those constraints address excessive variability and model risk. **Perishable — India’s domestic position changes under final Directions effective 1 April 2027; UK Basel 3.1 restrictions take effect 1 January 2027.** India must not be taught as an IRB domestic regime after that date. +----------------------+ | Credit exposure | +----------------------+ | v +----------------------+ | Internal rating | | system | +----------------------+ | +---+---+ | | v v +-----------+ +-----------+ | F-IRB | | A-IRB | | bank | | bank | | estimates | | estimates | | fewer | | more | | inputs | | inputs | +-----------+ +-----------+ \ / v v +----------------------+ | Basel risk function | +----------------------+ IRB means supervisory permission to estimate specified inputs inside a prescribed regulatory framework, not permission to set capital internally. Calling an internal credit scorecard an “IRB model” because it estimates PD ignores the regulatory approval, use-test, data and governance requirements. **F-IRB** — IRB variant in which the bank estimates fewer regulatory risk components and supervisors prescribe more inputs. --- **A-IRB** — IRB variant permitting bank estimates for more risk components where the framework allows and the supervisor approves them. — RBI has chosen the **Standardised Approach**, effective 1 April 2027, for covered commercial-bank banking-book credit risk; IRB should therefore be treated as international knowledge, not the Indian domestic credit-capital regime. [RBI 2026 SA Directions] — Basel 3.1 retains IRB subject to PRA permission and revised modelling-scope restrictions from 1 January 2027. [PRA PS1/26] — CRR3 continues a permission-based IRB framework with Basel-finalisation restrictions and the output floor. [Regulation (EU) 2024/1623 / CRR3] — The March 2026 package proposes a materially revised capital architecture for the largest banks; because it remains proposed, its final treatment of internally modelled credit-risk capital must not be presented as settled law. [Federal Reserve, 19 March 2026]

title: The IRB Risk-Weight Function
one_screen: The IRB function turns PD, LGD, EAD and maturity into a capital measure while applying a supervisory correlation structure. Higher default likelihood, larger loss severity, larger exposure or longer effective maturity generally increase capital, but the function is nonlinear because it is designed around adverse portfolio loss rather than a simple PD × LGD calculation.
bodyText: **PD**, probability of default, measures the likelihood that the obligor defaults over the prescribed horizon. **LGD**, loss given default, measures the proportion of exposure lost if default occurs, after appropriate recoveries and costs under the regulatory definition. **EAD**, exposure at default, measures the amount expected to be outstanding if default occurs. **Maturity**, where applicable, adjusts for the period over which credit deterioration can affect the exposure. Basel specifies these as core IRB risk components. The function also includes a **correlation** assumption. Intuitively, two borrowers whose fortunes move closely with the same systematic economic factor create more common-tail risk than two independent borrowers. Basel does not ask each bank to choose this portfolio correlation freely; the supervisory function embeds prescribed relationships. The formula is intentionally not just expected loss. PD × LGD × EAD is a useful expected-loss intuition under simplified assumptions. IRB capital targets the unexpected-loss portion of the distribution at a high adverse confidence level, with maturity and systematic dependence affecting the tail. That is why a small change in PD need not produce the same percentage change in capital at every starting PD. The regulatory mapping is nonlinear. **Perishable — India’s final Standardised Approach becomes effective on 1 April 2027. The formula described here is therefore not the Indian domestic banking-book credit-capital method.** +------+ +------+ +------+ +----------+ | PD | | LGD | | EAD | | Maturity | +------+ +------+ +------+ +----------+ \ | / / \ | / / v v v v +----------------------+ | Supervisory | | correlation + formula| +----------------------+ | v +----------------------+ | Capital requirement | | / credit RWA | +----------------------+ IRB capital is a supervisory portfolio-tail calculation using modelled inputs; it is not the arithmetic product of PD, LGD and EAD. Using expected loss as a proxy for IRB capital misses correlation, maturity and the unexpected-loss calibration embedded in the risk-weight function. **Expected loss** — a central loss estimate often simplified as PD × LGD × EAD. --- **IRB capital requirement** — the regulatory unexpected-loss result generated by the prescribed function and applicable adjustments. — From 1 April 2027, covered commercial banks use RBI’s Standardised Approach rather than the Basel IRB function for domestic banking-book credit RWA. [RBI 2026 SA Directions] — The IRB function remains relevant to exposures permitted under the PRA Basel 3.1 IRB framework from 1 January 2027. [PRA PS1/26] — IRB remains within CRR3 subject to model restrictions, parameter constraints and the output floor. [CRR3] — The March 2026 capital package remains proposed; no proposed feature should be treated as a final domestic IRB rule. [Federal Reserve, 19 March 2026]

title: IRB Input Floors and Parameter Constraints
one_screen: Input floors stop internally estimated risk parameters from falling below prudential lower bounds even when a model produces a smaller number. They constrain the ingredients of the IRB calculation; the output floor constrains the final aggregate RWA result.
bodyText: Internal models can generate extremely low PDs, LGDs or other parameters for portfolios with benign observed histories. That may reflect genuinely low risk, but it may also reflect limited defaults, favourable economic periods, data scarcity or model specification. Basel therefore imposes **parameter constraints**, including prescribed floors for relevant IRB inputs. An input floor works before the risk-weight function. If the model estimates a parameter below the applicable regulatory floor, the floor is used for capital purposes. The model estimate may remain useful for internal risk management, but it is not allowed to drive regulatory capital below the prescribed prudential boundary. Parameter constraints also include rules on estimation horizon, downturn treatment, eligible exposure classes, maturity and the circumstances in which bank estimates may be used. Their collective purpose is to reduce excessive model variability and make capital less dependent on sparse or optimistic data. The **output floor** operates at a different level. Input floors constrain individual parameters; the output floor compares total internally modelled RWA with a percentage of standardised RWA after the model calculations have been performed. A bank can therefore satisfy every input floor and still be constrained by the output floor. **Perishable — India’s revised commercial-bank credit framework effective 1 April 2027 is standardised, so IRB input floors are not domestic Indian credit-capital parameters.** +----------------------+ | Internal estimate | | e.g. PD or LGD | +----------------------+ | v +----------------------+ | Compare with | | regulatory input floor| +----------------------+ | v +----------------------+ | Use permitted input | +----------------------+ | v +----------------------+ | IRB risk function | +----------------------+ | v +----------------------+ | Modelled RWA | +----------------------+ An input floor changes or bounds a model parameter before the risk-weight calculation; it does not directly impose a percentage floor on total RWA. Calling the 72.5% output floor a “PD floor” mixes an aggregate RWA backstop with parameter-level constraints. **Input floor** — a lower bound on an IRB risk parameter or model input. --- **Output floor** — an aggregate lower bound on model-based RWA relative to standardised RWA. — RBI’s covered commercial-bank framework from 1 April 2027 uses the Standardised Approach, so Basel IRB parameter floors are not the domestic method for those credit exposures. [RBI 2026 SA Directions] — PRA Basel 3.1 implements revised IRB constraints from 1 January 2027 for exposures remaining eligible for IRB. [PRA PS1/26] — CRR3 implements revised model constraints alongside the output floor from 2025, subject to transition. [CRR3] — The March 2026 package remains proposed; proposed model constraints are not final US rules. [Federal Reserve, 19 March 2026]

title: The Output Floor
one_screen: The output floor prevents approved internal models from reducing total RWA below 72.5% of the amount produced by the prescribed standardised comparison at full implementation. It is an aggregate backstop against model risk and excessive RWA variability, not a rule that replaces internal models with a 72.5% risk weight.
bodyText: The calculation requires two views of risk. First, the bank calculates RWA using the approaches it is authorised to use, including internal models where permitted. Second, it calculates a **standardised total** under the rules specified for the floor. The regulatory RWA relevant to the floor becomes the higher of the model-based amount and the applicable floor percentage of the standardised amount. Example: model-based total RWA is 60; standardised RWA is 100; fully phased floor is 72.5. The floor raises regulatory RWA from 60 to 72.5. If model-based RWA were 80, the floor would not bind. The purpose is not to declare models wrong. Basel preserves modelling incentives above the floor while limiting how far model outputs can diverge downward from a common standardised benchmark. The PRA describes the 72.5% multiplier as a backstop that maintains incentives to pursue model approval. **Perishable — phase-in is jurisdiction-specific.** In the EU the floor is 55% during 2026, rises to 60% in 2027, 65% in 2028, 70% in 2029 and 72.5% from 1 January 2030. The UK starts its Basel 3.1 implementation on 1 January 2027 and is scheduled to reach the fully phased level by January 2030. The US has not implemented the final Basel output floor as a binding rule as at 27 August 2026; the March 2026 package remains proposed. +----------------------+ +----------------------+ | Model-based RWA | | Standardised RWA | | 60 | | 100 | +----------------------+ +----------------------+ \ / v v +----------------------+ | 72.5% x 100 = 72.5 | +----------------------+ | v +----------------------+ | Higher of 60 / 72.5 | | = 72.5 | +----------------------+ The 72.5% figure applies to the standardised RWA benchmark at full phase-in; it is not a universal asset risk weight. Multiplying each individual IRB exposure by 72.5% misunderstands an aggregate RWA comparison as an exposure-level risk weight. **Output floor** — aggregate lower bound on model-based RWA relative to standardised RWA. --- **Risk weight** — exposure-level or formula-derived scaling factor used inside an RWA methodology. — RBI has selected the Standardised Approach for covered commercial-bank banking-book credit risk from 1 April 2027; an IRB-versus-standardised credit output-floor architecture is therefore not the domestic Indian credit regime. [RBI 2026 SA Directions] — Basel 3.1 takes effect 1 January 2027; the UK output floor begins then and is scheduled to reach full 72.5% calibration by January 2030. [PRA PS1/26; European Commission 2026 comparative implementation table] — CRR3 output floor is **55% in 2026**, then 60%, 65%, 70%, and **72.5% from 1 January 2030**. [CRR Article 465(1); European Commission SWD 2026] — The final Basel output floor is not a binding US rule as at 27 August 2026; the March 2026 capital package remains proposed. [Federal Reserve proposal; European Commission comparative implementation review]

title: Specialised Lending and Supervisory Slotting
one_screen: Slotting converts a specialised-lending exposure into a supervisory quality category and assigns the corresponding regulatory treatment rather than relying on an ordinary corporate PD/LGD model. It is designed for financing whose repayment depends materially on the performance of a specific asset, project or cash-flow structure.
bodyText: **Specialised lending** describes exposures where repayment is closely tied to the cash flows generated by a financed asset or undertaking and where the lender has substantial control or security over those assets under the regulatory definition. Such transactions can behave differently from ordinary diversified corporate lending. Under Basel’s **supervisory slotting approach**, the bank evaluates prescribed qualitative and quantitative characteristics and places an eligible exposure into a supervisory category. The assigned “slot” then determines the applicable risk weight and expected-loss treatment under the Basel framework. The intuition is classification before calibration. Rather than saying “the internal PD is x and LGD is y”, slotting asks whether the transaction’s financial strength, political and legal environment, transaction structure, collateral or other specified characteristics place it in a stronger or weaker supervisory bucket. Slotting is therefore not an external credit rating. The classification is produced through the prudential specialised-lending framework. Nor is it simply a standardised corporate risk weight; it sits within the Basel IRB architecture for specialised lending where the relevant conditions apply. **Perishable — India’s covered commercial-bank banking-book credit regime becomes the revised Standardised Approach on 1 April 2027, so Basel IRB slotting should not be presented as the Indian domestic capital method.** +----------------------+ | Specialised-lending | | exposure | +----------------------+ | v +----------------------+ | Assess prescribed | | supervisory factors | +----------------------+ | v +----------------------+ | Assign quality slot | +----------------------+ | v +----------------------+ | Supervisory risk | | weight / EL treatment| +----------------------+ Slotting maps the whole specialised-lending risk profile into a supervisory category; it is not merely another name for a borrower rating. Applying ordinary corporate PD/LGD logic automatically to every project-style exposure ignores the specialised-lending classification and approach rules. **Slotting category** — prudential category assigned to qualifying specialised lending from prescribed risk characteristics. --- **External rating** — assessment produced by an eligible external credit assessment institution and used only where the applicable rules permit. — RBI’s revised domestic banking-book credit rules use the Standardised Approach from 1 April 2027; Basel IRB supervisory slotting is not the Indian domestic IRB regime. [RBI 2026 SA Directions] — Slotting remains relevant where specialised-lending exposures fall within the PRA’s permitted IRB framework under Basel 3.1 from 1 January 2027. [PRA PS1/26; Basel CRE33] — CRR3 retains supervisory treatment for specialised-lending exposures within the EU’s permission-based modelling architecture, subject to the applicable CRR provisions. [CRR3; Basel CRE33] — The March 2026 proposal remains non-final; its final treatment of specialised lending must be verified against any eventual final US rule. [Federal Reserve, 19 March 2026]

title: Credit Risk Mitigation: Collateral, Guarantees and Netting
one_screen: Credit risk mitigation reduces regulatory exposure only when the protection is eligible, legally effective and recognised by the applicable capital rules. Collateral changes the loss available from pledged assets, guarantees transfer specified credit risk to a protection provider, and netting reduces exposure by recognising enforceable offsetting claims.
bodyText: **Collateral** gives the bank recourse to specified assets if the borrower fails. Prudential recognition depends on the collateral type, valuation, legal enforceability, maturity, currency and method used. Economic security that cannot be recognised under the capital framework may reduce internal risk without reducing regulatory RWA. A **guarantee** is unfunded credit protection: another party undertakes to pay if the protected obligor fails under the guarantee’s terms. Under Basel’s standardised CRM framework, eligible guarantees can alter the relevant risk treatment where operational and legal requirements are satisfied. **Netting** recognises that two legally enforceable offsetting claims need not create the same exposure as their gross amounts. For example, where the capital rules recognise an enforceable on-balance-sheet netting arrangement, the exposure can be measured on the prescribed net basis rather than simply summing gross claims. Netting recognition is conditional; informal commercial expectations that parties will “settle net” are not enough. The sequence matters. Start with the regulatory exposure, identify an eligible CRM technique, verify documentation and enforceability, apply the prescribed valuation or substitution treatment, then determine the protected exposure used for RWA. A practitioner should never reduce exposure merely because collateral exists operationally. Basel CRE22 codifies the standardised approach’s permitted CRM techniques and conditions, including collateral, guarantees and applicable haircut methodologies. +----------------------+ | Gross exposure | +----------------------+ | v +----------------------+ | Eligible CRM? | +----------------------+ | yes v +----------------------+ | Collateral / | | guarantee / netting | +----------------------+ | v +----------------------+ | Legal + operational | | requirements met? | +----------------------+ | v +----------------------+ | Adjusted exposure / | | risk treatment | +----------------------+ Risk mitigation reduces regulatory capital only to the extent the prudential framework recognises the protection. Subtracting the market value of every pledged asset from EAD ignores eligibility, haircuts, maturity mismatch, currency mismatch and legal-enforceability requirements. **Collateral** — funded protection provided through an asset or right available against the exposure. --- **Guarantee** — unfunded protection in which an eligible protection provider assumes specified credit risk. **No delta.** Eligibility lists and calculations differ locally, but collateral, guarantees and enforceable netting are distinct CRM mechanisms across Basel-style frameworks.

title: Substitution and Comprehensive CRM Approaches
one_screen: Substitution changes whose credit quality drives the protected portion of an exposure; the comprehensive collateral approach changes the exposure value after recognising collateral and prescribed valuation adjustments. One changes the relevant risk weight, the other changes the amount to which risk weighting is applied.
bodyText: Consider an eligible guarantee. If the rules permit **substitution**, the protected portion of the borrower exposure receives the prudential treatment associated with the eligible protection provider, subject to the framework’s conditions. The borrower is still the original obligor economically, but the capital calculation recognises that another eligible party bears the specified default risk. The **comprehensive approach** to eligible financial collateral works differently. Rather than merely replacing one counterparty risk weight with another, it adjusts the exposure and collateral values using regulatory haircuts and other prescribed adjustments. The resulting net exposure amount is then risk weighted. Basel’s CRM chapter sets out the recognised approaches and the requirements governing financial collateral and guarantees. A simple conceptual example makes the distinction clear. An exposure of 100 protected by an eligible sovereign guarantee on 60 may apply the guarantor’s treatment to the protected 60 and the borrower’s treatment to the residual 40 under a substitution structure.
