By contrast, eligible financial collateral worth 60 does not necessarily reduce exposure by exactly 60 under the comprehensive approach: haircuts can reduce the recognised collateral value or increase the effective exposure before netting. The methods therefore cannot be mixed casually. A guarantee is not “collateral with a zero haircut”, and collateral is not automatically a substitute counterparty. Each CRM instrument follows the method prescribed for its legal and risk characteristics. +----------------------+ | Protected exposure | +----------------------+ | | v v +-----------+ +-----------+ | Guarantee | | Financial | | | | collateral| +-----------+ +-----------+ | | v v +-----------+ +-----------+ | Substitute| | Adjust | | eligible | | E and C | | risk | | by haircuts| | treatment | | | +-----------+ +-----------+ | | v v +----------------------+ | Post-CRM credit RWA | +----------------------+ Substitution operates on the credit-risk treatment of the protected portion; comprehensive collateral recognition operates through adjusted exposure and collateral values. Applying a guarantor’s risk weight to collateral because both are “security” uses the wrong CRM mechanism. **Substitution approach** — replaces the original obligor’s risk treatment with that of an eligible protection provider for the protected amount. --- **Comprehensive collateral approach** — adjusts exposure and eligible collateral values, including prescribed haircuts, before calculating the residual exposure. **No delta.** Detailed eligibility differs, but the conceptual distinction between unfunded-protection substitution and collateral-value adjustment is common to Basel-style CRM.

title: Haircuts
one_screen: A haircut is a prudential valuation adjustment that recognises that exposure and collateral values can move before a position is closed or collateral is realised. It deliberately prevents yesterday’s collateral market value from being treated as perfectly certain protection against tomorrow’s exposure.
bodyText: Suppose eligible financial collateral has a current market value of 100. If the applicable supervisory haircut is 10%, only 90 is recognised for the relevant calculation before other adjustments. The 10 is not a forecasted loss on the collateral; it is a prudential allowance for value volatility over the regulatory holding period. Haircuts may apply on both sides of the calculation. An exposure in a security can be adjusted upward for potential price movement, while collateral can be adjusted downward. A further adjustment may apply when the exposure and collateral are denominated in different currencies because exchange-rate movements can reduce the effective protection. The **holding period** matters because collateral cannot always be liquidated instantaneously after default or margin failure. The longer the period during which values can move, the greater the potential mismatch. Basel therefore links supervisory haircut structures to transaction characteristics and prescribed holding periods. Haircuts are distinct from credit risk weights. The haircut adjusts the value recognised for CRM; the risk weight subsequently calibrates the credit risk of the remaining exposure. A highly rated security can therefore have both a low risk weight when held as an exposure and a non-zero haircut when serving as collateral. The same word “haircut” also appears in market practice for financing discounts, but a contractual repo haircut and a regulatory supervisory haircut need not be numerically identical. +----------------------+ | Collateral MV = 100 | +----------------------+ | v +----------------------+ | Supervisory haircut | | = 10% | +----------------------+ | v +----------------------+ | Recognised value = 90| +----------------------+ | v +----------------------+ | Offset against | | adjusted exposure | +----------------------+ | v +----------------------+ | Residual exposure | +----------------------+ A regulatory haircut adjusts recognised value for potential change during the relevant risk period; it is not the collateral’s credit risk weight. Subtracting the full current market value of volatile collateral assumes perfect liquidation at today’s price and defeats the purpose of the comprehensive approach. **Haircut** — valuation adjustment to an exposure or collateral amount for volatility and related risks. --- **Risk weight** — prudential factor applied to a resulting exposure to determine RWA. **No delta.** Supervisory haircut tables and eligible collateral differ by rulebook, but the valuation-adjustment principle does not.

title: Pillar 1 and Pillar 2
one_screen: Pillar 1 standardises minimum capital for risks that can be captured through common formulas; Pillar 2 asks whether those formulas leave material institution-specific risk uncovered. Pillar 2 is therefore the deliberate completeness check on Pillar 1.
bodyText: A common capital framework requires standardisation. Credit RWA, market risk, operational risk and CVA can be measured through prescribed approaches that allow comparison across institutions. That is the strength of **Pillar 1**. Its weakness is equally important: no finite rulebook can anticipate every concentration, business-model vulnerability, governance weakness or emerging risk. Two banks with the same Pillar 1 ratio can have very different sensitivity to interest rates, concentration, pension risk, strategic risk or deficiencies in risk controls. **Pillar 2** addresses that gap through the supervisory review process. Basel requires banks to maintain a process for assessing overall capital adequacy in relation to risk profile and strategy, and supervisors must review that process, evaluate capital adequacy and take action where necessary. Pillar 2 can therefore affect capital even when a Pillar 1 calculation is perfectly correct. That does not mean Pillar 1 was “wrong”; it means its standardised scope was not intended to be exhaustive. The distinction also prevents double counting. A supervisor assessing Pillar 2 should understand which risks are already captured by Pillar 1 before adding capital for residual risk. Conversely, management should not exclude a material risk from internal capital assessment merely because no dedicated Pillar 1 formula exists. The conceptual sequence is formula first, residual-risk analysis second, supervisory judgement third. +----------------------+ | Pillar 1 calculation | +----------------------+ | v +----------------------+ | Identify material | | risks and limitations| +----------------------+ | v +----------------------+ | What is not fully | | captured? | +----------------------+ | v +----------------------+ | Pillar 2 assessment | +----------------------+ | v +----------------------+ | Supervisory response | +----------------------+ Pillar 2 begins where standardised minimum requirements stop being a complete description of the bank’s material risk. Adding capital under Pillar 2 without identifying what Pillar 1 already captures can create hidden double counting. **Pillar 1 requirement** — capital generated by prescribed minimum-risk methodologies. --- **Pillar 2 requirement or supervisory assessment** — capital and supervisory response arising from risks or weaknesses not adequately captured by Pillar 1, according to the local framework. **No delta.** Legal labels and calibration differ, but the conceptual function of Pillar 2 as a complement to Pillar 1 is common.

title: ICAAP and the Supervisory Review Process
one_screen: ICAAP is the bank’s own disciplined assessment of how much capital it needs for its actual risk profile and strategy; supervisory review tests whether that assessment is credible. It is not a worksheet for reproducing regulatory minima.
bodyText: The **Internal Capital Adequacy Assessment Process**, or ICAAP, begins with the bank’s risk inventory. Management identifies material risks arising from the balance sheet, business model, concentrations, operations and forward strategy. The bank then assesses how those risks could create losses or capital depletion and determines the capital resources needed to remain adequately capitalised. The process is broader than a point-in-time calculation. Basel expects capital assessment to be connected to risk management, governance and strategy. Supervisors review whether the bank has a sound process for assessing overall capital adequacy relative to its risk profile and whether the resulting capital position is sufficient. Stress testing is a central input. A base-case capital plan may show ample headroom, yet an adverse scenario can reveal that losses, lower earnings and rising RWA consume that headroom quickly. Basel’s supervisory-risk-management framework therefore links stress testing with internal capital assessment. The **supervisory review process** then challenges assumptions, risk coverage, governance, models, management actions and capital conclusions. A supervisor need not accept the amount management considers adequate. It may require remedial action, stronger controls or additional capital under the applicable domestic framework. ICAAP is therefore an argument supported by evidence: these are the risks, this is how severe they can become, these are available loss absorbers, this is the resulting capital need, and these are the actions available if conditions deteriorate. +----------------------+ | Identify material | | risks | +----------------------+ | v +----------------------+ | Measure / assess | | risk severity | +----------------------+ | v +----------------------+ | Stress capital plan | +----------------------+ | v +----------------------+ | Determine internal | | capital adequacy | +----------------------+ | v +----------------------+ | Supervisory review | | and challenge | +----------------------+ ICAAP must start from the institution’s actual material risks, not from the desire to reverse-engineer a predetermined capital number. Copying Pillar 1 capital into an ICAAP and adding a generic percentage defeats the process because it never identifies which residual risks require capital. **ICAAP** — management’s internal assessment and governance process for capital adequacy. --- **Supervisory review** — the authority’s independent evaluation of that assessment and the bank’s resulting prudential position. **No delta.** “ICAAP” and the formal supervisory process are implemented differently in national law, but the Basel sequence of internal assessment followed by supervisory review is common.

title: Stress Testing and Capital Transmission
one_screen: A capital stress test is a causal chain: define an adverse scenario, translate it into risk drivers and financial losses, project earnings and RWA, then recalculate capital resources and ratios. Reverse stress testing runs the chain backwards from failure to identify combinations of events capable of breaking the business model.
bodyText: **Scenario design** defines the macroeconomic or idiosyncratic shock. Variables may include economic contraction, unemployment, asset prices, interest rates, exchange rates, funding conditions or sector-specific stresses. The scenario should be severe enough to reveal vulnerabilities without being mistaken for a forecast. Basel describes stress testing as a critical element of bank risk management and a core supervisory tool. The scenario must then be **transmitted** into the bank. Credit quality deteriorates, defaults increase, collateral values change, market positions revalue, operating losses may rise and funding or revenue can weaken. Those effects flow into profit and loss and the balance sheet. Capital is affected through both numerator and denominator. Losses reduce retained earnings and therefore CET1. At the same time, rating migration, defaults or market volatility can increase RWA. A bank can therefore suffer a larger decline in its capital ratio than would be inferred from losses alone. Credible management actions may then be considered under the governing framework, but actions must be feasible under the stressed environment. Assuming instant capital issuance, perfect hedging or unlimited balance-sheet reduction can make a stress test mechanically pass while providing little information. **Reverse stress testing** begins with a defined point of non-viability or business-model failure and asks what events could cause it. Its objective is vulnerability discovery, not prediction. +----------------------+ | Adverse scenario | +----------------------+ | v +----------------------+ | Risk-factor changes | +----------------------+ | v +----------------------+ | Losses + lower income| | + RWA movement | +----------------------+ | v +----------------------+ | Capital numerator | | and denominator | +----------------------+ | v +----------------------+ | Stressed ratios | +----------------------+ Reverse: +----------------------+ | Failure condition | +----------------------+ | v +----------------------+ | What combination of | | shocks could cause it| +----------------------+ A capital stress test must transmit scenario variables through losses, earnings, balance-sheet behaviour and RWA before drawing a capital conclusion. Applying a single percentage loss directly to CET1 while leaving RWA and income unchanged can miss the most important transmission channels. **Scenario stress test** — starts with adverse events and projects their consequences. --- **Reverse stress test** — starts with a failure condition and identifies events capable of producing it. **No delta.** Scenario variables and regulatory exercises differ, but forward and reverse stress-testing logic is universal.

title: Supervisory and Internal Stress Tests
one_screen: Internal stress tests are management tools tailored to the bank’s own vulnerabilities; supervisory stress tests are authority-led or authority-specified exercises designed to assess prudential resilience and comparability. The same scenario can serve both purposes, but ownership, objectives and consequences are different.
bodyText: An **internal stress test** is designed and governed by the bank. It should reflect the institution’s particular concentrations, products, funding structure and strategic risks. Its value lies in decision-making: capital planning, risk limits, contingency actions and identification of vulnerabilities that broad industry scenarios may miss. A **supervisory stress test** is conducted or specified by a prudential authority. Basel distinguishes banks’ own internal stress testing, bank-run supervisory tests and supervisor-run tests. Common scenarios or methodologies can improve comparability across institutions and allow supervisors to evaluate system-wide vulnerabilities. The distinction is not simply “private versus published”. A bank may execute calculations itself using a supervisory scenario, while the authority determines methodology or evaluates results. Conversely, an internal exercise can use public macroeconomic variables but remain a management-owned stress test. Consequences can also differ. An internal test may lead management to change limits or capital targets. A supervisory exercise may inform formal capital requirements, buffers, supervisory expectations or remediation depending on the jurisdiction. The United States provides a clear example: the Federal Reserve’s supervisory stress test feeds the stress capital buffer architecture for large banks. In February 2026 the Board maintained then-current stress capital buffer requirements until 2027 while model feedback is considered. That is a jurisdiction-specific capital consequence, not a universal feature of all internal tests. +----------------------+ | Stress testing | +----------------------+ | | v v +-----------+ +-----------+ | Internal | | Supervisory| | bank-owned| | authority- | | | | led/set | +-----------+ +-----------+ | | v v +-----------+ +-----------+ | Decisions | | Prudential | | + limits | | assessment | +-----------+ +-----------+ A bank cannot outsource understanding of its vulnerabilities to the supervisory stress test; internal stress testing must remain tailored to its own risk profile. Treating the supervisory scenario as the bank’s only severe scenario can leave material institution-specific concentrations unstressed. **Internal stress test** — management-owned assessment designed for the institution’s risks and decisions. --- **Supervisory stress test** — authority-run or authority-specified assessment used for prudential oversight and, in some regimes, capital calibration. **No delta.** Supervisory consequences differ, but Basel expressly recognises internal, bank-run supervisory and supervisor-run stress tests as distinct uses of the same stress-testing discipline.

title: Basel Does Not Bind Banks Directly
one_screen: Basel is an international prudential standard, not a supranational banking statute. The Basel Committee expressly has no formal supranational authority and its decisions have no legal force; binding obligations arise only when competent jurisdictions implement the standards through their own law and supervisory rulebooks.
bodyText: The Basel Committee on Banking Supervision develops common standards to strengthen banking regulation and promote comparability. Its membership includes central banks and supervisory authorities, but the Committee is not a legislature with direct jurisdiction over banks. Its Charter is explicit: the BCBS “does not possess any formal supranational authority” and its decisions “do not have legal force”. Implementation relies on members’ commitments and domestic action. That creates three levels a practitioner must keep separate. First is the **Basel text**: the international benchmark. Second is **jurisdictional implementation**: legislation, regulations, directions or supervisory rules that transpose, modify, defer or supplement Basel. Third is the **firm-specific requirement**: the actual rule, permission, buffer or supervisory decision applicable to a particular institution. Those layers explain why implementation dates diverge. The EU began applying major CRR3 elements from 1 January 2025; the UK’s Basel 3.1 final rules begin 1 January 2027; India’s revised standardised credit-risk Directions begin 1 April 2027; and the United States’ March 2026 package remains proposed as at 27 August 2026. A sentence such as “Basel requires this bank to hold 8%” is therefore legally incomplete. Basel sets a global standard; the applicable jurisdictional rule determines the bank’s binding requirement and may be higher or structurally different. +----------------------+ | Basel standard | | international text | +----------------------+ | v +----------------------+ | National / regional | | implementation | +----------------------+ | v +----------------------+ | Supervisory rules, | | permissions, buffers | +----------------------+ | v +----------------------+ | Binding requirement | | on the bank | +----------------------+ For a bank, the binding rule is the applicable domestic or regional legal framework, not the Basel publication standing alone. Quoting a Basel minimum as though it automatically overrides a higher local minimum can understate the bank’s actual regulatory requirement. **Basel standard** — internationally agreed prudential benchmark issued by the BCBS. --- **Binding capital rule** — requirement made legally effective by the competent national or regional authority. **No delta.** Basel’s non-binding supranational legal status is stated in the BCBS Charter itself.

title: UK Basel 3.1 and the SDDT Regime
one_screen: **Perishable — final rules, pending commencement.** The PRA’s Basel 3.1 package takes effect on **1 January 2027**; the FRTB Internal Models Approach is delayed separately to **1 January 2028**. Small Domestic Deposit Takers enter the PRA’s simplified capital regime on **1 January 2027**, creating a deliberately different domestic framework for eligible smaller firms.
bodyText: PRA Policy Statement PS1/26, published on 20 January 2026, contains the final Basel 3.1 rules. The main implementation date is 1 January 2027. The package revises credit risk, output-floor and other Basel 3.1 elements and updates the scope and operation of internal-model permissions. Market risk has a separate timing wrinkle. The PRA delayed the **FRTB Internal Models Approach** to 1 January 2028. During the interim beginning 1 January 2027, existing IMA permissions may continue for positions within their existing scope, while positions outside those permissions move to the new standardised market-risk approaches under the PRA’s final framework. This is a delay to FRTB-IMA, not a delay of the entire Basel 3.1 package. The UK also operates the **Strong and Simple Framework** for qualifying Small Domestic Deposit Takers. PS4/26 confirms that the SDDT capital regime takes effect on 1 January 2027, although specified changes concerning ICAAP, reverse-stress-testing and ILAAP update frequency took effect when the policy was published on 20 January 2026. The simplified regime is designed to reduce prudential complexity for eligible smaller domestic firms rather than forcing the full large-bank framework onto them. The practical UK question is therefore always scope first: ordinary Basel 3.1 firm, SDDT, or another relevant category. +-------------------------+ | UK prudential firm | +-------------------------+ | v +-------------------------+ | Determine PRA scope | +-------------------------+ | | v v +-----------+ +-----------+ | Ordinary | | Eligible | | Basel 3.1 | | SDDT | | regime | | regime | +-----------+ +-----------+ | | v v | 1 Jan 2027 | | 1 Jan 2027 | | v +-------------------------+ | FRTB-IMA separately | | from 1 Jan 2028 | +-------------------------+ UK implementation dates must be read by component: 1 January 2027 is the main Basel 3.1 date, while FRTB-IMA starts on 1 January 2028. Saying “UK Basel 3.1 was delayed to 2028” incorrectly converts the FRTB-IMA delay into a delay of the whole package. **Basel 3.1 commencement** — main PRA final-rule commencement on 1 January 2027. --- **FRTB-IMA commencement** — separate UK implementation date of 1 January 2028 for the new market-risk internal-model approach. — Final PRA Basel 3.1 rules: 1 January 2027; FRTB-IMA: 1 January 2028; SDDT simplified capital regime: 1 January 2027, with specified ICAAP/reverse-stress/ILAAP frequency changes effective 20 January 2026. [PRA PS1/26; PRA PS4/26]

title: EU CRR3 Implementation
one_screen: **Perishable — partially implemented with a pending market-risk date.** CRR3 has applied major Basel-finalisation reforms since **1 January 2025**; the output floor is **55% during 2026** and reaches **72.5% on 1 January 2030**. Binding FRTB market-risk own-funds requirements have been postponed to **1 January 2027**, while specified FRTB calculations continue to matter for the output floor.
bodyText: Regulation (EU) 2024/1623, commonly called **CRR3**, implements major elements of the final Basel III reforms in the EU capital framework. The main package began applying on 1 January 2025, including revised treatment across credit, operational and CVA risk and the introduction of the output-floor architecture. The output floor is intentionally phased. Article 465(1) CRR establishes a transition of 50% in 2025, **55% in 2026**, 60% in 2027, 65% in 2028, 70% in 2029 and **72.5% from 1 January 2030**. This means “EU output floor = 72.5%” is correct only as the fully phased destination, not the current 2026 calibration. Market risk follows a different timeline. The Commission initially postponed binding FRTB own-funds requirements by one year and subsequently adopted a further postponement to **1 January 2027**. During postponement, pre-FRTB methodologies continue for the binding market-risk own-funds requirement, while the FRTB Standardised Approach remains relevant to the market-risk component of the output-floor calculation. That distinction prevents a common implementation error: “FRTB postponed” does not mean every FRTB-derived calculation disappears from the EU prudential framework during the postponement. +-------------------------+ | CRR3 main application | | 1 Jan 2025 | +-------------------------+ | v +-------------------------+ | Output floor transition | +-------------------------+ | 2025 50% | | 2026 55% | | 2027 60% | | 2028 65% | | 2029 70% | | 2030 72.5% | +-------------------------+ | v +-------------------------+ | Binding FRTB market | | risk: 1 Jan 2027 | +-------------------------+ A postponed FRTB own-funds commencement does not repeal CRR3 or suspend the output floor. Applying 72.5% as the EU output-floor multiplier in 2026 overstates the current transitional floor, which is 55%. **CRR3 application date** — the main package began applying on 1 January 2025. --- **FRTB binding market-risk date** — separately postponed to 1 January 2027. — CRR3 applies from 1 January 2025; output floor 55% in 2026, fully phased to 72.5% on 1 January 2030; binding FRTB market-risk requirements postponed to 1 January 2027. [Regulation (EU) 2024/1623; CRR Article 465(1); Commission/EBA FRTB measures]

title: India’s Commercial-Bank Capital Framework
one_screen: **Perishable — a final revised credit-risk framework is pending commencement.** Indian commercial banks have higher domestic Basel-style minimums of **5.5% CET1, 7% Tier 1 and 9% total capital**; leverage minima are **4% for D-SIBs and 3.5% for other banks**. RBI’s final revised **Standardised Approach** for banking-book credit risk becomes effective on **1 April 2027**.
bodyText: RBI’s 2025 Commercial Banks – Prudential Norms on Capital Adequacy Directions prescribe an ongoing minimum CET1 ratio of 5.5% of RWA, minimum Tier 1 of 7% and minimum total capital of 9%, plus a 2.5% CET1 capital conservation buffer and other applicable requirements. These are domestic binding minima; Basel’s 4.5%, 6% and 8% global minima must not be substituted for them. The leverage-ratio rule is also explicitly higher than the Basel 3% baseline: RBI prescribes **4% for a Domestic Systemically Important Bank and 3.5% for other banks**. For banking-book credit risk, RBI issued final *Commercial Banks – Capital Charge for Credit Risk – Standardised Approach Directions, 2026* on 27 April 2026, effective **1 April 2027**. The Directions state that banking-book exposures are risk weighted using prescribed categories or eligible external ratings as applicable, and that RWA is the product of the standardised risk weight and exposure amount. **IRB must not be taught as the Indian domestic commercial-bank credit-capital regime.** Accounting is a separate issue. RBI’s 22 March 2019 circular deferred Ind AS implementation for scheduled commercial banks until further notice. Indian scheduled commercial banks therefore must **not** be described as being on Ind AS 109 merely because expected-loss concepts arise in banking regulation. Relevant NBFCs required to implement Ind AS are subject to RBI guidance interacting with Ind AS 109, which is a different institutional perimeter. +-------------------------+ | Indian commercial bank | +-------------------------+ | v +-------------------------+ | Capital minima | | CET1 5.5% | | Tier 1 7% | | Total 9% | +-------------------------+ | v +-------------------------+ | Leverage ratio | | D-SIB 4% / other 3.5% | +-------------------------+ | v +-------------------------+ | Credit-risk SA | | effective 1 Apr 2027 | +-------------------------+ | v +-------------------------+ | NOT bank Ind AS 109 | | implementation | +-------------------------+ For an Indian commercial bank, start with RBI’s domestic directions: Basel minima, IRB teaching or Ind AS 109 cannot be substituted for the applicable RBI banking rules. Writing “India = Ind AS 109 + IRB” commits two distinct errors: scheduled commercial banks have not implemented Ind AS under the deferred timetable, and RBI’s final 2027 credit-capital framework selects the Standardised Approach. **RBI Standardised Approach** — domestic commercial-bank credit-capital methodology effective 1 April 2027. --- **Ind AS 109** — financial-instrument accounting standard relevant to entities within its accounting scope; RBI deferred Ind AS implementation for scheduled commercial banks until further notice. — CET1 minimum 5.5%, Tier 1 minimum 7%, total capital minimum 9%; leverage ratio 4% for D-SIBs and 3.5% otherwise; revised banking-book Standardised Approach effective 1 April 2027. Scheduled commercial banks are not to be treated as having implemented Ind AS 109 under RBI’s deferred bank timetable. [RBI Capital Adequacy Directions 2025; RBI/DOR/2026-27/397; DBR.BP.BC.No.29/21.07.001/2018-19]

title: The US March 2026 Capital Reproposal and Stress Capital Buffer
one_screen: **Perishable — proposal, not rule.** On **19 March 2026** the US federal banking agencies issued a new capital package, including a proposal for the largest and most internationally active organisations, a broader standardised-capital proposal and a Federal Reserve GSIB-surcharge proposal. As at 27 August 2026, the package must be treated as **proposed**, while the existing stress capital buffer architecture remains the operative large-bank stress-capital mechanism.
bodyText: The first March proposal is aimed primarily at the largest, internationally active banking organisations. The agencies describe it as completing US implementation of final Basel III components while improving risk sensitivity and replacing the existing dual-stack calculation for covered firms with a single risk-based capital calculation if adopted. The second proposal generally applies more broadly and revises the standardised capital treatment of traditional lending and other exposures. The third, issued by the Federal Reserve, revises the method for measuring systemic risk for the GSIB surcharge. Comments on the proposals were due by 18 June 2026. **A proposal does not change the binding capital rule merely because its intended implementation is described in detail.** The US architecture must also be separated from the European combined-buffer/MDA model. Since 2020 the Federal Reserve has integrated supervisory stress testing with non-stress capital requirements through the **stress capital buffer**. The buffer is forward-looking and firm-specific because supervisory stress results affect the applicable capital requirement for covered large banks. For the 2026 cycle, the Federal Reserve decided to maintain then-current stress capital buffer requirements until 2027 while it considers public feedback on supervisory stress-test models. Thus “US Basel finalisation proposal” and “current US SCB requirement” are separate objects. +-------------------------+ | Binding US capital | | framework | +-------------------------+ | +------------------+ | | v v +------------------+ +----------------------+ | Existing SCB | | 19 Mar 2026 | | architecture | | capital proposals | +------------------+ +----------------------+ | | v v +------------------+ +----------------------+ | Current prudential| | NOT binding unless | | requirement | | finalised | +------------------+ +----------------------+ A US notice of proposed rulemaking remains non-binding until the agencies complete the legally required rulemaking process and issue a final rule with an effective date. Teaching the March 2026 reproposal as “the US Basel rule” converts an unsettled proposal into law and can produce the wrong capital calculation. **March 2026 capital reproposal** — proposed revisions to the US regulatory capital framework. --- **Stress capital buffer** — existing Federal Reserve large-bank capital mechanism tied to supervisory stress testing. — The 19 March 2026 package remains a proposal as at 27 August 2026; current SCB requirements were maintained until 2027 while stress-test-model feedback is considered. [Federal Reserve 19 March 2026 joint release; Federal Reserve 4 February 2026 stress-test release]

title: Cross-Jurisdiction Basel Implementation Map
one_screen: **Perishable — status as at 27 August 2026.** Basel supplies the common vocabulary, but the live rule differs sharply by jurisdiction: EU CRR3 is already in application, UK Basel 3.1 starts 1 January 2027, India’s revised credit-risk Standardised Approach starts 1 April 2027, and the US March 2026 capital package remains proposed.
bodyText: The safest implementation workflow is **jurisdiction → legal status → effective date → institutional scope → methodology**. Starting with a Basel formula and asking later whether it applies reverses the legal hierarchy. In the **UK**, the PRA has issued final rules. The principal Basel 3.1 commencement is 1 January 2027; FRTB-IMA starts separately on 1 January 2028. Eligible Small Domestic Deposit Takers enter their simplified capital regime on 1 January 2027. In the **EU**, CRR3 has already applied major finalisation measures since 1 January 2025. During 2026 the output floor is 55%, rising in annual stages to 72.5% from 1 January 2030. Binding FRTB market-risk own-funds requirements are postponed to 1 January 2027. In **India**, current domestic commercial-bank minima are CET1 5.5%, Tier 1 7% and total capital 9%; the leverage minimum is 4% for D-SIBs and 3.5% for other banks. RBI’s final revised banking-book credit-risk framework uses the Standardised Approach from 1 April 2027. Scheduled commercial banks must not be labelled Ind AS 109 banks: RBI deferred their Ind AS implementation until further notice. In the **US**, the March 2026 capital package is still a proposal, not the binding final Basel-endgame rule. The existing large-bank architecture continues to include the Federal Reserve stress capital buffer. +----------------------+ | Start: jurisdiction | +----------------------+ | v +----------------------+ | UK | | Final | | Basel 3.1: 1 Jan 27 | | FRTB-IMA: 1 Jan 28 | +----------------------+ +----------------------+ | EU | | CRR3 already applies | | Floor 55% in 2026 | | 72.5%: 1 Jan 2030 | +----------------------+ +----------------------+ | India | | Final revised SA | | effective 1 Apr 2027 | | CET1/T1/Total | | 5.5% / 7% / 9% | +----------------------+ +----------------------+ | US | | Mar 2026 package | | PROPOSAL, not rule | +----------------------+ Never infer a bank’s binding capital treatment from Basel alone: identify the jurisdiction, current legal status, commencement date, scope and any transitional treatment first. Putting UK, EU, India and US into a single “Basel 3.1 effective” column erases the most operationally important facts: different dates, different methodologies and, in the US, proposal status. **International standard** — BCBS benchmark that jurisdictions commit to implement. --- **Jurisdictional implementation** — the binding or proposed local rule, with its own scope, dates, transitions and deviations. — Final revised credit-risk Standardised Approach effective **1 April 2027**; domestic commercial-bank minima are CET1 **5.5%**, Tier 1 **7%**, total capital **9%**; leverage **4% D-SIB / 3.5% other banks**. Scheduled commercial banks remain outside implemented Ind AS under RBI’s 2019 deferral. [RBI 2025 Capital Adequacy Directions; RBI 2026 SA Directions; RBI 2019 Ind AS deferral] — PRA Basel 3.1 final rules effective **1 January 2027**; FRTB-IMA effective **1 January 2028**; SDDT capital regime effective **1 January 2027**. [PRA PS1/26; PS4/26] — CRR3 applied from **1 January 2025**; output floor **55% in 2026**, fully phased to **72.5% on 1 January 2030**; binding FRTB market-risk requirement postponed to **1 January 2027**. [Regulation (EU) 2024/1623; CRR Article 465(1); Commission/EBA] — The **19 March 2026** capital package remains a **proposal, not a rule**, as at 27 August 2026; the existing stress capital buffer architecture remains relevant to large-bank capital requirements. [Federal Reserve 19 March 2026; Federal Reserve supervisory-capital materials]

title: Counterparty Credit Risk
one_screen: Counterparty credit risk is the risk that a counterparty defaults before final settlement of a transaction, exposing a bank to potential loss. It differs from standard loan credit risk because exposure is contingent on market movements, not a fixed loan balance. Either party can owe a positive amount in derivative trades, making it a bilateral risk.
bodyText: In a derivative trade, the credit exposure at any time is the replacement cost (current market value if positive) plus any expected future exposure. The exposure is never equal to the notional amount of the contract; instead it varies with underlying prices. Unlike a one-sided loan, both parties in a derivative trade can be in-the-money or out-of-the-money. If one party defaults, the surviving party may suffer loss equal to the mark‑to‑market value of the contract. CCR therefore depends on both counterparty credit quality and the volatility of the derivative’s value. Banks typically net exposures under enforceable master agreements and may require collateral. Managing CCR requires measuring current exposure and forecasting potential future exposure. Basel guidelines define metrics like expected exposure to capture these dynamics. CCR contrasts with normal credit risk: a loan’s exposure is usually the principal, while a derivative’s exposure is uncertain and can reverse direction as market prices change. Bank A <-------- Netting & Collateral --------> Bank B (Derivative trade / netting set) Counterparty credit exposures must account for current mark-to-market values and any future potential changes – not just notional amounts. Assuming a derivative’s credit exposure equals its notional or treating CCR as a one-sided loan risk. In reality, exposure fluctuates and is bilateral. **Credit risk (loans)** — Risk of borrower default on funded loan balance, usually fixed (principal). --- **Counterparty credit risk (derivatives)** — Risk of counterparty default on contingent obligations; exposure is mark-to-market and can be positive or negative for either party. **No delta.** The basic concept of bilateral, contingent exposure applies universally.

title: Current vs Potential Exposure
one_screen: CCR measurement distinguishes between current exposure (replacement cost) and potential future exposure. Current exposure is the positive mark-to-market value of a trade today. Potential future exposure is an estimate of how much the exposure could increase over time due to market movements, reflecting the contract’s uncertainty.
bodyText: Current exposure is simply the contract’s current market value (if it is positive to the bank). For example, if a bank has an interest rate swap that is in-the-money by $1 million, its current exposure is $1 million. Potential future exposure (PFE) represents a statistically high percentile of the future distribution of exposures. It accounts for volatility: even if current exposure is small, markets could move. PFE is computed using models or add-on factors to the notional. Together, current and potential exposures are used to calculate Expected Exposure (EE) and Expected Positive Exposure (EPE) profiles over the life of the contract. An exposure profile shows how exposure might evolve. Initially, current exposure starts at the trade date’s mark‑to‑market. Over time, without frequent cash settlement (as in uncollateralized trades), exposure can grow. Banks use either simulation or standardized add-ons to gauge PFE at future dates. Current and potential exposures are summed and multiplied by a buffer (alpha) in SA-CCR to get Exposure At Default (EAD). Current Exposure (CE) = max(mark-to-market, 0) Potential Future Exposure (PFE) = high-percentile of future exposure increase EAD = 1.4 × (CE + PFE) (under SA-CCR) When measuring CCR, always include both current exposure (today’s value) and potential future exposure (possible increase). Considering only current exposure (ignoring future volatility) will understate CCR. Conversely, overstating exposure by using notional without adjustments is also wrong. **Current Exposure** — Today’s positive mark-to-market value. --- **Potential Future Exposure (PFE)** — A modeled high-percentile future exposure. PFE is *not* the same as current exposure or an average; it is an estimate of future increase and is typically larger. **No delta.** The concepts of current vs potential exposure are part of the Basel CCR framework and apply universally.

title: Exposure Metrics (EE, EPE, Peak)
one_screen: Banks summarize CCR over time using metrics like Expected Exposure (EE), Expected Positive Exposure (EPE), and peak exposure. These metrics aggregate exposure profiles into single numbers for capital and limit setting. EPE is essentially the time-weighted average of expected exposures (only when positive) over the first year; peak exposure is the high percentile of exposures.
bodyText: Expected Exposure (EE) is the average potential exposure at a specific future date. It includes only positive exposures (zero is the floor). Expected Positive Exposure (EPE) is the average of EE over multiple future dates, usually up to one year. The Basel CCR guidelines define EPE as the weighted average of expected exposures over time. “Effective EPE” is a slight variant used in IMM that applies the max of EPE or certain floors. Banks may cap EPE at the maximum expected exposure to reflect worst-case scenarios. Peak exposure (or “Peak EEPE”) is the (say) 95th or 99th percentile of all future exposure values, representing a stress point. This is used for limit-setting to ensure capital covers extreme outcomes. Typically, banks’ exposure profiles start low (time-zero exposure is often zero if no up-front payment) and rise as time passes, then fall near maturity for some products. The shape depends on the type of derivative. For example, a vanilla interest rate swap might have exposures that rise and then fall. Exposure Profile (by date) /\ /\ / \ / \ / \_______/ \____ Time EE = expected exposure at dates EPE = (EE1+EE2+...)/N (average over time) Peak = max(EE_t at percentile) Regulatory capital for CCR often uses EPE (a weighted average exposure) and peak exposures, not just point-in-time values. Using one date’s exposure as representative, or confusing average (EPE) with worst-case (peak). EPE is an average, not a worst-case measure. **Expected Positive Exposure (EPE)** — The time-weighted average of expected exposures (only positive) over a horizon. --- **Peak Exposure** — A high percentile (e.g. 95%) of exposure across time. Peak exposure is *not* the same as EPE (average); it typically exceeds EPE. **No delta.** Basel CCR metrics like EPE and peak are used globally; all jurisdictions adopting SA-CCR follow this.

title: Wrong-Way Risk
one_screen: Wrong-way risk arises when market movements that increase exposure to a counterparty coincide with an increase in that counterparty’s default probability. In general WWR, the counterparty’s credit quality worsens with adverse market factors. In specific WWR, a direct link exists (e.g. the counterparty has credit exposure to the underlying).
bodyText: Wrong-way risk (WWR) means exposure and credit risk are positively correlated. If exposure to a bank is higher exactly when that bank is more likely to default, losses can be severe. Specific WWR examples include: a bank sells credit protection on itself, or an airline enters a fuel swap where fuel price spikes hurt the airline’s credit. General WWR examples include: a corporate bond dealer holds interest rate swaps with companies; if interest rates rise, swap exposure grows while those companies’ creditworthiness may fall. Banks must identify both general and specific WWR. Specific WWR often comes from linked transactions or collateral (e.g. dealer pledges defaultable collateral). General WWR emerges from broad market shifts (e.g. recession). Basel rules and supervisory guidance require monitoring of WWR through stress tests. According to Fed guidance: “Wrong-way risk occurs when the exposure to a counterparty is positively correlated with the probability of default of the counterparty itself. Specific WWR arises from the nature of the transactions; general WWR arises from market factors”. Banks must identify WWR and avoid taking on transactions where exposure and counterparty strength move together. WWR should be quantified in stress scenarios. Ignoring correlations between market moves and credit risk. For example, assuming collateral fully protects without considering if collateral value is itself at risk in the same scenario. **General Wrong-Way Risk** — Exposure correlated with broad market factors affecting credit (macro-driven). --- **Specific Wrong-Way Risk** — Exposure directly linked to counterparty’s default risk (contract-specific link). **No delta.** WWR concepts are universal in Basel/ICS framework.

title: Close-Out Netting
one_screen: Close-out netting is a legal mechanism allowing a bank to terminate all transactions with a defaulted counterparty and net them into a single amount owed by one party to the other. If enforceable, netting greatly reduces exposure, since only the netted positive value is at risk rather than each trade’s full value.
bodyText: Netting is documented in master agreements (like an ISDA Master). Upon default, all trades in a netting set are “closed out” at current market values and netted. The surviving bank then has a single net claim or obligation. Enforceability of netting depends on jurisdiction and legal opinions. If netting fails (e.g. in bankruptcy some local law does not recognize it), the bank faces each trade’s exposure separately. Netting reduces CCR by off-setting gains and losses. For example, if bank A owes $5 on one swap but is owed $3 on another with the same counterparty, netting lets A owe only $2 instead of risking $8. Banks rely on netting to lower capital and collateral needs. Supervisors require proof that netting agreements are legally valid. A broken netting could double-count exposure and increase losses. Counterparty A ----- Master Agreement ----- Counterparty B | \ / | +--- Swap 1 (+$5) Swap 2 (+$3) ---+ \_____ Swap 3 (-$2)______/ Close-out: A owed $(5+3-2) = $6 net Only legally enforceable netting agreements count toward reducing exposure. Without enforceability, netting benefits cannot be recognized. Assuming netting always works. If a jurisdiction or failure scenario prohibits close-out netting, exposures cannot be netted. Each contract’s exposure must then be held separately. **Bilateral Netting (Master netting)** — Offsetting trades between two parties under one agreement, where obligations are legally netted. --- **Portfolio Compression** — A multilateral process of reducing notional without involving close-out netting. It does not affect legal netting sets. **No delta.** Netting rules vary by law, but the concept of enforceability is universal. Banks obtain legal opinions country by country.

title: Collateral and Margin
one_screen: Collateral is a key mitigation tool for CCR. Variation margin (VM) and initial margin (IM) are two collateral types. VM is exchanged to cover current mark-to-market exposure daily, protecting against immediate losses. IM is posted upfront or periodically to cover potential future exposure over a margin period of risk.
bodyText: Under a margin agreement (CSA), counterparties exchange VM whenever the contract’s market value changes. VM ensures that current exposures are collateralized. Initial margin (sometimes called independent amount) is additional collateral that covers the risk during the margin period of risk (the time to close out trades after default). Thus IM protects against volatile moves that occur between margin calls. Collateral agreements may include **thresholds** (amounts below which no VM is exchanged) and **minimum transfer amounts** (small amounts exempt). These can leave small exposures uncollateralized. IM is typically applied symmetrically (both parties must post if in scope). Once posted, collateral is often rehypothecated (re-used) by the receiver, which can introduce risk if that receiver fails. Margin requirements for non-cleared trades (BCBS-IOSCO rules) phased in from 2016–2022; by 2022 most large participants must exchange both VM and IM on bilateral trades. These global rules standardize collateral for non-centrally-cleared derivatives. Variation margin is typically transferred daily, while initial margin amounts depend on regulatory formulae or models. Collateral must be valued daily, and variation margin called frequently (often daily). Collateral credit quality should be high (e.g. cash, sovereign debt) to avoid further risk. Treating posted collateral as risk-free. If collateral is rehypothecated or volatile, it may not fully protect against loss. Also, assuming thresholds or IM exempt all risk. **Variation Margin (VM)** — Collateral exchanged to cover current exposure (daily mark-to-market). --- **Initial Margin (IM)** — Up-front collateral to cover potential future exposure over a margin period. **No delta.** BCBS-IOSCO margining standards apply globally for regulated participants. Some jurisdictions (e.g. India) are still using older models with updated add-on factors.

title: Margin Period of Risk & Related Terms
one_screen: The margin period of risk (MPR) is the time assumed between a counterparty’s default and the liquidation or hedging of the position. It determines how much additional future price movement risk the initial margin must cover. Regulators often assume 10 days or more for the MPR.
bodyText: When a counterparty defaults, trades do not immediately settle; the surviving party needs time to revalue or replace trades. The MPR covers this lag. For example, if a bank assumes a 10-day MPR, it calculates potential exposure assuming markets move during those 10 days. IM posted is meant to cover losses that could arise in that period. A longer MPR means greater PFE (since more days of potential move), so higher IM. Other collateral terms: **Threshold** is the uncollateralized exposure allowed (e.g. $0 for major banks), **Minimum Transfer Amount (MTA)** is a floor below which no margin is transferred, and **Independent Amount (IA)** is an extra fixed IM buffer. These terms are specified in the CSA. A bank must model the MPR correctly; underestimating it can leave exposure when collateral is stale. When computing PFE (in SA-CCR or IMM), include an appropriate margin period of risk. Regulators mandate conservative MPR assumptions (often 10–20 days for non-cleared). Forgetting that collateral calls aren’t instantaneous. A default may occur during periods when collateral isn’t updated (e.g. weekend or holiday), so exposure can grow. **Margin Period of Risk (MPR)** — The assumed time to close out positions after default, used in PFE calculation. --- **Maturity (T)** — The time until a trade’s normal expiration. These get mixed up but MPR is usually much shorter than T. **No delta.** Basel SA-CCR and IMM define MPR parameters; implementations are consistent across major regulators.

title: Rehypothecation
one_screen: Rehypothecation is the practice where the collateral receiver re-uses (re-pledges) the client’s collateral to fund its own activities. This can create risk: if the receiver defaults, the original pledgor might not get full collateral back.
bodyText: Many counterparties allow rehypothecation of collateral (especially cash), effectively giving the collateral-receiver a lien on it. This can improve liquidity for dealers but introduces systemic risk. If the client counterparty defaults but its posted collateral is rehypothecated and then lost or seized, the client cannot reclaim it. As a result, regulators have restricted rehypothecation in some cases (e.g. segregated accounts), and banking regulations may require some client collateral be held in special segregated accounts. Rehypothecation issues arose in past crises (e.g. 2008 Bear Stearns). Current guidelines encourage limiting rehypothecation or requiring full disclosure to clients. In CCR terms, rehypothecated collateral may not provide full protection: banks should consider the availability of collateral in stress (if collateral is encumbered elsewhere). Do not double-count rehypothecated collateral. Once collateral is rehypothecated, the receiving party’s obligation to return it remains, but the collateral may not be free to use for own risk. Assuming posted collateral is safe and available even if rehypothecated. In reality, if the receiving bank is insolvent, the collateral may be tied up. **Pledged Collateral** — Collateral a counterparty provides as security. --- **Rehypothecation** — The reuse of pledged collateral by the receiver. These are not the same; rehypothecated collateral may be co-mingled with others’ assets. **No delta.** Rules on rehypothecation may vary legally, but concept is global. Many jurisdictions allow limited rehypothecation under CSAs.

title: Uncleared Margin Rules
one_screen: The global “Uncleared Margin Rules” (UMR) require banks and other dealers to post both variation and initial margin on non-centrally-cleared OTC derivatives. Phased implementation began in 2016, with the last group of counterparties complying by 2022. UMR ensure broad use of VM/IM even for bilateral trades.
bodyText: UMR (BCBS-IOSCO) mandated that each phase, based on aggregate notional, requires IM for entities above a threshold. The key goal is to mitigate tail risk by ensuring collateral is posted on nearly all large OTC trades. Before UMR, many bilateral trades had no margin except VM for regulated dealers; now even unregistered entities might need to post VM/IM when counterparties are in scope. Under UMR, variation margin was required from 2016 for the largest dealers, and initial margin was phased in by 2022 for basically all participants with US$50bn+ notional. By 2022, most major dealers globally must exchange VM (daily) and IM (initial margin) for new and legacy trades. This rule is enforceable via regulations in each jurisdiction (e.g. US final rule, EU regulation, etc.). Global margining standards under UMR must be incorporated. Failing to post required margin can lead to capital add-ons or regulatory penalties. Overlooking smaller counterparties. Even many hedge funds, asset managers, and corporates are now subject to initial margin requirements once thresholds were reduced in phase 6. **Uncleared Margin Rules (UMR)** — Global regulatory requirements for posting IM/VM on non-cleared derivatives. --- **Clearinghouse Margin** — Collateral required by a CCP for cleared trades. UMR applies to bilateral trades only. **No delta.** UMR are a global BCBS-IOSCO standard; all G20 jurisdictions have rules implementing the schedule.

title: Central Clearing and CCPs
one_screen: Central counterparties (CCPs) mitigate bilateral CCR by interposing themselves between participants. When two parties clear through a CCP, each party’s counterparty becomes the CCP. The CCP nets trades among all members and manages default risk via margins and a waterfall. CCP clearing removes bilateral credit exposure but introduces new exposures to the CCP itself.
bodyText: A CCP provides multilateral netting: all trades in a given product with the CCP are netted across parties daily. This significantly lowers gross exposures. CCPs require initial and variation margin from members, and maintain a default fund contributed by members (and sometimes the CCP’s own capital). If a member defaults, its margin is used first; then its default fund contribution; then the CCP’s “skin in the game”; then possibly a mutualized fund of other members. Thus, CCP risk is mutualized. However, CCPs do not eliminate all risk. Members now face the CCP’s credit and liquidity risk. A CCP could face simultaneous defaults (e.g. extreme market moves), in which case default fund and possibly additional loss-sharing can be used. Clients clearing through a member have either “house” or “client” accounts; in some models, client positions are segregated, reducing risk of using client funds to cover a dealer’s losses. Central clearing is usually mandated or incentivized for standardized derivatives (e.g. interest rate swaps). Studies show CCPs greatly reduce systemic exposure but can concentrate risk in the CCP, so regulators treat CCP exposures carefully. Participants: A, B, C, ... \ | / \|/ +--------+ | CCP | +--------+ /|\ /|\ / | \ / | \ (netted exposures between CCP and each clearing member) When a trade is centrally cleared, CCR is replaced by the CCP’s counterparty risk. A bank must hold capital for its exposure to the CCP under special rules. Assuming central clearing removes all CCR. Even with a CCP, residual risk (e.g. gap risk, liquidity, CCP default) remains. **Clearing Member** — A firm that is a direct member of a CCP. --- **Client** — An end-user or customer whose trades are cleared by a member. Clients have indirect exposure to the CCP through the member. **No delta.** Basel and major regulators recognize CCP clearing similarly. Entities are categorized (e.g. QCCP) under capital rules.

title: Default Waterfall
one_screen: A CCP’s default waterfall is its ordered pool of resources to cover a member’s losses. Typically, waterfall layers are: the defaulting member’s initial margin → the member’s default fund contribution → the CCP’s own capital (“skin in the game”) → the mutualized default fund of surviving members. If losses exceed all, additional measures (like assessments or equity auction) are used.
bodyText: For example, if Member X defaults on a large loss, the CCP applies X’s margin first. If that is insufficient, it takes X’s share of the default fund. If still short, the CCP’s own capital absorbs the remainder (to align incentives). Finally, non-defaulting members’ default fund contributions cover any further shortfall. This ensures that members have “skin” in the outcome of defaults. Waterfalls vary by CCP, but all include these layers. An incentivized contribution (skin in game) is usually 5–10% of required default fund. Capital regulations may allow partial offset for default fund contributions. The structure ensures losses are contained and predictable. Client clearing often has special default procedures: for example, a clearing member’s default may lead to porting client positions to other members or liquidating client trades separately, depending on segregation arrangements. Only pledged margin and default fund contributions are at risk first. The order of the waterfall must be respected. Clearing members must cover their contributions on demand to ensure the waterfall is fully funded. Assuming mutualized funds are available immediately. In a crisis, liquidity to cover losses may not be instant, and clawback provisions may differ. **Initial Margin** vs **Default Fund Contribution**. Initial margin is collateral posted for each member. Default fund contributions are shared resources by all members. They serve different roles in the waterfall. **No delta.** Global CCP frameworks (CPMI-IOSCO Principles) require similar default waterfalls. Details (e.g. mandatory skin-in-game) are converging internationally.

title: Client Clearing Structures
one_screen: When clients clear through a clearing member, there are typically two models: omnibus and segregated. In omnibus clearing, all client positions are pooled under the member’s account; the member’s risk to the CCP is net of all its clients. In segregated clearing, each client’s positions are separately collateralized, isolating them in case the member defaults.
bodyText: In the omnibus model, a client’s margin might be held with other clients’, so if a client defaults or the member goes under, there can be confusion over entitlements (to be unwound by legal agreement). Segregated models (e.g. client-specific accounts) protect clients’ collateral from each other. Regulators often require at least partial segregation. If a clearing member defaults, segregated client positions can be ported or liquidated without affecting other clients; omnibus positions require more coordination. Clearing members must report client exposures to regulators and meet margin calls including client trades. The client still faces the clearing member credit risk unless the clearing is fully segregated (in which the client’s only counterparty is the CCP, effectively). Capital rules often treat client-cleared positions differently from house positions (e.g. risk weights, recognition of client collateral). A clearing member must disclose and segregate client funds and trades as per CCP rules. Clients must be informed how their positions are held (omnibus vs segregated). Assuming client collateral fully covers client losses even if pooled with others. In omnibus accounts, one client’s losses can erode others’ assets. **House Account** — The clearing member’s own trading account with the CCP. --- **Client Account** — The account (omnibus or segregated) holding client trades. **No delta.** Most regulators require client fund protection but allow either omnibus or segregated models, with slight preference for segregation (e.g. Dodd-Frank requires segregation for many customer positions).

title: CCP Exposures and Capital Treatment
one_screen: Even with clearing, banks must hold capital for exposures to CCPs. Under Basel rules, a clearing member’s trade exposure to a qualifying CCP generally gets a low risk weight (often 2%) reflecting the CCP’s risk-absorbing structure. Client exposures to a CCP (via a member) also have regulatory treatment recognizing default fund offsets.
bodyText: Basel III (Chapter 5) provides special capital formulas for CCPs. For example, a clearing member may assign a 2% risk weight to its trade exposure (after netting) to a well-regulated CCP (QCCP). For contributions to a CCP’s default fund, banks may use a haircut approach or even deduction if not performing obligations. The goal is to encourage central clearing by lowering capital. However, non-clearing member (client) exposures can be higher risk – often treated like a bank loan to the member, adjusted for collateral. Thus, CCP exposures are not risk-free: banks cannot fully ignore them. Nonetheless, the capital charges are far lower than for bilateral OTC. This incentivizes central clearing of standard products. Identify CCPs that qualify as “QCCPs” (per supervisory list) to apply favorable capital treatment. Always ensure margin and default fund contributions are included in exposure measures. Overlooking CCP contributions. For example, thinking collateral to the CCP doesn’t affect capital – regulators usually require including posted margin and default fund contributions in exposure calculations (albeit with reductions). **Trade Exposure to CCP** — The current and future exposure to the clearing house (subject to 2% RW). --- **Default Fund Exposure** — The risk from loss mutualization. Banks must separately calculate capital for this (often higher). **No delta.** Global Basel standards treat CCP exposures similarly. National regulators (e.g. SEC/CFTC or PRA/EBA) list recognized CCPs (QCCPs) for capital rules.

title: SA-CCR (Standardized Approach to CCR)
one_screen: SA-CCR is the Basel III capital approach for measuring CCR exposure. It computes Exposure at Default (EAD) as **EAD = α × (Replacement Cost + Potential Future Exposure)**, with α=1.4. Replacement Cost (RC) is the positive current value net of haircut collateral. Potential Future Exposure (PFE) is derived from standardized add-on factors by asset class, aggregated by hedging sets and offset by correlation, then net of initial margin (subject to a small 5% floor). This approach accounts for margining, netting, asset classes, and uses a higher multiplier for safety.
bodyText: SA-CCR’s formula: **EAD = 1.4 × (RC + PFE)**. For example, RC = max(MTM, 0) – collateral. PFE add-ons use supervisory notional * factors (similar to old CEM add-ons but more refined). Trades are grouped by asset class and hedging sets to allow some offset. Initial margin reduces PFE but only up to 95% (the multiplier means at least 5% of IM benefit is ignored, ensuring some capital). SA-CCR replaced the older CEM and SM and was calibrated to be risk-sensitive (accounting for netting, hedges, margin). It avoids banks’ using bespoke models (except IMM). SA-CCR became effective 2017 globally (though actual regulatory implementation varied by jurisdiction). +-------------------------+ | EAD = 1.4 × (RC + PFE) | +-------------------------+ / \ +--------+ +--------+ | RC | | PFE | +--------+ +--------+ | Current| | Add-on | | exposure (MTM)| (std. potential exposure) | EAD under SA-CCR always uses α=1.4 as a conservatism buffer. Replacement Cost cannot be negative (floor at zero). Ignoring netting sets or collateral: SA-CCR explicitly nets trades and collaterals first. Also, forgetting to use correct supervisory factors for add-ons by product type and maturity. **Replacement Cost (RC)** — Current exposure (MTM) minus collateral. --- **Potential Future Exposure (PFE)** — The supervisory-derived add-on component for future risk. RC is “today’s” risk, PFE is “future” risk. **No delta.** Basel SA-CCR formula is standard. Jurisdictions implement it verbatim (e.g. EU CRR, UK PRA rules, Fed final rule).

title: Internal Model Method (IMM)
one_screen: The Internal Model Method (IMM) allows a bank to use its own approved models to compute CCR exposures (particularly PFE) for capital, subject to strict regulatory criteria. It is most often used for calculating CVA capital under Basel. For exposure, IMM required sophisticated simulation of netting sets and collateral to estimate expected and unexpected exposures. Basel has largely phased out the IMM shortcut (except for CVA) in favor of SA-CCR, but some large banks use IMM for advanced CCR metrics.
bodyText: Under IMM, banks simulate future exposures (e.g. via Monte Carlo) to compute EPE or CVA capital directly. IMM can capture portfolio-specific correlations and netting more precisely than SA-CCR. However, only very large institutions with approved models may use it, and they must back-test their results. The “IMM shortcut method” of Basel (an alternative simplistic approach) was eliminated once SA-CCR took effect. Now “Internal Model Method” usually refers to CVA exposure models or bilateral EAD models used for regulatory capital, with extensive validation and restrictions on collateral. IMM requires supervisory approval and continuous validation. Models must be conservative and cover wrong-way risk and stress. Assuming one can freely choose IMM. Regulators often discourage new IMM approval because SA-CCR exists; IMM is complex, costly, and under scrutiny after the crisis. **Internal Model Method (IMM)** — A regulatory capital method using advanced models for CCR exposures. --- **Initial Margin (IM)** — Collateral posted to cover future exposure (not a modeling method). **No delta.** IMM rules (for CVA and CCR) are largely superseded by Basel SA-CCR except as grandfathered. Regulators generally stick to SA-CCR except for CVA VaR models.

title: CEM and SM Retirement
one_screen: The old methods for CCR, the Current Exposure Method (CEM) and the Standardized Method (SM), have been replaced by SA-CCR. CEM (used since Basel II) computed CCR as RC + add-on factors on notional by asset class and maturity. SM was a simpler approach for certain transactions. Both were considered insufficiently risk-sensitive. Basel finalized SA-CCR to replace these from 2017 onward.
bodyText: Under CEM, each trade’s PFE was a percentage of notional (e.g. 1% per year on interest rate swaps, up to caps). CEM did not recognize hedging across asset classes or margin. The Standardized Method applied broad risk weights or a CEM variant. Neither captured netting or actual collateral effects well. Basel Committee’s 2014 standard explicitly “replaced both the Current Exposure Method and the Standardized Method” with SA-CCR. Thus, for capital calculations, banks must use SA-CCR (or IMM if allowed). CEM and SM are now obsolete except as possible fallbacks for small institutions until SA-CCR is implemented. After SA-CCR’s effective date, do not use CEM or SM for capital purposes. Any regulatory references to CEM/SM are historical or transitional. Mistakenly applying CEM factors or SM calculations. For example, calculating add-ons on notional as under CEM will understate capital if SA-CCR is mandated. **Current Exposure Method (CEM)** — Old CCR method: RC + fixed add-ons on notional. --- **Standardized Method (SM)** — An older Basel approach for CCR (e.g. index-based factors). **No delta.** All Basel members have moved to SA-CCR for regulated banks. Any national capital rules referencing CEM/SM should be updated.

title: Default vs CVA Capital
one_screen: Basel requires two separate capital charges for counterparty risk: a **default risk charge** (credit risk capital) and a **CVA risk charge**. The default charge covers expected loss if the counterparty outright defaults; CVA capital covers volatility in mark-to-market credit spreads (the risk of the counterparty’s changing credit quality).
bodyText: Default capital is calculated like any credit exposure: EAD × PD × LGD (for IRB banks) or risk-weighted under standardized. CVA capital (also called “Market risk” for CVA) is designed to capture losses from sudden widening of credit spreads on derivatives. Basel frameworks include a standardized CVA charge (and previously an advanced CVA VaR approach) to ensure banks hold capital against this risk. Notably, hedges (like single-name CDS) can reduce CVA capital if recognized. Thus banks need both: default capital (part of credit risk RWA) and CVA capital (part of market risk RWA in trading or CVA desks). These are distinct: a low-default-probability counterparty could still incur large CVA losses if its credit spreads move. Always compute capital for CCR exposure under credit risk rules *and* for CVA risk. Don’t double-count (deduct CVA exposures when already in default RWA). Thinking credit risk capital is enough for CCR. CVA capital is separate for mark-to-market movements. Some banks once tried to net CVA and default exposures – Basel forbids netting them for capital. **Default Risk Capital** — Capital against expected loss from default (PD × LGD). --- **CVA Capital** — Capital for mark-to-market credit spread risk on counterparty exposures. **No delta.** The need for two charges is a global standard. The methods (basic vs standardized CVA) vary slightly: final Basel rules now use standardized CVA capital for all banks.

title: Credit Valuation Adjustment (CVA)
one_screen: CVA is the adjustment to the fair value of a derivative portfolio reflecting the counterparty’s credit risk. It is effectively the market value of expected loss from counterparty default, similar to “credit spread” on the portfolio. Banks include CVA in pricing and may hold hedges for it.
bodyText: Mathematically, CVA = ∑ (Discounted Expected Exposure × LGD × PD). It is the amount by which a portfolio’s value is marked down to price in default risk. Basel requires capital for CVA risk changes, and accounting rules require recognition of CVA in mark-to-market (e.g. IFRS 13). CVA exists because bilateral contracts would not otherwise price in default risk. CVA is widely hedged using credit derivatives. Managing CVA involves modeling exposure profiles (EPE) and counterparty credit spreads. Market CVA desks track and capitalise CVA. After the financial crisis, regulators required explicit CVA capital requirements since CVA swings caused bank losses. Value derivatives portfolios including CVA to reflect counterparty risk, and hold capital for CVA volatility. CVA must be revalued as the counterparty’s credit quality changes. Ignoring CVA in pricing or hedging. A bank that marks trades without CVA or hedging CVA can underprice risk and build uncapitalized positions. **CVA (Credit Valuation Adjustment)** — Adjustment reflecting the counterparty’s credit risk in valuation. --- **DVA (Debit Valuation Adjustment)** — Similar adjustment reflecting the bank’s own credit. CVA (debit to bank) and DVA (credit to bank) often confuse people (see next atom). **No delta.** Basel and accounting standards (IFRS 13/ASC 820) recognize CVA. Some specific rules exist for which trades count in CVA (e.g. some sovereigns are exempt in standardized CVA formula).

title: Debit Valuation Adjustment (DVA) and Funding Costs
one_screen: DVA is the opposite of CVA: it is the value adjustment reflecting the bank’s own credit risk on its liabilities. In practice, DVA means the bank would mark a gain if its own credit spread widens (bad for stakeholders but accounting shows a profit). DVA is controversial because it ties reported earnings to the bank’s health.
bodyText: When a bank owes a counterparty, its deteriorating credit actually reduces the expected payment, hence an accounting gain (DVA). However, regulators typically do not allow banks to rely on DVA gains to reduce capital or to distribute to shareholders. DVA mainly matters for pricing certain trades. Some regulators net CVA and DVA differently for capital. Funding Valuation Adjustment (FVA) is another concept: it accounts for the cost of funding collateral. If a bank must borrow to post collateral, that funding cost reduces trade value (FVA). FVA debates arose around whether to include it in fair value; many banks include FVA/MVA (margin valuation adjustment) in their pricing for completeness. Include DVA in valuations if following mid-market accounting, but regulatory capital ignores DVA (no capital relief). FVA should be considered in pricing, but typical regulatory capital frameworks do not have a specific FVA charge (it is considered in IRRBB, not CCR capital). Double-counting or incorrect offset of CVA by DVA. While both arise from same framework, regulations treat them asymmetrically (CVA is capitalized, DVA is not). **CVA** (benefit from widening credit spreads of the counterparty) vs **DVA** (benefit from widening credit spreads of yourself). They cancel in a risk-neutral value if both are allowed, but only CVA is capital-adjusted. **No delta.** These valuation adjustments are accounting concepts; regulatory treatment is broadly similar: CVA capital is required, DVA yields no capital benefit.

title: FVA, MVA, KVA and the XVA Family
one_screen: Beyond CVA and DVA, a suite of valuation adjustments (XVAs) addresses other costs. The key ones are: Funding Valuation Adjustment (FVA), Margin Valuation Adjustment (MVA), and Capital Valuation Adjustment (KVA). FVA is the cost of funding collateral flows. MVA is specifically the cost of funding initial margin. KVA is a charge reflecting the cost of holding regulatory capital. These are mainly used in internal pricing rather than capital rules.
bodyText: In practice, banks often compute FVA and MVA when pricing uncollateralized or margined trades, particularly since replacement to central clearing became common. KVA is a newer concept: it estimates the present value of future capital costs from holding exposures. Collectively, these adjustments ensure a derivative’s price covers not only market risk, but also funding, liquidity and capital costs. Importantly, regulators do not yet require capital for FVA/MVA/KVA. These are internal or accounting adjustments. They are included here for completeness of CCR context. CVA (and DVA) are the primary regulator-view adjustments. FVA/MVA are aligned to CVA in cost-of-carry models; KVA is still largely theoretical. Banks should clearly separate risk capital from valuation adjustments. XVAs beyond CVA are modeling/ALM issues, not additional capital requirements. Confusing FVA with regulatory charges. Banks sometimes thought FVA could be offset by CVA profits; regulators clarified that XVA hedges only apply to CVA capital. **FVA** — Cost of funding derivative exposures. --- **Capital Charge** — A regulatory cost (separate from FVA). KVA is an internal pricing layer for this charge. **No delta.** XVA concepts are primarily driven by internal risk management and accounting. No jurisdiction requires KVA hold.

title: CVA Capital Charge
one_screen: Capital rules specify methodologies for CVA capital. Basel 3.1 (Basel IV) replaced the Advanced CVA approach with two standardized approaches: a “standardized approach for CVA” (SA-CVA) using risk weights on counterparty exposures and CDS spreads, and a “basic approach” (BA-CVA) using broad factors. Under SA-CVA, a bank computes a regulatory CVA VaR or formula-based capital based on net exposures, counterparty risk weights, and allows limited hedge recognition. The details are complex and specified in regulatory texts. In all approaches, recognized CVA hedges (single-name CDS or index) can reduce capital, up to 50% by Basel rules.
bodyText: The **Basic Approach** is a simpler formula (often a flat rate on net expected exposures). The **Standardized Approach** is more risk-sensitive, effectively charging against CVA volatility at the 99% quantile. Eligible hedges (credit derivatives) get offsets. Only standardized methodology is allowed for large internationally active banks now. Small banks or some portfolios may use the BA. Key point: under Basel’s finalized CVA framework, banks must hold capital for CVA risk using these global formulas. EU/UK transposed these in CRR3/UK Basel 3.1 (effective ~2025) and the US is updating its rule. Hedging rules (what qualifies and to what extent) follow Basel’s main text. When calculating CCR capital, CVA risk is a separate add-on: follow the prescribed CVA framework (basic or standardized) based on bank size and model usage. CVA hedges can reduce CVA RWA only as explicitly permitted. Mixing CVA and default exposures incorrectly. For example, one should not double-count risk reduction. Also, misidentifying which hedges are recognized (only certain counterparty CVA hedges). **Basic CVA Approach (BA-CVA)** — Simple standardized calculation (like fixed factor * EAD). --- **Standardized CVA Approach (SA-CVA)** — Basel’s detailed formula or CVA VaR-based method. — RBI’s draft CCR circular focuses on CEM add-ons; India has not yet mandated a separate CVA capital charge for banks. (NBFCs under Ind AS would follow global norms, but banks follow RBI norms). — Basel 3.1 includes the revised CVA framework (implemented by mid-2025, final CRR3 expected Jan 2025). — CRR3 (approved by end-2023) implements Basel’s new CVA rules from Jan 2025. — Agencies have proposed changes (Nov 2022) to align with Basel 3.1 CVA rules, but finalization is pending.

title: Settlement vs Pre-Settlement Risk
one_screen: Pre-settlement risk is the counterparty credit risk during the life of a trade (as described above). Settlement risk (often called Herstatt risk in FX) is the risk that one party pays while the other does not at settlement time, usually due to timing differences. For instance, in an FX trade across time zones, a bank may deliver EUR but not yet receive USD if the counterparty fails.
bodyText: Herstatt risk famously arose when a German bank failed mid-day, causing FX payments to be one-sided. To mitigate settlement risk in FX, most participants now use payment-versus-payment (PvP) systems like CLS, which ensure the final transfer of one currency occurs only if the other currency’s payment is finalized. PvP is mandated or recommended for major FX pairs. Settlement risk can also occur in securities (delivery vs payment), but standard solutions exist (DVP settlement at exchanges or clearinghouses). In short, pre-settlement (counterparty) risk is before trade completion; settlement risk is the risk of final exchange of value. Both affect CCR practice, but capital for CCR typically concerns pre-settlement exposures. Implement PvP (e.g. through CLS) for FX trades to eliminate Herstatt risk when possible.
