Use delivery-versus-payment (DVP) for securities. Equating CCR capital with settlement risk. Regulators require CCR capital for trades that are bilateral; settlement risk is operational/liquidity risk, not included in CCR capital. **Pre-settlement risk (CCR)** — Counterparty default risk before and up to settlement of cash flows. --- **Settlement risk (Herstatt)** — Risk of loss due to one party failing to make payment at settlement time (e.g. FX PvP risk). **No delta.** Settlement risk management is driven by market infrastructure (CLS, clearinghouses). Basel mandates PvP where available. Regulatory capital for settlement risk is not separate; it is managed via operational standards.

title: Basel Framework (Global Standard)
one_screen: The Basel Committee’s published standards (Basel III, Basel 3.1, etc.) are the definitive source for CCR methodologies and capital. Key texts include BCBS 279 (SA-CCR standard) and the Basel III Revised Framework for market risk/CVA. These set the universal baseline for capital and definitions in all jurisdictions.
bodyText: For example, BCBS 279 (2014) finalized SA-CCR. Basel 3.1 (2023) updated CCR/CVA for capital (implemented by 2025 in many countries). Regulators in each jurisdiction (Fed, PRA, EBA, RBI) transposed these rules but cannot deviate from core calculations. Thus, for universal CCR concepts (like SA-CCR formula, CVA definitions, netting rules), citing the Basel text is authoritative. Always refer to the latest Basel Framework text for definitions and formulas of CCR metrics. National rules follow this text. Using outdated or local circulars instead of Basel standards for universal concepts. **Basel III Standards** — Internationally agreed rules by BCBS. --- **Local Regulations** — Jurisdictional laws implementing Basel (may lag or add conservatism). **No delta.** Basel standards themselves do not vary by country. Differences arise only in national adoption timetables or stricter add-ons, not in the core mathematics.

title: UK/EU Implementation
one_screen: The UK and EU have adopted Basel CCR and CVA rules through their capital regulations. The EU’s CRR3 (part of Basel 3.1 package) was agreed in late 2023 and takes effect Jan 1, 2025. It includes SA-CCR for calculating exposures and the new standardized CVA capital approach. The UK’s PRA released draft standards (PS17/23) on CCR/CVA, finalizing them for implementation by July 2025.
bodyText: In detail, EU CRR2 already implemented SA-CCR (from Jan 2023) and amended CVA rules. CRR3 (Basel 3.1) further updates CVA capital (transition Jan 2025) and keeps SA-CCR as is. The UK follows the same schedule: the PRA’s policy says Basel 3.1 reforms (CVA and margining) will be in force by mid-2025. Both jurisdictions require qualifying CCP (QCCP) treatment for exposures (EU and UK lists). They also follow the same definitions of EE/EPE, WWR, etc, as Basel. Use CRR or UK Prudential Regulation Authority rules for final figures in these jurisdictions. Generally, EU/UK text mirrors Basel with local choices (e.g. sovereign CVA exemptions in EU). Forgetting conversion factors or treatment differences. For instance, EU CVA rules used to exempt certain sovereigns; UK may diverge post-Brexit. **CRR2/3 (EU)** — European regulations implementing Basel (CRR3 is latest, full Basel 3.1). --- **UK PRA rules** — UK’s onshore regs (PRA policy statements for Basel 3.1). — PRA announced Basel 3.1 implementation by July 2025, including CCR and CVA changes (reducing SA-CCR alpha to 1.0 for non-financials, transitional treatment). — CRR3 (Basel 3.1) adopted with application date Jan 1, 2025; CRR2 already moved banks to SA-CCR in 2023 and updated CVA.

title: India’s CCR Regulation
one_screen: The RBI currently uses Basel III’s CCR guidance but has not fully adopted SA-CCR yet. In India, the Basel III Capital Regulations (Master Circular) still prescribe the Current Exposure Method (CEM) with updated add-on factors. In August 2025 RBI invited comments on revisions to CEM add-ons in its Basel III circular. It has indicated a phased move towards SA-CCR after FY26–27 (2026–27), subject to market readiness (industry sources).
bodyText: Thus, while Basel global rules exist, Indian banks (scheduled commercial banks) have not implemented SA-CCR for now. They continue to compute PFE using CEM add-ons (recently revised to align with BCBS). RBI’s master circular (April 2025) discusses the future potential of SA-CCR in context of investment funds, but general bank norms will likely shift later. CCIL (Clearing Corp of India) provides CCP services for interest rate and FX derivatives, facilitating clearing, but netting benefits and new global standards are gradually being incorporated. For Indian banks, follow RBI’s Basel III master directions. As of now, CCR capital uses CEM (not SA-CCR) for banks. Check RBI circulars for updates on implementation timelines. Assuming India already uses SA-CCR for banks. It does *not*. RBI is aligning CEM parameters and planning SA-CCR in the future, but until then use CEM as per RBI’s instructions. **RBI Master Directions (Basel III)** — Indian regulations (CEM-based CCR for banks). --- **Ind AS 109 (IFRS)** — Indian accounting standard on impairment, not applicable to banks’ prudential CCR. (Banks have separate RBI norms.) — RBI’s draft capital rules (Apr 2025) keep CEM with revised add-ons. SA-CCR adoption is indicated for the future, not yet mandatory. CCIL is India’s main CCP for IRS/FRA (see CCIL FAQs).

title: US CCR Regulation
one_screen: The US banking regulators have implemented SA-CCR for U.S. banks. A final rule (Nov 2019) required bank holding companies and large banks to use SA-CCR for derivatives exposures (effective April 2020, with mandatory compliance by Jan 2022). This rule also updated hedging recognition and collateral treatment. For CVA, the U.S. agencies in late 2022 released proposals to revise the CVA capital charge in line with Basel, but no final rule is in force yet.
bodyText: Specifically, U.S. rules now use SA-CCR in place of the previous Current Exposure Method. The FFIEC and Basel rules define the calculation. U.S. guidance also harmonizes with global standards for netting and margin. For CVA capital, banks currently use the standardized CVA approach (Basel-aligned) as per existing regulations, but agencies have sought comment on further changes. Large U.S. banks must compute CCR RWA under SA-CCR. For capital, counterparty exposures use SA-CCR EAD, and CVA risk uses the standardized CVA approach. Misapplying older Basel I/II rules. Also, small U.S. banks had the option to use the simpler exposure method but even those are encouraged to adopt SA-CCR. **Fed/OCC rules** — U.S. regulations implementing Basel (SA-CCR, CVA). --- **FRB’s Exchange Act rules** — Another set of U.S. rules (generally consistent). — SA-CCR has been mandatory since Jan 2022. U.S. regulators are aligning CVA standards with Basel 3.1 (proposed in 2022). No separate CVA regime in India; UK/EU have updated theirs as noted above.

title: Obligor, borrower and counterparty
one_screen: Credit risk attaches to a person that owes performance, not to a customer label. **Obligor** identifies the legal or natural person responsible for the credit obligation; **borrower** and **counterparty** describe roles that may coincide with the obligor but need not.
bodyText: ### Core mechanism | Object | What it means | Why credit risk cares | | :--- | :--- | :--- | | Obligor | Person contractually responsible for an obligation | Default status and wholesale borrower risk normally attach here | | Borrower | Person receiving or using borrowed funds | Often the obligor in loans; not a safe synonym in every structure | | Counterparty | Other contractual party to a transaction | Central for derivatives, securities financing and settlement exposures | | Commercial customer | Relationship-management label | May contain several legal obligors and therefore several credit risks | One corporate group can contain several obligors. One obligor can have many facilities. A derivative counterparty can create a credit exposure whose amount changes with market value even though no conventional loan exists. Upstream: Legal identity · Contract · Transaction role This: Identify the person that owes performance Downstream: Facility mapping · Default status · Limits · PD · Exposure aggregation ### Ownership | Role | Responsibility | | :--- | :--- | | Produces | Front office / onboarding establishes legal identity and contractual roles | | Approves | Credit / legal functions confirm the risk-bearing entity and structure | | Consumes | Underwriting, limits, modelling, collections, capital and reporting | | Challenges | Independent risk, legal, compliance and audit test entity mapping and aggregation | Credit risk must be mapped to the legal or natural person responsible for the obligation before ratings, defaults, limits or exposures are aggregated. **Obligor** — the person responsible for a credit obligation. --- **Counterparty** — the other party to a transaction; the term describes the transactional relationship and may or may not coincide with a loan borrower. Using “customer”, “borrower”, “obligor” and “counterparty” as database synonyms can propagate one entity’s rating, default or limit status to legally separate persons. **No delta.** Legal definitions and regulatory wording vary, but identifying the person responsible for an obligation is universal.

title: Product, facility and account
one_screen: A product is a reusable lending design, a facility is a specific contractual grant of credit, and an account is an operational record used to book and service activity. Credit risk measures become ambiguous unless they declare which level they attach to.
bodyText: ### Core mechanism | Level | Owns | Typical examples of fields | | :--- | :--- | :--- | | Product | Reusable commercial design | Product type, standard terms, target segment | | Facility | Actual contractual credit availability | Limit, currency, maturity, repayment schedule, covenants, security | | Account | Operational booking and servicing | Balance, postings, due dates, arrears, interest, fees | | Obligor | Person responsible for obligations | Rating, default state, aggregate limits | A simple term loan may be one facility with one account. A revolving facility can have several operational accounts. One obligor can hold facilities with different collateral, seniority and drawdown behaviour even when a common obligor PD is used. Upstream: Obligor · Product design · Credit decision This: Product → Facility → Account Downstream: Exposure · Delinquency · LGD · EAD · Collections · Reporting Every risk measure must state its level: product, facility, account, obligor or a defined aggregate. **Facility** — the contractual grant or commitment of credit, including its limit and terms. --- **Account** — the operational record through which balances, payments and arrears are booked; one facility need not equal one account. Treating an account-level delinquency flag as automatically equivalent to an obligor-level credit state can misclassify other facilities when the governing default framework applies a different propagation rule. **No delta.** Regulatory rules differ on when account or facility events propagate to an obligor, but the object hierarchy itself is universal.

title: Exposure and aggregation levels
one_screen: Exposure is the amount or value subject to credit loss for a stated purpose; it is not automatically today’s drawn balance. The same relationship can produce different valid exposure numbers at account, facility, obligor, connected-group and portfolio levels.
bodyText: ### Core mechanism | Level | Question answered | What may be included | | :--- | :--- | :--- | | Account | What is booked here now? | Outstanding principal, accrued items | | Facility | What credit position belongs to this contract? | Drawn amount plus relevant undrawn or contingent exposure | | Obligor | How much depends on this legal person? | Relevant facilities to the same obligor | | Connected group | How much depends on one linked economic risk? | Exposures to connected counterparties | | Portfolio | How much exposure exists across the book? | All included obligors/groups under the chosen perimeter | Funded and non-funded positions can both create credit exposure. A commitment or guarantee may have little or no current loan balance while still creating future or contingent loss potential. Account exposure → Facility exposure → Obligor exposure → Connected-group exposure → Portfolio exposure ↓ Limits · Concentration · EAD / EL / capital views Upstream: Accounts · Limits · Commitments · Transactions This: Account → Facility → Obligor → Connected group → Portfolio Downstream: Limits · EAD · Concentration · Expected loss · Capital Every exposure number requires both a **measurement basis** and an **aggregation level**. **Outstanding balance** — the amount currently booked as drawn or owed. --- **Exposure** — the amount relevant to a stated credit-risk question; it can include future drawings, contingent claims or aggregation above account level. Setting exposure equal to current drawn balance for revolving or committed facilities can omit the amount that may be drawn or become due before default. #### IN (RBI) The RBI Commercial Banks IRACP Directions define exposure to include funded and non-funded exposures, including underwriting and similar commitments. #### UK (PRA) Detailed regulatory exposure values depend on the applicable prudential approach; the conceptual distinction between booked balance and risk exposure does not change. #### EU CRR exposure-value rules vary by exposure type and credit-risk approach; the aggregation principle is unchanged. #### US US regulatory capital rules define exposure measures by asset and approach; current balance is not a universal substitute for exposure at default.

title: Connected counterparties and economic groups
one_screen: Legal separation does not guarantee independent credit risk. Connected-counterparty analysis aggregates persons when control or economic interdependence creates a common failure channel, so one concentrated risk cannot be disguised as several names.
bodyText: ### Core mechanism | Connection test | Core question | Credit consequence | | :--- | :--- | :--- | | Control | Does one person directly or indirectly control another, or are several under common control? | Treat connected exposures as one concentration where the rule requires | | Economic interdependence | Would financial difficulty at one likely cause funding or repayment difficulty at another? | Aggregate because apparent legal diversification is not economic diversification | | Mere commercial relationship | Are entities simply customers/suppliers without material dependency? | Investigate; do not aggregate automatically | Connection for concentration purposes is not the same as default propagation. Two companies can be aggregated for a large-exposure limit yet retain separate ratings and default statuses if the applicable default rules assess them separately. Legal entities ↓ Control test OR economic-interdependence test ↓ Connected group → Aggregate exposure → Concentration limit / monitoring Upstream: Legal entities · Ownership · Funding links · Revenue dependencies This: Test control OR economic interdependence → connected group Downstream: Aggregate exposure · Large-exposure limits · Concentration monitoring ### Ownership | Role | Responsibility | | :--- | :--- | | Produces | Relationship teams and credit analysis identify ownership and dependency evidence | | Approves | Credit risk / designated governance confirms connected-group treatment | | Consumes | Limits, portfolio risk, regulatory reporting and capital assessment | | Challenges | Independent risk, compliance and audit test completeness and consistency | Count common failure mechanisms, not merely legal names. **Connected counterparties** — separate persons aggregated because their risks are linked by control or economic dependency. --- **Single obligor** — one legal or natural person responsible for obligations. “Same corporate group” does not automatically mean “same defaulted obligor”, and separate incorporation does not automatically mean independent concentration risk. #### IN (RBI) RBI’s Large Exposures Framework applies Indian prudential aggregation and limits to single counterparties and groups of connected counterparties; use the RBI framework in force for the reporting date. #### UK (PRA) PRA SS3/25 sets expectations for groups of connected clients using control and economic dependency concepts. #### EU The CRR large-exposures framework uses groups of connected clients and tests based on control and economic interconnection. #### US US legal lending-limit and aggregation rules use US-specific control/common-enterprise tests; they should not be assumed identical to the Basel connected-counterparty test.

title: Underwriting and the credit decision
one_screen: Underwriting converts information about the obligor, facility and environment into a governed decision to approve, decline or reshape credit. The decision starts with a sustainable **primary source of repayment**; collateral and guarantees can reduce loss if repayment fails, but they do not repair weak repayment capacity.
bodyText: ### Core mechanism | Decision layer | Question | Output | | :--- | :--- | :--- | | Credit policy | What business and risk will the institution accept? | Target markets, criteria, limits, prohibited/exception cases | | Repayment capacity | From what recurring cash flow or resources will contractual payments be made? | Base-case debt service assessment | | Downside resilience | What happens if revenue, rates, costs or asset values move adversely? | Stressed repayment capacity and weaknesses | | Structure | Can tenor, amortisation, covenants, limit or pricing make the risk acceptable? | Proposed terms and controls | | Mitigants | What secondary recovery exists if primary repayment fails? | Collateral / guarantee assessment | | Approval authority | Who may accept this size, risk and exception profile? | Approve / decline / approve with conditions / escalate | A sound decision is not “good borrower versus bad borrower”. It is **borrower + purpose + amount + structure + repayment source + downside + mitigants + price**, all within policy and delegated authority. Purpose + amount + obligor ↓ Policy eligibility ↓ Primary repayment source → Repayment capacity → Downside resilience ↓ Structure → Secondary mitigants → Approval authority ↓ Approve / conditions / escalate / decline Upstream: Obligor · Facility request · Financial/behavioural data · External credit data · Policy This: Repayment capacity → Downside → Structure → Mitigants → Approval authority Downstream: Sanction terms · Documentation · Disbursement · Monitoring · Rating ### Ownership | Role | Responsibility | | :--- | :--- | | Produces | Front office / credit analyst assembles facts, cash-flow analysis and recommendation | | Approves | Delegated credit officer, committee, senior management or board according to authority | | Consumes | Documentation, operations, monitoring, portfolio management and finance | | Challenges | Independent credit risk, second-line policy governance and internal audit | Approve credit primarily on sustainable repayment capacity. Treat collateral and guarantees as secondary protection unless the product is explicitly designed to repay from asset sale or liquidation. **Credit policy** — sets what risks may be taken and under what criteria. --- **Approval authority** — determines who may accept a particular exposure, size, risk or exception. A high collateral value can make an uneconomic loan look safe. If the borrower cannot service the debt, the bank has underwritten a workout, not a performing credit. **No delta in the core rule.** Local consumer-protection, responsible-lending, related-party and governance requirements vary, but sound underwriting universally requires defined criteria, repayment-capacity analysis and controlled approval authority.

title: Collateral, security and guarantees
one_screen: Collateral, security interests and guarantees are credit-risk mitigants only to the extent that the bank can legally rely on them and realise value when needed. Their underwriting job is to provide a credible **secondary way out**; their later LGD role is separate and depends on realised recovery cash flows.
bodyText: ### Core mechanism | Mitigant | What must be true | Main failure mode | | :--- | :--- | :--- | | Collateral asset | Identifiable, valued, controllable and realisable | Value falls, asset disappears, sale is delayed | | Security interest | Validly created and perfected under applicable law | Priority or enforceability fails | | Guarantee | Legally effective claim on a capable guarantor | Guarantor lacks capacity or defaults with borrower | | Covenant / structural protection | Trigger and remedy are clear and monitorable | Breach occurs too late or remedy is weak | **Eligible value is not appraisal value.** A lending or risk value normally considers valuation uncertainty, volatility, liquidation time, prior claims, currency mismatch, concentration and policy/regulatory haircuts. `Adjusted collateral value = Market / appraised value × (1 − haircut)` `Haircut` — reduction for uncertainty, volatility, liquidation and other prescribed risks. Haircut ↑ → recognised collateral value ↓ → unsecured exposure / loss severity pressure ↑. This is a teaching relationship; regulatory frameworks prescribe their own eligible collateral, valuation and haircut rules. Collateral / guarantee identified ↓ Due diligence → Legal creation / perfection → Valuation → Haircut ↓ Monitoring ↓ Default / enforcement need ↓ Realisation / guarantor payment → Net recovery Upstream: Approved structure · Asset/guarantor due diligence · Legal documentation This: Create → Perfect → Value → Haircut → Monitor → Enforce if needed Downstream: Lending terms · Limit usage · Recovery strategy · LGD evidence ### Ownership | Role | Responsibility | | :--- | :--- | | Produces | Credit, legal, valuation and collateral-management teams establish evidence | | Approves | Credit authority accepts the mitigant within policy | | Consumes | Operations, monitoring, workout, capital and LGD estimation | | Challenges | Legal, independent risk, valuation review and audit test perfection and values | A mitigant is worth only what can be legally enforced and economically realised when the borrower is under stress. **Collateral value** — secondary recovery value available if repayment fails. --- **Repayment capacity** — the borrower’s ability to meet contractual payments from the primary repayment source. **Guarantee** — a contractual promise by another person to perform or pay if the obligor does not. --- **Collateral** — an asset or property interest available to secure recovery. Counting a guarantee at face value without testing legal effectiveness, coverage and guarantor credit quality merely moves the credit risk to an unmeasured second obligor. **No delta in the economics.** Perfection, priority, insolvency treatment, valuation standards and regulatory recognition are jurisdiction-specific; production treatment must follow local law and the applicable prudential framework.

title: Default: defining the event
one_screen: Default is a governed credit state, not a synonym for arrears, loss, bankruptcy or write-off. Every PD, default rate, cure rate and LGD inherits the unit and events used in the default definition, so the event must be fixed before the metric.
bodyText: ### Core mechanism | Component | Question that must be answered | | :--- | :--- | | Unit | Does default apply to an obligor, facility, account or retail pool? | | Event | Which qualitative and quantitative conditions trigger default? | | Materiality | Which past-due amounts are material enough to count? | | Propagation | Does one facility’s default affect other facilities? | | Exit | What permits return to non-default? | | History | Which date and state are preserved for modelling and recovery? | Basel’s IRB reference definition uses two routes for an obligor: **unlikeliness to pay in full without recourse to actions such as realising security**, or **more than 90 days past due on a material credit obligation**. The routes are alternatives; later atoms own their mechanics. Performing ↓ Qualifying credit deterioration ↓ UTP trigger OR material past-due trigger ↓ Default state ↓ Cure test / recovery lifecycle Upstream: Legal obligor · Contract · Payment history · Credit information This: Apply governed default definition → default / non-default state Downstream: PD labels · LGD sample · Cure · Recovery · Capital · Reporting Define default before measuring default risk, then preserve that definition across development, calibration, validation and reporting. **Default** — entry into a defined credit-risk state. --- **Loss** — the economic or accounting shortfall arising from outcomes around or after default; default can still produce substantial recovery. Combining historical “bad” flags that mean 90 DPD, charge-off, bankruptcy or NPA creates a target variable with no stable economic meaning. #### IN (RBI) RBI commercial-bank asset classification is built around prudential **NPA** rules, not a word-for-word Basel IRB default definition. The IRACP Directions also cross-reference “default” in RBI’s stressed-asset resolution framework; mappings must state which definition is used. From **1 April 2027**, RBI’s 2026 Asset Classification, Provisioning and Income Recognition Directions mandate an expected-credit-loss provisioning framework for commercial banks; that future provisioning regime does not make the Basel IRB default definition and RBI prudential classifications interchangeable. #### UK (PRA) The current UK framework remains CRR-derived. The January 2026 PRA SS3/24 version is **future policy effective 1 January 2027**, not the framework in force on 29 August 2026. #### EU CRR Article 178 uses UTP and past-due criteria. EBA’s May 2026 amended Guidelines have an **application date of 19 October 2026** and are future-effective on 29 August 2026. #### US Advanced Approaches rules distinguish wholesale and retail default definitions; specified retail categories use different mechanical thresholds.

title: Arrears, days past due and delinquency states
one_screen: Arrears measure unpaid contractual amounts; days past due measure how long payment has remained unpaid; delinquency buckets convert that clock into operational states. These are payment facts, not loss estimates or the complete definition of default.
bodyText: ### Core mechanism | Measure | What it answers | Typical mistake | | :--- | :--- | :--- | | Arrears | How much required payment is unpaid? | Treating amount as duration | | DPD | How long has the relevant payment been overdue? | Starting the clock from statement or month-end instead of due date | | Delinquency bucket | Which monitoring state does the DPD fall into? | Treating a bucket boundary as a universal default rule | | Out-of-order test | Is a revolving/OD/CC facility persistently irregular under its rule? | Applying instalment logic to revolving credit | DPD describes payment behaviour; the default definition determines when that behaviour, or separate qualitative evidence, becomes a governed credit state. Contractual due date → Unpaid amount = arrears ↓ DPD clock starts → Delinquency bucket advances ↓ Collections / early warning → Governed default test Upstream: Contractual due date · Required payment · Credits received This: Due → Overdue → DPD count → Delinquency state Downstream: Collections · Early warning · Default test · Roll rates · Vintage analysis `DPD = observation date − relevant unpaid contractual due date` The exact counting convention belongs to the governing policy or regulation. DPD ↑ → delinquency severity usually ↑, but default still requires the applicable rule. Calculate delinquency from the contractual obligation and the specified counting convention; do not infer default merely from an informal bucket label. **Arrears** — the unpaid amount. --- **Days past due** — elapsed time associated with an unpaid contractual obligation. Changing due-date logic, allocation of payments or day-end convention can create apparent credit deterioration or improvement without any change in borrower behaviour. #### IN (RBI) RBI requires overdue, SMA and NPA status to be determined through the day-end process for the relevant date. Its illustration moves a continuously overdue account to SMA-1 after 30 days, SMA-2 after 60 days and NPA after the applicable 90-day progression; OD/CC products use the defined “out of order” test. #### UK (PRA) Past-due status and materiality are inputs to the current regulatory default framework; arrears buckets used operationally are not themselves the complete definition of default. #### EU CRR/EBA rules distinguish days-past-due mechanics, materiality and unlikeliness-to-pay indicators; reporting past-due bands do not replace Article 178 default. #### US Different regulatory purposes and retail categories use different delinquency/default thresholds; there is no safe universal “90 DPD for everything” rule.

title: Unlikeliness to pay
one_screen: Unlikeliness to pay identifies default from the substance of credit deterioration before a delinquency clock necessarily reaches its backstop. It asks whether full payment remains likely without extraordinary recovery action; it is governed judgement, not a discretionary weakness label.
bodyText: ### Core mechanism | Evidence | Question | | :--- | :--- | | Repayment capacity deterioration | Can expected cash flow still service the obligation in full? | | Distressed restructuring | Would the borrower fail or suffer material difficulty without a concession? | | Credit-related write-down / sale loss | Does the bank’s own action evidence material deterioration? | | Insolvency / bankruptcy event | Does legal distress indicate repayment will be avoided or delayed? | | Security dependence | Is repayment only credible through enforcement or realisation of collateral? | A watch-list flag, downgrade or adverse news item is an **input**, not automatically default. Documented triggers and evidence standards prevent UTP from drifting across teams or cycles. Adverse evidence ↓ Assess sustainable full payment without extraordinary recovery action ↓ Full payment likely → No UTP → Continue monitoring Full payment unlikely → UTP → Default Upstream: Underwriting baseline · Monitoring · Adverse events · Financial information This: Evidence → Assess full payment without extraordinary action → UTP yes/no Downstream: Default state · Collections/workout · PD labels · Provisioning/capital consequences ### Ownership | Role | Responsibility | | :--- | :--- | | Produces | Relationship/credit monitoring identifies deterioration and evidence | | Approves | Credit risk or delegated default governance determines UTP status | | Consumes | Collections, restructuring, modelling, finance and regulatory reporting | | Challenges | Independent risk, model validation and audit test consistency | Assess UTP on the ability and likelihood to pay the credit obligation in full, not on how much the bank expects to recover after failure. **Unlikely to pay** — a default-likelihood conclusion about full contractual payment. --- **High LGD** — a severity conclusion about the size of loss conditional on default. Calling a fully secured exposure “not defaulted” because collateral should cover the debt confuses borrower repayment with recovery from security. #### IN (RBI) RBI commercial-bank NPA classification is its own prudential framework. Do not import a Basel IRB UTP label into RBI NPA reporting without an explicit mapping to the RBI rules in force. #### UK (PRA) The current UK framework includes unlikeliness-to-pay indicators. PRA SS3/24 provides the future Basel 3.1 expectations from 1 January 2027. #### EU UTP is an independent limb of CRR Article 178. The May 2026 EBA amendments apply from 19 October 2026 and should be treated as future-effective until then. #### US Advanced Approaches wholesale default expressly includes a determination that the obligor is unlikely to pay in full without recourse to actions such as realising collateral.

title: Past-due backstops and the 90-day rule
one_screen: A past-due backstop is an outer mechanical trigger, not permission to wait for the clock when earlier evidence already establishes default. In the Basel wholesale reference definition, UTP and more-than-90-days-past-due are joined by **OR**, not by a sequence requiring both.
bodyText: ### Core mechanism UTP trigger met first → Default now Past-due clock reaches applicable material backstop first → Default now Neither met → Continue non-default monitoring The backstop constrains optimism. It preserves an objective point beyond which prolonged material non-payment cannot remain outside default merely because judgement has not acted. Qualifying UTP → Default now ↓ OR ↓ Past-due clock → Material backstop reached → Default now Upstream: DPD · Materiality · UTP evidence This: Earlier of qualifying UTP or applicable mechanical backstop Downstream: Default date · Cure clock · Model labels · Workout and reporting The backstop is the latest mechanical trigger under its rule, not a grace period that overrides earlier qualitative default evidence. **Backstop** — an outer mechanical trigger based on elapsed delinquency under a specified rule. --- **Definition of default** — the full set of qualitative and quantitative conditions governing entry to default. Writing “default = 90 DPD” into data dictionaries suppresses early defaults, mixes products with different rules and trains models on a delayed target. #### IN (RBI) For commercial banks, a term loan is classified NPA when interest and/or principal remains overdue for **more than 90 days**. RBI also prescribes distinct tests for OD/CC, working-capital irregularity, bills, agricultural exposures and other categories; asset classification is borrower-wise subject to specified exceptions. #### UK (PRA) The current UK CRR-derived default framework uses past-due and materiality rules alongside UTP. The updated PRA Basel 3.1 package, including the January 2026 SS3/24 version, takes effect on 1 January 2027. #### EU CRR Article 178 uses a past-due limb alongside UTP, supported by materiality rules. The EBA’s May 2026 amended Guidelines become applicable on 19 October 2026. #### US Advanced Approaches wholesale default includes more than 90 days past due on a material obligation, while specified retail categories use different mechanical thresholds; “90 days everywhere” is therefore wrong.

title: Restructuring, forbearance and distressed concessions
one_screen: Restructuring changes contractual terms; forbearance is a concession associated with the debtor’s financial difficulty. A modification can preserve value, but cannot erase the deterioration that made the original terms unsustainable.
bodyText: ### Core mechanism | Situation | Credit interpretation | | :--- | :--- | | Healthy commercial amendment | Terms change for ordinary business reasons; distress not implied | | Concession because of financial difficulty | Forbearance / distressed modification analysis required | | Material forgiveness or postponement | Test whether diminished financial obligation indicates UTP/default | | New contract after old arrears are capitalised | Preserve pre-modification history; do not reset the borrower to “new” | | Repeated restructuring | Escalating evidence that apparent cure may be unstable | The key question is **why terms changed and what risk the concession reveals**. Extending maturity may restore short-term affordability; capitalising arrears can clean DPD without improving cash generation; principal forgiveness changes expected recovery. Original terms → Financial difficulty → Concession / restructuring ↓ UTP / default test ↓ Revised cash flows → Performance monitoring ↓ Cure / probation OR re-default Upstream: Deterioration · Missed/expected missed payments · Negotiation This: Modify terms → Was concession driven by financial difficulty? → Default/forbearance test Downstream: Revised cash flows · Default status · Cure/probation · LGD and recovery history ### Ownership | Role | Responsibility | | :--- | :--- | | Produces | Workout / relationship team documents distress, proposal and economics | | Approves | Restructuring authority / credit committee approves within policy | | Consumes | Operations, finance, default management, modelling and reporting | | Challenges | Independent credit risk and audit test classification and economic substance | A new contractual schedule must not erase the borrower’s prior distress, default date or economic concession. **Restructuring** — a modification of contractual credit terms. --- **Forbearance** — a concession linked to the debtor’s financial difficulty; not every restructuring is forbearance. Evergreening converts unpaid amounts into a formally current contract while leaving repayment capacity unchanged; operational current status is not proof of economic cure. #### IN (RBI) Commercial banks apply the IRACP Directions together with the RBI *Commercial Banks – Resolution of Stressed Assets Directions, 2025* where relevant; restructuring classification and provisioning must follow those rules rather than a generic Basel label. #### UK (PRA) Distressed restructuring can be an UTP indicator under the definition-of-default framework; forbearance and regulatory default remain distinct classifications. #### EU CRR/EBA rules distinguish forbearance, non-performing exposure and default. The May 2026 EBA amendment retains the 1% NPV-loss threshold in the relevant distressed-restructuring guidance and becomes applicable on 19 October 2026. #### US Accounting modification, troubled-credit treatment and regulatory default are separate determinations; Advanced Approaches default remains governed by 12 CFR Part 217.

title: Cure, probation and re-default
one_screen: Cure is the governed transition from default back to non-default after the default conditions have ceased and renewed performance is credible. Re-default is a later return to default; a temporary payment or zero-DPD snapshot is not enough to prove a durable cure.
bodyText: ### Core mechanism Default ↓ Original trigger ceases ↓ Required arrears / viability conditions met ↓ Probation or observation requirement, where applicable ↓ Cured / non-default ↓ New qualifying trigger? ↓ Re-default A sound data model keeps the entire state history: first default date, cause, restructuring events, cure date, probation, re-default and recovery. Deleting default history after cure produces survivorship bias and makes weak restructurings look successful. Default ↓ Original trigger ceases → Arrears / viability conditions met ↓ Probation / observation where required ↓ Cured / non-default ↓ New qualifying trigger → Re-default Upstream: Default state · Payments · Financial recovery · Restructuring performance This: Test exit conditions → probation where required → cure Downstream: Migration · Re-default · PD calibration · Recovery analysis · Monitoring Cure removes the current default state; it does not remove the historical fact that default occurred. **Cure** — return to non-default under the complete exit criteria. --- **Arrears clearance** — payment of overdue amounts; UTP or other default conditions may still remain. Resetting a cured customer to “never defaulted” inflates apparent portfolio quality and corrupts PD, transition and restructuring-performance analysis. #### IN (RBI) Under the current commercial-bank IRACP Directions, an NPA may be upgraded to standard only when the **entire arrears of interest and principal are paid**; where the borrower has more than one facility with the bank, arrears across all those credit facilities must be repaid, subject to additional restructuring rules where relevant. #### UK (PRA) Return-to-non-default is governed under the current definition-of-default framework. The updated PRA SS3/24 sets the future Basel 3.1 expectations from 1 January 2027. #### EU EBA Guidelines govern return-to-non-default and probation concepts. The May 2026 amended version has an application date of 19 October 2026, so the applicable version must be identified by observation date. #### US Advanced Approaches rules provide return-from-default standards for wholesale obligors and retail exposures under the US framework; the relevant unit must be preserved.

title: Write-off, recovery and economic loss
one_screen: Write-off changes the carrying amount or prudential treatment of an exposure; recovery records value collected after credit failure; economic loss measures what was ultimately lost after recoveries, costs and timing. None of these events should erase the default lifecycle that produced them.
bodyText: ### Core mechanism | Lifecycle item | What it means | What must stay in history | | :--- | :--- | :--- | | Default | Governed credit state begins | Default date, trigger, EAD | | Provision / allowance | Loss is recognised or reserved under the applicable framework | Amount, basis, date | | Write-off / charge-off | Carrying amount is reduced or removed under relevant rules | Written-off amount and date | | Recovery | Cash or value is collected after default/write-off | Gross proceeds, source and timing | | Workout cost | Legal, collection, maintenance and disposal costs | Cash outflow and timing | | Economic loss | Net shortfall measured on a consistent basis | Final discounted loss calculation | Post-write-off recoveries are economically real. A technical write-off can coexist with continuing collection activity and legal liability; the database therefore needs both accounting status and recovery status. Default → Workout → Recoveries + workout costs ↓ Discounted net recovery → Economic loss Default ↓ Provision / allowance → Write-off when required → Post-write-off recovery can continue Upstream: Default · Exposure · Provisioning / accounting rules This: Provision → Write-off if required → Recoveries and costs → Final economic loss Downstream: LGD estimation · Workout strategy · Finance · Tax / reporting `Economic loss = EAD − PV(net post-default recoveries)` `Net recoveries = borrower payments + collateral/guarantee proceeds − workout costs` Longer recovery time ↑ → present value of recovery ↓ → economic loss and LGD ↑, all else equal. Never delete default, write-off or post-default recovery history merely because the balance sheet carrying amount has changed. **Write-off** — accounting or prudential reduction/removal of carrying amount under the applicable framework. --- **Debt forgiveness** — release of the debtor’s legal obligation; write-off does not necessarily produce forgiveness. Using the write-off amount as “LGD” automatically ignores later recoveries, workout costs, timing and the exposure actually outstanding at default. #### IN (RBI) The commercial-bank IRACP Directions recognise write-offs, technical write-offs and subsequent recoveries. A partial or technical write-off does not permit the remaining exposure to be shown as standard merely because part has been written off. The current IRACP provisioning regime is replaced for covered commercial banks from **1 April 2027** by RBI’s 2026 expected-credit-loss-based Asset Classification, Provisioning and Income Recognition Directions. #### UK (PRA) For IFRS reporters, IFRS 9 write-off requirements operate separately from prudential regulatory default. The two statuses must be mapped, not conflated. #### EU IFRS-reporting entities apply IFRS 9 write-off principles while CRR regulatory default remains a separate prudential state. #### US CECL allowance and charge-off practice is separate from regulatory default and nonaccrual classifications; modelling must preserve those distinctions.

title: Probability of default
one_screen: Probability of default is the probability that a defined obligor, facility or pool enters a defined default state over a specified future horizon, conditional on information available at an observation date. A number labelled “PD” is incomplete until its **unit, event, horizon and conditioning information** are known.
bodyText: ### Core mechanism | Component | Required statement | Why it matters | | :--- | :--- | :--- | | Unit | Obligor, facility or homogeneous pool | Changes what can default | | Event | Regulatory default, internal default or other defined target | Changes the outcome being predicted | | Horizon | One year, 12 months, lifetime or another period | Changes probability mechanically | | Observation date | Information available at prediction time | Prevents hindsight and leakage | | Calibration basis | Mapping from score/grade to probability | Turns ranking into a probability estimate | PD is not a declaration that a named borrower “will default”. It is a probability assigned before the outcome is known. Across repeated comparable populations, realised default frequencies should be consistent with well-calibrated probabilities within sampling and cyclical variation. Defined unit + default event + horizon + observation date ↓ Score / rating / model estimate ↓ Calibration ↓ PD Upstream: Default definition · Observation date · Borrower/pool information · Score/rating This: Estimate and calibrate probability over stated horizon Downstream: Pricing · Expected loss · Rating grades · Capital · Monitoring For a population observed at time `t`: `PD_h = P(default during horizon h | information available at t)` Horizon ↑ → cumulative probability of at least one default event generally ↑, all else equal. A one-year PD cannot be substituted mechanically for a lifetime probability. No PD is interpretable without its unit, default definition, horizon and observation date. **PD** — a calibrated probability of a specified future default event. --- **Credit score** — a ranking or predictive output that need not itself be a probability. Multiplying a raw score by LGD and EAD because the score “looks like a probability” creates a loss number with no valid probabilistic interpretation. **No delta in probability mathematics.** Regulatory frameworks can prescribe different default definitions, parameter floors, horizons and calibration standards; those rules change the parameter specification, not what probability means.

title: Point-in-time and through-the-cycle PD
one_screen: Point-in-time and through-the-cycle describe how strongly a rating or PD responds to current versus cyclical conditions. They are conditioning philosophies on a spectrum, not synonyms for short-horizon and long-horizon probability.
bodyText: ### Core mechanism | Dimension | Point-in-time tendency | Through-the-cycle tendency | | :--- | :--- | :--- | | Current borrower information | High sensitivity | Greater emphasis on persistent characteristics | | Current macro conditions | More direct response | Temporary cyclical effects damped | | Rating migration | Typically more frequent through the cycle | Typically more stable through ordinary cycles | | Near-term risk monitoring | Naturally responsive | Can lag rapid cyclical change if used alone | | Long-run calibration | May still require long-run anchoring depending on use | Does not automatically satisfy any regulatory calibration rule | A one-year PD can be PIT, TTC-like or somewhere between. Likewise, a lifetime forecast can use changing point-in-time macroeconomic paths. **Horizon and cyclical conditioning are separate axes.** Current borrower / macro conditions deteriorate ↓ PIT risk signal ↑ → PIT PD / migration ↑ Cycle-neutral design ↑ ↓ Cyclical responsiveness ↓ → Rating stability ↑ Upstream: Rating drivers · Macroeconomic information · Calibration philosophy This: Choose degree of current-condition sensitivity Downstream: PD movement · Rating migration · Pricing · Provisioning · Stress analysis PIT/TTC describes sensitivity to current and cyclical conditions; it does not by itself specify the PD horizon. **Point-in-time** — strong conditioning on information and conditions at the observation date. --- **Short horizon** — a forecast interval; it says nothing by itself about how cyclical information enters the model. **Through-the-cycle** — a rating philosophy designed to damp temporary cyclical movements. --- **Long-run average PD** — a calibration concept; averaging observed defaults is not by itself a TTC rating system. Calling a multi-year average default rate “TTC” without examining rating assignment, macro sensitivity and calibration confuses statistical smoothing with rating philosophy. **No delta.** Supervisors and accounting standards may require particular calibration or forward-looking treatment for specific uses, but PIT/TTC remains the same conceptual distinction.

title: Loss given default and recovery rate
one_screen: Loss given default is loss severity **conditional on default**. Collateral and guarantees influence LGD only through legally available, economically realised recovery value; an appraisal at origination is therefore an input to recovery expectations, not the LGD itself.
bodyText: ### Core mechanism | LGD driver | Effect on net recovery | | :--- | :--- | | Borrower post-default payments | Increase recovery | | Collateral sale proceeds | Increase recovery after priority and costs | | Guarantee proceeds | Increase recovery if guarantee is enforceable and guarantor performs | | Legal / collection / maintenance costs | Reduce recovery | | Delay to recovery | Reduces present value | | Seniority and prior claims | Determine how recovery value is shared | | Downturn conditions | Can reduce collateral prices and recovery capacity together | A simple `1 − recovery rate` relationship is valid only when recovery rate and LGD use the same exposure base, cash-flow perimeter, costs and discounting convention. Default → Gross recoveries ↓ Subtract workout costs ↓ Discount to default date ↓ Net recovery / EAD → Recovery rate ↓ LGD = 1 − recovery rate Upstream: Default · EAD · Security/guarantee rights · Workout cash flows This: Collect gross recoveries → subtract costs → discount → compare with EAD Downstream: Expected loss · Pricing · Capital parameters · Workout benchmarking `LGD = (EAD − PV(net recoveries)) / EAD` `Recovery rate = PV(net recoveries) / EAD` Under aligned definitions: `LGD = 1 − recovery rate`. Recovery delay ↑ or workout costs ↑ → PV(net recoveries) ↓ → LGD ↑. Measure LGD from the default event using a consistent exposure base and economically complete recovery cash flows. **Collateral value** — one potential source of recovery, subject to legal rights, priority, sale value, time and costs. --- **LGD** — total economic loss severity conditional on default across all recovery sources and costs. `LGD = 1 − collateral value / current balance` ignores pre-default drawings, borrower payments, guarantor proceeds, senior claims, costs, timing and collateral-value stress. **No delta in the economic mechanism.** Prudential frameworks differ in recognised collateral, supervisory or internal LGDs, downturn treatment, floors and discounting rules.

title: Exposure at default and credit conversion factors
one_screen: Exposure at default estimates or prescribes how much is exposed when default occurs, not how much is drawn today. Credit conversion factors translate undrawn or contingent amounts into exposure, making pre-default utilisation behaviour part of credit risk.
bodyText: ### Core mechanism | Facility component | Credit question | | :--- | :--- | | Current drawn amount | What is already exposed? | | Undrawn commitment | How much can still be drawn before default? | | Contingent item | What amount can crystallise into a claim? | | Accrued interest/fees | What additional amount may be outstanding at default under the chosen basis? | | Limit cancellation / draw-stop behaviour | How much future drawdown is actually possible? | For a fully drawn amortising loan, EAD can be close to expected balance at default. For cards, overdrafts and revolving commitments, distressed borrowers may draw further before failure, so current utilisation can materially understate EAD. Current drawn amount + Undrawn / contingent amount ↓ Apply drawdown / CCF logic ↓ Additional pre-default exposure ↓ EAD at default Upstream: Facility limit · Drawn balance · Undrawn amount · Behaviour · Default date This: Convert relevant off-balance / undrawn amount → add to default exposure Downstream: Expected loss · LGD denominator · Regulatory RWA · Limit analysis Teaching decomposition: `CCF = additional pre-default drawing / undrawn amount at reference date` `EAD = current drawn amount + CCF × undrawn amount` CCF ↑ → EAD ↑, all else equal. This is not a universal regulatory formula; applicable frameworks prescribe treatment by exposure type and approach. EAD is anchored to the default event. Current balance is an input, not the definition. **EAD** — exposure expected or prescribed at default. --- **Current utilisation** — amount drawn now, often expressed relative to the facility limit. Estimating revolving-credit loss on today’s balance while LGD is measured against default-date exposure creates a denominator mismatch and usually understates drawdown risk. **No delta in the mechanism.** Regulatory conversion factors, modelling permissions and off-balance-sheet exposure rules differ by jurisdiction and prudential approach.

title: Expected loss: PD × LGD × EAD
one_screen: `EL = PD × LGD × EAD` is a compact one-period loss decomposition only when the three inputs describe compatible default events, horizons, populations and economic conditions. The arithmetic is trivial; parameter alignment is the real mechanism.
bodyText: ### Core mechanism | Parameter | Role in loss | Alignment test | | :--- | :--- | :--- | | PD | Chance default occurs | Same default event and horizon as the loss measurement | | LGD | Severity if default occurs | Conditional on that same default definition and exposure basis | | EAD | Amount exposed at default | Measured for the same default event and population | For a low-PD loan, the most likely realised loss may be zero while expected loss is positive. EL is an average across possible outcomes, not a prediction that every individual exposure will lose a fractional amount. Dependence can hide inside the inputs. Revolving utilisation and recovery severity can both worsen around default or in recessions. Multiplying three independently estimated averages without considering their conditional meaning can therefore misstate the true expectation. Align PD event / horizon + LGD conditional basis + EAD default basis ↓ PD × LGD × EAD ↓ Expected loss ↓ Aggregate across exposures → Portfolio EL Upstream: PD · LGD · EAD with aligned definitions This: Probability × Severity × Exposure Downstream: Pricing · Portfolio EL · Provision/capital comparison · Profitability `EL = PD × LGD × EAD` Example: `2% × 40% × 100 = 0.8` monetary units. PD ↑, LGD ↑ or EAD ↑ → EL ↑, holding the other inputs constant. Reconcile event, horizon, population, observation point and valuation basis before multiplying PD, LGD and EAD. **Expected loss** — probability-weighted average loss over the defined horizon. --- **Most likely loss** — the modal outcome; for many low-PD exposures it is zero. Combining a regulatory one-year PD, a lifetime accounting LGD and today’s balance creates a numeric answer whose components do not describe one coherent loss experiment. #### IN (RBI) For covered commercial banks, RBI’s 2026 Asset Classification, Provisioning and Income Recognition Directions mandate an expected-credit-loss provisioning framework from **1 April 2027**. **No delta in the probability decomposition.** Regulatory capital, accounting ECL and internal economics prescribe different parameter horizons, conditions and treatments; the same formula label does not make those calculations interchangeable.

title: Retail versus wholesale credit modelling
one_screen: Retail credit is usually managed through large pools of comparatively homogeneous exposures, making repeated statistical patterns powerful evidence. Wholesale credit is usually more obligor-centred because exposures are larger, populations are smaller and borrower-specific financial, structural and legal information matters more.
bodyText: ### Core mechanism | Dimension | Retail tendency | Wholesale tendency | | :--- | :--- | :--- | | Number of exposures | Large | Smaller | | Individual exposure size | Comparatively small | Often material | | Homogeneity | Higher within designed segments | Lower | | Primary modelling unit | Pool / segment / facility behaviour | Obligor rating plus facility analysis | | Data evidence | Repeated behavioural observations | Financial statements, sector, management, structure, expert judgement | | Default application | Can permit facility/pool treatment under applicable rules | Generally obligor-centred in Basel-style wholesale frameworks | “Retail = model” and “wholesale = judgement” is too crude. Retail systems still need policy, overrides and fraud controls; wholesale ratings can use powerful quantitative models. The difference is how much **repeatable population evidence** versus **case-specific information** can support the decision. Exposure population ↓ Size + homogeneity + data density + materiality ↓ Retail-like → Pool / segment statistical treatment Wholesale-like → Obligor-centred rating + facility analysis Upstream: Exposure type · Population size · Homogeneity · Data density · Materiality This: Choose pooled statistical treatment or obligor-centred assessment Downstream: Segmentation · Scorecards · Ratings · PD/LGD/EAD estimation · Validation Choose the modelling unit and method to match the economic homogeneity, data density and materiality of the exposures. **Retail modelling** — pool-oriented estimation using repeated observations with similar risk characteristics. --- **Automated lending** — an operational decision process; retail credit can include manual review, and wholesale credit can use automation. Applying a mass-retail scorecard to a small, heterogeneous set of large corporates creates apparent statistical precision without a genuinely comparable population. **No delta in the economic logic.** Regulatory definitions determine which exposures qualify for retail or wholesale treatment and can impose size, pooling or management criteria.

title: Application, behavioural and bureau credit data
one_screen: Application models use information available at or before origination; behavioural models use information generated after the relationship exists; bureau or credit-information data add externally reported indebtedness and repayment history. Their common discipline is **time**: only information genuinely available at the decision or observation date may enter the prediction.
bodyText: ### Core mechanism | Information source | Observation point | Typical content | Limitation | | :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- | | Application | Origination | Declared/verified income, financials, demographics permitted by law, requested facility | No future account behaviour exists yet | | Internal behaviour | Post-origination | Payments, utilisation, arrears, balance trends, excesses | Requires account seasoning and clean observation windows | | Bureau / credit information | External reported history available at observation date | Other obligations, balances, enquiries, repayment history | Coverage, reporting lag, errors and thin files | | Policy / affordability | Decision-time rules | Eligibility, repayment capacity, limits | Not itself a statistical score | A bureau score or internal score is not automatically a PD. It must have a defined target, population and calibration. A “clean” thin file is also weaker evidence than a long clean history: absence of observed problems can mean absence of observation. Application data + bureau data available at origination ↓ Application score → Calibration → PD / credit decision Account opens ↓ Internal behaviour + refreshed bureau data ↓ Behavioural score → Calibration → PD / monitoring Upstream: Decision date · Application data · Bureau snapshot · Internal account history This: Define observation window → build score/ranking → calibrate if probability needed Downstream: Approve/decline · Limit/pricing · Behavioural monitoring · PD · Collections A model may use only information that was available at the point in time at which the prediction is supposed to be made. **Application score** — risk ranking from information available around origination. --- **Behavioural score** — risk ranking from subsequent account-performance information. **Clean bureau** — no adverse event observed in the covered reported history. --- **Strong repayment capacity** — sustainable ability to meet future obligations from cash flow or resources; bureau history is only one input. Allowing later delinquency, post-decision bureau updates or other future information into an origination model creates target leakage and makes model performance look unrealistically strong. **No delta in the modelling logic.** Data availability, permissible variables, consumer rights, credit-reporting frequency and automated-decision requirements vary materially by law and jurisdiction.

title: Rating grades, master scales and migration
one_screen: A rating grade is a discrete class of borrower credit quality; a master scale defines the ordered meaning of all grades; migration records movement through that scale over time. A grade is not meaningful because it is called “4” or “BBB-like”—its meaning comes from assignment criteria, ordering, default boundary and calibrated risk.
bodyText: ### Core mechanism | Element | Owns | Test of quality | | :--- | :--- | :--- | | Rating criteria | How an obligor is assigned | Consistent use of relevant risk drivers | | Master scale | Ordered risk states | Clear monotonic deterioration from strong to weak | | Grade PD | Probability attached to grade/pool | Calibration consistent with observed/default definition | | Override | Governed expert departure | Reason, authority and performance tracked | | Migration | Movement between grades | Stable state definitions through time | | Default grade | Terminal/default state for the relevant system | Aligned with governed default definition | A transition matrix counts or estimates movement from each starting grade to each ending grade over a fixed interval, including default. Migration separates a static stock of weak borrowers from a portfolio actively deteriorating toward those grades. Borrower information → Rating assessment / score → Grade ↓ Master-scale position → Grade PD ↓ New information → Upgrade / downgrade / default Upstream: Borrower information · Rating philosophy · PD calibration This: Assign grade → map to master scale → observe migration through time Downstream: Limits · Pricing · Monitoring · PD validation · Capital · Early warning ### Ownership | Role | Responsibility | | :--- | :--- | | Produces | Rating model/process assigns and documents the grade | | Approves | Credit authority or rating governance confirms assignment/override where required | | Consumes | Underwriting, portfolio monitoring, pricing, capital and reporting | | Challenges | Independent credit risk, model validation and audit test scale performance | A grade must retain a stable, documented meaning if historical default and migration statistics are to remain comparable. **Rating migration** — the obligor moves from one risk grade to another. --- **PD recalibration** — the probability mapped to a grade or score changes; the grade label can remain unchanged. Changing grade criteria and then analysing the old and new labels as one continuous transition history produces false migration statistics. **No delta in the concept.** Regulatory frameworks differ in rating-system granularity, approval, floors, use tests and validation requirements.

title: Vintage analysis and roll rates
one_screen: Vintage analysis follows exposures originated at similar times as they season; roll-rate analysis follows movement between delinquency or credit states. Both restore the time dimension that a portfolio snapshot destroys.
bodyText: ### Core mechanism | Method | Groups by | Compares | Best at revealing | | :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- | | Vintage | Origination period | Performance at the same months-on-book | Underwriting/channel/cohort changes | | Roll rate | Current credit state | Next-period movement to worse, same or better state | Direction and speed of delinquency | | Snapshot | Observation date | Stock in each state today | Current composition only | A six-month-old cohort and a three-year-old cohort have had different time to season. Comparing their cumulative defaults on the same calendar date confounds credit quality with age. Vintage curves instead align performance at month 1, month 2, month 3 and so on. Roll rates answer a different question: of accounts now at 30–59 DPD, how many cure, stay, move to 60–89 DPD or default next period? Identical current delinquency stocks can therefore hide opposite future directions. Vintage: Origination cohort → MOB 1 → MOB 2 → MOB 3 → … → cumulative delinquency / default ↓ Compare later vintages at the same months-on-book Roll rate: Current → Early delinquency → Later delinquency → Default state ↓ At each step: cure / stay / worsen Upstream: Origination date · Account age · DPD/default states · Observation history This: Cohort by vintage OR transition by state Downstream: Early warning · Collections capacity · Forecasting · Policy review · Model validation Illustrative one-step roll rate: `Roll rate(i → j) = count/exposure moving from state i to state j / starting count/exposure in state i` The numerator and denominator must use the same population basis and interval. Compare like with like in time: equal seasoning for vintages, and fixed start/end states and intervals for roll rates. **Vintage analysis** — follows origination cohorts through account age. --- **Roll-rate analysis** — follows transitions between credit or delinquency states through time. A fast-growing young book can look safer than a mature book simply because many accounts have not existed long enough to reach default. **No delta.** These are analytical methods; local definitions determine the delinquency and default states being tracked.

title: Concentration and diversification
one_screen: Concentration risk arises when too much exposure depends on the same name, connected group, sector, geography, collateral type or underlying economic driver. Diversification comes from genuinely different sources of loss, not from the number of rows, facilities or legal entities in a dataset.
bodyText: ### Core mechanism | Concentration form | Common failure source | Example diagnostic | | :--- | :--- | :--- | | Single name | One obligor | Exposure / capital or portfolio share | | Connected group | Control or economic dependency | Aggregated group exposure | | Sector | Common industry conditions | Sector share and stressed sector loss | | Geography | Local economy / law / property market | Regional exposure share | | Product / collateral | Common underwriting or recovery mechanism | Product or collateral-type share | | Hidden factor | Shared commodity, customer, currency or funding driver | Factor mapping / scenario analysis | Ten equal exposures to genuinely independent obligors diversify idiosyncratic failure better than one exposure of the same total size. One thousand borrowers can still be concentrated if most depend on the same property market or commodity price. Shared obligor / group / sector / geography / factor ↓ Common exposure dependence ↓ Concentration ↑ → Diversification benefit ↓ ↓ Tail-loss sensitivity ↑ Upstream: Aggregated exposure · Connected groups · Sector/geography/factor tags This: Identify common loss drivers → measure concentration → compare with limits/appetite Downstream: Limit actions · Portfolio steering · Stress testing · Pillar 2 / capital assessment ### Ownership | Role | Responsibility | | :--- | :--- | | Produces | Risk data and portfolio teams aggregate exposures and common drivers | | Approves | Board/senior risk governance sets appetite and concentration limits | | Consumes | Underwriting, limits, strategy, stress testing and capital planning | | Challenges | Independent risk and audit test aggregation, taxonomy and limit exceptions | Diversification must be judged by independence of loss drivers, not by nominal borrower count. **Concentration** — dependence on a common source of loss, which may be name, sector, geography, collateral or another factor. --- **Large exposure** — an exposure or connected-group exposure meeting a defined regulatory or internal size threshold; concentration is broader. Splitting one economic group across subsidiaries or one common sector across narrow industry codes can improve a report while leaving the underlying loss concentration unchanged. #### IN (RBI) RBI’s Large Exposures Framework governs prudential single-counterparty and connected-counterparty aggregation and limits. Internal concentration management must still capture sector and common-factor risks outside the legal large-exposure perimeter. #### UK (PRA) PRA large-exposure rules and SS3/25 govern connected-client identification; concentration risk also feeds broader supervisory and Pillar 2 assessment. #### EU CRR large-exposure rules constrain single clients and groups of connected clients; broader concentration risk remains a risk-management and supervisory concern. #### US US legal lending limits use US-specific aggregation rules. Internal sector and factor concentration management is broader than statutory single-borrower limits.

title: Correlation and systematic credit risk
one_screen: Credit correlation means default and loss outcomes are not independent because common economic forces move many borrowers together. Idiosyncratic risk can be diversified across sufficiently independent exposures; systematic risk cannot be removed by adding more borrowers exposed to the same underlying conditions.
bodyText: ### Core mechanism | Risk source | Example | Diversification effect | | :--- | :--- | :--- | | Idiosyncratic | Fraud, plant failure, loss of one customer | Falls as many independent names are added | | Sector systematic | Commodity-price collapse, industry disruption | Persists across borrowers in the same sector | | Macro systematic | Recession, unemployment, rate shock | Can affect many sectors and borrowers together | | Recovery dependence | Property prices fall during mortgage defaults | Defaults and LGDs can worsen together | | Utilisation dependence | Revolvers draw in stress | Defaults and EAD can worsen together | Correlation does not require equal PDs. A 1% PD firm and a 5% PD firm can still become riskier at the same time because both respond to recession, rates or a common customer base. Idiosyncratic shock → One / few obligors → Diversification impact ↓ Systematic shock → Many obligors deteriorate together → Correlated defaults ↓ Clustered losses → Portfolio tail ↑ → Capital pressure ↑ Upstream: Individual PDs · Common economic factors · Sector/geography links This: Common shock → joint deterioration/default → clustered losses Downstream: Portfolio loss tail · Stress testing · Diversification benefit · Capital For default indicators `D₁` and `D₂`, positive dependence means: `P(D₁ = 1 and D₂ = 1) > P(D₁ = 1) × P(D₂ = 1)` in the simple comparison to independence. Positive dependence ↑ → probability of clustered losses ↑ → tail loss ↑, all else equal. Adding exposures diversifies risk only to the extent that their failure drivers are not the same. **Correlation** — dependence between credit outcomes. --- **Concentration** — disproportionate exposure to names or common drivers; concentration magnifies the consequence of dependence but is not the same concept. Assuming legal independence implies default independence systematically understates loss clustering during common economic stress. **No delta.** Correlation and systematic risk are economic and statistical properties; prudential frameworks differ in how dependence is parameterised, stressed or capitalised.

title: Unexpected loss and capital
one_screen: Expected loss is the average credit cost under a defined measurement; unexpected loss is adverse variation around that average. Capital protects solvency against sufficiently severe outcomes above ordinary expected-loss capacity, so portfolio dispersion and dependence matter even when exposure-level EL is unchanged.
bodyText: ### Core mechanism | Layer | Question | Main drivers | | :--- | :--- | :--- | | Expected loss | What loss is anticipated on average? | PD, LGD, EAD and their aligned conditioning | | Loss volatility | How much can realised loss vary? | Granularity, parameter variation, migration | | Tail / unexpected loss | How severe can adverse loss become above the mean? | Concentration, correlation, systematic stress | | Capital | What loss-absorbing resources protect solvency? | Prudential/economic confidence standard and capital rules | Two portfolios can have identical EL but very different tail risk. One may contain thousands of diversified exposures; another may depend on a few correlated names. Their average loss can match while their severe-loss quantiles do not. Exposure losses ↓ Expected loss = mean ↓ Concentration + correlation + systematic stress ↓ Loss distribution widens ↓ Tail above EL = unexpected loss ↓ Capital Upstream: Exposure-level EL · Concentration · Correlation · Stress This: Build portfolio loss distribution → identify adverse tail above EL Downstream: Regulatory/economic capital · Risk appetite · Pricing return-on-capital · Limits Conceptual decomposition: `Unexpected loss ≈ high loss quantile − expected loss` This is a mental model, not a universal regulatory capital formula. Basel IRB risk-weight functions incorporate prescribed dependence, confidence and other parameters rather than applying this subtraction mechanically. Expected loss and capital answer different questions: average credit cost versus protection against adverse loss beyond that average. **Expected loss** — probability-weighted average credit loss for the defined measurement. --- **Capital** — loss-absorbing resources held under a regulatory or internal solvency framework; it is not simply `PD × LGD × EAD`. Calling exposure-level EL “capital” ignores diversification, correlation, concentration and the shape of the portfolio loss distribution. **No delta in the conceptual split.** Regulatory capital formulas, buffers, Pillar 2 practices and accounting/provision regimes vary materially across jurisdictions.

title: The credit-loss architecture
one_screen: Credit risk is one continuous system: identify the person and exposure, decide whether repayment is sustainable, recognise default consistently, measure probability, severity and exposure, then aggregate common loss drivers into portfolio tail risk. The architecture fails when adjacent layers are collapsed—for example, collateral into repayment capacity, DPD into default, score into PD, or expected loss into capital.
bodyText: ### Core mechanism | Layer | Owns the question | Core objects | | :--- | :--- | :--- | | Credit object | Who owes what? | Obligor · Facility · Account · Exposure · Connected group | | Credit decision | Should this risk be taken and on what terms? | Policy · Repayment capacity · Approval · Mitigants | | Credit state | Has contractual credit performance failed under the governed rule? | DPD · UTP · Default · Restructuring · Cure · Write-off | | Risk parameters | How likely, how severe, how much exposed? | PD · LGD · EAD | | Expected loss | What is the average loss cost? | PD × LGD × EAD under aligned definitions | | Risk measurement system | How is risk ranked and observed through time? | Retail pools · Scores · Bureau data · Ratings · Migration · Vintages | | Portfolio tail | What can fail together? | Concentration · Correlation · Systematic risk | | Solvency protection | What absorbs severe loss above the mean? | Unexpected loss · Capital | Obligor + Facility + Exposure ↓ Underwriting: repayment capacity first ↓ Collateral / guarantees as secondary mitigants ↓ Performing → Deterioration → Default → Cure / Re-default / Recovery ↓ PD + LGD + EAD ↓ Expected loss ↓ Concentration + Correlation + Systematic stress ↓ Unexpected loss ↓ Capital Keep each layer’s question separate, then connect the outputs deliberately. A precise answer at the wrong layer is still the wrong risk measure. **Expected loss capacity** — pricing, provisions/allowances or other mechanisms that recognise and absorb anticipated credit cost under the applicable framework. --- **Capital** — resources protecting solvency against adverse outcomes beyond ordinary expected loss, under the applicable capital regime. A credit pack becomes incoherent when the same label is used for several layers—for example “risk” meaning score, PD, EL, provision and capital depending on the page. Always name the object, state and measure. **No delta.** The architecture is universal. Jurisdictions differ in prudential definitions, accounting treatment, regulatory formulas, thresholds and legal enforceability, but those variants sit inside the same object → state → parameter → portfolio-loss chain.

title: Risk Data as a Discipline
one_screen: In the 2007–2009 financial crisis, banks could not aggregate their risk exposures quickly or accurately. This failure impaired timely decision-making, prompting regulators to formalize risk data management as a discipline (e.g. Basel BCBS 239) to ensure banks maintain accurate, timely, end-to-end risk data aggregation and reporting.
bodyText: Banks historically maintained data in silos and spreadsheets, impeding a holistic risk view. When Lehman Brothers collapsed in 2008, many institutions realized their systems could not tell the board or regulators the full picture of their exposures. The Basel Committee responded with BCBS 239 (2013) to “strengthen banks’ risk data aggregation capabilities and internal risk reporting practices”. Globally systemically important banks (G-SIBs) had to comply by 2016; supervisors applied similar standards to domestic SIBs. In practice, risk data discipline means implementing corporate-wide data governance, architecture and controls so that any material risk metric can be produced “fully, quickly and accurately.” This underpins effective risk management and regulatory compliance. Key outcomes of this discipline include board-level data governance, documented processes, and accountability for data quality. It also requires banks to invest in integrated data architectures and automation, since manual consolidation is deemed unacceptable. The discipline encompasses ongoing improvement: recent Basel progress reports note that, years on, many banks still need work to fully meet BCBS 239. +----------------+ +----------------+ +----------------+ | Risk Data in |-----> | Data Governance|-----> | Risk Decisions | | Siloes | | Frameworks | | and Reporting | +----------------+ +----------------+ +----------------+ Timely, accurate risk data is essential for sound decision-making and regulatory compliance. Relying on last-minute, manual spreadsheet aggregations (especially during stress) can give a false sense of security. **Risk data** — Information on potential losses or exposures (e.g. credit, market risk metrics). It is forward-looking and used for risk management. --- **Accounting (financial) data** — Realized financial transactions (P&L, balance sheets) as recorded in accounts.
