Risk data and accounting data serve different purposes and must be reconciled, not conflated. **No delta.** The need for robust risk data aggregation and reporting is a universal lesson from the financial crisis.

title: Risk Data Aggregation vs Risk Reporting
one_screen: Risk data aggregation is the internal process of collecting and consolidating all relevant risk data across the bank. Risk reporting is the output of that process, conveying the aggregated data in reports. BCBS 239 treats them as separate obligations: the former ensures data is accurate and complete; the latter ensures reports are clear and delivered on time.
bodyText: Risk data aggregation focuses on gathering data points (e.g. exposures, positions) from all business lines, legal entities and regions into a single view. It requires data warehousing, reconciliation with accounting systems, and automated controls to meet BCBS 239’s principles on accuracy, completeness, timeliness and adaptability. By contrast, risk reporting is about designing and distributing the reports themselves. It covers how aggregated data is formatted, explained and delivered to decision-makers and regulators. Reporting practices include ensuring reports are “accurate, comprehensive, and written for their intended audience” with appropriate frequency and escalation paths. In effect, aggregation is about the data pipelines (the “back office” work) and reporting is about the presentation. For example, Principle 4 (completeness) demands data from *all* material sources be captured, whereas Principle 9 (clarity) demands that reports be understandable to non-technical users. A bank may have strong data pipelines but still produce poor reports if it fails the latter principle. BCBS 239 Group II (Principles 3–6) governs aggregation; Group III (Principles 7–11) governs reporting. Both must be in place: good aggregation without clear reporting fails to inform stakeholders, and good reports without sound data defeat regulators’ objectives. Data Aggregation Data Reporting +--------+ +---------+ | Systems|--extract/ETL-->| Reports |---> Stakeholders +--------+ mapping +---------+ | ^ v | Aggregate, Reconcile Validate (content, format) Aggregation and reporting are distinct steps: you must first consolidate all required data, then use it in reports designed for the audience. Fixating on report templates or dashboards without ensuring the underlying data is comprehensive and reconciled leads to misleading outputs. **Risk data aggregation** — Internal consolidation of all risk data (the “what” and “how” data is collected). --- **Risk reporting** — The communication of aggregated risk metrics (the “presentation” of that data to management/regulators). **No delta.** All jurisdictions distinguish between banks’ data-processing capabilities and the reports they deliver to supervisors.

title: BCBS 239 Principles Overview
one_screen: BCBS 239 comprises 14 principles organized in four groups: (I) Governance & Infrastructure (board accountability, data architecture), (II) Risk Data Aggregation Capabilities (accuracy, completeness, timeliness, adaptability), (III) Risk Reporting Practices (comprehensiveness, clarity, frequency, distribution), and (IV) Supervisory Review (how regulators assess banks). Together they form a principles-based framework requiring banks to implement robust data policies and systems.
bodyText: BCBS 239’s purpose is to ensure banks can identify their risk exposures at any time. It mandates that the board of directors oversee data quality, and that the Chief Risk Officer is accountable day-to-day. Principle 1 demands “strong governance” consistent with other Basel standards, and Principle 2 requires a data architecture that supports aggregation in normal and stress conditions (avoiding last-minute spreadsheets). The second group (Principles 3–6) then focuses on aggregation: data must reconcile with accounting, cover all material sources (at least ~95%), be updated rapidly (daily or intraday for critical metrics), and support ad hoc queries under stress. The third group (Principles 7–11) covers reporting: risk reports must be “accurate, comprehensive, and written for their intended audience,” delivered at appropriate frequency, and distributed along the approved chain of command. Finally, Principles 12–14 describe supervisory review: they guide how regulators should evaluate compliance, require remediation plans for deficiencies, and address home/host coordination for global banks. BCBS 239 is principles-based: it does not prescribe specific IT architectures but sets outcomes. National supervisors (e.g. PRA in the UK, Fed in the US, RBI in India) expect banks to meet these outcomes, potentially imposing Pillar 2 add-ons for serious shortcomings. The standard has no formal legal force by itself; compliance is enforced through local regulation and supervision. +------------------------+ +----------------------------+ | Governance & Infra | | Risk Reporting Practices | | (Principles 1–2) | | (Principles 7–11) | +------------------------+ +----------------------------+ | ^ v | +------------------------+ +----------------------------+ | Data Aggregation | | Supervisory Review | | (Principles 3–6) | | (Principles 12–14) | +------------------------+ +----------------------------+ The board of directors must ultimately own the risk data framework, not just delegate it to IT – strong governance is mandatory. Treating BCBS 239 as optional guidance; in practice, major regulators treat it as mandatory for significant banks. **BCBS 239** — Basel Committee principles for risk data aggregation and reporting. Its focus is data and reporting quality. --- **Basel III/CRR** — Regulatory framework for capital and liquidity. While related to risk, Basel III addresses capital adequacy, not data architecture. **No delta.** The 14 principles and their objectives are identical globally; they were adopted for G-SIBs with the same intent by all major regulators.

title: Risk Data Aggregation Capabilities (Accuracy, Completeness, Timeliness, Adaptability)
one_screen: BCBS 239 mandates that a bank’s risk data aggregation be **accurate, complete, timely, and adaptable**. In practice, this means automated data pipelines, extensive reconciliations, and flexible reporting capabilities. Banks must reconcile risk data with accounting records, cover ~95% of exposures across all entities, refresh data fast (daily or intraday for critical metrics), and be able to run ad-hoc reports on demand.
bodyText: The principle of **Accuracy and Integrity** (Principle 3) requires that risk data reconcile with the general ledger and management reports, and that automated checks minimize manual errors. Any manual adjustments must have documented rationale and approval. **Completeness** (Principle 4) means capturing data across all material business lines, legal entities and geographies. Supervisors typically expect banks to cover at least 95% of risk sources; any gaps trigger examination findings. **Timeliness** (Principle 5) demands that consolidated risk metrics be available fast enough for decision-making in stress; for example, daily VaR and credit portfolio reports as a baseline, potentially intraday for key measures. Finally, **Adaptability** (Principle 6) requires systems to produce new, ad-hoc reports quickly – for instance, answering a one-off supervisory query without months of coding. Banking institutions implement these requirements by building data warehouses or data lakes that collect source-system data nightly (or more frequently) and standardizing it. They set quality rules so that any discrepancy (e.g. mismatched values) is flagged. Importantly, the infrastructure must operate in crisis scenarios as well (e.g. with market freezes or system outages) to ensure data is still deliverable. The perpetual struggle is that legacy siloed systems and manual processes often fall short of these standards, which is why many banks have ongoing data improvement programs. Nonetheless, under BCBS 239, the **permanent requirement** is clear: all material risk data must be consolidated accurately and on time. ```text Risk aggregation must cover all material data and reconcile to accounting — incomplete or unverified data is unacceptable. Assuming that old processes (e.g. monthly spreadsheet closes) are sufficient; BCBS 239 expects daily or intraday capabilities and automation. **Completeness** — capturing *all* relevant risk data (nearly 100% coverage). --- **Consistency (or validity)** — ensuring data adheres to business rules. While related, completeness means no gaps, consistency means matching definitions. **No delta.** Data aggregation requirements (accuracy, completeness, etc.) are consistent under BCBS 239 across jurisdictions, as these are quantitative targets not subject to local modification.

title: Risk Reporting Practices
one_screen: BCBS 239 requires risk reports to be **accurate, comprehensive, clear, frequent, and properly distributed**. Reports must be tailored to their audience (e.g. board vs risk manager) and sufficiently granular. This ensures stakeholders get the right information at the right time.
bodyText: A bank’s risk reports should paint a complete picture: covering all major risk types (credit, market, liquidity, etc.) and including both totals and trend analysis. They must be error-free and understandable; jargon must be explained for non-experts. BCBS 239 (Principle 7–11) says reports should be of high quality (“comprehensive, timely, clear”) and delivered at the mandated frequency. For instance, daily and weekly dashboards for market risk, and periodic reports for portfolios, with exceptions escalated as needed. The reports must include documented definitions (so recipients know what each metric means) and must follow a regular schedule. Distribution (Principle 11) demands reports go to the right people (board, risk committee, regulators) and that escalation paths exist if limits are breached. In summary, risk reporting is about governance of the report content and process: it involves standard templates, sign-off procedures, and validation checks (ensuring the report matches the aggregated data). A common failure (trap) is producing reports without reconciling them back to source data (so-called “data drift”). Another mistake is listing raw data without analysis. Regulators have noted banks sometimes produce stat sheets but not insightful narrative or exception lists. Under BCBS 239, the **permanent expectation** is that reports translate data into actionable intelligence, validated end-to-end. Each risk report must be accompanied by context and definition, and approved by the appropriate officer; raw numbers alone are insufficient. Dumping large tables of figures in a report with no explanatory content or without ensuring they match the underlying data. **Frequency** vs **Response Time**: Frequency — how often reports are published (e.g. daily, monthly). Response Time (Timeliness) — how quickly updated data is produced during stress. Reporting frequency must align with decision needs but is not the same as intraday data availability. **No delta.** These qualitative reporting expectations are set at the global level by BCBS 239; national supervisors typically echo them.

title: Supervisory Review and Compliance Record
one_screen: The final BCBS 239 principles cover supervisory review (Principles 12–14) and require banks to act on regulators’ findings. By 2023, global reports show banks remain at “different stages” of compliance and need significant work to meet the standard.
bodyText: Principles 12–14 instruct how supervisors should review the data framework and require remediation if the bank’s practices are deficient. They encourage cross-border coordination for global groups, and detail potential supervisory measures (e.g. requiring capital add-ons for data weaknesses). In effect, they push banks to treat risk data as a first-class issue. Recent Basel progress reports note that almost a decade after BCBS 239’s publication, no major bank is fully compliant. The press release observes “banks are at different stages of alignment” and “additional work is required at all banks to attain or sustain full compliance”. Supervisors worldwide (Fed, ECB, PRA, RBI, etc.) have been pressing banks via Stress Test frameworks and Pillar 2 dialogues to close gaps. A critical point: BCBS 239 itself has no formal legal force (it relies on member commitments). In the UK, the PRA explicitly incorporates its expectations into SREP for major banks. The ECB can impose Pillar 2 guidance for data issues, and the Fed expects high-quality data for its FR Y-14 stress tests. Thus, compliance is enforced locally. Globally, the common narrative is that risk data deficiencies have been a repeat finding in audits and reviews. The **permanent expectation** is that any material data issue must be escalated and fixed, and supervisors will hold senior management accountable. BCBS 239 principles must be embedded institution-wide and are enforced by national regulators. Formal remediation plans are expected when issues are found. Treating audit comments on data as mere “to-dos” rather than core risk-control failures. Senior management must lead remediation. **BCBS 239** — A supervisory standard, not a law. --- **Accounting standard** — (e.g. IFRS) Rules for financial statements. BCBS 239 is about data systems, not accounting treatment. **No delta.** All major jurisdictions (UK PRA, ECB, Fed, RBI etc.) regard BCBS 239 outcomes as required for SIBs, though enforcement mechanisms vary.

title: Golden Source of Data
one_screen: A golden source is the single authoritative source of truth for a given data element across the organization. It contains the most accurate and up-to-date version of that data, and all systems reference this “one source” to avoid discrepancies.
bodyText: For example, a bank might designate one system or database as the golden source for the exchange rate used in all risk reports, or the official customer master record. All downstream processes then draw from that gold record. This prevents situations where different departments have conflicting values for the same metric. Building a golden source requires strong data governance: clear ownership of the data field, defined quality rules, and processes to update the source whenever new information arrives. The golden source concept is vital under BCBS 239 Principle 2 (Data Architecture): it supports reconciliation and ensures “a single, authoritative source” for each risk metric. Without it, banks often hit the trap of “multiple authorities” – e.g. one system reporting Value-at-Risk one way, another giving a different number. A common rule is that only the golden source can feed regulators; any other calculation must reconcile back to it. Golden source is sometimes synonymous with “source of truth” or “master dataset.” It is not static: it is updated continuously to reflect the latest true data. Achieving a golden source typically involves integrating data pipelines and may use technologies like master data management (MDM) tools. The permanent expectation is that *every key data field* has one golden source designated, so that accuracy and consistency are maintained. +-------------------------+ | Golden Source Database | +-------------------------+ ^ ^ ^ ^ | | | | +-----+ +---+ +---+ +---+ | CRM | | Trade | Market| ... | Sys | | Sys | Data | +-----+ +---+ +---+ +---+ For each key data element, the bank must designate one authoritative source and use it consistently. Allowing multiple “masters” for the same data field (e.g. one report using Core banking data, another using Risk system) causes conflicts and undermines trust. **Golden source** — The official, authoritative dataset for a piece of information. --- **Data lake** — A repository of raw data. A data lake is not by itself an authoritative source unless governance ensures it contains only validated data. **No delta.** The concept of a single authoritative source is best practice worldwide; regulators expect banks to avoid conflicting data sources.

title: Critical Data Elements (CDEs)
one_screen: Critical Data Elements (CDEs) are the data points an organization deems essential to its core operations, decision-making, and compliance. In banking, CDEs include fields like customer ID, credit exposure amounts, collateral valuations, etc. They require special governance attention since errors in CDEs can have significant impact.
bodyText: Organizations identify CDEs based on risk and business significance. For example, any data field that feeds risk-weight calculations or capital models would be a CDE. Under BCBS 239, regulators effectively treat all material risk data as CDEs. Good data governance frameworks inventory CDEs and assign them owners and stewards. The owner (often a senior business manager) is responsible for the definition and quality of each CDE; stewards implement controls and fixes. Marking data as “critical” means prioritizing quality rules, monitoring, and issue management for those fields. The idea is to avoid the opposite of the CDE philosophy: that all data gets equal, impractical scrutiny. By focusing on CDEs, banks can allocate resources to where mistakes matter most. Identifying CDEs is not a one-time task; it must be revisited as regulations and products change. +--------------+ | Data Governance Framework | +--------------+ | +-----------------------------+ | Critical Data Elements List | +-----------------------------+ / | \ / | \ [Customer ID] [Loan Amount] [FX Rate] ... Banks must explicitly identify and govern their critical data elements (CDEs) to ensure governance efforts focus on high-impact fields. Treating all data elements alike; without highlighting CDEs, governance becomes spread too thin. **CDE** — A specific field deemed critical (e.g. a risk exposure amount). --- **Data catalog** — A comprehensive inventory of all data assets (it may list CDEs but also all other fields). **No delta.** The notion of identifying and governing CDEs is best practice internationally (no one sets different rules on which fields count as “critical”).

title: Data Lineage (Business vs Technical)
one_screen: Data lineage tracks the journey of data from its origin to its final use. *Business lineage* is a high-level, user-friendly map of what data comes from where for reporting purposes; *technical lineage* is the detailed breakdown of data flows through systems and code. Both are essential for understanding and troubleshooting data issues.
bodyText: Business lineage answers “what data needed to produce a report and why.” It’s often documented in a business requirements document (BRD): e.g. a line item in a report is defined as “sum of loan commitments by country.” Technical lineage, by contrast, traces exactly how that sum is calculated: which tables in the core banking system, what transformations (aggregations, currency conversion) were applied, and how it moved into the data warehouse. Regulators and auditors require lineage evidence to trust reports. For instance, if a regulator sees a credit risk report, they may ask the bank to show the chain of systems and transformations leading to each number. Clear lineage helps identify root causes of data discrepancies. If a report number is wrong, technical lineage lets data engineers pinpoint where the anomaly occurred in the pipeline. Business lineage helps managers understand the impact (e.g. which products are affected). Both together provide a “complete picture.” Under BCBS 239, documenting lineage is part of demonstrating data governance; many banks include lineage diagrams in their data management plans. +---------------------+ | Business Lineage | +---------------------+ | Loan Commitments --| | by Region -> Report | +---------------------+ | v +-------------------------------+ | Technical Lineage | +-------------------------------+ | CoreBanking.Loans -> ETL -> | | DataWarehouse -> Report DB | +-------------------------------+ Always document both business and technical lineage when creating data flows or reports. This double perspective ensures clarity for both business and IT stakeholders. Providing only high-level lineage (“loans come from system X”) without the technical detail needed for audit. **Business lineage** — A high-level mapping (for example, “Loan system ⇒ (sum) ⇒ monthly risk report”), understandable by non-IT stakeholders. --- **Technical lineage** — A precise record of ETL steps, database tables and transformations that produce the data. **No delta.** Both forms of lineage are part of global data governance expectations (e.g. BCBS 239 Principle 2’s call for documented architecture).

title: Metadata and Business Glossary
one_screen: Metadata is “data about data” – information that defines and describes data elements. A business glossary is a centralized catalog of business terms and their definitions. Together, they ensure everyone has a common understanding of data definitions.
bodyText: For example, a report might include a column “Non-Performing Asset Ratio.” Metadata would record that this is calculated as “Total NPA amount / Total advances” and has business unit “Retail Loans.” The business glossary would define “Non-Performing Asset” (e.g. a loan overdue >90 days). Good metadata systems also track data source, format, and constraints for each field. Under RBI guidance, banks are urged to use common taxonomies and sync metadata across systems. This means aligning internal definitions with external ones (e.g. RBI’s definition of NPA). A single business glossary prevents mismatches where one department uses one term differently from another. Both metadata and glossary entries should have clear ownership, and be updated when policies change. This is a cornerstone of data governance: without metadata, reports can’t be properly interpreted and controls on data validity are weak. +----------------------+ | Business Glossary | +----------------------+ | Term | Definition | | NPA | ... | | PD | ... | +----------------------+ | v +-----------------------------+ | Metadata Repository | +-----------------------------+ | Field | Source | Type | ... | | NPA_Amount | CoreBanking | Curr. | ... | +-----------------------------+ All regulatory and risk data fields must have definitions and metadata documented, linked to the official business glossary. Assuming everyone understands a term; failing to codify definitions causes inconsistent reporting and confusion. **Metadata** — Details about data fields (type, format, source, lineage). --- **Business glossary** — A dictionary of business terms with plain-language definitions (bridges business and technical meaning). **No delta.** Standardizing metadata and glossaries is universally recommended (e.g. BIS mentions using international codes and definitions for RBI reporting).

title: Data Dictionary and Data Model
one_screen: A data dictionary is a detailed catalog of all fields (data elements), describing each one’s attributes (name, type, description, format, valid values, etc.). A data model (conceptual or logical) is a diagram showing entities and relationships between them. Together they help design systems and prevent misinterpretation.
bodyText: For instance, in a bank’s credit risk data model, entities might include `Customer`, `Loan`, `Collateral`. The data dictionary would list that `Loan.Amount` is a numeric field in rupees, defined as “principal outstanding.” The dictionary is a repository of these definitions for technical staff, while the model visualizes how `Loan` relates to `Customer` and `Collateral`. Having a data model ensures database tables and fields align with business concepts (avoids missing fields). The dictionary ensures anyone writing queries or reports knows exactly what each field means. Both should be version-controlled. When regulations introduce new report items, the dictionary/model must be updated. Without them, even a simple mapping exercise is error-prone, and data integration between systems becomes guesswork. +----------------+ +--------------+ +--------------+ | Customer |<----| Account |---->| Product | +----------------+ +--------------+ +--------------+ CustomerID AccountID ProductID Name CustID (FK) Name DOB Balance Type ... ... ... Every data field in any regulatory report or risk system must be defined in the data dictionary and accounted for in the data model. Skipping the dictionary for “obvious” fields; even basic terms like “balance” need precise definition in a banking context. **Data dictionary** — A detailed list of fields and technical specs for developers and analysts. --- **Data catalog** — A broader inventory (often tool-based) that may include the data dictionary and also lineage, quality metrics, etc. **No delta.** The use of data dictionaries and models is a technical practice not dictated by law; best practices are common globally.

title: Reference Data vs Master Data
one_screen: Master data consists of core business entities (e.g. customers, accounts, products) that are critical to operations, while reference data consists of standardized code sets or classifications (e.g. country codes, currency codes, security identifiers). Master data changes as business grows; reference data is relatively stable and often global (ISO codes, etc.).
bodyText: For example, a customer record (with name, KYC info) is master data; the country code “IN” used in an address is reference data. Master data is usually owned by business functions (e.g. front office), whereas reference data can be managed centrally (often by risk or finance teams). Both must be maintained carefully: a glitch in master data can misstate exposure for an entity; a stale reference code (like an outdated ISIN) can disrupt reporting. Regulatory data reporting relies on reference data standards (e.g. RBI may mandate ISO country codes in returns). Master data alignment ensures all systems recognize the same legal entity (which ties into entity resolution and LEIs). In practice, data governance tracks both types. Tools like MDM systems often manage master data, while governance tools or data catalogs manage reference codes. But conceptually, **never confusing** them is key. Reference data supports interpretation of master data. Master Data Reference Data +------------+ +--------------------+ | Customer | | Currency Codes | | Product | | Country Codes | | Account | | ISIN, Tickers | +------------+ +--------------------+ Maintain a single master record for each core entity and use standard reference data sets (e.g. ISO codes) across the bank. Letting departments define their own “local” reference lists (e.g. local sector codes instead of international standards), leading to integration headaches. **Master data** — Business-critical records (customers, accounts) that the bank transacts with. --- **Reference data** — Shared classification codes and lists (currency codes, country codes, industry codes) used for categorizing data. **No delta.** Distinction between master vs reference data is a general data management concept, not subject to regulatory variation.

title: Data Quality Dimensions
one_screen: Data quality is multi-dimensional. Key dimensions include **accuracy** (data correctly reflects reality), **completeness** (no missing values), **consistency** (data aligns across sources), **timeliness** (data is up-to-date and available when needed), **validity** (data follows defined formats and rules), and **uniqueness** (no duplicates).
bodyText: For regulatory reporting, all dimensions matter. For example, an asset balance must be accurate (matches the general ledger), complete (every balance is reported), valid (currency format, non-negative), and timely (as of the report date). Consistency ensures that if two reports reference the same exposure, they use the same amount. Defining these dimensions allows setting measurable targets: e.g. 99% of accounts must be filled (completeness threshold), or 100% of country codes must match ISO lists (validity). Banks implement data quality frameworks that automate checks against these dimensions. Scorecards might flag any loans with null values (completeness) or duplicate customer IDs (uniqueness). Working these dimensions into BCBS 239 compliance means building controls for each: reconciliation for accuracy, data completeness reports, etc. Data Quality Dimensions +-----------+-----------+-----------+ | Accuracy | Timeliness| Consistency| | Completeness| Validity| Uniqueness| +-----------+-----------+-----------+ All regulatory data must meet the necessary quality dimensions for its use. Missing or outdated key data invalidates a report. Focusing on only one dimension (e.g. only completeness) while ignoring others (like not verifying that “complete” data is accurate). **Accuracy** — Data matches the true value or source system. --- **Consistency** — Data is uniform across systems (e.g. same value for Customer ID in trading vs risk systems). **No delta.** Data quality dimensions are agreed best practice in all jurisdictions; regulators expect rigorous checks regardless of country.

title: Data Quality Rules, Thresholds, and Exception Management
one_screen: Data quality rules are specific checks or constraints (e.g. “loan amount ≥ 0”, “interest date must not precede loan date”). Thresholds set acceptable levels for quality metrics (e.g. “95% of records must be complete”). When data fails a rule or threshold, it is flagged as an exception to be investigated and resolved.
bodyText: For example, a completeness rule might state that 99% of trade records must have an associated counterparty ID. If only 97% do, that misses the threshold and triggers an exception report. Exception management then enters: the issue is logged with severity, root causes are analyzed (e.g. missing entries in a source feed), and corrective action is taken (perhaps a process fix or data backfill). Exception tracking tools or ticket systems typically record these issues. Banks document quality rules in their governance frameworks, often aligning with BCBS 239’s accuracy/integrity principle. At each reporting cycle, automated validators run the rules. Validations can be cross-checks (e.g. sum of sub-portfolios equals total) or plausibility checks (e.g. a ratio must lie in [0,100]). When thresholds are narrowly missed, some banks issue warnings; larger gaps may halt report submission until fixed. The **permanent expectation** is that no data anomaly goes unchecked. Adopting robust exception management means assigning issues to data stewards or owners, tracking SLA for fixes, and reporting status to management. Regulators have become wary of banks “papering over” persistent exceptions. Best practice is to classify and resolve high-impact exceptions immediately, while monitoring low-impact ones until clearance. Data Quality Framework +-------------------------+ +-------------+ +------------+ | Data Quality Rules |-->| Data Checks |-->| Reports | +-------------------------+ +-------------+ +------------+ Thresholds: 95% compliant ^ | v +--------------------------+ | Exceptions (tickets) | +--------------------------+ Every failed quality check must be logged and owned; unresolved exceptions compromise report integrity. Archiving known data issues without resolution, assuming they are “small” or won’t recur. **Data quality rule** — A specific constraint (e.g. a value range). --- **Threshold** — The allowable error rate (e.g. 1% missing data). **No delta.** These practices are part of robust data governance everywhere; regulators everywhere expect strict validation and issue tracking.

title: Reconciliation (Front-to-Back and Risk-to-Finance)
one_screen: Reconciliation is the process of comparing data between systems to detect and resolve differences. *Front-to-back* reconciliation ensures that transactions recorded in front-office systems (trading, loans booking) match entries in the back-office accounting system. *Risk-to-finance* reconciliation ensures that risk metrics (e.g. aggregated exposures) reconcile to financial accounts (e.g. total assets or regulatory capital). Both are critical controls for data integrity.
bodyText: Front-to-back reconciliation typically involves comparing trade tickets or loan disbursements against the general ledger entries. Any mismatch (e.g. a trade missing from the ledger) is investigated. For example, the Risk data might sum all counterparty exposures and compare to the Finance system’s total asset value. Discrepancies often arise from timing differences or mapping errors. A common permanent rule is to run these reconciliations daily or at least monthly; material breaks must be cleared before period-end. Risk-to-finance reconciliation is especially vital under BCBS 239. If a bank reports a credit exposure of ₹100 bn to risk management, the finance team’s asset ledger should also reflect ₹100 bn (allowing for minor classification differences). Regulators expect banks to explain any gaps. A perennial trap is to ignore small mismatches that then grow unnoticed. Instead, banks should categorize breaks (e.g. expected timing lag vs error) and resolve root causes. Reconciliation tasks often uncover underlying data issues (bad mappings, missing code standards) that feed back into data quality improvement. Perform both front-to-back and risk-to-finance reconciliations regularly; document and fix all significant breaks. Only reconciling at quarter-end or audit time. Instead, reconciliation must be integrated into daily processes. **Front-to-back reconciliation** — Comparing transactional data (front office) to accounting ledgers (back office). --- **Risk-to-finance reconciliation** — Comparing risk aggregate data (used in risk reports) to financial statements or accounting reports. **No delta.** These reconciliations are standard controls in all banks worldwide.

title: Data Ownership vs Stewardship
one_screen: **Data owners** are senior business managers who are accountable for data assets; **data stewards** are specialists who manage data quality day-to-day. The owner defines data policies and sets quality standards, while the steward implements these standards and handles operational issues.
bodyText: For each CDE or data domain, an owner is formally assigned (often at executive or business-unit level). The owner’s responsibilities include approving definitions and prioritizing data initiatives. A data steward (usually in risk or finance department) is then responsible for monitoring data quality, investigating issues, and coordinating fixes with IT and business teams. The Reserve Bank recommends clarifying these roles: assigning ownership of key data elements and requiring data stewards to update the data governance committee. In practice, confusion between these roles is a trap. If nobody is accountable, issues languish; if too many claim ownership, governance muddles. Clear role definitions – documented in a data governance policy – are essential. For example, the data owner might be the Head of Credit Risk for loan data, while the data steward is a risk analyst reporting to them. Together they ensure questions like “Who decides loan classification rules?” have an answer. Every critical data element must have a single business owner assigned (with ultimate accountability) and one or more stewards (with operational responsibilities). Assigning ownership to IT or multiple owners by default. Ownership should reside in the business line that “owns” the risk. **Data owner** — Business executive responsible for a domain or data set (e.g. loans, market data). Accountable for policies. --- **Data steward** — Practitioner who enforces data standards and quality, reports to the owner. **No delta.** Defining data ownership and stewardship is a standard governance practice across banks globally.

title: Data Governance Models
one_screen: Data governance models define how oversight is structured. Common models are *centralized* (a single data governance committee sets policies for all) and *federated* (each business unit has its own governance under corporate guidelines). RBI notes typical models based on process, subject area, or geography, but emphasizes business-function-based ownership.
bodyText: In a centralized model, a bank-wide data council or steering committee makes decisions on data standards and conflicts. This ensures consistency but can be slow to react. In a federated model, each line of business governs its own data (loans, payments, etc.) with a chief data steward, under high-level corporate policy. This is more agile but risks inconsistent rules. Many banks use a hybrid: enterprise-wide standards set by a central group, with subcommittees or local owners refining for their area. Choosing a model depends on bank size and culture. Large global banks often need a strong central committee (reporting to the board) to coordinate regional offices. A smaller bank might use a subject-based structure (e.g. separate governance for retail vs corporate banking data). RBI’s guidance suggests ownership should follow business functions, with an executive data governance committee and clear roles. Regardless of model, a permanent rule is that the structure and responsibilities must be documented. A trap is letting data governance stay informal or ad hoc. Best practice: publish an operating model (committees, roles, processes), and review it periodically. The goal is a sustainable model where policies are enforced, quality is measured (e.g. via KPIs), and issue remediation is managed end-to-end. Centralized Model +-----------------------------+ | Corporate Data Governance | | Steering Committee (Board) | +------+----------------------+ | +------+------+ | Department A | (Data Stewards) +-------------+ | Department B | +-------------+ Federated Model +---------------------+ +---------------------+ | Dept A Governance | | Dept B Governance | | (Loan Data Council) | | (Market Data Council)| +---------------------+ +---------------------+ ^ ^ Corporate Data Governance (policy framework) Define and publish your data governance structure (committees, roles, processes) and measure its effectiveness. Believing “one size fits all” – e.g. centralizing without business input can lead to resistance. Balance central oversight with local expertise. **Centralized governance** — A single corporate body governs all data decisions. --- **Federated governance** — Each division/business unit has autonomy (within overall guidelines). **No delta.** These are organizational choices; regulators expect some governance model, but don’t mandate a specific structure.

title: Issue Management and Remediation
one_screen: Data issues must be formally managed: identified, tracked, and remediated through a controlled process. This typically involves logging issues in an issue-tracking system, prioritizing by severity, performing root-cause analysis, and implementing fixes under governance oversight.
bodyText: In practice, once a data validation or reconciliation uncovers an error (for example, a daily report mismatch), an issue ticket is created. The ticket includes description, severity (e.g. Critical if it affects a report submission), and owner (often a data steward). Root cause might be a system defect, a mapping error, or missing data. The solution plan is documented – e.g. code correction or process change – with milestones. Senior management tracks progress via dashboards or committee reports. BCBS 239 requires that material data/reporting issues be escalated “to the highest appropriate level” and that timely action be taken. A bank’s “issue management” process is a key part of its data governance framework. A trap is failing to monitor slow fixes; regulators expect permanent resolution, not temporary workarounds. A permanent rule is that any critical data quality issue (especially those impacting regulatory reports) should be escalated through the risk committee or even board if needed. Remediation may involve multiple steps: short-term manual fixes (to enable report filing) and long-term system changes. Banks often set a standard (e.g. 30 days to fix a critical break). Progress is reported to risk committees, often via heatmaps of outstanding issues. Ultimately, management sign-off on the fix closes the loop. Issue Detected | v Log Ticket (ID, Owner, Severity) | v Root Cause Analysis | v Action Plan (short-term, long-term) | v Implement Fix -> Test | v Verify Resolution | v Close Ticket Every significant data discrepancy or report error must be tracked until fully resolved, with evidence of the fix. Treating issue tickets as “done” when a report is patched, rather than fixing the underlying data problem. **Remediation** — The corrective actions taken to fix a data defect (code fixes, process changes). --- **Workaround** — A temporary solution to allow reporting to proceed (e.g. manual data entry) before full remediation. Both need controls and tracking. **No delta.** All regulators expect banks to have formal issue remediation processes (though naming may vary).

title: Regulatory Returns and Production Cycle
one_screen: A *regulatory return* is a standardized report or form that banks must submit to supervisors (e.g. capital, liquidity, or risk data). The production cycle involves: extracting data from source systems, transforming and mapping it to the return’s schema, aggregating as needed, validating the report against business rules, then submitting and attesting.
bodyText: Concretely, a bank’s risk data team gathers the necessary raw data (from trading, lending, finance systems) and runs it through a predefined mapping specification. This mapping (often in code or ETL tools) converts internal field names and units into the regulatory template fields. Aggregation steps consolidate records (e.g. summing exposures by counterparty type). Once the draft return is built, a series of validation checks ensures the filing is consistent (e.g. column sums match subsidiary filings, no negative values). Issue items from validations are resolved by adjusting mappings or cleaning data. Finally, the return is submitted electronically (often in XBRL or other formats) and signed off. Attestation and sign-off are usually required: typically a senior executive or compliance officer must certify the return is true and correct. Restatements occur when errors post-submission require a corrected filing; these must be communicated to the regulator. In data projects, understanding this full cycle is crucial: changes in business definitions or systems can break mappings, so any reporting change project must consider end-to-end impact. A sample production flow: Source Systems | v Extract Data | v Transform/Map (spec: source→return fields) | v Aggregate/Summarize | v Validate (quality checks) | +--> Exceptions? -> Investigate and correct | v Submit Return | v Attest/Sign-off Every field in a regulatory return must be traceable back to source data via the mapping logic. Neglecting to re-validate mappings after source system changes; a code update might redirect a column without testers noticing. **Regulatory return** — A formal submission to a supervisor with pre-defined data items. --- **Regulatory report (internal)** — An internal risk report (like VaR reports) which is not directly submitted to regulators. **No delta.** All regulators require banks to follow this general extract-transform-validate-submit cycle for returns. (The details of formats differ.)

title: Attestation, Restatements, and Reporting Change Programs
one_screen: **Attestation and sign-off:** Senior management (often the board, CEO or Chief Risk Officer) must formally attest that each regulatory report is accurate and complete. This is both a legal requirement in many jurisdictions and an internal control. **Restatements:** If a material error is discovered after submission, the bank must correct (“restatement”) the return. Restatements can impact capital calculations or regulatory standings, so timely correction and explanation are critical. **Reporting change programs:** When regulations change or new reports are added, a change program is launched. This involves requirement analysis, mapping updates, system development, testing, and parallel runs.
bodyText: In practice, attestation is typically documented via a cover letter or checkbox in the submission portal. It holds senior officers legally responsible if the data is faulty. Restatements usually follow a defined protocol: e.g. notify the regulator, submit a corrected report, and explain the cause. Each restatement is logged to avoid repeat mistakes. Reporting changes (like new BCBS rules or formats) require project management. For instance, moving from manual to XBRL filing or adding a new COREP schedule. Such projects demand coordination between IT, data teams, and regulators. They produce new mapping specs and update test packs. A common trap is underestimating the regression testing needed across old reports. Compliance requires that all related reports still match after change. No report is final until attested. All corrections must be documented: one should never “forget” a restatement or leave an unexplained discrepancy. Thinking of reporting change as just a format switch; in reality it often involves changing data definitions, so deep validation is needed. **Attestation** — Management’s certification of a report’s accuracy. --- **Audit** — Independent verification by internal or external auditors. Attestation is self-certification; audit is independent checking. **No delta.** Attestation/sign-off processes and requirements for restatements are universal (though e.g. Indian banks may align with Companies Act and RBI letters).

title: Delivery Layer: Requirements, Mapping, and Testing
one_screen: The delivery layer in a data program consists of business requirements, mapping specifications, and testing. A Business Requirements Document (BRD) defines *what* reports/data are needed (with business context). A Data Mapping Specification details *how* each target field is derived from source fields with transformation logic. Testing involves pre-defined result sets and user acceptance testing (UAT) to validate that the implemented mappings produce the expected outputs.
bodyText: **BRD:** In regulatory/risk contexts, the BRD describes needed data points, calculation methods, timing, and exceptions. It often cites regulatory definitions. The BRD ensures developers and analysts understand the objectives. **Data Mapping Spec:** This is the core deliverable. It is typically a spreadsheet or document listing: Source Field → Transformation Rule → Target Field. For example: “LoanBook.EndDate → Calendar Quarter End for report.” Each mapping should include any conversion (currency, units) and business rules applied. It serves as the blueprint for ETL developers. **Testing:** Test packs with known inputs and results are prepared. For example, a small dataset with calculated expected totals. During UAT, business users verify that outputs match these expectations. Automated regression tests and reconciliation reports are also built to compare results against legacy systems or previous runs. UAT covers functional correctness and edge cases. A strong delivery approach uses examples: e.g. test that negative balances or unusual security types still produce correct report lines. Downstream extracts (e.g. FINREP extracts sent to ECB) should also be checked – that is, one might run a script on the final data extract to verify totals against source systems. The process is iterative: any discrepancies found in UAT or extracts feed back into the mapping (looping through the cycle again until clean). Business Requirements | v Data Mapping Spec | v ETL/Development | v Unit Testing | v UAT (with test packs) | v Go-live and Parallel Runs Every data transformation must be traceable (via the mapping spec) and tested with expected results before production use. Skipping UAT or not involving actual report users. Testing by IT alone often misses business logic errors. **Business Requirements Document (BRD)** — Describes the *what* and *why* (business needs, regulatory requirements). --- **Mapping Specification** — Details the *how* (the exact field mappings and calculations). **No delta.** These delivery practices apply to any data/reporting project, regardless of jurisdiction.

title: Jurisdiction-Specific Reporting Frameworks
one_screen: Regulatory reporting frameworks differ by jurisdiction. BCBS 239 itself is a global set of principles with **no direct legal force**. In practice:
bodyText: **IN** — India’s RBI has instituted the *Automated Data Flow (ADF)* system. Since 2010, banks build a Centralised Data Repository (CDR) to consolidate required data elements, and submit many returns in XBRL format. RBI’s standards (e.g. on coding, unique IDs) govern data in this system. **UK** — The Prudential Regulation Authority (PRA) expects UK banks (especially “significant institutions”) to apply BCBS 239 outcomes. Reporting is done under the UK Rulebook (Capital Requirements Regulations adapted from CRR). Banks submit COREP and FINREP returns (via PRA-run systems) consistent with EU rules, although UK now diverges post-Brexit. PRA Supervisory Statements reinforce BCBS 239 principles, and breaches can affect SREP. **EU** — Eurozone banks file EBA-developed COREP/FINREP returns under the CRR/CRD IV framework. COREP covers credit, market and operational risk and capital ratios. FINREP covers financial statements for IFRS-adopters. The EU is moving to an integrated framework (IReF) which by 2030 will unify multiple ECB statistical and supervisory returns. **US** — Banks file *Call Reports* (FFIEC 031/041) quarterly with regulators. Large bank holding companies (BHCs) file Federal Reserve FR Y series (e.g. FR Y-9C) and FR Y-14 for stress testing. These cover balance sheet, income and risk data. The Fed incorporates BCBS 239 expectations into its supervisory processes, especially for Systemically Important BHCs. BCBS 239 (Global principles) | v +-----+ +-----+ +-----+ +-----+ | India| | UK | | EU | | US | +-----+ +-----+ +-----+ +-----+ ADF/XBRL PRA returns EBA COREP/ FFIEC Call (central (BCBS239 & FINREP, Reports; data repo) UK SREP) integrated Fed FR Y series (IReF) Regulatory return taxonomies differ by jurisdiction, but underlying risk data governance expectations (BCBS 239) remain universal. Assuming a regulatory report mapping in one jurisdiction automatically satisfies the data definition rules of another. **COREP/FINREP** — European Supervisory Authority (EBA) reporting frameworks for capital and financial statements. --- **FFIEC Call Reports** — US prudential regulatory return filings required for insured depository institutions. — RBI’s ADF requires banks to channel return data into a centralized repository and submit XBRL filings. — The PRA expects banks to meet BCBS 239 outcomes; capital and risk data are reported via PRA’s forms (based on CRR/CRD) in the sub-set of COREP/FINREP where applicable. — Banks submit EBA COREP (capital/risk) and FINREP (financial statements) under CRR/CRD IV. The future Integrated Reporting Framework (ECB IReF) will consolidate data collection from 2030. — Insured depository institutions file Call Reports (FFIEC 031/041) to regulators, and large BHCs file Fed FR Y-series (e.g. FR Y-9C for consolidated data).

title: Bank as a Balance Sheet
one_screen: A bank is a balance sheet before it is a building, app, or lender. It owns assets, owes liabilities, and has equity equal to the residual difference: **Assets = Liabilities + Equity**.
bodyText: A **balance sheet** is a snapshot of financial position at a particular date. An **asset** is a present economic resource controlled by an entity as a result of past events; a **liability** is a present obligation to transfer an economic resource; **equity** is the residual interest after liabilities are deducted from assets. Those definitions make the basic accounting identity unavoidable rather than optional. For a bank, the labels can initially feel reversed. A loan made to a customer is normally an **asset of the bank** because the customer owes future payments to the bank. A customer deposit is normally a **liability of the bank** because the bank owes the depositor money and must honour valid withdrawals or payments. Cash, balances with central banks, securities and loans are common asset categories; deposits and wholesale borrowings are common liability categories. Equity sits beneath them as the residual claim. Suppose a bank has assets of 110 and liabilities of 100. Its equity is 10. If an asset subsequently loses 4 in value and nothing else changes, assets become 106 and equity becomes 6. The loss does not disappear because it was non-cash; it reduces the residual available to absorb losses. This is the mechanical reason capital matters to a bank. The identity does **not** say that every asset is safe, every liability is payable immediately, or equity is a pile of cash. It only says that recognised resources and obligations must balance through the residual interest. Accounting recognition and measurement determine the amounts assigned to each item; prudential regulation may then make additional adjustments when determining regulatory capital. +-----------------------+ | ASSETS | | cash, securities, | | loans, other claims | +-----------------------+ | | financed by v +-----------------------+ | LIABILITIES | | deposits, borrowings | +-----------------------+ | | plus residual v +-----------------------+ | EQUITY | | assets - liabilities | +-----------------------+ Assets = Liabilities + Equity Every recognised balance-sheet amount must fit the identity **Assets = Liabilities + Equity**. A loss that reduces assets without reducing liabilities reduces equity. Reading a customer's loan as the bank's liability because the bank "gave the money". The remaining repayment claim belongs to the bank, so the loan is the bank's asset. **Asset** — a recognised economic resource controlled by the bank. --- **Equity** — the residual after liabilities are deducted from assets; it is not another asset or a dedicated cash reserve. **No delta.** The accounting identity and the asset-liability-equity relationship do not depend on jurisdiction.

title: Deposits and Loans: Opposite Sides of the Bank
one_screen: **Deposits fund the bank and are liabilities; loans use the bank's balance sheet and are assets.** The words are usually spoken from the customer's perspective, which is why beginners instinctively put them on the wrong sides.
bodyText: A **deposit** is money the bank owes to a depositor. From the customer's perspective, a positive deposit balance is an asset: the customer has a claim on the bank. From the bank's perspective, exactly the same contract is a liability. Perspective determines the label. A **loan** reverses the direction. The customer receives funds and promises future repayment of principal and usually interest. The customer therefore has a liability; the bank holds the corresponding contractual claim and therefore records an asset. The bank earns interest on many such assets and pays interest on many funding liabilities. This symmetry explains a large part of bank accounting. When a depositor adds cash to an existing account, the bank can receive an asset such as cash or settlement balances while simultaneously increasing its deposit liability. When a borrower repays principal, the bank's loan asset declines. Where repayment comes from a deposit at the same bank, that deposit liability can decline at the same time. **Funding** means the liabilities and equity that support the asset side of the balance sheet. Deposits are a major form of bank funding, but not the only form: a bank can also borrow from financial markets or other institutions and can fund itself with equity. Saying that deposits are funding therefore does not mean every individual deposited currency unit can be traced to a particular loan. The balance sheet must always be read from the reporting bank's perspective. That single discipline prevents the common reversal of deposits and loans and prepares the ground for understanding how lending can create deposits. CUSTOMER VIEW BANK VIEW +--------------+ +--------------+ | Deposit |-------------->| Deposit | | = asset | same contract | = liability | +--------------+ +--------------+ +--------------+ +--------------+ | Loan |-------------->| Loan | | = liability | same contract | = asset | +--------------+ +--------------+ Classify a financial instrument from the perspective of the entity whose balance sheet is being read. Calling deposits "bank assets" because the money is physically or electronically at the bank. The depositor's claim is an amount the bank owes, so it is a bank liability. **Deposit** — a customer's claim on the bank and therefore normally a liability of the bank. --- **Loan** — a bank's claim on the borrower and therefore normally an asset of the bank; the perspective reversal makes the two easy to mix up. **No delta.** Contractual perspective and the asset-versus-liability logic are universal.

title: Loan Creation, Deposits and Funding
one_screen: When a bank grants a loan and credits the borrower's account, it can create a **loan asset and a deposit liability simultaneously**. That does not make funding irrelevant: payments out of the bank create settlement outflows, while liquidity, capital, risk and profitability constrain sustainable lending.
bodyText: Consider a new loan of 100 whose proceeds are credited to the borrower's account at the lending bank. At origination, the bank can record **+100 loan asset** and **+100 deposit liability**. Its balance sheet expands by 100 on each side. Commercial bank lending is therefore capable of creating deposit money; lending need not mechanically wait for a specific existing depositor's money to be reassigned first. The Bank of England describes bank lending as creating deposits in this manner. That mechanism is frequently stretched into the false claim that a bank needs no funding. Suppose the borrower immediately pays 100 to somebody who banks elsewhere. The deposit created at the lending bank may leave it. Settlement between banks then requires an asset acceptable for interbank settlement, ordinarily central-bank money within the relevant payment system. The originating bank must manage the resulting liquidity position and may replace lost deposit funding with other deposits or wholesale funding. Lending is also constrained by more than settlement cash. The bank must expect the loan to compensate for funding costs, operating costs, credit losses and the use of scarce balance-sheet resources. Prudential capital requirements constrain how much risk can be supported by loss-absorbing resources, while liquidity requirements constrain vulnerability to cash outflows. Risk appetite and underwriting standards impose further limits. Basel standards therefore contain separate capital and liquidity frameworks rather than treating deposit creation as an unlimited process. "Loans create deposits" describes an accounting and monetary mechanism. "Banks need funding" describes the continuing requirement to finance assets and survive payment outflows. Both statements can be true at the same time. Loan approved | v +------------------+ +------------------+ | +100 Loan asset | | +100 Deposit | | | | liability | +------------------+ +------------------+ \ / \ / v v Balance sheet expands | v Customer pays away | v +--------------------------------+ | Deposit may leave the bank; | | settlement liquidity is needed | +--------------------------------+ Loan origination can create a deposit, but a bank must still fund and settle the balance sheet that remains after customers move money. Interpreting "banks create deposits by lending" as "banks can lend without capital, liquidity, funding costs or settlement constraints". **Deposit creation** — the simultaneous balance-sheet creation of a loan asset and deposit liability. --- **Funding** — the liabilities and equity supporting assets over time, including after newly created deposits are transferred elsewhere. **No delta.** The double-entry mechanism is universal; local monetary, capital and liquidity rules determine the constraints around it.

title: Net Interest Income and Bank Earnings
one_screen: A traditional bank earns a spread by receiving interest on interest-earning assets and paying interest on funding. **Net interest income = interest income − interest expense**, but final profit also reflects fees, market-related income, operating expenses, credit losses and taxes.
bodyText: **Interest income** is income generated by interest-bearing assets such as loans and debt securities. **Interest expense** is the cost recognised on interest-bearing liabilities such as deposits and borrowings. Their difference is **net interest income (NII)**. The Federal Reserve uses this definition when analysing bank earnings. Suppose a bank recognises 8 of interest income and 3 of interest expense during a period. NII is 5. The calculation is simple; interpreting it is not. NII depends on the amount of interest-earning assets, the rates earned on them, the amount and mix of funding, the rates paid for that funding, and how quickly asset and liability rates reprice. **Net interest margin (NIM)** scales NII relative to earning assets. A common supervisory presentation annualises net interest income and divides it by average earning assets. NII is therefore an amount of income; NIM is a ratio. A bank's earnings are broader than interest. Fees and commissions can arise from services. Securities and other financial instruments can generate gains or losses. Staff, technology and premises create operating costs. Credit deterioration can create impairment or provisioning expense under the applicable accounting or regulatory framework. Taxes then reduce pre-tax earnings. Consequently, a large NII does not guarantee a large profit. The economic spread also cannot be read from two headline interest rates alone. Funding and asset balances differ, instruments reprice at different times, some balances pay or earn no interest, and defaults can prevent expected interest from being collected. Bank profitability analysis therefore begins with NII but cannot end there. +---------------------+ | Interest income | | on earning assets | +---------------------+ | | minus v +---------------------+ | Interest expense | | on funding | +---------------------+ | v +---------------------+ | Net interest income | +---------------------+ | | +/- non-interest items, | expenses, credit losses, tax v +---------------------+ | Profit or loss | +---------------------+ NII measures the accounting difference between interest income and interest expense; it is not the same as total bank profit. Comparing the average loan rate directly with the average deposit rate and calling the difference NIM without weighting balances, other funding or the denominator. **Net interest income** — an amount: interest income minus interest expense. --- **Net interest margin** — a ratio relating net interest income to earning assets; the similar names conceal different units. **No delta.** The economic distinction between interest income, interest expense and their net amount does not change across jurisdictions.

title: Capital Versus Liquidity
one_screen: **Capital absorbs losses; liquidity meets payments when due.** A bank can have positive capital yet fail through a cash shortage, or hold abundant cash yet be economically insolvent because its assets are worth less than its obligations.
bodyText: Bank **capital** is the loss-absorbing financial base protecting creditors and depositors against declines in asset value. Accounting equity and regulatory capital are related but not identical: prudential rules define eligible capital instruments and make regulatory deductions and adjustments. Basel standards therefore specify capital measures separately from ordinary financial-statement equity. **Liquidity** is the ability to meet payment obligations when they fall due without unacceptable loss. Liquid assets can be converted into settlement cash quickly and reliably. A bank needs liquidity because deposit withdrawals, outgoing payments, maturing borrowings and other obligations can require cash before longer-term assets such as loans repay. The distinction can be seen numerically. A bank with assets economically worth 105 and liabilities of 100 has positive residual value of 5. But if almost all 105 is locked in long-dated, non-saleable assets while 20 of liabilities must be paid today, it can face a liquidity crisis despite being solvent in value terms. Conversely, a bank could hold 30 of immediately available cash but have total assets worth only 90 against liabilities of 100. It is liquid in the immediate sense but has negative economic net worth. Prudential frameworks therefore maintain distinct capital and liquidity requirements. Basel III includes risk-based capital and leverage requirements as well as liquidity standards. The UK PRA and EU framework likewise treat liquidity as a dedicated prudential risk rather than a synonym for capital. A capital injection may also improve liquidity if it brings in cash, but that transaction does not collapse the concepts into one. The capital describes loss-bearing capacity; the incoming cash describes an asset available for payments. BANK RESILIENCE | +---------+---------+ | | v v +------------------+ +------------------+ | CAPITAL | | LIQUIDITY | | absorbs losses | | meets cash | | | | outflows on time | +------------------+ +------------------+ | | v v solvency protection payment capacity Capital answers **"Can losses be absorbed?"** Liquidity answers **"Can payments be made when due?"** Calling a bank "well capitalised" because it has a large cash balance. Cash is an asset; capital is a loss-absorbing funding concept. **Solvency** — having sufficient asset value relative to obligations and an adequate loss-absorbing base. --- **Liquidity** — having resources available at the required time to settle obligations; a solvent institution can still become illiquid. **No delta.** Regulatory calibration differs, but capital and liquidity remain economically distinct in every jurisdiction.

title: The Financial Statements and How They Link
one_screen: The three-statement shorthand is **balance sheet, profit and loss statement, and cash-flow statement**. Profit changes equity, cash flows explain movements in cash, and every recognised closing balance must end up on the closing balance sheet.
bodyText: The **balance sheet** reports financial position at a date. The **profit and loss statement** reports income and expenses over a period. The **cash-flow statement** reports cash inflows and outflows during the period, commonly classified into operating, investing and financing activities under IAS 7. They measure different things. If interest income of 10 is accrued but only 8 has been received in cash, profit can include 10 while cash increases by only 8; the remaining 2 appears through a receivable or carrying amount elsewhere on the balance sheet. Similarly, depreciation or a credit-loss charge can reduce profit without producing an equal current-period cash payment. Profit normally feeds equity through retained earnings after dividends and other equity movements. Cash movements change the closing cash balance. Transactions such as new borrowing can increase cash and liabilities without creating profit. Repaying principal can reduce cash and debt without creating an equivalent expense. The statements therefore reconcile economic performance, financial position and cash movement rather than repeating one another. "Three statements" is practitioner shorthand, not a claim that a complete set of accounts literally contains only three documents. Under IFRS, a complete set also includes a statement of changes in equity, notes and comparative information, while profit or loss and other comprehensive income form part of the prescribed presentation. For banks, the linking logic is the same even though line items differ markedly from an industrial company's accounts. The applicable reporting framework determines recognition, measurement and presentation; prudential reports may use accounting values as a starting point and then apply regulatory definitions. +-----------------------+ | Opening balance sheet | +-----------------------+ | v +-----------------------+ | Profit or loss | | income - expenses | +-----------------------+ | +---------> changes equity | v +-----------------------+ | Cash-flow statement | | explains cash movement| +-----------------------+ | v +-----------------------+ | Closing balance sheet | +-----------------------+ Profit is not cash, and cash movement is not profit; both ultimately reconcile into closing balance-sheet positions. Forcing the change in cash to equal reported profit and treating any difference as an error. **Profit and loss statement** — measures recognised income and expenses over a period. --- **Cash-flow statement** — measures cash movements over a period; accruals and non-cash items make it differ from profit. — Scheduled commercial banks prepare statutory financial statements under the Banking Regulation Act framework and RBI presentation/disclosure directions; this does not mean they apply Ind AS 109. [RBI, Commercial Banks – Financial Statements: Presentation and Disclosures Directions, 2025] — Entities reporting under UK-adopted international accounting standards use the applicable UK-endorsed IFRS requirements, including IAS 1/IFRS presentation requirements. [UK Endorsement Board, UK-adopted international accounting standards] — EU law requires EU-adopted international accounting standards for specified consolidated accounts, notably those of companies whose securities trade on an EU regulated market. [Regulation (EC) No 1606/2002; Regulation (EU) 2023/1803] — Applicable US entities report under US GAAP; the FASB establishes and improves financial accounting and reporting standards for nongovernmental entities. [FASB Mission]

title: Reading a Bank Balance Sheet
one_screen: Read a bank balance sheet by asking three questions in order: **what assets generate or preserve value, how those assets are funded, and how much residual loss absorption sits beneath the liabilities**. A bank's debtors are often its customers, while its customers' deposits are its funding.
bodyText: A useful first pass starts with **assets**. Cash and central-bank balances provide settlement capacity. Securities can provide income, liquidity or investment exposure depending on their nature and classification. Loans represent claims on borrowers and are commonly a major source of interest income and credit risk. Other financial and non-financial assets complete the asset side. Next read **liabilities** as funding and payment obligations. Customer deposits can differ substantially in stability, interest rate and maturity. Wholesale borrowings are funds obtained from financial markets or institutional counterparties. Other liabilities can include settlement obligations, derivatives and accrued expenses. The maturity and behavioural characteristics of liabilities matter because an asset may remain economically sound while funding against it becomes unavailable. Then read **equity** and, separately where relevant, prudential capital disclosures. Equity is the accounting residual. Regulatory capital applies regulatory eligibility, deductions and other adjustments and therefore should not be assumed to equal book equity. A bank balance sheet should also be read by **quality**, not merely size. Two loan portfolios with equal carrying amounts may have different credit quality. Two security portfolios may have different market sensitivity or liquidity. Two deposit bases of equal size may behave differently under stress. Balance-sheet analysis therefore combines amounts with information about maturity, concentration, valuation, impairment and contractual terms. This differs from the intuitive reading of many non-financial corporates. Inventory and physical plant may dominate a corporate asset side, while bank assets are heavily financial claims. Debt is funding for both, but customer deposits are distinctive because they simultaneously represent funding to the bank and money-like assets to customers. Read top to bottom +-----------------------+ | ASSETS | | What does the bank | | own or have claims on?| +-----------------------+ | v +-----------------------+ | LIABILITIES | | Who funds the bank? | | What must be paid? | +-----------------------+ | v +-----------------------+ | EQUITY / CAPITAL | | What absorbs losses? | +-----------------------+ | v +-----------------------+ | QUALITY + MATURITY + | | CONCENTRATION | +-----------------------+ Never assess a bank balance sheet from totals alone; composition, quality, maturity and funding structure determine what the totals mean. Treating a large deposit balance as evidence of a large liquid-asset buffer. Deposits are funding liabilities, not liquid assets. **Book equity** — the accounting residual of assets minus liabilities. --- **Regulatory capital** — capital recognised under prudential rules after eligibility criteria and adjustments; it can differ from book equity. **No delta.** Reporting templates differ, but the analytical sequence of assets, funding, residual loss absorption and balance-sheet quality is jurisdiction-neutral.

title: Accrual Versus Cash
one_screen: **Accrual accounting recognises economic effects when the recognition criteria are met, not simply when cash moves.** Cash accounting asks when money moved; accrual accounting asks what asset, liability, income or expense exists because of what happened.
bodyText: Suppose a bank earns 10 of interest during December but receives the cash in January. Under accrual accounting, December can contain the interest income even though the corresponding cash receipt occurs later. The unpaid amount is reflected in a recognised asset or in the carrying amount of the financial instrument as required by the applicable accounting framework. The opposite timing also occurs. A bank can pay cash before an expense belongs economically to the current period, creating a prepaid asset until the service is consumed. It can recognise an expense before paying the cash, creating or increasing a liability. The presence or absence of a current-period cash movement therefore does not determine whether income or expense exists. This distinction is especially important for **provisions and impairment**. A deterioration in expected recoveries can create an accounting loss before a borrower actually fails to pay cash. The financial statements are attempting to represent the changed economic value or expected collectability under the applicable measurement rules, rather than waiting for the final cash shortfall to become certain. The cash-flow statement then restores visibility over actual cash movements. Under IAS 7, cash flows are presented by operating, investing and financing activities, while the balance sheet contains the resulting closing cash and cash-equivalent positions. Accrual accounting does not permit arbitrary forecasting to be booked as profit or loss. Recognition and measurement must follow the applicable accounting requirements. The foundational point is narrower: **timing of accounting recognition and timing of cash settlement can differ**. Understanding that separation prevents provisions, accrued interest, receivables and payables from being mistaken for cash transactions. Economic event occurs | v +-----------------------+ | Recognition criteria | | satisfied? | +-----------------------+ | v +-----------------------+ | Accrual accounting | | records effect | +-----------------------+ | | cash may move | earlier or later v +-----------------------+ | Cash-flow statement | | records cash timing | +-----------------------+ An income or expense can be recognised without an equal cash movement in the same reporting period. Reversing a valid provision merely because "no cash has been lost yet". The absence of cash settlement does not by itself invalidate accrual recognition. **Accrual** — recognition based on the economic event and applicable recognition requirements. --- **Cash movement** — settlement or transfer of cash; its date can differ from the accounting recognition date. **No delta.** Specific recognition rules vary by accounting framework, but the distinction between accrual recognition and cash timing is universal.

title: Provisions and Credit-Loss Allowances
one_screen: A credit-loss allowance recognises that the amount expected to be collected from credit exposures may be less than their contractual amount. **The economic idea is shared; the recognition and measurement rule is jurisdiction- and reporting-framework-specific.**
bodyText: A borrower can owe 100 contractually while the bank expects to recover less. Credit-loss accounting provides a mechanism for reflecting that deterioration before the final cash loss necessarily occurs. The resulting **allowance** is an accounting adjustment associated with expected credit losses; the related charge ordinarily affects profit or loss under the applicable framework. The allowance must not be confused with cash placed in a separate account. Under US CECL, for example, the allowance for credit losses on financial assets measured at amortised cost is a **valuation account deducted from amortised cost** to present the amount expected to be collected. Under IFRS 9, expected credit losses are probability-weighted and the impairment model distinguishes 12-month and lifetime expected credit losses according to the applicable stage and conditions. The Indian banking position requires special discipline. RBI deferred implementation of Ind AS for scheduled commercial banks in April 2019 **until further notice**. Their prudential asset classification and provisioning operate under RBI directions, not an assumption that Ind AS 109 applies to banks. Relevant NBFCs that are required to apply Ind AS have separate RBI guidance dealing explicitly with impairment allowances under **Ind AS 109**. This distinction matters operationally because "expected loss", "provision", "allowance", "stage" and "NPA" can belong to different rule systems. Similar economic concerns do not make the accounting mechanics interchangeable. Credit exposure | v +----------------------+ | Estimate / determine | | loss under applicable| | framework | +----------------------+ | v +----------------------+ | Allowance / provision| +----------------------+ | v +----------------------+ | Profit or loss effect| | + carrying-value / | | regulatory treatment | +----------------------+ A credit-loss allowance is a measurement or valuation mechanism, not a segregated pot of cash. Applying IFRS 9 staging and ECL rules to an Indian scheduled commercial bank merely because Ind AS 109 exists for other Indian financial entities. **Credit-loss allowance** — an accounting valuation adjustment reflecting credit losses under the applicable reporting framework. --- **Regulatory provision** — an amount required by prudential rules; it may interact with accounting allowances but need not be calculated on the same basis. — RBI deferred Ind AS implementation for scheduled commercial banks until further notice; bank income recognition, asset classification and provisioning therefore operate under RBI prudential directions. Relevant Ind AS-applying NBFCs use Ind AS 109 subject to RBI regulatory guidance.
