[RBI DBR.BP.BC.No.29/21.07.001/2018-19; RBI DOR(NBFC).CC.PD.No.109/22.10.106/2019-20; RBI Commercial Banks IRACP Directions] — For entities reporting under UK-adopted IFRS, IFRS 9 contains the expected-credit-loss impairment model. [UK Endorsement Board, UK-adopted IFRS 9] — For reporting within the scope of EU-adopted IFRS, IFRS 9 is part of the EU-endorsed accounting framework. [Regulation (EU) 2023/1803] — ASC Topic 326 uses CECL for applicable financial assets; CECL estimates expected credit losses over the contractual term, considering specified historical, current and reasonable-and-supportable forecast information. [FASB ASU 2016-13; Federal Reserve CECL FAQ]

title: Other Comprehensive Income
one_screen: **Other comprehensive income (OCI) is a reporting route for specified recognised income and expense that the applicable accounting standard does not put in current profit or loss.** It is not "less real" income, and it is not a discretionary parking place for inconvenient volatility.
bodyText: Under IFRS presentation requirements, **other comprehensive income** comprises items of income and expense that other IFRS requirements require or permit to be recognised outside profit or loss. Profit or loss and OCI together contribute to **total comprehensive income**. Accumulated effects generally sit within equity, subject to the classifications and reclassification rules applicable to each item. Why does OCI exist? Some accounting standards distinguish between changes that belong in current profit or loss and specified changes whose presentation is outside current profit or loss. The classification can preserve information about different sources of performance and measurement without pretending that the recognised change did not occur. The key discipline is that management cannot simply decide that an unpleasant loss belongs in OCI. The relevant accounting standard determines whether an item goes to profit or loss, OCI, or directly to equity and whether a later **reclassification** into profit or loss occurs. Different instruments and elections can therefore produce different treatments. Indian scheduled commercial banks require particular care. They are not on Ind AS 109. Under RBI's investment-portfolio directions, valuation movements on the bank's **Available for Sale (AFS)** portfolio are dealt with through an **AFS-Reserve** under RBI-prescribed mechanics; debt-instrument amounts can be recycled to profit and loss on derecognition, while other treatment depends on the instrument. RBI does not thereby convert scheduled commercial banks into Ind AS 109 reporters. US GAAP also contains other comprehensive income and accumulated other comprehensive income, but the detailed eligible items and recycling mechanics come from US GAAP rather than IFRS. Recognised income / expense | v +--------------------------+ | Applicable standard asks | | where it is presented | +--------------------------+ | | v v +-------------+ +-------------+ | Profit or | | OCI | | loss | | if required | +-------------+ +-------------+ | v +-------------+ | Equity / | | accumulated | | OCI effects | +-------------+ An item belongs in OCI only because the applicable accounting framework puts it there; management preference cannot create OCI eligibility. Calling every valuation change recorded outside a bank's profit and loss account "OCI", including the RBI AFS-Reserve of an Indian scheduled commercial bank. **OCI** — an accounting-framework category for specified recognised income and expense outside current profit or loss. --- **AFS-Reserve under RBI bank directions** — an RBI-prescribed reserve mechanism for relevant bank investment valuation changes; it should not be relabelled automatically as Ind AS 109 OCI. — Scheduled commercial banks remain outside Ind AS implementation following RBI's deferment; RBI's investment-portfolio directions prescribe an AFS-Reserve for relevant AFS valuation movements. [RBI DBR.BP.BC.No.29/21.07.001/2018-19; RBI/DOR/2023-24/104] — UK-adopted international accounting standards retain the IFRS architecture of profit or loss and OCI for entities within that reporting framework. [UK Endorsement Board, UK-adopted standards] — EU-adopted IFRS provides the applicable IFRS presentation architecture for entities and accounts within the IAS Regulation's scope. [Regulation (EC) No 1606/2002; Regulation (EU) 2023/1803] — US GAAP contains comprehensive-income and accumulated-OCI requirements under Topic 220; detailed classifications are governed by US GAAP rather than IFRS. [FASB ASC Topic 220]

title: Present Value and Discount Factors
one_screen: **Present value converts money at different dates into values at one common date.** A discount factor is the multiplier that performs that conversion: for one annual rate \(r\), the time-\(t\) factor is \(1/(1+r)^t\).
bodyText: Money received now and the same nominal amount received later are not economically identical when a positive required return exists. Current money can be invested, while a future payment cannot be used until it arrives. **Present value (PV)** expresses a future cash flow in today's value using a **discount rate**. For a cash flow \(CF_t\) received \(t\) annual periods from now at a constant annually compounded rate \(r\): \[ PV=\frac{CF_t}{(1+r)^t} \] The term \[ DF_t=\frac{1}{(1+r)^t} \] is the **discount factor**. Thus \(PV=CF_t\times DF_t\). If 110 is certain to arrive one year from now and the relevant annual discount rate is 10%, its present value is \(110/1.10=100\). At the same rate, 110 due two years away is worth less today because it is discounted for two periods. Discounting is not synonymous with predicting whether payment occurs. A cash flow can first be probability-weighted for uncertainty and then discounted for timing. Probability changes the expected amount; discounting changes the value assigned to its timing. That distinction becomes essential in expected-loss calculations. The rate and cash-flow convention must match. Annual cash flows require a rate expressed consistently with annual periods. Monthly timing requires a compatible periodic or appropriately converted rate. Cash flows at the start versus end of a period also produce different results. A perfectly correct formula with mismatched timing assumptions still gives the wrong answer. Present value is mathematics rather than a banking-specific rule. Accounting standards, valuation frameworks and risk models decide **which** cash flows and **which** rate to use; the discounting operation itself does not change by jurisdiction. Future cash flow CF_t | v +----------------------+ | Discount factor | | 1 / (1+r)^t | +----------------------+ | v +----------------------+ | Present value | | CF_t x discount | | factor | +----------------------+ Cash flows at different dates cannot be compared economically until timing has been put on a common basis. Discounting a monthly cash flow with an annual rate as though one month were one annual period. **Discount rate** — the rate used to translate value across time. --- **Discount factor** — the numerical multiplier produced from the rate and timing; the rate is an input, while the factor performs the multiplication. **No delta.** Present-value mathematics does not change across jurisdictions.

title: Compounding and Discounting Conventions
one_screen: **Compounding moves value forward through time; discounting moves it backward.** The mathematics only works when the rate, compounding frequency, day-count or period convention, and cash-flow dates are internally consistent.
bodyText: With annual compounding, an amount \(P\) invested for \(n\) years at annual rate \(r\) grows to: \[ FV=P(1+r)^n \] where **FV** is future value. Reversing the operation gives: \[ PV=\frac{FV}{(1+r)^n} \] Compounding and discounting are therefore inverse operations under the same assumptions. Rates can be quoted under different **compounding conventions**. If a nominal annual rate \(r_{nom}\) is compounded \(m\) times per year for \(n\) years, one common representation is: \[ FV=P\left(1+\frac{r_{nom}}{m}\right)^{mn} \] A quoted annual rate of 12% compounded monthly is therefore not mechanically identical to 12% compounded annually. More frequent compounding changes the effective annual growth when the nominal quote is held constant. Timing conventions matter just as much. A cash flow received today has no one-period discounting. A payment received at the end of year one receives one period of discounting. A payment occurring halfway through a year needs timing that reflects that half-period under the chosen convention. In real financial contracts, day-count conventions and payment calendars can further affect the calculation. The most common modelling error is not sophisticated mathematics; it is **unit mismatch**. A model may combine annual probability assumptions, monthly cash flows and quarterly discount rates without converting them to a common time basis. Another error is comparing rates whose quotation conventions differ and treating the numerical percentage as sufficient. The safe method is to identify the cash-flow dates first, state the rate convention explicitly, convert rates consistently where necessary, then apply the corresponding factors. Only after that should results be aggregated. Present value | | compound forward v +----------------------+ | P x (1+r)^n | +----------------------+ | v Future value | | discount backward v +----------------------+ | FV / (1+r)^n | +----------------------+ | v Present value Rate frequency and cash-flow frequency must use the same time basis before compounding or discounting. Treating a nominal 12% rate compounded monthly as economically identical to an effective 12% annual rate. **Nominal annual rate** — a quoted annualised rate whose economic effect depends on its compounding convention. --- **Effective annual rate** — the one-year growth rate after the specified intra-year compounding has been reflected. **No delta.** Compounding identities and the need for consistent conventions are mathematical rather than jurisdictional.

title: Effective Interest Rate
one_screen: The **effective interest rate (EIR)** is the single periodic rate that makes the present value of the relevant contractual cash-flow stream equal to the instrument's initial carrying amount under the stated methodology. It converts price, interest, fees and timing into one internally consistent yield.
bodyText: A loan can contain more economics than its headline coupon. There may be an initial price different from principal, fees integral to the yield, transaction costs, instalment timing and a final repayment. The **effective interest rate** expresses those relevant cash flows as one rate that solves a present-value equation. In simplified form, for an initial carrying amount \(P\) and future relevant cash flows \(CF_t\), EIR \(i\) solves: \[ P=\sum_t\frac{CF_t}{(1+i)^t} \] This makes EIR an **internal rate of return** for the specified cash-flow definition. Suppose 100 is advanced and the only contractual receipt is 110 one year later. The EIR is 10%. If the initial amount and contractual cash flows differ because of qualifying fees or transaction costs, the EIR can differ from the stated coupon even when contractual interest payments use that coupon. Under IFRS 9, the effective interest method uses an EIR determined through the standard's specified estimated cash flows and incorporates fees, transaction costs and other premiums or discounts that are integral to that rate. The accounting definition controls which items enter the calculation. The general mathematical concept nevertheless remains the same: solve for the rate that equates a present value to the relevant carrying amount. EIR is therefore not merely "the interest rate printed on the contract". Nor is it automatically the market yield observed today. Once an accounting EIR has been established, the relevant framework determines when it remains fixed and when special rules apply. +----------------------+ | Initial carrying | | amount | +----------------------+ ^ | | find rate i such that | +----------------------+ | PV of relevant | | future cash flows | | discounted at i | +----------------------+ PV = initial amount => i = effective interest rate EIR is defined by a present-value equality across a specified set of cash flows; changing the cash-flow definition can change the rate. Using the contractual coupon as the EIR without checking fees, premiums, discounts, transaction costs and timing. **Coupon rate** — the contractual rate or formula used to determine stated interest payments. --- **Effective interest rate** — the yield solving the relevant present-value equation; it can differ from the coupon. **No delta.** The rate-solving mathematics is universal; accounting frameworks determine the precise cash flows included and subsequent accounting use.

title: NPV and Discounting Expected Loss
one_screen: **Net present value (NPV) adds cash flows after converting them to one valuation date.** Expected loss is time-sensitive when the applicable methodology discounts shortfalls: the same nominal shortfall occurring later has a different present value.
bodyText: For dated cash flows \(CF_t\) and a consistent discount rate \(r\), a simple NPV is: \[ NPV=\sum_t \frac{CF_t}{(1+r)^t} \] Inflows are usually represented with one sign and outflows with the opposite sign. Discounting prevents a loss or benefit occurring far in the future from being treated as economically identical to the same nominal amount occurring immediately. Consider an expected shortfall of 100 one year from today and a 10% annual discount rate. Its present value is \(100/1.10=90.91\). If the same 100 shortfall occurred two years away, its present value would be \(100/1.10^2=82.64\). The nominal loss is unchanged; its valuation date is not. Expected-credit-loss accounting adds another layer: **uncertainty**. Possible credit shortfalls can be probability-weighted, while discounting separately reflects the timing of those shortfalls. IFRS 9 explicitly requires expected credit losses to be discounted to the reporting date using the effective interest rate determined at initial recognition, or an approximation, subject to specified rules for particular instruments. That IFRS requirement must not be exported mechanically to every jurisdiction. US CECL does not prescribe one mandatory estimation technique; discounted cash-flow methods are available, but other compliant methods can be used. Indian scheduled commercial banks remain under RBI prudential provisioning rather than Ind AS 109. The permanent mathematical lesson is that timing matters. The regulatory or accounting question is **whether, how and at what rate the applicable framework requires that timing to enter the loss measure**. Possible credit shortfalls | v +-----------------------+ | Weight for uncertainty| | where methodology | | requires | +-----------------------+ | v +-----------------------+ | Place shortfalls on | | their expected dates | +-----------------------+ | v +-----------------------+ | Discount where the | | framework requires | +-----------------------+ | v Present-value loss measure NPV compares dated amounts only after translating them to a common valuation date. Applying IFRS 9's EIR discounting rule to an Indian scheduled commercial bank or assuming US CECL requires a discounted-cash-flow method in every case. **Expected cash shortfall** — the relevant difference in cash flows under a loss methodology. --- **Present value of a cash shortfall** — that shortfall after adjusting for its timing using the applicable discount rule. — Scheduled commercial banks use RBI prudential income-recognition, asset-classification and provisioning rules; Ind AS implementation for banks remains deferred until further notice. [RBI DBR.BP.BC.No.29/21.07.001/2018-19; RBI Commercial Banks IRACP Directions] — For entities applying UK-adopted IFRS 9, ECL is discounted to the reporting date using the EIR determined at initial recognition or an approximation, subject to IFRS 9's instrument-specific rules. [IFRS 9 B5.5.44; UK-adopted IFRS 9] — The same IFRS 9 discounting principle applies where EU-adopted IFRS 9 governs the reporting entity and exposure. [IFRS 9 B5.5.44; Regulation (EU) 2023/1803] — ASC Topic 326 CECL permits multiple estimation methods; a discounted-cash-flow approach is not universally mandatory. [FASB ASU 2016-13; Federal Reserve CECL FAQ]

title: Exposure: What Is Actually at Risk
one_screen: **Exposure is the amount or position whose value can be affected by a risk event; it is not the loss itself.** The relevant exposure may include more than today's booked principal because commitments, accrued amounts, derivatives or future drawings can also be at risk.
bodyText: For a simple fully drawn loan, the first approximation to **credit exposure** is often the amount currently owed. If 80 of principal remains outstanding, 80 is an obvious starting point for asking what is exposed to borrower default. But exposure and loss are different quantities. If the bank is exposed to 80 and ultimately recovers 60, the realised loss is 20, not 80. Collateral, guarantees, repayments and recoveries can reduce loss relative to exposure. Conversely, a facility can contain an undrawn amount that may be drawn before default, causing the exposure at the risk event to exceed today's drawn balance. The same distinction extends beyond loans. A derivative can create exposure when its replacement value becomes positive to the bank. A security position creates exposure to market-value changes. A foreign-currency position creates exposure to exchange-rate movements. Operational processes can create exposure to losses even without a conventional financial claim. "Exposure" therefore needs both a **risk type** and a **measurement date or horizon**. Practitioners should ask: exposed to **what event**, over **what horizon**, measured using **which amount**, and after **which recognised risk mitigants**? Without those qualifiers, an exposure number can look precise while referring to different economic concepts. Later credit-risk measures may distinguish current exposure, exposure at default, committed amounts and conversion of undrawn commitments. The foundational discipline comes first: the amount at risk must be identified before probability or severity can be calculated. +----------------------+ | Contract / position | +----------------------+ | v +----------------------+ | What risk event? | +----------------------+ | v +----------------------+ | What amount is | | exposed at that time?| +----------------------+ | v +----------------------+ | What is recovered? | +----------------------+ | v Loss Exposure is an input to loss measurement, not a synonym for loss. Using today's outstanding principal as exposure for an undrawn or revolving facility without asking whether further drawings can occur before default. **Exposure** — the amount or position subject to adverse change from a specified risk. --- **Loss** — the adverse economic outcome after the risk event and relevant recoveries or offsets; exposure can exist without an equal loss. **No delta.** Regulatory definitions of particular exposure measures can differ, but the conceptual distinction between amount exposed and realised loss does not.

title: Probability and Expected Value
one_screen: **Probability says how likely an outcome is; expected value combines each possible outcome with its probability.** A 1% probability of losing 100 is not a loss of 1%, but in a two-outcome example it contributes an expected loss of 1.
bodyText: A **probability** is a number between 0 and 1 representing the likelihood assigned to an event under a specified probability model. A probability of 0.01 corresponds to 1%; a probability of 1 corresponds to certainty within that model. An **expected value** is a probability-weighted average of possible numerical outcomes. For a discrete random variable \(X\) with outcomes \(x_i\) and probabilities \(p_i\): \[ E[X]=\sum_i p_i x_i \] Suppose a position loses 100 with probability 1% and loses zero with probability 99%. Expected loss is: \[ 0.01\times100+0.99\times0=1 \] Nothing in that calculation predicts that a realised loss will equal 1. In an individual period, the simplified position loses either 0 or 100. The value 1 describes the probability-weighted mean across the modelled distribution or across repeated comparable situations. That is why probability and expected loss must carry units correctly. Probability is dimensionless: 1%, 5%, 20%. Expected loss is measured in currency or another loss unit. Multiplying a probability by a loss amount can contribute to expected loss; the probability itself is never the amount of loss. Expected value is also sensitive to the modelled outcome set and assigned probabilities. Missing a severe state or mis-estimating its probability changes the answer. A mathematically correct weighted average does not rescue incorrect assumptions. This distinction forms the base for credit-risk reasoning. Default probability describes likelihood. Exposure describes what is at risk. Loss severity describes what portion is lost if the event occurs. Combining such quantities can create an expected-loss measure, but each answers a different question. Possible outcomes | v +----------------------+ | Assign probability | | p_i to each outcome | +----------------------+ | v +----------------------+ | Multiply | | p_i x outcome_i | +----------------------+ | v +----------------------+ | Sum across outcomes | +----------------------+ | v Expected value Probability is a likelihood; expected value is a probability-weighted amount. Reporting "1% expected loss" when the calculation actually produced a 1% probability of a monetary loss event. **Probability** — likelihood of an event under the stated model. --- **Expected value** — the probability-weighted average amount across possible outcomes. **No delta.** Probability axioms and expected-value mathematics do not depend on jurisdiction.

title: Variance and Volatility
one_screen: **Variance measures average squared dispersion around a mean; standard deviation is its square root.** In finance, volatility usually refers to a standard-deviation measure over a stated horizon, so volatility is meaningless without the variable, data frequency and time horizon.
bodyText: For a random variable \(X\) with mean \(\mu\), **variance** is: \[ Var(X)=E[(X-\mu)^2] \] It asks how far outcomes tend to lie from the mean, squares those deviations so positive and negative deviations do not cancel, and averages them according to the probability model. Variance has squared units. If \(X\) is measured in percentage points, variance is measured in squared percentage points. The **standard deviation** is: \[ \sigma=\sqrt{Var(X)} \] Taking the square root restores the original units, which makes standard deviation easier to interpret alongside the variable itself. NIST makes this unit distinction explicitly when describing measures of scale. In financial usage, **volatility** usually means a standard deviation of price changes, returns, rates or another chosen variable over a defined interval and observation scheme. A daily volatility calculated from daily observations and an annual volatility are not automatically the same number. Conversion can require assumptions about how changes behave through time; multiplying by an arbitrary number of days is not a general solution. Variance also treats upside and downside deviations symmetrically. A return far above the mean increases variance just as a similarly distant return below the mean does. That can be useful for measuring dispersion but makes volatility different from a pure downside-loss measure. Finally, equal variance does not imply equal tail behaviour. Two distributions can have the same mean and variance yet place very different probability in extreme outcomes. Variance and volatility therefore summarise spread; they do not fully describe risk. Outcomes X | v +----------------------+ | Mean = mu | +----------------------+ | v +----------------------+ | Deviations X - mu | +----------------------+ | v +----------------------+ | Square and average | | = variance | +----------------------+ | v +----------------------+ | Square root | | = standard deviation | +----------------------+ A volatility number is incomplete unless its underlying variable and measurement horizon are known. Comparing a daily standard deviation directly with an annual standard deviation because both are labelled "volatility". **Variance** — expected squared dispersion around the mean, expressed in squared units. --- **Standard deviation** — square root of variance, expressed in the original units and commonly called volatility in financial contexts. **No delta.** Variance and standard-deviation mathematics do not vary by jurisdiction.

title: Quantiles and Tail Risk
one_screen: A **quantile** is a threshold in a distribution: an \(\alpha\)-quantile has approximately \(\alpha\) of probability at or below it under the stated convention. **Tail risk is what happens in the extreme region beyond such thresholds; a quantile is not a maximum possible loss.**
bodyText: Take a modelled loss variable \(L\). A 99th-percentile loss quantile is a threshold such that roughly 99% of modelled losses lie at or below it and roughly 1% lie above it, subject to the precise quantile definition and whether the distribution is continuous or discrete. NIST illustrates percentiles through this cumulative-probability interpretation. This is the foundation of **Value at Risk (VaR)**-type thinking: a high loss quantile gives a boundary associated with a selected confidence level. But the quantile says little by itself about the severity of losses once that boundary has been breached. Consider two hypothetical loss distributions that both have a 99% quantile of 10. In one, the worst remaining 1% clusters around 11. In another, the remaining 1% includes losses of 100 or more. Their 99% quantiles can look similar while their tail severities are radically different. **Tail risk** concerns these extreme outcomes and their distribution. A heavier loss tail places relatively more probability or severity in extreme losses than a lighter-tailed alternative. Measures focusing on loss conditional on being beyond a quantile can therefore provide information that the quantile alone does not. A quantile also depends on horizon and model. A one-day 99% loss quantile and a one-year 99% loss quantile answer different questions. Changing the probability distribution, dependence assumptions or data window can change the estimated threshold. The phrase "99% confidence" is frequently miscommunicated as "there is only a 1% chance of any loss". That is wrong. It means approximately 1% of modelled outcomes exceed the stated loss threshold, not that the other 99% have zero loss. Loss distribution 0 ---------------------------------------> severe loss | | |<------ about 99% ------>|<-- tail -->| ^ | 99% quantile | v NOT maximum loss A quantile identifies a distribution threshold; it does not cap outcomes beyond the threshold. Describing a 99% VaR-type number as "the most that can be lost with 99% certainty". **Quantile** — a threshold associated with a cumulative probability level. --- **Tail risk** — the probability and severity of extreme outcomes beyond a chosen region; a single quantile does not describe the whole tail. **No delta.** Quantiles and probability tails are mathematical concepts independent of jurisdiction.

title: Expected Loss Versus Unexpected Loss
one_screen: **Expected loss is the probability-weighted average loss built into the centre of the loss distribution; unexpected loss is adverse variation around and beyond that expectation.** Provisioning and pricing address expected loss in different ways, while prudential capital is fundamentally concerned with resilience to losses beyond the expected level.
bodyText: Return to a simple position that loses 100 with 1% probability and zero otherwise. Its expected loss is 1. But no actual outcome in that example equals 1: realised loss is either 0 or 100. The gap between the average and adverse realisations is the intuition behind **unexpected loss**. Expected loss can be written generically as the probability-weighted mean of possible losses: \[ EL=E[L] \] In simple credit-risk shorthand, later frameworks may approximate expected loss using components for probability of default, exposure and loss severity. That decomposition does not change the fundamental definition: expected loss is an average over a loss distribution. Unexpected loss is not ordinarily a second amount that simply gets added to every loan's invoice. It describes variability around expected outcomes, particularly adverse states for which the institution needs resilience. The Basel credit-risk framework explicitly states that risk-weighted assets under its internal-ratings-based architecture are designed to address **unexpected losses**, while expected-loss amounts and provisions receive separate treatment. This makes the distinction foundational to banking. Expected losses should influence economics such as pricing and loss recognition under the applicable framework. Capital exists to provide loss-absorbing capacity when actual losses are worse than expected, though precise prudential treatment is more complex than "provisions equal EL and capital equals UL" in every circumstance. The distinction also prevents a dangerous error in risk reporting: a portfolio can have a modest expected loss but a severe tail. Low average loss does not imply low capital need, because concentration and dependence can make rare outcomes extremely damaging. Loss distribution | v +----------------------+ | Expected loss | | probability-weighted | | average | +----------------------+ | | adverse variation v +----------------------+ | Unexpected loss | | outcomes worse than | | the expected level | +----------------------+ | v +----------------------+ | Capital resilience | | against severe loss | +----------------------+ Expected loss describes the centre of a loss distribution; resilience must also address the possibility that realised losses are materially worse. Subtracting expected loss from a high quantile and treating the result as a universally defined accounting or regulatory "unexpected loss" number without checking the framework. **Expected loss** — probability-weighted average loss. --- **Unexpected loss** — adverse variation around expected loss, especially the severe outcomes for which additional resilience is required. **No delta.** The statistical distinction is universal; national prudential and accounting frameworks determine exactly how provisions and capital interact with it.

title: Risk Appetite
one_screen: **Risk appetite is the aggregate level and types of risk an institution is willing to assume within its risk capacity while pursuing its objectives.** Appetite becomes operational only when translated into limits, monitored against the actual risk profile, and linked to escalation and decisions.
bodyText: The Financial Stability Board's **risk appetite framework (RAF)** links four ideas: risk capacity, risk appetite, risk limits and risk profile. **Risk capacity** is the maximum level of risk the institution can bear before breaching constraints such as capital, liquidity, regulatory or operational viability. **Risk appetite** is how much and what types of risk the institution chooses to take within that capacity to pursue strategy. **Risk limits** translate appetite into practical boundaries. The **risk profile** is the institution's actual risk exposure at a point in time. Capacity should therefore sit outside appetite, not the other way round. A bank might have the capacity to tolerate a particular level of credit concentration but choose a lower appetite because its strategy favours diversification. Limits can then constrain exposures by sector, counterparty, geography, product or another measurable dimension. A useful appetite statement combines quantitative and qualitative dimensions. Some risks can be expressed directly through ratios or limits. Others require statements about activities the institution will avoid, control conditions that must be satisfied, or circumstances requiring escalation. Risk appetite is not a forecast. A statement that a bank is willing to accept a certain level of loss does not mean that loss is expected to occur. Nor is appetite simply a regulatory minimum. A regulatory boundary is an external constraint; internal appetite should define chosen risk-taking within the institution's capacity and applicable constraints. The framework closes through monitoring. Actual risk profile is compared with appetite and limits. Approaching or breaching a limit should trigger the predetermined escalation, remediation, acceptance or governance response rather than silent relabelling of the boundary. +----------------------+ | Risk capacity | | maximum bearable | +----------------------+ | v +----------------------+ | Risk appetite | | willing to assume | +----------------------+ | v +----------------------+ | Risk limits | | operational bounds | +----------------------+ | v +----------------------+ | Decisions / exposures| +----------------------+ | v +----------------------+ | Actual risk profile | +----------------------+ | v Monitor and escalate Risk appetite must remain within risk capacity and must connect to measurable or otherwise enforceable decision boundaries. Raising a limit after a breach solely so that the reported position becomes compliant, without treating the change as a governed risk-appetite decision. **Risk capacity** — the maximum risk the institution can bear subject to its binding constraints. --- **Risk appetite** — the risk the institution chooses to accept within that capacity; willingness and ability are not the same. **No delta.** Supervisory expectations vary, but the capacity-appetite-limits-profile architecture is a cross-jurisdictional governance principle.

title: The Three Lines Model
one_screen: The Three Lines Model separates **management's ownership and management of risk**, specialist support and challenge, and **independent internal-audit assurance**. The lines are roles in governance, not walls that permit one function to outsource responsibility to another.
bodyText: The Institute of Internal Auditors' current framework is called the **Three Lines Model**, updating the older "three lines of defence" terminology. It places the governing body, management and internal audit in related but distinct roles and rejects an overly rigid interpretation in which functions operate as isolated silos. The **first line** consists of management roles closest to delivering products, services and operations. First-line management owns and manages the risks arising from those activities and maintains the controls needed to keep risk within approved boundaries. The **second line** comprises management roles providing specialist expertise, support, monitoring and challenge on risk-related matters. Risk management and compliance functions are common examples. The second line can set frameworks, monitor exposures, challenge decisions and escalate concerns, but that does not transfer ownership of business risk away from first-line management. The **third line** is internal audit. Its defining feature is independence from management responsibilities so that it can provide objective assurance and advice regarding governance, risk management and internal control. The third line should not become the owner of controls it later audits; doing so can compromise its ability to assure them independently. The **governing body** sits above this operating distinction. It is accountable for governance and oversight and receives information and assurance from management and internal audit. Cooperation among the lines is desirable, but accountability and independence must remain clear. The model is therefore less about organisational charts than about answering: who owns the risk, who supports and challenges management, and who independently assures the governance and control system? +--------------------------+ | Governing body | | oversight + accountability| +--------------------------+ | v +--------------------------+ | FIRST LINE | | business / management | | owns and manages risk | +--------------------------+ | v +--------------------------+ | SECOND LINE | | expertise, monitoring, | | support and challenge | +--------------------------+ | v +--------------------------+ | THIRD LINE | | independent internal | | audit assurance | +--------------------------+ Management retains responsibility for managing risk; internal audit must remain sufficiently independent to provide objective assurance. Writing a control failure off as "second line's responsibility" because the risk function monitors it, even though the business process creating the risk sits in the first line. **Second line** — management functions providing expertise, monitoring, support and challenge. --- **Third line** — independent internal audit assurance; it is not simply a stronger version of second-line risk management. **No delta.** The IIA Three Lines Model is a governance model rather than a jurisdiction-specific banking rule; local supervisory requirements can add role-specific obligations.

title: Policy, Standard and Procedure
one_screen: A useful control hierarchy is **policy = required intent and principles; standard = mandatory control or design criteria; procedure = steps for execution**. The terminology is not legally universal, so authority and content matter more than the document label.
bodyText: A **policy** states what the institution requires and why. It usually establishes principles, scope, responsibilities, risk boundaries or mandatory outcomes. For example, a credit-risk policy might require independent approval above defined thresholds and prescribe high-level principles for acceptable lending. A **standard** converts policy into more specific mandatory requirements. It might define minimum information needed for an approval, required control frequencies, quantitative thresholds, modelling conventions or documentation fields. A standard should be sufficiently precise that compliance can be tested. A **procedure** describes how people or systems execute the requirement. It normally specifies a sequence: obtain information, perform checks, record evidence, obtain approvals, book the transaction and retain documentation. Procedures are closest to day-to-day operations and usually change more often than governing policy. This three-level hierarchy is a governance convention, not a globally fixed legal taxonomy. One institution may call a document a "policy" where another calls similar content a "standard", "framework", "manual" or "rulebook". Regulatory texts can also use these words differently. The reliable test is therefore the document's **authority, mandatory force, scope, owner and approval route**, not its title. The hierarchy should flow downward without contradiction. A procedure cannot legitimately authorise activity prohibited by the governing policy. A standard cannot silently widen risk appetite beyond an approved boundary. Where lower-level documents conflict with higher-authority requirements, the conflict must be resolved through governance rather than by choosing whichever text is operationally convenient. Version control matters for the same reason. Users need to know which document is effective, who approved it, what it superseded and how exceptions are authorised. +------------------------+ | POLICY | | intent, principles, | | mandatory outcomes | +------------------------+ | v +------------------------+ | STANDARD | | detailed mandatory | | requirements | +------------------------+ | v +------------------------+ | PROCEDURE | | execution steps | +------------------------+ | v +------------------------+ | Evidence / records | +------------------------+ Lower-authority documents may implement higher-authority requirements but cannot validly contradict them. Treating the word "policy" as proof of board approval, or "procedure" as proof of low authority, without checking the institution's actual governance taxonomy. **Standard** — a set of specific mandatory criteria translating higher-level requirements into testable controls. --- **Procedure** — the operational sequence used to perform those requirements; detailed steps do not themselves establish higher authority. **No delta.** There is no universal statutory taxonomy fixing these three document labels; institution-specific governance and applicable local rules determine formal authority.

title: What a Regulator Actually Does
one_screen: A banking regulator turns law and statutory objectives into enforceable boundaries, while **supervision** tests how institutions actually operate inside those boundaries. Depending on the mandate, the toolkit can include authorisation, rules, reporting, examinations, remediation and enforcement.
bodyText: **Regulation** establishes binding or otherwise formally applicable requirements under a legal mandate. In banking these can concern capital, liquidity, governance, risk management, permissible activities, reporting or customer treatment. **Supervision** is the continuing process of assessing institutions against applicable requirements and supervisory objectives, including through data, meetings, inspections, examinations and judgement. The two functions reinforce each other. A capital rule might specify a minimum ratio; supervision asks whether the bank calculates it correctly, manages the underlying risks, maintains credible controls and can remain resilient under stress. The Federal Reserve describes supervision as evaluating institutions' financial condition, governance, controls and ability to manage risks, complementing the regulatory framework. A regulator or supervisor can also possess **authorisation or licensing** powers that determine whether an institution may conduct regulated business, and **enforcement** powers to require remediation or impose consequences where legal conditions are met. Exact powers differ by statute and agency. The OCC, for example, charters, regulates and supervises national banks within its remit and conducts examinations focused on safety, soundness and compliance. Not every body called a "regulator" performs every function. The EU's EBA develops the Single Rulebook and promotes supervisory convergence, while institution-level supervision involves competent authorities under the EU architecture. Accounting standard-setters are different again: they prescribe financial-reporting standards rather than supervising bank safety and soundness. Law / statutory mandate | v +----------------------+ | Regulation / rules | +----------------------+ | v +----------------------+ | Authorisation and | | ongoing supervision | +----------------------+ | v +----------------------+ | Reporting, review, | | examination | +----------------------+ | v +----------------------+ | Remediation / | | enforcement where | | legally available | +----------------------+ Regulation defines applicable requirements; supervision assesses institutions and their risk management against law, rules and supervisory objectives. Assuming a bank is safe because it met a reported minimum ratio on one date, while ignoring supervisory assessment of governance, controls, concentrations and risk management. **Regulation** — the body of legally or formally applicable requirements made under the relevant mandate. --- **Supervision** — ongoing assessment of institutions and their practices; it tests reality rather than merely publishing rules. — RBI exercises statutory regulation and supervision of banks under powers including those derived from the Banking Regulation Act, with on-site and off-site supervisory mechanisms. [RBI Department of Supervision; Banking Regulation Act framework] — The PRA is responsible for prudential regulation and supervision of firms within its remit, focused on safety and soundness and related statutory objectives; the FCA separately carries major conduct responsibilities. [Bank of England/PRA prudential regulation; FCA mandate] — The EBA develops and maintains the Single Rulebook and supports supervisory convergence; it should not be mistaken for the direct supervisor of every EU bank. Institution-level supervisory responsibility depends on the EU and national competent-authority architecture. [EBA Single Rulebook; EBA Missions and Tasks] — Banking supervision is multi-agency. The Federal Reserve supervises institutions within its statutory remit, while the OCC charters, regulates and supervises national banks and federal savings associations. [Federal Reserve supervision framework; OCC mandate]

title: Prudential Regulation, Conduct Regulation and Accounting Standards
one_screen: **Prudential regulation asks whether a financial institution is safe and resilient; conduct regulation asks whether it behaves properly toward customers and markets; accounting standards determine how financial position and performance are recognised, measured and reported.** The three systems interact, but none is a substitute for another.
bodyText: **Prudential regulation** concerns the financial resilience and safe operation of regulated institutions. Its tools can include capital, liquidity, large-exposure, governance and risk-management requirements. The Basel framework is an international prudential standard architecture, while national and regional authorities implement their own legally applicable regimes. **Conduct regulation** concerns behaviour: how firms treat customers, design or distribute products, communicate, manage conflicts and comply with applicable market or consumer-protection obligations. The UK illustrates the institutional distinction clearly: the PRA is the prudential regulator for firms within its remit, while the FCA regulates conduct across a broad population of financial-services firms. **Accounting standards** answer another question: how transactions and economic events enter general-purpose financial statements. They establish recognition, measurement, presentation and disclosure rules. The FASB's mission, for example, is financial accounting and reporting standard-setting for nongovernmental US entities, not prudential bank supervision. The systems meet at important boundaries. Accounting values can be inputs into prudential measures, but supervisors can impose regulatory definitions, deductions and adjustments. A credit-loss allowance can affect accounting equity, while prudential rules determine how provisions interact with regulatory capital. A firm can therefore comply with an accounting standard yet breach a prudential requirement, or satisfy a capital rule yet breach a conduct obligation. India provides the strongest warning against collapsing the categories. RBI has deferred Ind AS implementation for banks until further notice, so scheduled commercial-bank provisioning remains governed by RBI prudential norms rather than Ind AS 109. Relevant NBFCs applying Ind AS occupy a different accounting position. BANK | +-------------+-------------+ | | | v v v +----------+ +----------+ +----------+ |PRUDENTIAL| | CONDUCT | |ACCOUNTING| |resilience| | behaviour| | reporting| +----------+ +----------+ +----------+ | | | v v v capital / customers / recognition / liquidity / markets / measurement / governance fairness presentation Accounting compliance does not prove prudential compliance, and prudential compliance does not prove conduct compliance; each framework answers a different regulatory or reporting question. Using an accounting label as though it determines prudential treatment automatically—for example, assuming an IFRS or Ind AS impairment allowance is identical to the regulatory provision or regulatory-capital deduction. **Prudential regulation** — requirements and supervision directed principally at institutional safety, soundness and financial resilience. --- **Accounting standards** — financial-reporting rules governing recognition, measurement, presentation and disclosure; they supply important numbers but do not themselves constitute prudential supervision. — RBI combines major prudential and banking-conduct regulatory responsibilities within its statutory remit. Scheduled commercial banks remain outside Ind AS implementation following RBI's deferment and use RBI prudential provisioning norms; relevant Ind AS-applying NBFCs are treated separately. [RBI DBR.BP.BC.No.29/21.07.001/2018-19; RBI prudential directions; RBI NBFC Ind AS guidance] — The PRA is the principal prudential regulator for banks and other firms within its statutory remit; the FCA is the principal conduct regulator across financial services. Applicable UK-adopted international accounting standards form a separate financial-reporting framework. [PRA prudential-regulation mandate; FCA mandate; UK Endorsement Board] — The CRR/CRD architecture and EBA Single Rulebook form core elements of EU banking prudential regulation. The EBA also has consumer-protection responsibilities, while conduct supervision and enforcement can involve national and sector-specific authorities. EU-adopted IFRS under the IAS Regulation is a separate accounting framework for accounts within its scope. [EBA Single Rulebook; EBA Consumer Protection; Regulation (EC) No 1606/2002] — Prudential supervision is distributed among agencies according to charter and statutory remit; the Federal Reserve and OCC are major examples. Banking agencies also enforce specified consumer and compliance requirements, while FASB establishes US GAAP for nongovernmental entities rather than prudential rules. [Federal Reserve supervision framework; OCC mandate; FASB Mission]

title: Impairment and Expected Credit Loss
one_screen: Impairment is the accounting recognition that contractual credit cash flows will not all be collected. Expected-credit-loss accounting brings that recognition forward: the allowance reflects losses expected from credit risk before a loss event has necessarily occurred.
bodyText: A loan may remain a legally valid claim for its full contractual amount while its accounting carrying amount is reduced by a **loss allowance**. Impairment is therefore not cancellation of the borrower’s obligation. It is recognition in the financial statements that some contractual cash flows are not expected to be collected. Under IFRS 9, the impairment model recognises expected credit losses (ECL) and updates the allowance as expectations and credit risk change. The standard replaced the IAS 39 incurred-loss approach; the move towards forward-looking loss recognition responded directly to concerns exposed by the financial crisis about delayed credit-loss recognition. The change is fundamental. An incurred-loss model asks whether evidence of impairment has already emerged. An expected-loss model asks what credit loss is expected given information available at the reporting date, including relevant forecasts. Under IFRS 9, performing instruments generally carry an allowance from initial recognition: 12-month ECL where credit risk has not increased significantly, and lifetime ECL after a significant increase in credit risk. Expected loss does not mean recognising every adverse economic possibility as though it were certain. IFRS 9 requires an unbiased, probability-weighted estimate using reasonable and supportable information and the time value of money. The allowance is therefore an estimate under uncertainty, not a hidden reserve and not a forecast of one inevitable outcome. The US reached the same broad destination—earlier expected-loss recognition—but with different architecture. ASC 326 CECL recognises lifetime expected credit losses for financial assets measured at amortised cost from initial recognition rather than using IFRS 9’s Stage 1/Stage 2 threshold. +---------------------+ | Contractual asset | +---------------------+ | v +---------------------+ | Expected collection | | assessed | +---------------------+ | v +---------------------+ | Expected shortfall | +---------------------+ | v +---------------------+ | Loss allowance / | | impairment expense | +---------------------+ Impairment changes the accounting measurement of expected recoverability; it does not by itself extinguish the contractual claim. Treating “performing” as equivalent to “zero impairment” is wrong under expected-loss accounting: credit loss can be expected before default or delinquency appears. **Impairment** — accounting recognition of expected credit loss on an asset or exposure. --- **Default** — a credit-risk event concerning the obligor or facility; impairment can exist before default. — Scheduled commercial banks remain outside Ind AS implementation and, through March 31, 2027, are governed by RBI’s 2025 IRACP provisioning framework; RBI’s separate 2026 bank ECL Directions take effect April 1, 2027. Relevant Ind AS-implementing NBFCs apply Ind AS impairment requirements. [RBI 2019 Deferral; RBI 2025 IRACP; RBI 2026 ECL Directions; RBI 2020 NBFC guidance] — UK-adopted IFRS 9 contains the ECL impairment model; PRA supervision concerns sound implementation rather than replacing IFRS measurement rules. [UK-adopted IFRS 9; PRA thematic feedback] — EU-adopted IFRS 9 supplies the accounting ECL model, supplemented for banks by EBA supervisory guidance. [Regulation (EU) 2023/1803; EBA/GL/2017/06] — ASC 326 CECL uses expected credit losses but generally recognises lifetime expected loss from initial recognition for amortised-cost assets rather than IFRS 9 staging. [ASU 2016-13; Interagency CECL FAQ]

title: Credit Loss Is a Discounted Cash Shortfall
one_screen: Under IFRS 9, credit loss is fundamentally the present value of the difference between contractual cash flows due and cash flows expected to be received. PD, LGD and EAD are modelling components; the accounting target is the cash shortfall.
bodyText: A useful mental model for ECL starts with cash rather than risk parameters. IFRS 9 defines a **credit loss** through cash shortfalls: compare all contractual cash flows due under the contract with all cash flows the entity expects to receive, then discount the difference using the relevant effective interest rate. Timing matters as well as amount; receiving the full principal materially late can create a credit loss because delayed cash is worth less at the reporting date. This definition explains why the common formula `PD × LGD × EAD` is a method rather than the accounting definition. Probability of default (PD) estimates the chance of default, loss given default (LGD) estimates loss severity conditional on default, and exposure at default (EAD) estimates the amount exposed when default occurs. A well-built parameter model should reproduce the expected discounted cash shortfall required by the accounting framework. If the parameterisation conflicts with that measurement objective, the model—not the accounting definition—must yield. IFRS 9 deliberately does not prescribe one modelling technique. Expected recoveries affect the shortfall. Cash expected from the borrower, collateral realisation, guarantees or other credit enhancements can reduce expected loss where those recoveries are appropriately included under the applicable measurement requirements. Their **timing**, costs and uncertainty still matter. A nominal recovery expected after several years is not equivalent to the same amount received today. The distinction also explains why market-price movements are not automatically credit losses. Credit impairment focuses on expected contractual collection. Market value may change because risk-free rates, liquidity premiums or other non-credit factors move even when expected contractual collection is unchanged. +---------------------------+ | Contractual cash flows | | due | +---------------------------+ | v +---------------------------+ | Expected cash flows | | actually collected | +---------------------------+ | v +---------------------------+ | Difference in amount | | and/or timing | +---------------------------+ | v +---------------------------+ | Discount to measurement | | date | +---------------------------+ | v +---------------------------+ | Credit loss | +---------------------------+ The economic object being measured is expected non-collection of contractual value, including the effect of timing. Using `PD × LGD × EAD` mechanically without checking whether it reproduces discounted expected cash shortfalls can produce a technically elaborate but accounting-inconsistent allowance. **Credit loss** — the expected discounted contractual cash shortfall. --- **Fair-value loss** — a change in market value that may contain credit, interest-rate, liquidity and other effects. — Current scheduled-commercial-bank IRACP provisioning is rule-based rather than an Ind AS 109 cash-shortfall ECL regime; RBI’s bank ECL Directions effective April 1, 2027 introduce an ECL framework with PD/LGD mechanics and EIR discounting. Relevant Ind AS NBFCs already operate under Ind AS impairment requirements. [RBI 2025 IRACP; RBI 2026 ECL Directions; RBI 2020 NBFC guidance] — UK-adopted IFRS 9 uses the IFRS cash-shortfall definition. [UK-adopted IFRS 9] — EU-adopted IFRS 9 uses the same cash-shortfall measurement principle. [Regulation (EU) 2023/1803] — CECL defines the allowance for amortised-cost assets as the amount needed to reflect the net amount expected to be collected; it permits multiple estimation methods rather than requiring the IFRS 9 cash-shortfall technique in every case. [ASC 326; Interagency CECL FAQ]

title: Probability-Weighted Outcomes
one_screen: ECL is an expectation across possible credit outcomes, not the loss under the single scenario management considers most likely. Non-linearity matters: weighting scenario-specific losses can differ materially from calculating loss once at probability-weighted average macroeconomic inputs.
bodyText: IFRS 9 requires expected credit losses to reflect an **unbiased and probability-weighted amount** determined by evaluating a range of possible outcomes. The aim is neither a worst-case provision nor a best-case provision. Where credit losses can arise in some possible outcomes but not others, the probability of both loss and no-loss outcomes matters even when the most likely single outcome would show no loss. Suppose three internally coherent macroeconomic scenarios produce ECL estimates of 40, 100 and 250, with probabilities of 20%, 60% and 20%. Probability-weighted ECL is `0.20×40 + 0.60×100 + 0.20×250 = 118`. The calculation does not mean the entity predicts a loss of exactly 118. It means 118 is the expectation across the modelled distribution. A critical modelling issue is **non-linearity**. Credit risk often deteriorates disproportionately when unemployment, property values or borrower cash flows pass stress thresholds. Consequently, ECL evaluated under a single “average” macro path may not equal the weighted average of ECL calculated separately under multiple scenarios. IFRS 9 does not prescribe a fixed number of scenarios; the number and construction must be sufficient to capture material non-linear effects and satisfy the unbiased probability-weighted objective. Scenario probabilities are themselves estimates. They should correspond to coherent economic narratives, not be selected backwards to obtain a desired allowance. Governance therefore needs to address scenario design, probability setting, model sensitivity and changes from the previous reporting date. +----------------+ | Scenario A | | ECL = 40 | | Weight = 20% | +----------------+ | v +----------------+ | Scenario B | | ECL = 100 | | Weight = 60% | +----------------+ | v +----------------+ | Scenario C | | ECL = 250 | | Weight = 20% | +----------------+ | v +----------------+ | Weighted ECL | | = 118 | +----------------+ Probability weighting applies to possible credit-loss outcomes; it is not permission to select whichever scenario gives a comfortable provision. Running ECL once on average macroeconomic variables and calling the result “probability weighted” can miss material non-linear loss behaviour. **Most-likely scenario** — the individual scenario with the highest assigned probability. --- **Expected loss** — the probability-weighted result across relevant possible outcomes. — Current bank IRACP is not a probability-weighted ECL accounting regime. RBI’s final 2026 bank ECL framework, effective April 1, 2027, explicitly requires multiple scenarios and probability weights informed by historical experience and expert judgement; Ind AS NBFCs already apply expected-loss accounting. [RBI 2026 ECL Directions, paragraphs 47–49] — IFRS 9 probability weighting applies; PRA’s 2025 thematic work additionally emphasises governance over model limitations and adjustments. [IFRS 9 5.5.17; PRA thematic feedback] — EU-adopted IFRS 9 applies the same probability-weighted objective, with EBA supervisory expectations around robust ECL practices. [Regulation (EU) 2023/1803; EBA/GL/2017/06] — CECL also incorporates reasonable and supportable expectations about future conditions, but Topic 326 does not impose the IFRS 9 scenario architecture or prescribe one estimation method. [ASU 2016-13; Interagency CECL FAQ]

title: Effective Interest Rate Discounting
one_screen: IFRS 9 discounts expected cash shortfalls using the effective interest rate established from the instrument’s own economics, not a current market yield selected at the reporting date. The rule prevents changes in market discount rates from being mistaken for changes in credit loss.
bodyText: The **effective interest rate (EIR)** is the rate that discounts estimated contractual cash flows over the expected life of a financial instrument to its initial gross carrying amount, incorporating relevant fees, transaction costs, premiums and discounts. For ordinary IFRS 9 ECL measurement, expected credit losses are discounted to the reporting date using the EIR determined at initial recognition, or an approximation where permitted. Variable-rate instruments use the applicable effective rate under the standard’s requirements. Why not use today’s market lending rate? Because ECL is intended to measure deterioration in expected contractual collection, not revalue the asset to current market terms. Assume a fixed-rate loan was originated when its EIR was 6%, but equivalent new lending later yields 9% because general interest rates increased. Discounting expected cash shortfalls at 9% would mix a market-rate change into the credit-loss measurement. Retaining the instrument-specific EIR keeps the impairment estimate connected to the economics on which amortised cost was established. Discounting matters even when the nominal recovery amount is unchanged. A recovery of 100 expected in one year is worth more at the reporting date than 100 expected after five years. Recovery timing, foreclosure delays, restructuring schedules and collection costs can therefore materially affect loss severity. Purchased or originated credit-impaired assets are different: IFRS 9 uses a **credit-adjusted effective interest rate**, because expected credit losses are incorporated into estimated cash flows when that rate is established at initial recognition. +-----------------------+ | Expected future | | cash shortfalls | +-----------------------+ | v +-----------------------+ | Instrument EIR from | | initial recognition | +-----------------------+ | v +-----------------------+ | Discount shortfalls | | to reporting date | +-----------------------+ | v +-----------------------+ | Present-value ECL | +-----------------------+ A credit-loss discount rate must be consistent with the accounting measurement basis of the asset; changing the discount rate can change measured loss even when expected collections do not change. Replacing the original EIR with a current market yield in IFRS 9 ECL turns part of a market-rate movement into an apparent credit-loss movement. **Effective interest rate** — the instrument-specific yield used in amortised-cost accounting and IFRS 9 ECL discounting. --- **Current market rate** — the yield currently demanded for comparable new risk; it can move without any change in the borrower’s expected cash payments. — Current scheduled-commercial-bank IRACP provisioning does not use an Ind AS 109 EIR-based ECL framework. RBI’s 2026 bank ECL Directions require EIR discounting for instruments originated or invested from April 1, 2027 and provide a transition path for existing loans through March 31, 2030. [RBI 2026 ECL Directions, paragraphs 50–53] — UK-adopted IFRS 9 follows the original-EIR requirement. [IFRS 9 B5.5.44] — EU-adopted IFRS 9 follows the same EIR measurement rule. [Regulation (EU) 2023/1803; IFRS 9 B5.5.44] — CECL permits multiple estimation techniques; when a discounted-cash-flow method is used, Topic 326 uses the asset’s effective interest rate, but DCF is not mandatory for all amortised-cost assets. [ASC 326; Federal Reserve guidance]

title: Forward-Looking Information and Macroeconomic Scenarios
one_screen: ECL must respond to information about the future when that information is relevant, reasonable and supportable. Macroeconomic forecasts are inputs to credit-risk expectations, not independent reserves added on top of modelled loss.
bodyText: Historical default and recovery experience is a starting point, not the destination. IFRS 9 requires ECL to incorporate reasonable and supportable information available without undue cost or effort, including forecasts of future economic conditions. Forward-looking information (FLI) can affect the probability of default, expected exposure, recovery rates, staging, or several of these simultaneously. Relevant variables depend on the portfolio. Employment conditions may be important for unsecured household credit; property prices and interest rates may affect mortgage affordability and collateral recoveries; output, commodity prices or sector-specific demand can matter for corporate borrowers. The modelling question is not “Which macro variables are fashionable?” but “Which variables have a defensible causal or predictive relationship with the credit outcomes being estimated?” The **forecast horizon** and the **credit horizon** are different. A five-year loan can require lifetime ECL even when detailed macro forecasts are credible for only a shorter period. Beyond a reasonable and supportable forecasting horizon, models need a disciplined method for extrapolation or reversion rather than pretending to possess precise long-range forecasts. Under US CECL, Topic 326 expressly contemplates reversion to historical loss information for periods beyond the reasonable-and-supportable forecast horizon. FLI also influences staging. A borrower can experience a significant increase in credit risk before missing a payment when forward-looking evidence indicates material deterioration. That is why a purely arrears-driven staging system defeats the purpose of expected-loss accounting. +----------------------+ | Historical credit | | behaviour | +----------------------+ | v +----------------------+ | Current conditions | +----------------------+ | v +----------------------+ | Reasonable and | | supportable forecasts| +----------------------+ | v +----------------------+ | PD / LGD / EAD / | | staging effects | +----------------------+ | v +----------------------+ | Forward-looking ECL | +----------------------+ Forward-looking information belongs in ECL only through a defensible connection to expected credit outcomes. Adding a generic “macroeconomic buffer” after already incorporating the same macro deterioration in modelled PD or LGD can double-count the risk. **Forecast horizon** — the period over which specific forward-looking economic estimates remain reasonable and supportable. --- **ECL horizon** — the period over which expected credit losses must be measured; it can extend beyond the detailed forecast horizon. — Current bank IRACP remains primarily classification- and provisioning-rule based. RBI’s ECL Directions effective April 1, 2027 require macroeconomic variables and multiple scenarios, including documented treatment beyond standard forecast horizons; Ind AS NBFC ECL already requires forward-looking measurement. [RBI 2026 ECL Directions; RBI 2020 NBFC guidance] — IFRS 9 governs FLI; PRA’s 2025 review stressed monitoring model boundaries and risks not adequately captured by existing models. [IFRS 9 5.5.17; PRA 2025] — EU-adopted IFRS 9 applies, with EBA guidance and monitoring focused on sound forward-looking ECL implementation. [Regulation (EU) 2023/1803; EBA/GL/2017/06] — CECL uses historical experience, current conditions and reasonable and supportable forecasts, with reversion to historical information when forecasting beyond the supportable period. [ASC 326; FASB Staff Q&A Topic 326 No. 2]

title: The IFRS 9 Three-Stage Architecture
one_screen: IFRS 9 staging changes the horizon of loss recognition as credit risk changes: Stage 1 carries 12-month ECL, Stage 2 lifetime ECL after significant deterioration, and Stage 3 lifetime ECL once the asset is credit-impaired. Stage is a credit-risk state, not simply an arrears bucket.
bodyText: At each reporting date, IFRS 9 asks whether credit risk has increased significantly since initial recognition and whether the asset is credit-impaired. Those two assessments create the familiar three-stage architecture. Stage 1 generally contains instruments without a significant increase in credit risk and carries **12-month ECL**. Stage 2 contains instruments with a significant increase in credit risk (SICR) that are not credit-impaired and carries **lifetime ECL**. Stage 3 contains credit-impaired assets and also carries lifetime ECL. The jump from Stage 1 to Stage 2 is intentionally substantial: the allowance moves from losses associated with defaults possible in the next twelve months to losses associated with defaults over the remaining life. That makes staging economically important even if PD, LGD and EAD models themselves remain unchanged. Stage 2 is not “30–89 days past due”. Arrears are one indicator and the 30-day rule is a backstop, but SICR can and should be identified earlier when reasonable and supportable information indicates material deterioration. Similarly, Stage 3 is not defined merely by one delinquency count; it reflects evidence that the financial asset is credit-impaired, with IFRS 9 listing events such as significant financial difficulty, breach of contract or concessions related to financial difficulty. Stage assignment therefore depends on both **relative deterioration** and **current credit condition**. The reference point for Stage 2 is risk at initial recognition; the reference for Stage 3 is whether the asset is credit-impaired now. +-----------------------+ | Initial recognition | +-----------------------+ | v +-----------------------+ | Stage 1 | | 12-month ECL | +-----------------------+ | SICR v +-----------------------+ | Stage 2 | | Lifetime ECL | +-----------------------+ | Credit-impaired v +-----------------------+ | Stage 3 | | Lifetime ECL | +-----------------------+ Stage 1 versus Stage 2 determines **which default-event horizon feeds ECL**; Stage 3 additionally identifies credit impairment. Building stages directly from delinquency bands and treating forward-looking SICR indicators as optional reverses IFRS 9’s logic. **Stage 2** — significant deterioration since initial recognition without current credit impairment. --- **Stage 3** — a financial asset that is credit-impaired at the reporting date. — Scheduled commercial banks do not currently apply the IFRS 9 stage model. RBI’s final 2026 ECL Directions introduce a regulatory three-stage framework from April 1, 2027; relevant Ind AS NBFCs already operate under Ind AS 109-style ECL requirements. [RBI 2026 ECL Directions, paragraphs 25–26; RBI 2020 NBFC guidance] — UK-adopted IFRS 9 applies the three-stage model. [IFRS 9 5.5; UK-adopted IFRS 9] — EU-adopted IFRS 9 applies the same accounting staging structure, with EBA supervisory guidance. [Regulation (EU) 2023/1803; EBA/GL/2017/06] — CECL has no Stage 1/Stage 2/Stage 3 architecture for amortised-cost assets: lifetime expected loss is recognised from initial recognition. [ASC 326; Federal Reserve CECL FAQ]

title: Twelve-Month ECL
one_screen: Twelve-month ECL is not the cash loss expected during the next twelve months. It is the lifetime credit loss arising from default events that are possible within the next twelve months, weighted by the probability of those defaults.
bodyText: This is one of the most persistent IFRS 9 misunderstandings. Stage 1 does **not** estimate only cash shortfalls occurring during the next year. IFRS 9 defines 12-month ECL as the portion of lifetime expected credit losses representing losses resulting from default events that are possible within twelve months after the reporting date. Consider a five-year loan. A default could occur nine months from today, followed by restructuring and collateral recovery over the next three years. If that default event lies within the relevant twelve-month default horizon, the ECL calculation includes the full discounted loss consequences of that default, including cash shortfalls occurring after month twelve. Conversely, a default expected only in year four is outside Stage 1’s 12-month default-event horizon even though it may enter lifetime ECL after SICR. This also means 12-month ECL is not simply “lifetime ECL for loans expected to default within a year”. Every exposure can contribute through the probability that a default event occurs in the next twelve months, multiplied by the loss consequences if it occurs. IFRS 9’s application guidance explicitly distinguishes these concepts. For an instrument with less than twelve months remaining, the relevant period cannot exceed the remaining exposure period. The term “12-month” therefore describes the maximum default-event horizon for Stage 1, not a requirement to manufacture risk beyond contractual exposure. Reporting date | v +----------------------+ | Next 12 months | | Which defaults can | | occur? | +----------------------+ | v +----------------------+ | For each such | | default, measure | | full loss consequence| +----------------------+ | v +----------------------+ | Probability-weight | | and discount | +----------------------+ | v +----------------------+ | 12-month ECL | +----------------------+ “Twelve months” limits the **default-event window**, not the timing of subsequent cash shortfalls caused by those defaults. Truncating recoveries and losses at month twelve systematically misstates Stage 1 ECL on instruments whose post-default workout extends beyond a year. **12-month ECL** — lifetime loss consequences of defaults possible during the next twelve months. --- **Twelve months of cash loss** — cash shortfalls physically occurring during the next year; this is not the IFRS 9 definition. — Current bank IRACP has no Stage 1 12-month-ECL concept. RBI’s bank ECL framework effective April 1, 2027 adopts the same default-event-horizon definition of 12-month ECL. [RBI 2026 ECL Directions, definition of 12-month ECL] — UK-adopted IFRS 9 uses the IFRS definition. [IFRS 9 B5.5.43] — EU-adopted IFRS 9 uses the same definition. [Regulation (EU) 2023/1803; IFRS 9 B5.5.43] — CECL does not use a 12-month Stage 1 allowance for amortised-cost assets; expected losses are measured over the contractual term, subject to Topic 326’s treatment of expected prepayments and other scope rules. [ASC 326; Interagency CECL FAQ]

title: Significant Increase in Credit Risk
one_screen: SICR is principally a relative test: compare the risk of default over the remaining life at the reporting date with that risk at initial recognition. Absolute thresholds can operationalise or conservatively supplement the test, but they must not erase the origination benchmark.
bodyText: An IFRS 9 instrument moves to lifetime ECL when credit risk has increased significantly since initial recognition. The standard focuses on the **change in the risk of default**, not the change in the amount of ECL. The comparison is between default risk over the expected life at the reporting date and the corresponding risk at initial recognition. That makes SICR a **relative** concept. A movement from very low risk to moderate risk can be significant even though the current absolute PD remains below a portfolio-level “high risk” threshold. Conversely, a borrower originated at high risk may show a high current PD without having deteriorated significantly relative to origination. IFRS 9 specifically notes that an identical absolute change in default risk can have different significance depending on the starting level of risk. Practitioners nevertheless use **absolute indicators**: internal rating grades, watchlists, forbearance events, PD thresholds, pricing changes, sector stress or other risk signals. These can be useful operational triggers, particularly when they identify deterioration conservatively. They are not a licence to replace the IFRS 9 objective with a single current-risk cut-off. The design must still identify significant change since origination. IFRS 9 also permits a low-credit-risk practical expedient: where an instrument has low credit risk at the reporting date, an entity may assume credit risk has not increased significantly. “Low credit risk” concerns default risk and capacity to meet obligations; strong collateral alone does not make an otherwise weak borrower low risk. +-----------------------+ | Risk at origination | +-----------------------+ | v +-----------------------+ | Risk at reporting | | date | +-----------------------+ | v +-----------------------+ | Compare change over | | remaining life | +-----------------------+ | | v v +----------+ +----------+ | No SICR | | SICR | | Stage 1 | | Stage 2 | +----------+ +----------+ SICR is about deterioration relative to the credit risk accepted at initial recognition. Using one absolute current-PD threshold for every exposure can leave initially low-risk borrowers in Stage 1 after a proportionately severe deterioration. **Relative SICR test** — measures deterioration from the asset’s origination risk benchmark. --- **Absolute risk threshold** — measures the current level of risk without necessarily considering where the exposure started. — Current scheduled-commercial-bank IRACP does not use IFRS 9 SICR. RBI’s final bank ECL framework from April 1, 2027 requires a relative lifetime-risk comparison and allows documented operational parameters; relevant Ind AS NBFCs apply SICR requirements with RBI prudential guidance. [RBI 2026 ECL Directions, paragraphs 25–31; RBI 2020 NBFC guidance] — IFRS 9 SICR applies; PRA supervision expects robust and timely recognition of credit deterioration. [IFRS 9 5.5; PRA 2025] — EU-adopted IFRS 9 provides the SICR test; EBA/GL/2017/06 supplements bank supervisory expectations. [Regulation (EU) 2023/1803; EBA/GL/2017/06] — CECL has no SICR threshold controlling a switch from 12-month to lifetime allowance because lifetime expected losses are recognised from initial recognition. [ASC 326]

title: The Thirty-Day Past-Due Backstop
one_screen: More than 30 days past due creates a rebuttable IFRS 9 presumption that SICR has occurred. It is a backstop, not the normal definition of Stage 2, and rebuttal requires reasonable and supportable evidence rather than routine policy.
