bodyText: IFRS 9 contains a rebuttable presumption that credit risk has increased significantly since initial recognition when contractual payments are **more than 30 days past due**. “Rebuttable” matters: the presumption is strong but not irrebuttable. An entity may rebut it when reasonable and supportable information demonstrates that credit risk has not increased significantly despite the delinquency. The equally important point is what the rule does **not** mean. An entity must not wait for day 31 when other reasonable and supportable information identifies SICR earlier. IFRS 9 explicitly treats the delinquency presumption as a backstop. A rating downgrade, worsening liquidity, adverse covenant information or relevant macro deterioration can trigger Stage 2 before any payment is missed. Rebuttal should be evidence-based. A temporary administrative failure may support rebuttal where credible historical and current evidence shows that it does not signal higher lifetime default risk. A blanket policy that all 30–59 DPD cases remain Stage 1 would invert the presumption and is inconsistent with its purpose. Past-due status also must be computed consistently. Data-quality errors around due dates, payment allocation, moratoria, restructurings and account-level versus borrower-level delinquency can cause false stage transfers or conceal genuine ones. The backstop is simple conceptually but operationally dependent on reliable delinquency data. +----------------------+ | More than 30 DPD? | +----------------------+ | | No Yes | | v v +---------+ +------------------+ | Use all | | SICR presumed | | SICR | +------------------+ | evidence| | +---------+ v +------------------+ | Strong evidence | | to rebut? | +------------------+ | | No Yes | | v v +---------+ +---------+ | Stage 2 | | Continue| | | | full SICR| +---------+ | assessment| +---------+ A backstop catches deterioration missed by earlier indicators; it does not replace those indicators. Calling 30 DPD “the Stage 2 trigger” causes late recognition because it turns an outer backstop into the primary staging rule. **Rebuttable presumption** — a default conclusion that stands unless supported evidence demonstrates otherwise. --- **Optional indicator** — a factor that may simply be ignored; the 30-DPD presumption is not optional. — For Ind AS-implementing NBFCs, RBI reiterates the 30-DPD rebuttable presumption and additionally says exposures overdue beyond 60 days must not have SICR recognition deferred. Current scheduled-commercial-bank IRACP is different. RBI’s bank ECL Directions effective April 1, 2027 adopt a more-than-30-DPD rebuttable presumption, with a specific revolving-facility backstop. [RBI 2020 NBFC guidance; RBI 2026 ECL Directions, paragraphs 33–36] — UK IFRS 9 applies the more-than-30-DPD rebuttable SICR presumption. [IFRS 9 5.5.11] — EU-adopted IFRS 9 applies the same presumption. [Regulation (EU) 2023/1803; IFRS 9 5.5.11] — CECL has no 30-DPD staging backstop because there is no Stage 1-to-Stage 2 lifetime-loss switch. Delinquency remains relevant credit information within allowance estimation and credit administration. [ASC 326]

title: Stage Three and Credit-Impaired Assets
one_screen: Stage 3 means the financial asset is credit-impaired at the reporting date, not merely that its risk has increased. Lifetime ECL remains the allowance basis, while IFRS 9 changes interest recognition for assets that became credit-impaired after origination.
bodyText: IFRS 9 defines a financial asset as **credit-impaired** when one or more events have occurred that have a detrimental impact on estimated future cash flows. Evidence can include significant financial difficulty of the borrower, breach of contract such as default or delinquency, a concession granted for financial difficulty, probable bankruptcy or disappearance of an active market because of financial difficulties. Stage 3 therefore represents more than elevated probability of default. Stage 2 says risk has increased significantly but the asset is not yet credit-impaired; Stage 3 says impairment evidence has crystallised. IFRS 9 also contains a rebuttable operational presumption that default does not occur later than 90 days past due unless reasonable and supportable information justifies a more lagging criterion. The accounting definition still cannot be reduced to one DPD threshold. Both Stage 2 and Stage 3 carry lifetime ECL, but Stage 3 has an additional interest consequence. For a financial asset that was not credit-impaired when originated but later becomes credit-impaired, IFRS 9 calculates interest revenue by applying the original EIR to **amortised cost**, meaning the gross carrying amount net of the loss allowance, rather than to the gross carrying amount used for non-credit-impaired assets. That distinction prevents recognition of interest income on amounts the accounting measurement already expects not to collect. It is separate from the question of whether contractual interest remains legally due. +-----------------------+ | Performing / elevated | | risk | +-----------------------+ | v +-----------------------+ | Credit-impairment | | evidence occurs | +-----------------------+ | v +-----------------------+ | Stage 3 | | Lifetime ECL | +-----------------------+ | v +-----------------------+ | IFRS interest on | | amortised cost | +-----------------------+ Credit impairment concerns detrimental effects on expected cash flows, not merely a high risk score. Equating Stage 3 mechanically with “90 DPD” misses borrowers that become credit-impaired before 90 days and misunderstands the default backstop. **SICR** — material deterioration in default risk since initial recognition. --- **Credit-impaired** — evidence exists that events have detrimentally affected estimated future cash flows. — Current commercial-bank IRACP uses NPA, substandard, doubtful and loss-asset classifications rather than IFRS Stage 3; common NPA mechanics include 90-day overdue/out-of-order criteria. RBI’s ECL Directions from April 1, 2027 introduce Stage 3 while retaining prudential floors and specific income-recognition rules. [RBI 2025 IRACP; RBI 2026 ECL Directions] — UK-adopted IFRS 9 applies the credit-impaired definition and Stage 3 lifetime ECL/interest mechanics. [IFRS 9 Appendix A and 5.4.1] — EU-adopted IFRS 9 applies the same accounting definition; prudential default concepts remain separate regulatory concepts even where operational alignment is sought. [Regulation (EU) 2023/1803; EBA guidance] — CECL has no Stage 3 allowance category. US nonaccrual and regulatory classification practices are separate from Topic 326’s lifetime expected-loss measurement. [ASC 326; Interagency CECL policy]

title: Purchased or Originated Credit-Impaired Assets
one_screen: A POCI asset is already credit-impaired when first recognised, so ordinary Stage 1-to-Stage 3 logic does not describe its economics. IFRS 9 embeds initial expected credit losses in a credit-adjusted EIR and subsequently recognises only changes in lifetime ECL.
bodyText: **Purchased or originated credit-impaired (POCI)** financial assets are credit-impaired at initial recognition. A purchase at a deep discount because the borrower is in severe financial difficulty is a common economic pattern, although the accounting test is credit impairment at initial recognition rather than the size of the discount alone. POCI accounting avoids recognising a conventional Day-1 loss allowance on top of a purchase price that already reflects expected credit losses. Instead, expected credit losses at initial recognition are incorporated into expected cash flows used to calculate the **credit-adjusted effective interest rate**. Interest revenue is subsequently based on that credit-adjusted EIR. After initial recognition, the entity recognises the cumulative change in **lifetime ECL** as an impairment gain or loss. This can produce an impairment gain if expected collections improve relative to the credit-adjusted expectations embedded at purchase or origination. The asset does not first enter “Stage 1” merely because it has just been recognised; the ordinary staging model assumes an initially non-credit-impaired asset and therefore does not fit POCI economics. The concept is particularly important when comparing purchased distressed assets with loans that deteriorate after origination. Two assets can have identical current expected cash flows but different accounting histories because one was purchased already impaired and the other became impaired after initial recognition. +------------------------+ | Credit-impaired at | | initial recognition? | +------------------------+ | Yes v +------------------------+ | POCI | +------------------------+ | v +------------------------+ | Initial expected loss | | embedded in expected | | cash flows | +------------------------+ | v +------------------------+ | Credit-adjusted EIR | +------------------------+ | v +------------------------+ | Recognise subsequent | | change in lifetime ECL | +------------------------+ For POCI assets, initial credit deterioration is part of the asset’s starting economics rather than a post-origination stage migration. Booking a normal Day-1 Stage 3 allowance on top of a purchase price already reflecting credit impairment can double-count the initial expected loss under IFRS 9. **POCI** — an asset credit-impaired when first recognised by the reporting entity. --- **Stage 3 after origination** — an asset that was not credit-impaired initially but later became credit-impaired. — Current scheduled-commercial-bank IRACP does not operate the Ind AS 109 POCI model. RBI’s final bank ECL framework from April 1, 2027 separately identifies POCI, embeds initial ECL in a credit-adjusted EIR and recognises subsequent cumulative lifetime-ECL changes; relevant Ind AS NBFCs follow applicable Ind AS requirements. [RBI 2026 ECL Directions, paragraphs 24 and related POCI provisions] — UK-adopted IFRS 9 applies the POCI and credit-adjusted-EIR model. [IFRS 9 Appendix A, 5.4.1, 5.5.13] — EU-adopted IFRS 9 applies the same POCI treatment. [Regulation (EU) 2023/1803] — ASC 326 uses **purchased credit deteriorated (PCD)** accounting rather than IFRS 9 POCI: the acquisition-date allowance is added to purchase price to establish the initial amortised-cost basis, producing a gross-up rather than IFRS 9’s POCI credit-adjusted-EIR model. [ASC 326; Interagency CECL FAQ]

title: Transfers Back and Cure Asymmetry
one_screen: IFRS 9 allows transfer back from lifetime to 12-month ECL when the SICR criterion is no longer met, but reversal is not simply the mirror image of deterioration. The question is whether current lifetime default risk is no longer significantly above the origination benchmark—not whether the latest adverse symptom has merely disappeared.
bodyText: IFRS 9 requires the loss allowance to revert from lifetime ECL to 12-month ECL when the criterion for lifetime ECL is no longer met. That makes staging two-way: exposures can deteriorate and later improve. The apparent asymmetry arises from the reference point. Suppose a borrower entered Stage 2 after a sharp internal-rating downgrade. Six months later, the rating improves by one grade. The original trigger has partly reversed, but current risk may still be substantially worse than at origination. Stage 2 therefore remains appropriate. “Cure” is not simply the opposite movement in the latest indicator; it requires reassessing current credit risk against the original benchmark. The same principle prevents automatic cure immediately after an arrears balance is paid. Payment can be strong evidence of improvement, but the borrower may remain financially weak, recently restructured or exposed to adverse forward-looking conditions. All relevant reasonable and supportable information remains part of SICR assessment. Conversely, IFRS 9 does not establish a universal mandatory probation period for every Stage 2-to-Stage 1 transfer. Policies that require sustained performance can be evidential tools, but the accounting test remains whether SICR persists. Stage 3 cure adds another layer: first determine whether the asset remains credit-impaired; then determine whether SICR relative to origination still exists. A cured Stage 3 exposure need not jump directly to Stage 1 if credit risk remains significantly elevated. +--------------------+ | Stage 2 / Stage 3 | +--------------------+ | v +--------------------+ | Has current risk | | improved? | +--------------------+ | v +--------------------+ | Compare again with | | origination risk | +--------------------+ | | SICR remains SICR gone | | v v +---------+ +---------+ | Stage 2 | | Stage 1 | | lifetime| | 12m ECL | +---------+ +---------+ A stage reversal must reapply the same underlying credit-risk assessment objective used for deterioration. Automatically curing Stage 2 when DPD returns to zero can move an exposure to Stage 1 while its lifetime default risk remains materially above origination. **Symptom cure** — disappearance of a particular warning signal such as arrears. --- **SICR cure** — evidence that credit risk is no longer significantly increased relative to initial recognition. — Current bank IRACP has its own NPA-upgradation rules rather than IFRS stage cure. RBI’s ECL Directions effective April 1, 2027 contain specific Stage 3 upgradation and restructuring conditions alongside SICR assessment, so their prudential cure mechanics must be applied on their own terms. [RBI 2025 IRACP; RBI 2026 ECL Directions, paragraphs 78–81] — IFRS 9 permits reversion to 12-month ECL when lifetime-ECL criteria are no longer met; PRA expects robust monitoring rather than mechanical cures. [IFRS 9 5.5.7; PRA 2025] — EU-adopted IFRS 9 follows the same accounting reversal principle, supplemented by EBA supervisory guidance. [Regulation (EU) 2023/1803; EBA/GL/2017/06] — CECL has no Stage 2-to-Stage 1 cure because it has no staged allowance horizon; improved credit expectations reduce the lifetime allowance through remeasurement. [ASC 326]

title: Lifetime PD Term Structures
one_screen: Lifetime ECL needs the timing of default risk, not merely one lifetime default percentage. Marginal PD measures default probability in a particular future interval conditional on survival to that interval; cumulative PD measures the probability of having defaulted by a stated horizon.
bodyText: A **PD term structure** distributes default risk through time. This matters because ECL depends not only on whether default eventually occurs but also on when it occurs: exposure, recoveries and discount factors can all differ by period. Let cumulative PD to year 1 be 2%, to year 2 be 5%, and to year 3 be 9%. The unconditional probability of default specifically during year 2 is approximately `5% − 2% = 3%`; during year 3 it is `9% − 5% = 4%`. Those are **marginal** or interval default probabilities on an unconditional basis. A conditional hazard rate asks a slightly different question: given survival to the start of the interval, what is the probability of default during it? The denominator therefore excludes exposures that already defaulted. The distinctions matter operationally. Adding cumulative PDs across years double-counts earlier defaults because a borrower counted in the year-2 cumulative PD remains included in year 3. ECL engines normally need mutually exclusive default timing probabilities when they sum period-specific loss contributions. IFRS 9 does not mandate a `PD × LGD × EAD` implementation, but where that architecture is used, lifetime PD must represent default risk over the relevant lifetime and be consistent with forward-looking information. IFRS 9 also warns that changes in 12-month default risk are only an approximation for changes in lifetime risk when the circumstances make that approximation reasonable; concentrated risk beyond twelve months can make the shortcut inappropriate. +----------------------+ | Cumulative PD | | Y1 = 2% | +----------------------+ | v +----------------------+ | Cumulative PD | | Y2 = 5% | +----------------------+ | v +----------------------+ | Y2 marginal default | | probability ≈ 3% | +----------------------+ | v +----------------------+ | Apply Y2 EAD, LGD, | | discount factor | +----------------------+ Default probabilities used across periods must be mutually consistent so that an obligor cannot be counted as newly defaulting more than once. Summing one-year cumulative PD figures to construct lifetime PD overstates default risk by repeatedly counting defaults already included in earlier horizons. **Cumulative PD** — probability of default at any time from the starting date up to a stated horizon. --- **Marginal PD** — probability allocated to a particular future interval rather than all preceding intervals combined. — Current commercial-bank IRACP does not require lifetime PD term structures. RBI’s ECL Directions effective April 1, 2027 require 12-month PD for Stage 1 and lifetime PD for Stage 2 under a PD–LGD approach, and prohibit mechanically extending Stage 1 PD parameters without adjustment for lifetime and higher-risk characteristics. [RBI 2026 ECL Directions, paragraphs 45–46] — IFRS 9 governs the measurement objective but does not prescribe one PD-term-structure methodology. [IFRS 9 5.5 and B5.5] — EU-adopted IFRS 9 has the same accounting position; EBA supervisory work addresses sound ECL methodology. [Regulation (EU) 2023/1803; EBA/GL/2017/06] — CECL may use PD/LGD methods but does not require them; any selected method must estimate lifetime expected collectability consistently with Topic 326. [ASC 326; Interagency CECL FAQ]

title: Lifetime EAD and Revolving Behavioural Life
one_screen: Lifetime EAD is a path through time, not today’s balance copied into every future period. Revolving facilities are special because future drawdowns and the period of credit exposure can depend on borrower behaviour and the lender’s practical risk-management actions, sometimes extending beyond a nominal cancellation notice period.
bodyText: **Exposure at default (EAD)** represents the amount expected to be exposed when default occurs. For an amortising term loan, future EAD normally changes as scheduled principal is repaid, prepayments occur, additional drawings are made or interest and fees accumulate. A lifetime ECL model therefore needs an exposure profile aligned with each possible default period rather than one static balance. Undrawn commitments create another dimension. The borrower may draw additional funds before default, especially as financial condition weakens. Expected future utilisation must therefore be consistent with contractual rights, historical behaviour and the institution’s credit-management practices. Revolving products require special attention under IFRS 9. Ordinarily, the maximum ECL measurement period is the maximum contractual period over which the entity is exposed to credit risk. IFRS 9 contains a specific exception for certain financial instruments containing both a loan and an undrawn commitment component where contractual cancellation does not in practice limit exposure. For qualifying revolving products, ECL is measured over the period during which the entity is exposed to credit risk and expected losses would not be mitigated by credit-risk-management actions, even if that period extends beyond the contractual notice period. This is **behavioural life**, not licence to assume an unlimited horizon. The estimate should reflect observed account survival, drawdown patterns, limit management, cancellation practices and other actions that genuinely terminate or mitigate credit exposure. +-----------------------+ | Current drawn balance | +-----------------------+ | v +-----------------------+ | Scheduled repayment | | / prepayment | +-----------------------+ | v +-----------------------+ | Possible future | | drawdowns | +-----------------------+ | v +-----------------------+ | EAD by future period | +-----------------------+ | v +-----------------------+ | Combine with period | | PD and LGD | +-----------------------+ EAD must correspond to the exposure expected at the time of each modelled default, not merely the exposure reported today. Using the contractual cancellation notice period as behavioural life for a revolving portfolio without testing whether limits are actually cancelled in practice can materially understate ECL. **Contractual maturity** — the legal endpoint or cancellation period specified by the contract. --- **Behavioural exposure period** — the period during which credit exposure is expected to persist given actual borrower behaviour and credit-risk-management actions. — Current bank IRACP does not implement an IFRS behavioural-life ECL model. RBI’s ECL Directions from April 1, 2027 specify different lifetime treatments for drawn facilities, revolving commitments and auto-renewing products, including analysis of default, drawdown and limit-management behaviour. [RBI 2026 ECL Directions, paragraph 46] — UK-adopted IFRS 9 applies the contractual-period rule and revolving-facility exception in paragraph 5.5.20. [IFRS 9 5.5.19–5.5.20] — EU-adopted IFRS 9 applies the same revolving exposure-period requirements. [Regulation (EU) 2023/1803] — CECL estimates off-balance-sheet expected losses over the contractual period in which the entity is exposed to credit risk, but no allowance is recorded for an unfunded commitment that can be unconditionally cancelled by the institution; this differs structurally from IFRS 9’s revolving-product exception. [ASC 326; Interagency CECL FAQ]

title: Accounting LGD Versus Regulatory LGD
one_screen: Accounting LGD estimates the loss severity needed to satisfy an accounting ECL measurement objective; regulatory LGD is calibrated for prudential capital objectives. Regulatory parameters can be useful starting points, but they are not interchangeable because horizon, cyclicality, conservatism and prescribed floors can differ.
bodyText: **Loss given default (LGD)** is the proportion of exposure lost if default occurs. In accounting ECL models, LGD is a modelling component used to represent expected discounted cash shortfalls conditional on default. It should therefore capture expected recoveries, their timing, collateral and guarantee effects where appropriate, workout costs and forward-looking conditions consistently with the accounting framework. Regulatory-capital LGD answers a different question. Under the Basel internal-ratings-based framework, a bank’s LGD must reflect economic-downturn conditions where necessary to capture relevant risk. Basel capital parameters also operate within prudential calibration rules designed to protect solvency against unexpected loss. That difference is not semantic. A downturn-calibrated regulatory LGD may be deliberately more conservative than a neutral probability-weighted accounting estimate at a particular reporting date. Basel analysis has explicitly noted that regulatory-capital models can be useful starting points for accounting ECL but may require adjustment because regulatory PD and LGD have different objectives and inputs; for example, Basel regulatory LGD reflects downturn economic conditions, whereas accounting ECL is intended to produce an unbiased expectation rather than a permanently stressed estimate. Other mismatches can arise from prescribed regulatory floors, definitions of default, cure treatment, collateral eligibility, recovery costs and discounting conventions. Therefore, a mapping from regulatory LGD to accounting LGD needs an explicit bridge showing which prudential adjustments remain relevant and which must be removed or recalibrated. +-----------------------+ | Recovery experience | +-----------------------+ | v +-----------------------+ | Regulatory objective | | downturn / prudential | +-----------------------+ | v +-----------------------+ | Regulatory LGD | +-----------------------+ +-----------------------+ | Recovery experience | +-----------------------+ | v +-----------------------+ | Accounting objective | | unbiased expected | | cash shortfall | +-----------------------+ | v +-----------------------+ | Accounting LGD | +-----------------------+ A risk parameter inherits the objective and calibration rules of the framework for which it was built. Copying downturn regulatory LGD directly into accounting ECL without adjustment can embed prudential conservatism twice—once in the parameter and again in scenario weighting or overlays. **Accounting LGD** — expected loss severity calibrated to the financial-reporting ECL objective. --- **Regulatory LGD** — loss severity calibrated under prudential capital rules, potentially including downturn requirements and regulatory constraints. — Current scheduled-commercial-bank IRACP uses prescribed prudential provisioning rather than accounting LGD-based ECL. RBI’s ECL Directions from April 1, 2027 introduce PD/LGD modelling but overlay it with RBI prudential ECL floors, so modelled accounting-style loss and regulatory minimum provision remain distinct concepts. [RBI 2026 ECL Directions, paragraphs 82–95] — IFRS 9 ECL measurement and PRA capital-model requirements serve different objectives; regulatory parameters should not be imported into accounting without an accounting-consistent bridge. [IFRS 9; BCBS guidance] — EU banks applying IFRS 9 also operate under prudential capital requirements; EBA has separate guidance for IRB PD/LGD estimation, reinforcing the distinction between accounting and regulatory parameter frameworks. [EBA PD/LGD Guidelines; EBA ECL Guidelines] — CECL likewise measures accounting expected losses under Topic 326, while US regulatory-capital parameters and capital rules have separate prudential purposes. [ASC 326; Interagency ACL policy]

title: Overlays and Post-Model Adjustments
one_screen: An overlay or post-model adjustment changes model output when relevant credit risk is not adequately captured by the model. It is necessary when models have known blind spots, but dangerous when it becomes an undocumented plug, double-counts modelled risk or persists after the underlying deficiency should have been repaired.
bodyText: Every ECL model has a boundary. New risks may emerge faster than data can support model redevelopment; structural breaks can make historical relationships unreliable; a portfolio may contain concentrations not represented in model variables. **Post-model adjustments (PMAs)** and **management overlays** provide a controlled way to incorporate material information that the core model does not yet capture adequately. The correct logic starts with a named deficiency or omitted risk. Management should explain what is missing, why it matters, how the adjustment amount is estimated, which exposures it affects, what evidence supports the adjustment and what would cause it to be increased, reduced or removed. RBI’s 2020 Ind AS guidance for NBFCs expressly requires management overlays to be approved by the audit committee and their rationale and basis documented. The danger is that an overlay can bypass the discipline of a model. A vague “economic uncertainty” adjustment can conceal model weakness, earnings management or excessive conservatism. Double-counting is another common failure: if weaker macroeconomic conditions already raise scenario-weighted PDs and LGDs, an additional overlay for the same deterioration needs evidence of residual risk not already captured. Overlays should therefore have an exit strategy. PRA’s 2025 thematic feedback emphasised identifying new and evolving risks, assessing whether models capture them, and reducing PMAs as models and data improve. RBI’s future bank ECL framework similarly requires PMAs or management overlays to address model limitations under a consistent governance framework. +----------------------+ | Core ECL model | +----------------------+ | v +----------------------+ | Known missing risk | | or model limitation? | +----------------------+ | | No Yes | | v v +---------+ +------------------+ | Model | | Quantify PMA / | | output | | overlay | +---------+ +------------------+ | v +------------------+ | Governance, | | validation, exit | +------------------+ | v +------------------+ | Final ECL | +------------------+ An overlay must correspond to identifiable residual risk or model limitation that is not already captured adequately. Allowing an overlay to become a permanent unexplained percentage of the allowance converts judgement into an unvalidated parallel model. **Model calibration** — changing the model or its parameters so the model itself better represents risk. --- **Post-model adjustment** — an adjustment applied outside the core model because a specific limitation or emerging risk remains. — RBI already requires governance and audit-committee approval for overlays used by Ind AS NBFCs; scheduled commercial banks remain under IRACP until March 31, 2027, while the 2026 bank ECL Directions expressly govern PMAs under the future framework. [RBI 2020 NBFC guidance; RBI 2026 ECL Directions] — PRA’s September 2025 thematic feedback specifically addresses PMAs, model operating boundaries, evolving risks and the expectation that PMAs reduce as underlying models improve. [PRA 2025 thematic feedback] — IFRS 9’s measurement objective governs the final ECL; EBA supervisory guidance expects sound credit-risk and ECL practices, so overlays must remain consistent with unbiased accounting measurement. [IFRS 9 5.5.17; EBA/GL/2017/06] — CECL permits qualitative and quantitative factors and management judgement, but the resulting allowance must remain well supported under Topic 326 and supervisory ACL governance. [Interagency CECL FAQ; Interagency ACL Policy Statement]

title: ECL Model Validation and Backtesting
one_screen: Validation asks whether an ECL model is conceptually sound, implemented correctly and performing acceptably for its intended accounting use. Backtesting is one part of validation: compare predictions with realised outcomes, diagnose differences, and determine whether recalibration, redevelopment or a controlled adjustment is needed.
bodyText: ECL validation should cover more than a final allowance number. A model can produce a plausible aggregate ECL while its segmentation, PD term structure, LGD recovery timing or EAD behaviour is wrong. Validation therefore works from inputs through methodology to outputs. A practical sequence begins with **conceptual soundness**: does the methodology correspond to the accounting objective, portfolio economics and available data? Next comes implementation testing: are source data, transformations, code, parameter mappings and aggregation correct? Quantitative performance testing then evaluates discrimination, calibration, stability and realised outcomes where relevant. Finally, governance testing checks documentation, change control, limitations, approval and whether users understand the model’s intended boundaries. **Backtesting** compares model predictions with realised outcomes over appropriately defined periods. A PD backtest may compare forecast defaults with realised defaults; an LGD backtest can compare expected discounted recoveries with actual recovery experience; an EAD backtest can test drawdowns before default. Aggregate ECL-versus-write-off comparison is useful but insufficient because timing and portfolio composition can obscure component errors. Repeated material overprediction or underprediction is evidence requiring investigation, not automatic proof that a particular calibration change is correct. US interagency guidance explicitly expects periodic validation independent of credit approval and ACL estimation, including conceptual-soundness review, ongoing monitoring and output analysis; it notes that persistent material forecast error may indicate weakness. +----------------------+ | Conceptual design | +----------------------+ | v +----------------------+ | Data / implementation| | verification | +----------------------+ | v +----------------------+ | Quantitative testing | +----------------------+ | v +----------------------+ | Backtest predicted | | vs realised | +----------------------+ | v +----------------------+ | Remediate / approve | | / monitor | +----------------------+ Validation must test the model against its intended use and underlying risk mechanics, not merely reproduce the developer’s calculation. Declaring a model “validated” because aggregate provision is close to actual write-offs can hide offsetting PD, LGD, EAD or staging errors. **Validation** — independent challenge of conceptual soundness, implementation, performance and use. --- **Backtesting** — outcomes analysis comparing model predictions with realised experience; it is a component of validation, not the whole process. — Current commercial-bank IRACP requires automated classification controls and periodic system audit; RBI’s ECL Directions from April 1, 2027 add an explicit model inventory, independent validation, pre-implementation validation and post-implementation backtesting framework. [RBI 2025 IRACP; RBI 2026 ECL Directions, paragraphs 119–131] — PRA’s 2025 thematic feedback emphasises monitoring and validation of IFRS 9 ECL models and model operating boundaries. [PRA 2025 thematic feedback] — EBA/GL/2017/06 provides supervisory guidance on sound credit-risk-management and accounting-ECL practices alongside IFRS 9. [EBA/GL/2017/06] — Interagency ACL guidance expects periodic independent validation and initial and ongoing model-validation activities, including conceptual soundness, monitoring, benchmarking and model-output analysis. [Interagency ACL Policy Statement]

title: Staging Validation and ECL Disclosures
one_screen: Staging needs its own validation because a well-calibrated PD model can still produce wrong allowances if SICR thresholds move exposures too early or too late. Disclosures then make the framework observable by explaining staging policies, assumptions, forward-looking information, allowance movements and credit-risk concentrations.
bodyText: **Staging validation** tests the decision layer that determines whether IFRS 9 ECL uses a 12-month or lifetime horizon. It should therefore be separated analytically from PD model validation. An excellent lifetime PD term structure cannot compensate for a SICR framework that systematically leaves deteriorated exposures in Stage 1. Useful tests include migration analysis, transition rates between stages, the proportion of exposures entering Stage 3 directly from Stage 1, arrears status by stage, rating migration before Stage 2 transfer, Stage 2 cure behaviour, 30-DPD rebuttals and outcomes after cure. A high Stage 1-to-Stage 3 “cliff” can indicate that SICR recognition is too late, although the conclusion requires portfolio context rather than a mechanical threshold. Collective assessment also matters: IFRS 9 requires lifetime ECL where SICR is identifiable on a collective basis even when borrower-specific information has not yet emerged. IFRS 7 turns much of this judgement into required disclosure. Entities must explain how SICR is determined, including use of the low-credit-risk expedient and rebuttal of the 30-DPD presumption; define default; explain grouping for collective ECL; describe how credit-impaired assets are identified; and explain write-off and modification policies. IFRS 7 also requires disclosure of inputs, assumptions and estimation techniques, including forward-looking macroeconomic information, and reconciliations of loss allowances across 12-month, lifetime non-credit-impaired, credit-impaired and POCI categories. Disclosures are therefore a governance output, not merely a reporting appendix: unexplained stage migrations, opaque overlays or large assumption changes become visible to financial-statement users. +----------------------+ | Staging rules | +----------------------+ | v +----------------------+ | Migration / cure / | | backstop testing | +----------------------+ | v +----------------------+ | Validate timing of | | SICR recognition | +----------------------+ | v +----------------------+ | IFRS 7 explanations | | and reconciliations | +----------------------+ | v +----------------------+ | External visibility | +----------------------+ Staging validation must test **when** lifetime loss recognition begins and ends, not merely whether the underlying risk model predicts default. Validating PD calibration but never testing Stage 1→2→3 migration can leave the dominant source of ECL volatility and delayed recognition unchallenged. **Model-performance disclosure** — information explaining assumptions, methods and allowance movements. --- **Model validation** — independent evidence that the underlying process is fit for purpose; disclosure does not substitute for validation. — Current scheduled-commercial-bank IRACP has different classification and disclosure rules. RBI’s ECL Directions effective April 1, 2027 prescribe extensive methodology disclosures and first ECL reporting based on June 30, 2027 positions, with comparative presentation beginning from March 31, 2028; Ind AS NBFCs also face Ind AS/RBI disclosures. [RBI 2026 ECL Directions, disclosure chapter; RBI 2020 NBFC guidance] — IFRS 7 disclosure requirements accompany UK-adopted IFRS 9; PRA supervision adds prudential scrutiny of staging and model governance. [IFRS 7 35F–35M; PRA 2025] — EU-adopted IFRS 7/IFRS 9 apply, with EBA monitoring and supervisory guidance for institutions. [Regulation (EU) 2023/1803; EBA/GL/2017/06] — CECL has no staging disclosures; Topic 326 instead requires allowance and credit-quality information, including vintage-based credit-quality disclosures for relevant public business entities. [ASC 326-20-50; Interagency CECL FAQ]

title: US CECL Under ASC 326
one_screen: CECL and IFRS 9 are both forward-looking expected-loss frameworks, but CECL is not “IFRS 9 without stage labels”. For amortised-cost assets, CECL recognises lifetime expected credit losses from initial recognition, eliminating the IFRS 9 SICR gateway between 12-month and lifetime ECL.
bodyText: ASC Topic 326’s **current expected credit losses (CECL)** methodology measures expected credit losses on financial assets carried at amortised cost using information about historical experience, current conditions and reasonable and supportable forecasts. An allowance is established when an asset is originated or acquired; for assets in CECL scope, the objective is the net amount expected to be collected over the relevant contractual term. The structural contrast with IFRS 9 is the allowance horizon. IFRS 9 starts a non-credit-impaired asset in Stage 1 with 12-month ECL and moves to lifetime ECL after SICR. CECL generally starts at **lifetime expected loss**. Consequently, CECL has no SICR test, no Stage 1-to-Stage 2 allowance cliff and no 30-DPD staging presumption. Deterioration still changes the allowance, but it changes a lifetime estimate that already exists. CECL is also method-neutral. Topic 326 does not require one prescribed technique; acceptable approaches can include loss-rate, roll-rate, vintage, discounted-cash-flow and PD/LGD methods when they reasonably estimate expected collectability and are consistently supported. The lifetime concept is not identical to IFRS 9’s revolving-facility rule. CECL generally measures expected losses over the contractual term, considering expected prepayments but not expected extensions, renewals or modifications unless specified by the guidance. For off-balance-sheet commitments, expected losses are measured over the contractual period of exposure, but no allowance is recorded for commitments the institution can unconditionally cancel. Purchased credit-deteriorated assets use PCD gross-up accounting: the initial allowance is added to purchase price to establish amortised cost rather than charged as an ordinary acquisition-date provision expense. IFRS 9 +---------+ SICR +---------+ | Stage 1 | -------> | Stage 2 | | 12m ECL | | Life ECL| +---------+ +---------+ CECL +------------------------------+ | Initial recognition | | Lifetime expected credit loss| +------------------------------+ | v +------------------------------+ | Re-estimate lifetime loss | | every reporting date | +------------------------------+ The difference between CECL and IFRS 9 is structural measurement architecture, not merely terminology. Recreating IFRS 9 stages inside CECL and using them to decide whether lifetime ECL applies imports a threshold ASC 326 does not contain. **CECL lifetime allowance** — lifetime expected credit loss recognised from initial recognition for in-scope amortised-cost assets. --- **IFRS 9 lifetime ECL** — lifetime expected loss that ordinarily applies after SICR, to credit-impaired assets, and in specified other cases. — CECL does not govern Indian statutory bank provisioning. Indian scheduled commercial banks remain under RBI IRACP through March 31, 2027 and transition to RBI’s own three-stage ECL framework from April 1, 2027; relevant NBFCs may apply Ind AS 109, not ASC 326. [RBI 2025 IRACP; RBI 2026 ECL Directions; RBI 2020 NBFC guidance] — UK-adopted IFRS 9 uses staging and therefore differs structurally from CECL. [UK-adopted IFRS 9] — EU-adopted IFRS 9 likewise retains 12-month versus lifetime staging. [Regulation (EU) 2023/1803] — ASC 326 CECL is the applicable US GAAP expected-loss model for in-scope amortised-cost financial assets; it recognises lifetime expected losses from initial recognition without IFRS 9 staging. [ASU 2016-13; Interagency CECL FAQ]

title: India: IRACP, Ind AS and the Bank ECL Transition
one_screen: India must be read as three distinct tracks: scheduled commercial banks are not on Ind AS and remain under RBI IRACP through March 31, 2027; relevant NBFCs already apply Ind AS, including Ind AS 109 ECL; and RBI has issued a separate final three-stage ECL framework for commercial banks that becomes effective April 1, 2027. The January 2023 ECL discussion paper was a proposal; the April 2026 Directions are final future rules, not current rules as of August 28, 2026.
bodyText: The first boundary is non-negotiable: **Indian scheduled commercial banks are not currently applying Ind AS 109**. RBI’s March 22, 2019 circular deferred implementation of Ind AS for scheduled commercial banks “till further notice”. As of August 28, 2026, commercial banks covered by RBI’s 2025 Income Recognition, Asset Classification and Provisioning Directions remain on prudential IRACP rules. Those rules classify problem assets through NPA, substandard, doubtful and loss categories and prescribe provisioning rather than operating an IFRS 9 accounting-stage model. The second track is **Ind AS-implementing NBFCs and ARCs**. RBI’s March 13, 2020 guidance states that NBFCs covered by Rule 4 of the Companies (Indian Accounting Standards) Rules must prepare financial statements under Ind AS. RBI overlays prudential safeguards: such entities maintain Ind AS impairment allowances while also computing IRACP provisions, with any shortfall addressed through the prescribed impairment reserve mechanism. RBI also reinforces the 30-DPD SICR presumption and governance of ECL models and overlays. The third track is the **commercial-bank transition to RBI ECL**. RBI’s January 16, 2023 Discussion Paper proposed a three-stage IFRS-9-influenced ECL approach for scheduled commercial banks. That document was a consultation proposal, not operative provisioning law. RBI subsequently issued final *Commercial Banks – Asset Classification, Provisioning and Income Recognition Directions, 2026* on April 27, 2026. They take effect **April 1, 2027**; until then, the 2025 IRACP Directions continue to govern. The final framework uses Stage 1 12-month ECL, Stage 2 lifetime ECL after SICR and Stage 3 lifetime ECL for credit-impaired assets, while adding RBI-specific prudential floors, transition rules, model-risk requirements and income-recognition provisions. This is an RBI prudential ECL framework—not adoption of Ind AS 109 for banks. INDIA — 28 AUG 2026 +--------------------------------+ | Scheduled commercial banks | +--------------------------------+ | v +--------------------------------+ | RBI IRACP 2025 | | CURRENT through 31 Mar 2027 | | NOT Ind AS 109 | +--------------------------------+ | v +--------------------------------+ | RBI ECL Directions 2026 | | FINAL, effective 1 Apr 2027 | +--------------------------------+ +--------------------------------+ | Relevant NBFCs / ARCs | +--------------------------------+ | v +--------------------------------+ | Ind AS financial reporting | | + RBI prudential safeguards | +--------------------------------+ +--------------------------------+ | RBI Discussion Paper | | 16 Jan 2023 | +--------------------------------+ | v +--------------------------------+ | Historical proposal | | NOT current rule | +--------------------------------+ An accounting standard, a prudential provisioning regime and a proposed regulatory framework are different legal and conceptual objects even when they use similar ECL terminology. Writing “India uses Ind AS 109 for banks” collapses three different regimes and is factually wrong: scheduled commercial-bank Ind AS implementation was deferred, current bank provisioning remains IRACP through March 31, 2027, and RBI’s April 2026 ECL Directions are a separate prudential framework effective April 1, 2027. **Ind AS 109 for relevant NBFCs** — Indian accounting-standard ECL applied by entities within the applicable Ind AS implementation scope, subject to RBI prudential guidance. --- **RBI bank ECL framework** — RBI’s separately issued commercial-bank prudential provisioning regime, finalised in April 2026 and effective April 1, 2027; it is not bank adoption of Ind AS 109. — Three-way position: current scheduled-commercial-bank IRACP through March 31, 2027; Ind AS 109 for relevant Ind AS-implementing NBFCs/ARCs; and final RBI commercial-bank ECL Directions effective April 1, 2027. The January 16, 2023 Discussion Paper is historical proposal material, superseded for implementation purposes by the final April 27, 2026 Directions. [RBI 2019 Deferral; RBI 2020 NBFC guidance; RBI 2023 Discussion Paper; RBI 2025 IRACP; RBI 2026 ECL Directions] — UK companies within the relevant accounting scope use UK-adopted IFRS 9; there is no Indian-style IRACP/Ind AS split. [UK Endorsement Board, IFRS 9] — Relevant EU consolidated financial statements apply EU-adopted IFRS standards under Regulation (EC) No 1606/2002 and Regulation (EU) 2023/1803; banking supervision overlays accounting with EBA/CRR prudential requirements rather than replacing IFRS 9 with Indian IRACP. [Regulation (EU) 2023/1803; EBA/GL/2017/06] — US GAAP uses ASC 326 CECL rather than IFRS 9 or RBI IRACP; lifetime expected credit losses for in-scope amortised-cost assets are recognised from initial recognition without an IFRS-style SICR staging gateway. [ASU 2016-13]

title: RBI’s Mandate and Dual Role
one_screen: The Reserve Bank of India (RBI) is India’s central bank with a broad mandate that goes beyond prudential supervision. In addition to setting monetary policy and ensuring banking stability, RBI has a statutory “developmental role” – promoting national objectives like financial inclusion and credit to agriculture and MSMEs.
bodyText: The RBI Act (1934) empowers RBI as monetary authority and bank regulator, but also explicitly tasks it with supporting economic development. For example, RBI regularly revises the Priority Sector Lending norms to “ensure adequate flow of credit” to sectors crucial for socio-economic development. In practice, RBI issues prudential norms (capital, NPA rules, etc.) like any financial regulator, **and** enforces growth-oriented policies (such as mandatory loans to farmers, micro‐businesses, etc.). This dual mandate means RBI-issued guidelines often blend safety with directed targets. Unlike most central banks abroad, RBI’s charter includes credit-promotion – e.g. linking lending rates to an external benchmark to improve transmission – and priority targets for banks. The RBI’s remit thus spans monetary policy, foreign exchange, currency issuance, system oversight, and development. It supervises commercial banks, NBFCs, payments systems and more. The net effect is that Indian banking regulators regularly set both stability rules (asset classification, capital, audit) **and** development quotas (priority sectors, subsidies). Internationally, counterparts like the U.S. Fed focus on macro‐stability, but RBI also directly steers credit allocation. For India’s banks, this means compliance is both about risk control and social objectives. The RBI Act grants RBI objectives beyond bank supervision – including currency and monetary control **and** socio-economic development (e.g. credit to priority sectors). Assuming RBI’s role is *only* prudential oversight. In reality RBI imposes directed lending programs (priority sectors, subsidized refinancing, financial inclusion schemes) as part of its mandate. Ignoring these developmental mandates leads to misreading RBI guidelines. **Monetary Authority** — The role of setting interest rates and controlling money supply (e.g. policy repo rate). --- **Developmental Regulator** — RBI’s role in promoting growth (e.g. enforcing priority‐sector lending to agriculture/MSMEs). They often overlap, but the former is macro management, the latter is directed credit policy. — RBI is legally charged with developmental mandates such as priority sector lending to agriculture, MSMEs, etc.. **US/UK** — The Federal Reserve or Bank of England focus on monetary & prudential stability; no formal equivalent of India’s PSL targets exists (no legislative mandate for sectoral quotas).

title: Bank Categories in India (SCB, SFB, Payments, RRB, Coop)
one_screen: India’s banking system has multiple specialized categories.  *Scheduled Commercial Banks* (SCBs) – including public, private, foreign, regional rural, scheduled payments banks, small finance banks, and co-operative banks – have broad banking powers. Small Finance Banks focus on underserved segments; Payments Banks can take small deposits but cannot lend.  Co-operative banks and RRBs serve member or rural communities with limited geographic scope.
bodyText: A **Scheduled Commercial Bank (SCB)** is any bank included in the RBI Act’s Second Schedule. This umbrella covers public sector banks (like SBI), private sector banks (HDFC, ICICI, etc.), foreign banks’ Indian branches, plus scheduled RRBs, payments banks, SFBs and co-operative banks. SCBs can accept deposits (current, savings, term), lend, issue cards, participate in clearing, etc. They maintain CRR/SLR and have access to RBI facilities. A **Small Finance Bank (SFB)** is a niche bank licensed under the Banking Regulation Act (in 2015-16) to advance financial inclusion. SFBs can do most banking activities (taking deposits, lending) similar to SCBs, but they must primarily serve small businesses, marginal farmers, micro and small enterprises and underserved areas. SFBs were often conversions of microfinance institutions or coops, subject to phased licensing and branch expansion norms. They can issue loans (with limits under MFI norms, etc.) and accept savings/current/term deposits. A **Payments Bank** (PB) is a special bank that can accept deposits and make payments/remittances, but **cannot lend out funds**. PBs are allowed only savings/current accounts with a maximum balance per customer (currently ₹100,000), issue debit cards or wallets, and offer payment services. They often operate via agents/BCs. Since PBs cannot issue loans or credit cards, they cannot earn interest income from lending. They also hold large SLR portfolios because deposits are short-term. **Regional Rural Banks (RRBs)** are co-owned by the central & state governments and a sponsor bank, established under the RRB Act (1976). RRBs’ business area is restricted to specified rural districts. They aim to provide credit to agriculture and rural sectors (SMEs, etc.) in those areas. RRBs can take deposits and lend like other banks, but typically focus on small farmers and village enterprises. **Co-operative Banks** are member-owned banks (urban or rural cooperatives) registered under co-operative laws. They serve members of a local community (e.g. urban merchants’ coop banks or village credit cooperatives). Scheduled urban co-operative banks are also SCBs if in the Second Schedule; they abide by RBI’s banking regulations (though rural co-ops are jointly regulated with NABARD). Co-op banks can accept deposits and make loans, but usually within a limited area and to their members. Together, these categories create India’s banking architecture. For example, SCBs and SFBs have near-identical banking rights (except SFB branch restrictions), while Payments Banks are highly constrained. RRBs and coops have deposit/credit powers but are geographically or membership confined. Only SCBs (including SFBs, coop banks, etc.) can accept deposits *and* make loans. Payments Banks can accept deposits (₹100k limit per customer) but are **not permitted to lend**. Treating payments banks like normal banks. In reality, PBs cannot lend or issue loans – assuming they can leads to incorrect advice on their use. Likewise, assuming all SCBs have nationwide scope – RRBs and most coop banks have restricted areas/membership. **Small Finance Bank (SFB)** — a licensed bank focusing on underserved segments; it can take deposits and grant loans. --- **Payments Bank (PB)** — a bank limited to deposit and payment services; cannot issue loans, has per-customer deposit cap. — India defines these specific bank categories by law and RBI licensing. **No delta.** Other jurisdictions (US, UK, EU) do not have identical classes; they have full-service banks and separate non-bank lenders but no formal “payments bank” or “small finance bank” category.

title: NBFC Scale-Based Regulation (SBR)
one_screen: In 2022–2023, RBI moved to a four-tier, size-and-risk-based regulatory framework for NBFCs. The framework classifies NBFCs into Base, Middle, Upper and Top layers. Base-layer NBFCs are the smallest/non-deposit ones (assets < ₹1,000 crore) and fintech entities; middle-layer NBFCs include deposit-taking companies and larger NBFCs (assets ≥ ₹1,000 cr) and critical segments like HFCs, CICs, etc.; Upper and Top layers (ideally empty) are for systemically important NBFCs subject to enhanced scrutiny.
bodyText: Under RBI’s **Scale-Based Regulations (SBR)**, NBFCs are grouped by size and activity. *Base Layer*: mainly non-deposit NBFCs with assets below ₹1,000 crore, plus all NBFC-P2P, NBFC-AA, NOFHCs, etc.. These are subject to simpler rules. *Middle Layer*: all deposit-taking NBFCs and non-deposit NBFCs with assets ≥ ₹1,000 cr; also includes dedicated entities like SPDs, IDF-NBFC, CICs, HFCs, NBFC-IFCs. They face intermediate norms. *Upper Layer*: systemically important NBFCs identified yearly (no fixed list), facing the strictest capital and governance requirements. *Top Layer* is a potential category for any NBFC whose risk (possibly identified from the Upper layer) becomes a serious systemic concern; it is empty at inception. In essence, this regime applies graduated oversight: the smaller/lower-risk NBFCs in the Base Layer follow lighter prudential norms, while large NBFCs or critical ones are tightly regulated. The SBR came into effect October 2022 (with legal backing under various Acts). It replaced the older NBFC-ND-SI (systemic) vs NBFC-ND (non-systemic) classification. Now, for example, an HFC or CIC automatically goes into the Middle or Upper Layer (not Base). A group consolidation rule (from Oct 2022) ensures related NBFCs’ assets are summed to decide their layer. This means RBI can tailor capital, provisioning, group exposure rules by layer. All NBFCs in India must register with RBI (with minimum capital), but RBI now groups them by scale: smaller NBFCs (Base Layer) have lighter rules, while larger or deposit-taking NBFCs (Middle/Upper Layer) have stricter norms. Ignoring layer classification: applying the same rules to all NBFCs. For example, assuming an NBFC with ₹500 cr assets is treated like a ₹5,000 cr company is wrong – RBI’s SBR buckets mean they face different requirements. **NBFC–Base Layer (NBFC-BL)** — NBFCs with asset size < ₹1,000 crore (and fintech NBFCs like P2P, AA, etc.); subject to least stringent norms. --- **NBFC–Middle/Upper Layer (NBFC-ML/UL)** — larger or deposit-taking NBFCs (e.g. NBFC-D, HFC, CIC, etc.) with ₹1,000cr+; subject to higher capital and prudential standards. — RBI’s SBR framework is India-specific. It integrates HFCs and others into NBFC layer definitions. **No delta.** (No exact counterpart in UK/EU/US; other countries classify banks differently but India’s four-layer NBFC regime is unique.)

title: Housing Finance Companies under RBI
one_screen: As of August 2019, Housing Finance Companies (HFCs) were brought under RBI’s regulation. The Central Bank is now the regulator of HFCs (lenders specializing in home loans), integrating them into the NBFC framework.  During the transition, HFCs were allowed to follow existing NHB guidelines until RBI issues new rules.
bodyText: Prior to 2019, HFCs were regulated by the National Housing Bank (NHB) under the NHB Act. The Finance (No.2) Act 2019 amended the NHB Act to shift HFC regulation to RBI. From Aug 9, 2019, HFCs are treated as a category of NBFCs for regulatory purposes. RBI announced that it would “carry out a review” of HFC regulations and issue a revised framework in due course. Until that new RBI framework is in place, HFCs continue to comply with NHB-issued directions and returns. Under the new SBR regime (post-2022), all HFCs are to be classified either in the Middle Layer or Upper Layer (never Base Layer). In practice, this reflects that HFCs are treated as systemically important NBFCs. They now follow RBI’s prudential norms (e.g. capital adequacy, ALM) as per their NBFC layer, and ultimately will migrate fully to RBI’s directions (for example, RBI’s NBFC regulations including IRACP, provisioning, etc.). The NHB itself ceased primary supervision, though it continues as the housing finance policy body. HFCs are now regulated by RBI as NBFCs. Any housing finance company must register with RBI and follow RBI’s NBFC prudential norms once the transition is complete. Ignoring the shift: continue treating HFC regulations as per NHB. Post-2019, NHB guidelines apply only until RBI substitutes them. Compliance advisors must confirm whether RBI has issued a master direction for HFCs. **Housing Finance Company (HFC)** — a financial institution primarily extending home loans. After 2019, HFCs are NBFCs regulated by RBI. --- **Mortgage Refinance (NHB)** — NHB continues as a refinancing institution and policy authority, but **no longer supervises HFC prudentially**. — HFCs = NBFCs under RBI since 2019. There is no analogous transfer in other jurisdictions covered.

title: Banks vs. NBFCs: Key Distinctions
one_screen: Commercial banks and NBFCs in India differ in core functions and regulation.  Banks can accept demand deposits, offer cheque facilities, and participate in the payment system – NBFCs cannot.  NBFCs rely mostly on wholesale/market funding or term deposits (for deposit-taking NBFCs).  Banks have RBI-backed deposit insurance (DICGC cover), maintain CRR/SLR, and access RBI liquidity; NBFCs do not (except selective refinance schemes).  Banks require higher entry capital and stricter licensing; NBFCs have a lower ₹2 crore equity norm but face similar prudential norms scaled to their assets.  Because NBFCs cannot create money via demand deposits, their funding costs and leverage limits differ fundamentally from banks.
bodyText: In practice, an Indian bank is licensed under the BR Act and can grant loans (including overdrafts, credit cards) directly funded by deposits. NBFCs (except certain rare deposit-taking ones) cannot open current accounts or offer cheque books. They can only accept term/lien-marked savings deposits with restrictions, and they must invest most deposits in government securities (e.g. PBs keep 75% in SLR securities). Banks contribute to CRR and SLR at set ratios; NBFC deposit-takers have their own (lower) CRR rates and no CRR if non-deposit NBFC. NBFCs access RBI refinancing schemes (e.g. MSE financing, mortgages) but cannot borrow directly through standard bank routes like repo. Regulatory burdens also differ: banks need full Basel capital ratios and AML/KYC; NBFCs follow RBI NBFC Directions (now largely converging with Basel norms for larger NBFCs). NBFCs often face extra restrictions on leverage, lending (e.g. sub-limits on unsecured loans), and must maintain Asset-Liability limits. For example, only banks count as “scheduled banks” in inter-bank systems. Moreover, only banks have statutory liquidity injection roles (like government banking), whereas NBFCs do not. Banks are permitted to accept demand (current) deposits and to extend credit directly; NBFCs cannot accept current account deposits or create payment mechanisms. Only SCBs hold RBI-guaranteed deposit insurance and use CRR/SLR facilities. Treating an NBFC like a small bank. For example, assuming an NBFC’s deposits are instantly withdrawable (like a current account) – this is false. Also ignoring NBFC funding limits can lead to compliance errors (NBFCs must invest most deposits in govt bonds, etc.). **Bank** — a licensed entity that can take demand deposits (cheque/savings accounts) and provide a full suite of banking services. --- **NBFC** — a non-bank financial firm that cannot accept demand deposits or issue cheques; funding comes via term liabilities, and it is generally outside central-bank clearing. — RBI delineates banks (BR Act) vs NBFCs (RBI Act) sharply. NBFCs have limits (no current accounts, limits on deposits) not found in US/UK banking. **No delta.** The general difference that banks take deposits and NBFCs do not is universal. But India’s deposit cap rules (e.g. ₹100k for PBs) are local details.

title: Asset Classification and NPA Norms (IRACP)
one_screen: Banks must classify each loan into Standard, Sub-standard, Doubtful or Loss assets based on repayment delays. A loan becomes a Non-Performing Asset (NPA) when interest/principal is overdue for 90 days.  The Income Recognition, Asset Classification and Provisioning (IRACP) norms require daily monitoring (stamping) of accounts, with more provisions for higher-risk categories.
bodyText: Under RBI’s IRACP rules, a performing loan is **Standard** if not exhibiting any default and is repayable according to agreement. If a loan shows “signs of weakness” (like late payments but repaying) it may be classified as a **Special Mention Account** (SMA) first (see next atom) before becoming NPA. Once overdue beyond thresholds, it is classified as NPA with subcategories: - **Sub-standard**: NPA < 12 months, or assets showing incipient credit weakness. - **Doubtful**: NPA ≥ 12 months, significant uncertainty about recovery (e.g. liquidation value < book value). - **Loss**: NPA essentially uncollectible and fully written off (may be identified on a continuous basis and written off). For practical purposes, RBI mandates the *90-day rule*: any loan (principal or interest) unpaid for more than 90 days is an NPA. In many exposures (e.g. credit cards) RBI requires monthly (or more frequent) couponing into NPA status by 90 days overdue. The classification is updated daily through stamping in loan accounting systems. Banks must provide (p ) as per IRACP. Standard assets carry minimal provisions (0.4% or 1% of outstanding depending on secured status). Sub-standard assets require a **minimum 15%** provision (further if unsecured). Doubtful assets require higher provisions (20%–100% depending on how long in the bucket and available security). Loss assets have 100% provision. These provisioning rates and classification criteria are laid down in RBI’s IRACP Master Directions (updated periodically). A credit exposure is an NPA if interest/principal is overdue for more than 90 days. Once an asset is NPA, it must be classified as sub-standard, doubtful or loss according to RBI’s IRACP guidelines, and provisioning applied accordingly. Delaying NPA classification beyond 90 days past due. RBI requires daily stamping; waiting months to mark NPA breaches guidelines. Also, underestimating required provisioning for substandard and doubtful assets is a common mistake – RBI’s table mandates at least 15% for substandard, with more if unsecured. **Standard asset** — loan with no signs of default; provisioned at RBI’s base rate (often 0.4% or 1%). --- **Sub-standard asset** — NPA overdue <1 year; shows weakness; provision ≥15%. --- **Doubtful asset** — NPA overdue ≥1 year; high uncertainty; provision much higher (up to 100%). --- **Loss asset** — uncollectible; fully provided. — RBI’s 90-day NPA rule and IRAC categories are India’s regulatory norm; UK/US use 90 days too, but account aging and provisioning differ.

title: Special Mention Accounts (SMAs)
one_screen: **Special Mention Accounts (SMAs)** are categories for loans showing early warning signals of stress, before becoming NPAs. RBI defines three SMA levels by days past due or consistent irregular payments. SMAs ensure banks monitor these exposures closely.
bodyText: SMAs serve as a watchlist under RBI’s framework. When a loan installment is overdue for 31–60 days, it is an **SMA-0**. Overdue 61–90 days becomes **SMA-1**. Overdue 91–180 days is **SMA-2** (by then it is an NPA if >90 days). These buckets help banks report accounts approaching NPA status. For example, a loan 45 days past due is SMA-0. Any payment beyond 90 days makes it automatically NPA (substandard category). SMAs capture loans at risk of slipping: if a borrower is regularly late or temporarily stressed, the account is flagged as SMA even if NPA threshold not crossed yet. RBI introduced SMAs to improve risk monitoring and discourage “evergreening” accounts (extending new loans to cover interest on old ones). Banks must report SMA balances to RBI daily. Regulators use SMA data to assess sectoral asset quality and systemic risk. No additional provisioning is mandated for SMAs (they remain performing assets) but banks should increase watchful provisioning as accounts progress through SMA categories. When an SMA-2 account crosses 90 days, it is upgraded to NPA (sub-standard). Thus, SMAs act as intermediate flags. Accounts must be flagged in increasing SMA categories as soon as they cross due-date thresholds (31, 61, 91 days past due). This daily reporting is mandatory. Ignoring SMA flags or delaying them. SMA classification is not a choice; banks must stamp accounts promptly at 31+ days overdue. Treating a stressed loan as “still standard” before 30 days beyond due violates rules. **SMA-0** — overdue 31–60 days (early warning, pre-NPA). **SMA-1** — overdue 61–90 days. **SMA-2** — overdue 91–180 days (immediately becomes NPA if not resolved) SMAs are *not* regulatory categories with prescribed provisioning; they’re managerial flags. Once past 90 days, any SMA becomes NPA (Sub-Standard asset). — RBI’s SMA classification is used; similar watch-lists exist in some countries but not all regulators formalize 30/60/90 day buckets.

title: Provisioning Norms for Banks
one_screen: RBI’s norms prescribe minimum loan-loss provisions based on classification and security. Standard assets require low provisioning (often 0.4% for secured, 1% for unsecured). Sub-standard assets need at least 15% (further higher if unsecured). Doubtful assets carry higher provisions (20–100% depending on seasoning and collateral). Fully-provided Loss assets require 100% provisioning.
bodyText: For **Standard loans**, banks must maintain a floating provision. Current guidelines typically require 0.4% of outstanding for secured standard advances and 1.0% for unsecured standard advances. These may vary by loan type and are updated periodically. For **Sub-standard NPAs**, RBI mandates a **minimum 15%** provisioning against outstanding (additional for unsecured portion). For instance, a 15% provision is mandatory even if there is collateral; unsecured portion may require a higher rate (at least 25%). For **Doubtful NPAs** (NPA >1 year), provisioning depends on how long the asset has been in that bucket and realizable security. Schematically: - Less than 1 year in Doubtful: ~20% (subject to security coverage). - 1–3 years in Doubtful: ~50%. - Over 3 years in Doubtful: 100%. Finally, **Loss assets** are those considered unrecoverable; they carry 100% provision. Banks must also consider security coverage (loan-to-value) in computing the shortfall. RBI provides a detailed provisioning schedule in its IRACP directions. If collateral liquidation value significantly covers outstanding, banks can adjust provisions downwards (but not below minimums). All these rates are the **minimum** RBI requires; banks can and do often provision more (for prudence). The actual provisioning entries are critical for regulatory capital and profit. The RBI periodically issues circulars updating these percentages and classification rules (e.g. 15% sub-standard). Apply the RBI-prescribed provisioning percentages by asset class: 0.4–1% for Standard; ≥15% for Sub-Standard (more if unsecured); higher for Doubtful (up to 100% with aging). Under-provisioning. A common mistake is assuming low provisions suffice when assets slip into Sub-Standard or Doubtful. RBI’s table demands at least 15% on Sub-Standard, and up to 100% on old Doubtfuls. Also forgetting security cushion (banks must provision on the unsecured portion). **Standard asset provision** — minimal (0.4%/1%), since loan is performing. **NPA provision** — much higher: e.g. 15% (sub-standard) or more (doubtful). — RBI’s percentages are unique to India’s IRAC norms (see RBI master directions). Other countries have their own loss provisioning, but India’s 90-day definition and fixed rates are RBI-specific.

title: Restructuring and Resolution Framework
one_screen: Banks follow RBI’s restructuring guidelines when a borrower’s credit stress is resolved via concession. This includes Corporate Debt Restructuring (CDR), 5/25 refinancing, and more recently, the Resolution Frameworks (RBI’s COVID-19 and MSME frameworks). Under these, an NPAs may be restructured (terms changed) and classified as Standard again if conditions are met. Special norms apply to ensure loans aren’t “evergreened” without justification.
bodyText: Restructuring allows lenders to modify loan terms (extension of tenor, interest rate cut, etc.) for a viable borrower under stress. RBI has periodically issued frameworks: e.g. in 2014–15 the CDR mechanism (mostly phased out), and “5/25” for infrastructure. Post-COVID, RBI issued Resolution Frameworks (2020-21) letting banks restructure specified stressed loans with a benefit of preserving asset classification (subject to strict criteria). RBI also had schemes specifically for MSMEs (e.g. Mudra loans) and one-time restructuring packages for legacy stressed sectors. Under RBI policy, when a loan is restructured, it can be upgraded out of NPA only if it meets specific performance criteria over a period. RBI’s circular in 2015 clarified that a restructured advance must perform for at least one year (or two quarters) after restructuring to be considered Standard again. This avoids immediate upgrade fraud. If those conditions aren’t satisfied, the account remains an NPA. When restructuring occurs, banks must increase provisions (e.g. a minimum 5% on restructured standard loans, rising on restructured NPA). RBI’s norms spell out extra provisioning for restructured assets. Also, restructured loans carry enhanced reporting and are tagged on balance sheets. RBI’s resolution frameworks now overlap with the Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code (IBC). Banks can opt for IBC proceedings for large defaulters, or choose RBI’s guidelines for out-of-court settlement. Both routes have specific timelines and safeguards to protect creditors and equitable treatment of all lenders. Resolution under IBC requires strict timelines (270 days) and NCLT oversight. RBI’s preference is that viable debt should not require formal insolvency if banks can resolve it cooperatively. When loans are restructured, they remain NPAs until strict conditions (specified by RBI) are met. Absent that, the classification stays NPA even if payments resume. Upgrading only happens after sustained performance post-restructuring. Assuming a restructured loan is automatically ‘standard’. In India, a loan modified under a restructuring scheme must still run successfully for a mandatory period before being considered standard. Banks often mistakenly revert classification immediately. **Restructured loan** — a loan whose terms are modified to help a stressed borrower. It may still be NPA; upgrading depends on post-restructure performance. --- **Write-off** — outright removal of an asset from books. (Covered next.) — RBI’s circulars on restructuring (e.g. Resolution Frameworks) are India-specific. Other countries have workout rules, but RBI’s emphasis on performance post-restructure is a local regulatory detail.

title: Upgrades and Write-offs
one_screen: **Upgrading** means moving an asset from NPA back to Standard after the borrower cures delinquency. RBI requires strict criteria: the loan must be fully repaid for a mandatory period post-default (e.g. 2 successive quarters or 1 year) and provisions made. This prevents manipulating classification. **Write-off** is when a bank formally removes an asset from its books, fully providing for it. In India, write-off is a prudential (not tax) exercise: losses are absorbed only after thorough review, and even then such loans may be sold or recovered later.
bodyText: Upon successful resolution of an NPA (e.g. borrower makes good on arrears or loan is restructured), banks may upgrade the asset to Standard. RBI’s 2015 clarification mandates a “cooling period”: for a restructured account to be classified as Standard again, repayments must meet conditions (like no defaults for two quarters). Without that probation period, an upgrade is not allowed. This rule was highlighted by RBI when it cautioned banks against prematurely upgrading SME accounts in 2014-15. **Write-offs** occur when a loan is deemed unrecoverable. RBI allows two types: *prudential write-off* (for banks, as per regulatory guidelines) and *technical write-off* (often a bookkeeping exercise after 2 years of NPA, for income recognition, but banks continue recovery efforts). After prudential write-off, a bank can still pursue the borrower or recover via SARFAESI/IBC. A write-off does not necessarily extinguish the debt legally (banks still have claim on assets). RBI’s rules require certain conditions (security realization attempts, etc.) before prudential write-off. Many NBFCs (like some housing finance) have their own write-off timelines but must adhere to RBI’s broad norms. Practically, write-off reduces a bank’s taxable income (since provisions were already made) but is a regulatory decision to clean balance sheets. The outstanding balance after write-off may be reported as ‘Outstanding written-off assets’ for supervisor attention. Only after full write-off can a new loan be given to that borrower under banking laws. An NPA cannot be downgraded to Standard until RBI’s post-default performance period is satisfied. Banks may only write off loans after exhausting all recovery options and meeting prudential criteria. Improper early upgrade. A common error is reclassifying a restructured NPA as Standard immediately. RBI’s circular forces a waiting period – skipping it breaks rules. Another mistake is treating a write-off as forgiveness: even after write-off, banks pursue the borrower. **Upgrade** — reclassification of an NPA to Standard after borrower cures. Requires RBI-mandated wait period (e.g. no default for 2 quarters). **Write-off** — formally removing the loan from active books (after full provision); often a tactical cleanup, but the borrower’s liability remains. — RBI’s detailed upgrade criteria are India-specific. Many jurisdictions similarly prevent immediate NPA cures, but RBI’s exact timelines (e.g. 2Q after restructure) are local.

title: Priority Sector Lending (PSL) Targets
one_screen: Indian banks must lend a mandated share of their credit to specified “priority sectors” (agriculture, MSMEs, etc.) as defined by RBI, often 40% of net bank credit for domestic banks. Within this, sub-targets exist (e.g. farm credit, smaller loans, micro-enterprises, poorer sections). PSL quotas shape lending portfolios: banks issue loans just to meet these percentages and may sell excess obligation via certificates (PSLCs).
bodyText: Under current RBI rules, domestic banks’ overall PSL target is 40% of Adjusted Net Bank Credit (with RRBs at 75%). Within that, there are sub-targets: at least 18% to agriculture (including 8% to small farmers), 7.5% to micro-enterprises, etc. There is also a category of lending to weaker sections (10% of ANBC) and a target to small-scale industries (7.5%). Loans to export sectors, large industries, or corporates do NOT count. PSL has grown to cover new areas (education, housing, renewable energy) as per RBI prescriptions. Starting in 2016, RBI allowed banks that exceed PSL targets to sell Priority Sector Lending Certificates (PSLCs) to others who fall short. This “bank-on-bank trading” ensures goals are met system-wide. PSLCs come in types – e.g. Agriculture, Micro, General PSL – reflecting the underlying loan category. Priority sector rules profoundly shape Indian bank books: banks fund many low-yield rural loans simply to comply with the 40% mandate. This constrains their liquidity and profitability (since many PSL segments demand concessional rates or higher risk). Unlike any developed-country system, India’s mandatory directed-credit framework ties national policy to banking regulation. RBI-prescribed lending quotas (e.g. 40% to PSL) are mandatory. Banks must ensure each year’s lending meets or exceeds these sub-targets. Ignoring sub-categories and PSL certificates. A bank might focus only on agriculture without meeting MSME or weaker section targets, risking non-compliance. Also, some assume PSL is optional – it is not. **PSL quotas** — mandatory lending targets (40% of bank credit to certain sectors). **PSLC (certificates)** — tradable certificates representing excess PSL achievement; used to buy compliance. — Mandatory priority-sector quotas are unique to India’s financial system. (No similar directed-credit rules exist under PRA/Fed/FASB.)

title: Priority Sector Categories (Agri, MSME, Weaker)
one_screen: The “priority sectors” comprise several categories. Key ones include **Agriculture** (direct loans to farmers, etc.), **Micro and Small Enterprises (MSMEs)** (business loans up to specified limits), and **Weaker Sections** (targeted small borrowers). RBI regularly revises definitions: e.g. what constitutes a small farm or loan limit for microenterprise. Understanding each is crucial since only these count toward PSL quotas.
bodyText: **Agriculture (18% target):** Loans to farmers (individual or joint) for agriculture and allied activities. This includes crop loans, agricultural equipment loans, irrigation loans, and loans to agri-related services. Within agri, there is an 8% target specifically for small and marginal farmers (holding <2ha). Also loans to agri corporations, horticulture, and some farm sector supply chain are included. **MSMEs (7.5% target):** Loans to micro, small enterprises (as per MSME Act definitions) for business purposes.
