Also very small businesses (like retail shops, crafts). Recently, RBI expanded the definition to include loans to MSMEs up to ₹5 crore (and with turnover criteria). Loans to larger SMEs (beyond ₹5 cr) are out of PSL. **Weaker Sections (10% target):** This is a portion of PSL loans to small borrowers: it includes small farmers, microenterprises, borrowers from marginalized communities, and loans up to ₹50,000 (whichever sector). Essentially, a subset of agri, micro, and other small loans targeted at the bottom of economic pyramid (ST/SC, economically backward, etc.). Other PSL categories include education loans, housing loans (to EWS/LIG segments), renewable energy, and loans to specific small-scale service industries. Banks must use RBI’s PSL guidelines booklet to classify loans correctly. Only loans falling in these categories count; e.g. a big corporate loan does not. Overall, PSL shapes balance sheets: banks often build rural branches and specialized MSME credit teams to meet these targets. Satisfied PSL requirements can improve regulatory standing (e.g. risk weight relief), while shortfalls incur penalties. As RBI notes, PSL fosters socio-economic goals but also forces banks into lower-yielding lending. Only loans to RBI-defined priority categories count toward PSL. Agriculture loans, small enterprise finance, and weaker section lending have separate sub-targets. Misclassifying loans. E.g., making a small business loan to an urban store and hoping it counts as agriculture PSL – it does not. Each category has strict definitions. Also, banks sometimes ignore the ‘weaker sections’ requirement thinking general MSME lending covers it – but weaker sections is a distinct sub-target. **Agriculture credit** — includes crop/pump loans etc. (part of 18% PSL). **Weaker sections** — a subset of priority sector covering loans to marginalized and poorest borrowers, under the 10% sub-target of ANBC. — These exact sectoral categories (e.g. the 18% agri target) are unique to India’s RBI framework. Other countries may have development lending programs, but not tied to bank quotas.

title: Digital Lending Guidelines (Platforms and KFS)
one_screen: In 2022–2023, RBI issued comprehensive norms on digital lending to protect consumers from predatory fintech practices. It defines *Lending Service Providers* (LSPs) who partner with banks/NBFCs to distribute credit via apps. Key requirements include issuing a mandatory *Key Fact Statement (KFS)* for each loan, ensuring loans are disbursed into borrowers’ bank accounts (no third-party “pass-through” accounts), and capping upfront fees. LSPs also must register with RBI and have grievance officers. These rules address mis-selling and hidden charges that were rampant in unregulated lending apps.
bodyText: The context: unregulated loan apps led to harassment and exorbitant rates. In Feb 2022, RBI’s Master Directions on Digital Lending standardized the space. **Lending Service Providers** (non-bank fintechs who process applications) must follow KYC standards, get Permanent Account Number (PAN)/Aadhaar, and have a formal tie-up with a bank/NBFC. Every digital loan app must display, before disbursal, a *Key Fact Statement* summarizing the rate of interest, all fees and charges (incl. late payment fees), total amount payable, EMI/tenor etc. This ensures transparency. Borrowers must consent to these terms electronically. **Disbursal and repayment:** Loans must be disbursed directly to the customer’s bank account or their PSP wallet. Use of any “pass-through” account (e.g. an agent’s account) is banned. Similarly, repayments cannot flow through third-party accounts: they must go to the lender directly. This severed the practice of routing funds through shell accounts. **Fee and guarantee rules:** Fintech LSPs often offered “first loss default guarantees” to banks (promising to cover initial losses). RBI clarified these are not true securitizations but credit guarantees, and capped them at 20% of exposure or INR 5 cr. Also, LSPs cannot charge any fee at loan start except as explicitly disclosed – no pre-check fees. **Grievance redress:** Digital lenders must list a nodal grievance officer. Any user complaint must be addressed per RBI’s turnaround times. Ombudsman schemes also cover digital loans. Unfair collection by aggressive agents is prohibited under the Recovery Agent Code (see Consumer section). The RBI guidelines distinguish digital lending as a mechanism: *the loan contract is between lender and borrower*, while LSPs act as technology intermediaries. This “platform neutrality” means fintech apps cannot circumvent banking norms – borrowers can always refer to the original lender’s terms. Overall, these rules aim for consumer protection without stifling innovation: licensed entities can still use tech for underwriting (including data analytics, Aadhar/KYC), but must do so under RBI oversight. Digital lending platforms must issue a clear *Key Fact Statement* before loan disbursement, showing all charges and repayment terms. Loans must disburse directly to the customer’s own bank/wallet account, and no pass-through accounts are allowed. Loan sharks often created tech “platforms” outside regulation. A pitfall is thinking a fintech app can lend on its own terms. RBI’s rules require the actual loan to be from a bank/NBFC with digital co-lending only. Also, ignoring the KFS requirement can lead to non-compliance – every loan must show fully loaded APR and fees upfront. **Lending Service Provider (LSP)** — a non-bank platform or fintech that facilitates loan origination on behalf of a bank/NBFC. Not a lender itself. **Fintech loan** — an RBI-licensed lender’s loan disbursed via a digital channel. (Not simply “getting money from a random app”.) — RBI was among the first to regulate digital lending apps directly in such detail (re: KFS, pass-through ban). In UK/US, digital lending is allowed but individual states or laws handle disclosures (e.g. Truth-in-Lending Act) differently, and there is no blanket ban on pass-through accounts.

title: Digital Lending: Flow, Guarantees, and Securitisation
one_screen: Beyond transparency, RBI’s digital lending rules impose strict flow-of-funds and guarantee limits. Loans must be disbursed directly, and repayments must go to the original lender. The RBI also defined and capped “First Loss Default Guarantees” (FLDG) by fintechs, clarifying these are not true securitisation. Any arrangement where an app provider keeps collateral or routes funds illegitimately is prohibited.
bodyText: A key mandate: **Direct disbursal and repayment.** Any credit extended via a lending app must be paid into the customer’s own bank/PSP account – no money passes through the fintech or any third party. Similarly, loan repayments (EMIs) must be paid directly to the bank/NBFC. This is to prevent misappropriation. RBI explicitly forbids any “pooling or sweep accounts” that were used by some apps to skim funds. **Guarantee arrangements:** Fintechs used to offer to cover the bank’s losses (FLDG) up to some amount to motivate banks to lend. RBI treats an FLDG (capping around 20% of loan principal or ₹5 crore, whichever lower) as a credit enhancement, not traditional securitisation. Such guarantees must be explicit and capped by contract. They differ from securitisation: in a normal securitisation, credit risk is split among investors and not guaranteed by originator. Under RBI’s regime, if a fintech guarantees 20% of a loan’s loss, that fintech is effectively retaining part of credit risk (so regulator counts only 80% transfer as securitization). These agreements must be disclosed to borrowers. RBI’s limit (20%/₹5cr) prevents full risk transfer in a grey-camouflage way. RBI’s guidance also affirms that a fintech providing FLDG cannot park consumer funds. If a fintech receives payment from a borrower (say for processing), it must immediately route it to the bank. Collecting money and redisbursing it later is not allowed. Essentially, the fintech’s role is only origination & tech; money flows directly between borrower and bank. **First Loss Guarantee vs. Securitisation:** RBI emphasises they are distinct. In a securitisation, the originator may sell a pool of loans (and risk) to investors; there is no party assuring losses beyond already sold tranches. In a FLDG, the fintech agrees to compensate the bank for first losses. Because the guarantee can distort borrowers’ incentives and hides the true risk, RBI caps and requires disclosure of FLDGs. A FLDG is treated prudentially – the lender must still provision if a guarantee is in place (it’s not risk-free). No “pass-through” accounts in lending: funds must flow directly between borrower and lender. Any first-loss guarantee by a fintech must be contractually capped (max 20% of loan or ₹5 cr) and is **not** a pure securitisation. Using agent accounts to disburse or collect loan money. Some apps tried to appear as platforms but routed payments through their own accounts — RBI now explicitly forbids this. Also, fintechs believing they can guarantee entire losses – RBI caps such guarantees. **FLDG (First-Loss Default Guarantee)** — a fintech’s commitment to cover an agreed fraction (max 20%) of losses on a loan. This is a credit support, not full securitisation. **Securitisation** — selling loan assets and credit risk to investors (no partial guarantee by originator). — RBI’s treatment of fintech guarantees (FLDG) as limited and capping them is specific. Other countries allow fintech partnerships but often regulate them case-by-case (e.g. US banking regs). No identical cap is universal.

title: Digital Lending Grievance Redressal
one_screen: RBI mandates that all regulated entities using digital lending have formal grievance mechanisms. Lenders and fintechs must appoint nodal officers for customer complaints. Borrowers must be informed of escalation paths (including Banking Ombudsman). RBI also requires that both lenders and their tech partners resolve complaints quickly, tracking them in regular reports.
bodyText: The digital lending directions specify that every app or digital lender must provide clear contact details for grievance redressal. This includes an official Nodal Officer name/contact who handles issues. If a borrower complains (overcharging, collection practice, etc.), the lender must address it as per RBI’s standard timelines (e.g. 3-4 weeks resolution). Firms must also publish details of the Banking Ombudsman scheme, since appellants can approach it if unsatisfied. Moreover, under RBI’s 2016 Outsourcing guidelines (augmented in 2022 for recovery agents), banks must ensure their fintech partners and any recovery agents follow proper conduct. Customers should not face harassment or 24/7 calls. If needed, the customer’s complaint to the lender can be escalated through RBI’s Integrated Ombudsman Scheme. Tech-savvy customers often get quick redress via email or app, but the requirement is to maintain logs of all complaints and resolutions. In effect, RBI’s digital lending rules tighten accountability. A startup cannot avoid RBI oversight by claiming to be a “technology platform” – it must still honor consumer protection rules. Consumers have the same rights (transparency, appeals) as with brick-and-mortar banks when dealing via an app. For example, if a fintech breaches RBI’s guidelines, the bank’s grievance cell must still be answerable. Some fintechs go further (e.g. fintech ombudsmen) but legally the RBI framework covers all. All digital lenders must publish and operate a grievance redress system. Complaints must first go to a designated Nodal Officer. The Banking Ombudsman scheme covers digital loan disputes. Neglecting offline complaint channels. Assuming “if it’s digital, complaints must be emailed” – RBI requires accessible contact points and escalation. Also, sometimes start-ups think only their tech side is liable, but RBI holds the actual NBFC/bank accountable for the borrower’s redress. **Lending app support** — the platform or lender’s own customer service/email. **Banking Ombudsman** — RBI’s formal consumer forum. After exhausting internal redress, the borrower can approach it about digital loan issues (as with any bank). — RBI specifically requires digital loan grievance offices. Elsewhere, similar tech-lending regulations are nascent; EU has Digital Finance proposals, but no RBI-style scheme yet.

title: Co-Lending Framework (Banks-NBFCs)
one_screen: In 2018, RBI launched a co-lending scheme where banks and eligible NBFCs jointly finance borrowers. Under this, the bank must retain at least 20% of each co-lent loan portfolio (even if the NBFC originated most). Typically, the bank holds the larger share (say 80%) to keep better assets. The NBFC services the loan (e.g. documentation, collection) while sharing credit risk. Co-lending requires both parties to reconcile accounts and operations carefully, since each one-on-one partnership involves dual loan accounts and revenue splits.
bodyText: Under the *Co-Lending Model* (CoL), a bank and an NBFC enter a formal agreement. They extend credit to a common borrower at a predetermined ratio. One pattern is 80:20 (bank:NBFC) or 70:30, but RBI’s 2023 updates mandate minimum bank share of 20% for this scheme. In practice, many big banks take 80% and partner with smaller NBFCs (especially MFIs) that originate and service the loan to micro customers. All documentation must be in both names, and collections are shared. For example, the bank provides funds to NBFC (or directly to borrower), but NBFC handles field appraisal. The repayments are then split per the agreed ratio. This model aims to leverage NBFC outreach (last-mile distribution, quick appraisals) while giving banks a strong share of safer assets. Both parties must decide upfront on interest rate split, service fees to NBFC, and NPA handling. Operationally, co-lending adds complexity: two sets of ledgers (bank’s book and NBFC’s), reconciliation of cashflows, dual KYC checks, etc. If a borrower defaults, both share the loss per their ratio. RBI requires co-lending accounts to be reported correctly in their prudential returns (assets doubled: one on each book). Tax and accounting rules also reflect that a co-lent loan is partly a loan to NBFC (on bank book) and partly bank’s loan to borrower. The CoL framework was revised: initially introduced in 2018, it was formalized by Master Directions in 2021 and updated in 2023. The 2023 revision relaxed some earlier restrictions (like making NBFC proportion flexible up to 80%). It also allowed banks to lend their own share through partnerships (bank fraction can be higher). These policies aim to expand affordable credit (especially to underserved borrowers of NBFCs) by leveraging bank deposit base. In any RBI-approved co-lending arrangement, the bank must retain at least 20% (and typically holds the majority) of the credit amount. Both parties share risk and ownership accordingly. Misunderstanding who owns the loan: both do. A common mistake is booking the entire amount on one balance sheet; instead, each books its share. Also, forgetting that two payment schedules exist – banks must get their share. **Co-lending** — joint financing by bank + NBFC on a single loan to a borrower. Each funds part (min. 20% by bank) and shares title. --- **Syndication** — multiple banks lending separate portions to one borrower, each with own loan. (Co-lending keeps one loan, two lenders, not a consortium of loans.) — RBI’s co-lending model is unique (though other countries have bank–nonbank partnerships, they are usually simpler).

title: Co-Lending Operations and Reconciliation
one_screen: Practically, co-lending requires careful accounting on both sides. Each co-lending loan is reflected twice: a fraction on the bank’s books and the complementary on the NBFC’s books. Collections and disbursements must be reconciled to ensure each partner receives exactly its share. Often, the NBFC handles origination and collection (sometimes via its own BC network), remitting the bank’s portion of principal and interest as per the agreed split. The complexity of dual servicing and settlement is where most co-lending operations focus.
bodyText: Consider a ₹10 lakh loan co-lent at 80:20. The bank disburses ₹8L (possibly via the NBFC’s escrow), and the NBFC ₹2L. The NBFC may use its credit underwriting. When the borrower repays, the NBFC collects full EMI and must immediately allocate ₹8 of every ₹10 repayment to the bank’s account. RBI requires this flow to be documented, often via escrow or trustee arrangements. Both lenders then account: the bank books ₹8L asset, NBFC books ₹2L asset (showing ₹8L as a loan to NBFC if it was an advance). Reconciling these transactions is crucial each month. Banks and NBFCs often have joint MIS (Management Information System) to track co-lending pools. Differences (timing, rounding) must be resolved, or interest mismatches occur. RBI guidelines mandate that co-lending contracts clearly define default risk-sharing: if the borrower defaults, the bank and NBFC write off the respective shares in NPA. The NBFC’s share is often fully provided since the borrower mostly owes NBFC’s smaller part last (depending on waterfall, if any). Operational burdens include dual KYC process (both lenders verify the borrower), dual documentation, and regulatory reporting. For example, both lenders report their part of the loan in returns (one sees an inter-company advance, the other the borrower advance). Oversight demands that both sides have audit rights and controls over the loan pool. Despite the paperwork, co-lending is encouraged because it leverages NBFC outreach while using cheaper bank funds. Analysts must however note that it creates many micro-contractual relationships. Staff in banks and NBFCs must ensure cash flows match contractual splits exactly – failure can lead to compliance flags (like undisclosed bridging finance if the NBFC temporarily covers the bank’s share). Each co-lent account must be recognized on both the bank’s and NBFC’s balance sheets in the agreed ratio. Collections must be split immediately per that ratio. Neglecting reconciliation: assuming the NBFC’s collection is the end. In fact, the bank’s share must be remitted precisely each payment cycle. Failing to transfer promptly can violate regulations and trigger funding issues. **Disbursement ratio** — split of funds lent (e.g. bank:NBFC 80:20). **Risk ratio** — same as disbursement split (each bears losses in proportion). These two are identical in RBI’s co-lending rules. — Such formal bank-NBFC co-lending (with a fixed 20% bank retention) is currently unique.

title: Account Aggregators and GST Data in Lending
one_screen: The Account Aggregator (AA) ecosystem enables customers to share financial data from banks, investments and tax (GST) authorities with lenders upon consent. An AA is an RBI-regulated NBFC that securely fetches a borrower’s authenticated bank and other accounts data (like GST returns) to streamline credit assessment. In practice, a borrower can allow a prospective lender to view her bank statements and GST filings via the AA, replacing the need for manual document submission. This enhances underwriting accuracy for cash-flow lending.
bodyText: Under AA rules, banks and NBFCs must obtain explicit consent through the AA network before accessing a customer’s data. For MSMEs, RBI and government agencies are pushing use of GST returns to gauge cash flows. RBI now permits lenders to use GST-tracking (via AAs) as part of their credit appraisal. This is a paradigm shift from collateral-based to data-driven lending: for example, instead of using fixed assets, a bank can underwrite a shop owner’s ₹20 lakh loan by analyzing 6 months of GST invoices and bank inflows via an AA platform. The RBI’s digital lending guidelines implicitly encourage such open data models (as long as privacy is protected). Regulators (RBI, IBBI, GSTN) have jointly built frameworks: GSTN acts as a KYC and data provider (through Accounts Aggregator or NBFC-Factors). Lenders need to verify GSTIN status and utilization to validate turnover. The RBI’s 2022 standards require customer consent and confidentiality for all shared data. Meanwhile, data validation through GST filters out sham businesses. The government’s Unified Lending Interface (ULI) is an upcoming initiative to integrate this: ULI would let a lender fetch customer data (from AAs or government sources) through APIs, assess eligibility and disburse quickly. As of 2026, ULI pilots (e.g. with NBFCs and fintechs) are underway under RBI and IBA supervision. The idea is a one-stop-shop for loan origination: borrower consents once, and multiple lenders can exchange standardized credit data. Customer data (bank statements, GST returns, etc.) may be shared with lenders only through RBI-authorised channels (Account Aggregators) and only with customer consent. Assuming lenders can scrape GST data directly. In fact, only AAs or designated repositories (with consent) can transmit GST filings to banks. Also, neglecting to update borrower’s risk after changes in their GST activity can misstate credit risk. **Account Aggregator** — an RBI-regulated data intermediary that moves customer-permissioned data between institutions. --- **GST data** — tax return data of businesses. (Accessible by banks only through AAs or GSTN APIs with consent.) — The AA framework is Indian (launched 2021) and unique in mandating customer consent for banking data sharing. No similar centralized data sharing network is in place in UK/US.

title: Open Credit Enablement Network (OCEN) and Unified Lending
one_screen: OCEN is a public digital infrastructure initiated by RBI and others to promote standardized lending processes. It provides open protocols so any bank or NBFC can offer standardized lending products (LOAN service) to any borrower via their preferred interface (called Loan App Provider). The **Unified Lending Interface (ULI)** is an evolution of OCEN – a platform or API layer (conceptualized by IBA/RBI) that allows multiple lenders and tech-entities to interconnect seamlessly for loan origination. In practice, OCEN/ULI aims to let a borrower initiate a loan request once, then multiple lenders can compete or collaborate, all via technology rails.
bodyText: OCEN’s idea: separate *procurement of borrowers* (handled by digital aggregators or apps, called LAPs) from *funding* (banks/NBFCs). Using open APIs (like rupee-instant-pay, AA), a Loan App can share borrower’s data with many lenders using OCEN. Each lender then provides loan quotes. Final loan issuance happens through UPI’s LTI (loan transfer initiation) or direct credit. The OCEN framework is still evolving. It is mandated for certain government loan schemes (like for MSMEs). Under OCEN, lenders must publish their loan “schema” (min criteria) and pricing APIs. Borrowers see an offer comparison screen. Ongoing pilots involve fintech lending apps and major banks. The concept addresses fragmentation – instead of one bank-per-relationship, small borrowers can access many lenders digitally. Regulatory stance: RBI encourages this open network but underscores customer protection (same KFS, consent rules apply). OCEN/ULI bypass middlemen fees and aim for credit deepening. However, RBI has not mandated full roll-out; it’s voluntary with incentives. By 2026 RBI reports many pilots, but wide adoption is pending. Key point: OCEN/ULI are *not* separate entities, just infrastructure standards. Forthcoming RBI guideline: digital lenders can use the ULI (under OCEN) to interconnect, but all standard rules (KFS, KYC) still apply. For now, any participation is voluntary but encouraged for efficiency. Thinking OCEN/ULI replaces banks. In fact, banks/NBFCs remain the credit providers. OCEN just standardizes the way loan requests flow to them. Another mistake: assuming an app can lend via OCEN without partnering a regulated lender – regulatory approval is still needed. **OCEN** — a framework of open APIs and data standards for credit enabling (no single “company”). **ULI** — proposed RBI/IBA interface for unified loan origination/decision (still under development). — India’s OCEN/ULI initiative is pioneering an open credit network; no identical global standard exists.

title: Credit Information and CIBIL Scores
one_screen: Credit Information Companies (CICs) like CIBIL, Experian, Equifax (licensed by RBI) collect borrowers’ credit data (loans, credit cards, defaults) from banks/NBFCs and provide credit reports and scores. A bureau score (300–900 range) reflects an individual’s or firm’s credit history; lenders use it as a risk indicator. Each loan or card issued is reported to CICs. A CIBIL (now TransUnion CIBIL) *score* is a summary derived from one’s report; though popular, RBI treats it as *one* input, not a sole decision factor.
bodyText: CICs operate under the Credit Information Companies (Regulation) Act, 2005. By law, any institution granting loans above certain thresholds must report data (including repayment behaviour) to CICs. Thus, a “CIBIL report” may contain: outstanding loans, EMI payment history, credit inquiries, defaults or write-offs. A high credit score (e.g. 750+) typically leads to faster loan approval. However, some segments (like unsecured or newer forms of credit) still rely on alternate data, since CIC coverage has gaps (informal lending not always reported). RBI mandates that lenders consult at least one CIC before sanctioning any loan. Lenders are also regulated on sharing the score with customers (ECIR/ ECI guidelines requiring justification for rejection). Over the past decade, refinements have been made: e.g. CRILC (Central Repository of Information on Large Credits) to flag large defaults, and securitisation of card limits for bureau reporting. Debenture data (various corporate loans) is less visible in consumer credit reports. For corporate or MSME borrowers, there is no single “CIBIL score” standard. Instead, banks rely on financial statements, promoter history, and sometimes the promoter’s personal credit scores. Commercial credit intelligence (like Dun & Bradstreet ratings) complement it. Banks and NBFCs must submit borrower data to CICs and use bureau reports in credit decisions. Borrowers have a right to one free credit report per year from each bureau. Over-reliance on the numeric score. A common error is to treat a 750 CIBIL score as guarantee of repayment; lenders must still do underwriting. Conversely, a borrower’s poor score may have valid reasons (data errors or past minor defaults) – blindly rejecting such cases without manual review can be wrong. **Credit report** — detailed history of all borrowed accounts and repays (with any defaults) held by a CIC. **Credit score** — a numerical summary (e.g. CIBIL score) of that report. — System of multiple CICs (CIBIL, HDFC ERGO, etc.) is similar to US/UK bureau systems. But India’s credit scoring scale (300–900 for CIBIL) is proprietary (others use different ranges).

title: SARFAESI Act (Asset Enforcement)
one_screen: The SARFAESI Act (2002) empowers banks/ARCs to enforce securities against defaulting borrowers without court intervention. It allows a secured creditor (bank/NBFC/ARC) to take possession of collateral (land, factories, financial instruments) if a loan account is an NPA, subject to RBI’s prescribed triggers. This mechanism dramatically speeds up recovery in contrast to civil litigation. However, it only covers “secured” exposures: unsecured debts (like credit cards, personal loans) cannot be directly taken under SARFAESI.
bodyText: Under SARFAESI, upon default, an asset reconstruction company (or the bank itself) can issue a notice to the borrower (and guarantor) demanding payment within 60 days. If not paid, the creditor can auction the pledged assets (e.g. sell the mortgaged factory). The sale proceeds pay off the debt. Borrowers can appeal before DRTs (Debt Recovery Tribunals) if they believe wrongful action. SARFAESI’s enforcement is therefore final, with limited appeals – it is potent. Banks often syndicate bad loans to ARCs (Asset Reconstruction Companies) which use SARFAESI to reorganize or sell assets. For lenders, SARFAESI provides collateral realisation. Practically, banks must follow RBI’s “change of management” norms if a corporate account being taken over exceeds a threshold. RBI also requires lenders to classify any SARFAESI-induced partial recovery appropriately (e.g. as standard if current, else further NPA reduction). In stress scenarios, SARFAESI is often a precursor to invocation of IBC or other legal recovery if needed. A secured lender can take possession of pledged collateral if the borrower defaults and does not repay after notice. The process must follow SARFAESI procedures (notice, sale, use funds to settle debt). Trying to use SARFAESI on unsecured loans – it only applies to secured advances. Also, failing to issue the proper notice period (60 days) or not following RBI’s change-of-management rules when seizing a company. **SARFAESI** — enforcement law letting secured creditors seize and sell collateral after default (without courts). **Debt Recovery Tribunal (DRT)** — quasi-judicial body that borrowers can approach to challenge SARFAESI or other recovery actions. — Unique to India (introduced 2002). No direct analog in US/UK; other countries rely on normal foreclosure laws.

title: Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code (IBC) and DRT
one_screen: The Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code (2016) provides a structured process for resolving stressed corporate debts. If lenders collectively decide (typically 75% by value) that a default requires legal resolution, they can initiate corporate insolvency. A *Resolution Professional* then manages the company’s affairs, and creditors vote on a revival plan. The IBC has priority over SARFAESI in that once an insolvency petition is admitted, SARFAESI proceedings halt. For personal or small debtors, formal bankruptcy via IBC may not apply; instead, DRTs (for bank debts above a threshold) and debt recovery tribunals handle lower-value cases, including unsecured and smaller claims.
bodyText: Under IBC, any financial creditor (bank, NBFC, or even a supplier if admitted) can initiate proceedings when payment default occurs. A strict timeline (330 days max) forces quick action. Successful resolution under IBC often involves structural changes (equity dilution, takeover by new promoters, etc.). Recoveries under IBC have exceeded SARFAESI recoveries historically because of its collective mechanism. But IBC is mostly for corporate debt. For individual/business borrowers, RBI relies on SARFAESI and DRT (established by RDDBFI Act, 1993) and lok adalats. Debt Recovery Tribunals handle all debts of ₹10 lakh and above to banks/financial institutions. They can entertain cases on any credit, secured or not, and can order recovery from a debtor’s assets. There are separate DRTs for circular references from the RBI. The DRT process is formal (like a tribunal court), but faster than regular civil court. DRTs have been strengthened by digital filing and “DRAT” appeals. Banks usually prioritize SARFAESI for quick value, then DRT if borrower defends. IBC is the last resort for viable corporates or when persuasion fails. RBI’s provisions require reclassification of accounts when IBC is filed (they become NPA on petition filing). The IBC can wipe out shareholders; in one instance, leading to EMI refinance rather than further lending. Under IBC, when a corporate borrower defaults, lenders may trigger insolvency proceedings with RBI filing specified asset classification. DRTs handle recovery suits for any loan above ₹10 lakh. Missing the priority: initiating SARFAESI on a company after IBC has been filed – not allowed, since IBC is a binding multilateral process once admitted. Also, dismissing smaller claims (below 10 lakh) thinking only big debts go to DRTs – DRT jurisdiction starts at ₹10 lakh for banks. **IBC (Corporate)** — structured insolvency process for companies / FIs (time-bound, collective). **DRT (Debt Recovery)** — tribunal for creditor claims on individuals or businesses (₹10L+), including enforcement of guarantee by guarantors. — The IBC is India’s consolidated insolvency law (2016). Countries like the UK/US have different corporate insolvency regimes (Chapter 11, administration, etc.), but the IBC’s speed and creditor primacy are quite distinctive.

title: Fair Practices Code and Rate Transparency
one_screen: RBI mandates all banks/NBFCs adopt a *Fair Practices Code (FPC)* – a set of consumer-lending norms. The FPC requires clear, upfront disclosure of key loan terms (interest rates, all fees, prepayment and foreclosure conditions). Borrowers must receive written sanction letters. Lenders must not coerce borrowers into purchasing unrelated products. After 2019, RBI additionally requires all new floating-rate loans (e.g. mortgages, auto loans, corporate loans) to be linked to external benchmarks (like RBI’s repo rate or govt bond yields). This makes the rate formula transparent – borrowers know that if RBI changes repo, their EMI changes per a public index.
bodyText: For instance, every home loan borrower must be told the benchmark (now MCLR or an external rate) and margin. Any change in the base rate must be communicated one month in advance. Prepayment or foreclosure should be allowed per the FPC (sometimes with max 2% penalty). No hidden charges are allowed. If a bank refuses to lend, it must give a reason in writing (borrower’s right to information under FPC). The 2019 “external benchmark” circular mandated that by Oct 1, 2019 all new floating-rate personal, retail, and MSME loans link to external benchmarks, and from April 1, 2020 medium enterprise loans too. This revolutionized rate transparency: borrowers now see explicit linkage to, say, RBI’s repo. Banks cannot arbitrarily change rates without a rule. In essence, fair practices and rate guidelines aim to protect retail borrowers from predatory pricing and information asymmetry. While bankers often resent caps on lending rates, RBI views transparency (e.g. bench-marking) as non-negotiable. All retail credit product literature (e.g. home loans, auto, personal loans) must clearly detail these terms. Lenders must disclose all loan terms in writing (sanction letter or KFS) per RBI’s FPC. All new floating-rate loans must use an external benchmark (e.g. policy rate) for interest calculations. Failing to update borrowers on rate changes. RBI requires communication if the external benchmark shifts. Some banks adjust rates silently (not allowed). Also, bundling hidden fees into loan rate rather than showing them separately violates FPC. **Fair Practices Code (FPC)** — RBI’s consumer protection rules for lending (disclosure, no coercion, grievance mechanism). **External Benchmarking** — the requirement that floating rates link to public indices. This is part of FPC transparency. — RBI’s mandatory external benchmark linkage (repo or gilt) is specific to India’s circulars. Elsewhere, countries may require APR disclosure but not compulsory benchmark linking.

title: Recovery Agents Code of Conduct
one_screen: RBI’s 2022 guidelines reaffirm that financial institutions are fully responsible for their recovery agents’ actions. Banks must ensure recovery personnel treat borrowers respectfully, within prescribed hours, and without intimidation. Agents must carry ID cards. Borrowers can record collection calls and lodge complaints if the code is violated. This rule curbs the excesses of aggressive recovery practices prevalent especially in rural/tele-calling.
bodyText: The key directives (2022) state that banks/NBFCs must not use agents to harass borrowers. No coercion is allowed: no making calls before 8 am or after 7 pm, no abuse/insults, no shame-tactics. Agents must have clear ID/name tags; they must follow written guidelines. The regulated entity (bank or NBFC) remains liable for any breach by its agents. Prior RBI codes (2006 & 2010) prohibited many misbehaviors (e.g. third-party visits to workplaces for small debts). The 2022 circular specifically supplements these with updated instructions under the outsourcing framework, emphasizing that violations can lead to supervisory action. This is consumer protection in collections: borrowers have recourse to the bank’s grievance cell for any agent mis-step, and ultimately to the Ombudsman. Banks must train and monitor their agents (even if they are third-party contractors). Banks/NBFCs must ensure recovery agents comply with RBI’s conduct rules: no threat, no personal harassment, call only between 8am-7pm, respectful behavior. ID cards are mandatory. Assuming recovery can be “any means necessary.” RBI’s explicit code bans intimidation (Verbal/physical harassment, false claims, repeated late-hour calls). Non-compliance by agents is deemed violation by the lender. **Recovery Agent** — hired agent or third-party who collects overdue loans. (Subject to RBI’s code of conduct.) **Debt Collector** — similar role; RBI’s rules apply equivalently, unlike unregulated field agents for non-financial debts. — RBI’s Code for recovery agents is detailed and mandatory (2016/2022). Other countries regulate debt collectors (e.g. US Fair Debt Collection Practices Act) differently, but India’s code is specific to banking debts.

title: Market risk and risk factor classes
one_screen: Market risk is the risk of trading losses due to changes in market prices, covering exposures to interest rates, equity prices, FX, commodities, and credit spreads.
bodyText: Market risk arises when positions are marked‐to‐market, so portfolio value changes with market movements. It includes price risk on instruments from six risk categories: general interest rates, credit spreads (non-securitized and securitized), foreign exchange, equity, and commodity risk. Each of these risk factor classes drives the market value of trading positions (e.g. rising rates reduce bond values, widening credit spreads hurt credit-sensitive instruments). A market risk manager communicates risk in terms of sensitivities (delta, vega, curvature) to these factors (see MRK-03). For example, a bond portfolio’s delta sensitivity quantifies loss per basis-point move in rates. Each risk class is handled separately but then aggregated under capital rules. Market risk exposures: +--------------------------+ | Interest Rate Risk | | (e.g. bond prices) | +--------------------------+ | Credit Spread Risk | | (credit-sensitive bonds) | +--------------------------+ | Foreign Exchange Risk | | (currencies) | +--------------------------+ | Equity Risk | | (stock prices) | +--------------------------+ | Commodity Risk | | (oil, metals, etc.) | +--------------------------+ Market risk is always about price changes in trading positions, not credit defaults. Treating credit spread risk simply as credit default risk (credit risk capital) rather than as a market risk factor. **Interest rate risk** — loss from interest rate moves (fixed income valuation); **Credit spread risk** — loss from widening credit spreads on debt (a market risk factor). **No delta.** The definitions of market risk and its factor categories are uniform across jurisdictions.

title: Market risk vs credit risk capital
one_screen: Market risk capital covers mark-to-market losses on trading positions, whereas credit risk capital covers losses from counterparty or issuer default.
bodyText: Market risk and credit risk address different loss drivers. Market risk capital is held against losses from price or rate moves in tradable instruments (e.g. bond price declines, equity crashes). In contrast, credit risk capital covers expected losses from default or credit deterioration of borrowers/counterparties (covered under credit RWA frameworks). For example, widening credit spreads on a corporate bond affect its market value (market risk), whereas an actual default causing a loss beyond any resale value is credit risk. The Basel Committee explicitly includes credit spread and jump-to-default risk in the trading book market risk framework. This reflects that trading desks face both price volatility and potential default events. However, the capital for each risk type is calculated separately, since pricing risk and default risk behave differently. Market risk covers losses from market price or volatility changes; credit risk covers losses from defaults. Ignoring that credit exposures in the trading book incur both market (spread) and default risk; treating all credit exposures as only credit RWA. **Credit spread risk** — market loss from widening credit spreads on instruments (market risk factor); **Credit risk** — loss from default or credit event (covered by credit RWA). **No delta.** The conceptual separation between market and credit risk capital is universal.

title: Market risk sensitivities (delta, vega, curvature)
one_screen: Market risk is often quantified by first-order and second-order sensitivities: delta (linear price change), vega (volatility sensitivity), and curvature (non-linear/gamma effect).
bodyText: Instead of revaluing portfolios for every risk shock, traders and risk managers express exposure in sensitivities to risk factors. **Delta risk** is the linear change in value per unit move in the underlying (e.g. bond yield or stock price). **Vega risk** measures the change in instrument value for a change in implied volatility (important for options or caps). **Curvature risk** (sometimes called gamma/volga) captures the additional non-linear loss beyond the linear delta approximation when large shocks or optionality is present. For example, an at-the-money option has high vega and curvature: a spike in volatility or a large price move causes loss beyond the delta estimate. FRTB explicitly models separate charges for delta, vega, and curvature in each risk class. Key market risk sensitivities are delta, vega, and curvature; all must be quantified and aggregated. Ignoring vega and curvature in an options portfolio and using only delta risk (underestimating true risk). **Delta** — linear sensitivity to a small move in the underlying price; **Curvature** — additional non-linear effect (the loss beyond delta when larger shocks or optionality occur). **No delta.** The definitions of delta, vega, and curvature risk are set by the Basel framework and apply universally.

title: Value at Risk (VaR) definition
one_screen: VaR is the loss threshold which is not expected to be exceeded at a given confidence level over a specified time horizon.
bodyText: Value at Risk (VaR) is a statistical risk measure. For a chosen confidence level α (e.g. 99%) and horizon (e.g. 10 days), VaRα is the loss L such that there is a (1−α) probability the actual loss will exceed L. In practice, a bank says “99% 10-day VaR” of $X means there is a 1% chance the 10-day loss will exceed $X. Banks typically compute VaR daily for trading books to summarize total market risk exposure. Basel rules historically used 10-day 99% VaR (12-month window) for capital. FRTB replaces VaR with ES, but VaR remains key for backtesting and internal limits. VaR computation (conceptual): 1. Gather P&L distribution over horizon (simulation or historical returns). 2. Sort losses from smallest (best) to largest (worst). 3. Identify the 1% quantile (for 99% VaR). 4. VaR = loss at that quantile (not exceeded with 99% confidence). VaRα is always defined as the (100−α)th percentile loss over the chosen horizon. Treating VaR as the maximum possible loss or ignoring that beyond-VaR losses can be larger. **Value at Risk (VaR)** — the loss not exceeded at the confidence level (loss threshold); **Expected Shortfall (ES)** — the expected loss *beyond* the VaR threshold (average tail loss). **No delta.** The mathematical definition of VaR is universal across regulatory regimes.

title: VaR calculation methods
one_screen: VaR can be computed by historical simulation (replaying actual past returns), parametric (variance-covariance, assuming normal returns), or Monte Carlo simulation. Each method uses different assumptions about return distributions.
bodyText: **Historical simulation** VaR sorts actual historical portfolio returns (e.g. last 1,000 days) and picks the percentile loss. It assumes the future risk factor moves will resemble past moves (no distributional assumption). **Parametric (variance-covariance)** VaR assumes portfolio returns are multivariate normal and portfolios respond linearly to risk factors; it calculates VaR analytically from portfolio mean and covariance. This is computationally fast but can underestimate tail risk if returns are fat-tailed. **Monte Carlo simulation** VaR uses a risk model to generate many random return scenarios (e.g. from heavy-tailed or multi-factor distributions), revalues the portfolio under each, and then finds the loss percentile. It can capture complex distributions and non-linearities but is computation-intensive. +---------------------------+ | VaR Methods | +---------------------------+ | Historical Simulation | +---------------------------+ | (use actual past returns) | | | +---------------------------+ | Parametric (Var-Cov) | +---------------------------+ | (assume normal returns) | | | +---------------------------+ | Monte Carlo Simulation | +---------------------------+ | (simulate future paths) | +---------------------------+ Three main VaR methods: historical simulation, parametric (variance-covariance), and Monte Carlo. Using a parametric (normal) VaR model when returns are fat-tailed or portfolios are non-linear, thus underestimating actual risk. **Historical VaR** — derived from actual past return scenarios (no assumed distribution); **Parametric VaR** — calculated assuming normal returns (linearized portfolio). **No delta.** The conceptual VaR methods are the same everywhere.

title: Limitations of Value at Risk
one_screen: VaR does not describe the magnitude of losses beyond its threshold, and can be insensitive to extreme tail risk.
bodyText: VaR only tells you the cut-off loss at the confidence level, not what happens if losses exceed that. It ignores the severity of losses in the tail. In other words, portfolios with very different tail risk can have the same VaR. As one analyst notes, “VaR does not tell us anything about losses beyond the VaR level”. For instance, a portfolio with potential huge losses in rare events may have the same VaR as a benign portfolio up to that quantile. This gap became apparent during crises when losses far exceeded VaR predictions. VaR is also not a coherent risk measure (it lacks sub-additivity in some cases), which means diversifying positions could, counterintuitively, increase VaR. These shortcomings motivated the shift to Expected Shortfall in regulatory frameworks (see MRK-07). VaR at α% does **not** measure how large losses can be beyond that percentile. Treating VaR as if it were a worst-case loss or ignoring the tail beyond the VaR cutoff. **VaR** — the (1−α) percentile loss (threshold loss); **Worst-case loss** — an extreme possible loss (VaR does not guarantee worst-case). **No delta.** The mathematical limitations of VaR are inherent and do not depend on jurisdiction.

title: Expected Shortfall (ES) and rationale
one_screen: Expected Shortfall at confidence level α is defined as the average loss in the worst (1−α)% of cases. It was adopted by Basel because it captures tail losses that VaR ignores.
bodyText: Expected Shortfall (ES), also known as Conditional VaR or Tail VaR, is the mean loss given that losses exceed the VaR threshold. Formally, ESα is the expected loss in the worst (100−α)% scenarios. For example, 97.5% ES is the average of the worst 2.5% losses. ES addresses VaR’s blind spot: it incorporates how bad tail losses can be. Basel III.1 replaced 99% VaR with 97.5% ES for capital, explicitly to “overcome some weaknesses identified in VaR, in particular that it does not ignore tail losses”. ES is a coherent risk measure and responds more sensibly to extreme events. Under normal distributions, 99% VaR and 97.5% ES are numerically similar, but for fat-tailed markets ES is significantly larger. Basel’s switch to ES reflects a priority on capturing potential extreme losses in stressed conditions. ESα is the average loss beyond the α-VaR cutoff and ensures tail losses are included in risk capital. Using VaR instead of ES for capital calculations when regulators require ES, thereby underestimating tail risk. **VaR** — loss percentile at confidence α; **Expected Shortfall (ES)** — average of losses beyond that percentile (tail average). **No delta.** The expected shortfall calculation is a mathematical concept with no jurisdictional variation.

title: Confidence levels, holding periods, scaling
one_screen: VaR and ES must specify a confidence level and holding period.  Regulators typically use 99% VaR (10-day) or 97.5% ES (10-day) for capital.  Under iid returns, risk scales as √time, but real markets often violate that.
bodyText: Regulators set specific confidence levels and horizons for capital calculation. Basel II used 99% VaR over 10 trading days; FRTB uses 97.5% ES over 10 days. The longer holding period corresponds to liquidating or hedging positions under stress. One often scales 1-day VaR to a 10-day VaR by multiplying by √10 (assuming independent returns), but if volatility changes or liquidity constraints exist, that simple scaling breaks down. Under a normal return assumption, 10-day 99% VaR numerically equals 10-day 97.5% ES (both ≈2.33σ). Basel chose 97.5% ES in part to align capital ratios (since ES at 97.5% on a normal distribution roughly matches 99% VaR). Confidence level governs the tail probability (e.g. 99% VaR ignores top 1% losses). Basel also introduced a separate stressed calibration (see MRK-10) using a 250-day period. Capital VaR/ES increases with higher confidence and longer horizon. Under i.i.d. assumptions, risk approximately scales with the square root of time. Blindly scaling VaR by √time when returns are autocorrelated or volatility shifts; treating 99% VaR as equivalent to 97.5% ES without regard to distribution. **1-day VaR** vs **10-day VaR** (horizon difference); **99% VaR** vs **97.5% ES** (confidence difference). For a normal distribution, 99% VaR ≈ 97.5% ES, but this breaks in crisis. **No delta.** The concepts of confidence level and time horizon scaling are general; only the numeric standards (e.g. 97.5% ES vs 99% VaR) vary by regulation.

title: VaR backtesting and traffic light
one_screen: VaR backtesting checks model accuracy by counting daily exceptions.  Over 250 days, 0–4 exceptions (loss>VaR) is green, 5–9 yellow, ≥10 red.
bodyText: Banks compare realized P&L against VaR forecasts each day. An “exception” occurs when actual loss exceeds the VaR estimate. Basel prescribed a 250-day test window. If exceptions are within 0–4, the model is in the green zone; 5–9 exceptions is a yellow (caution) zone; ≥10 exceptions (4% rate) is red, implying the model likely underestimates risk. Consistently high exceptions trigger higher capital multipliers or require model review. Typically, about 2.5 exceptions are expected on average per 250 days at 99% VaR. A red-zone model would get a multiplier of 4× on VaR for capital. Notably, regulators use *hypothetical* P&L (revaluing yesterday’s closing positions) for backtesting, not intraday actual P&L, to avoid distortions from new trades. Counting actual P&L can inflate exceptions if intraday trades occur. 250-day backtesting: +-------------+--------+ | Exceptions | Action | +-------------+--------+ | 0–4 (Green) | Model OK (low exceptions) | | 5–9 (Yellow)| Investigate (some alarm) | | >=10 (Red) | Model invalid (4%+ breaches) | +-------------+--------+ An accurate 99% VaR model should yield roughly 2-3 exceptions in 250 days (green zone). Treating any exception as a model failure, or using actual P&L (with intraday trading) instead of hypothetical P&L. **Actual P&L** — realized daily P&L including new trades; **Hypothetical P&L** — P&L from revaluing prior-day positions (used in backtesting). **No delta.** The Basel backtesting traffic-light framework is applied uniformly. 4% exceptions)." />

title: Stressed VaR calibration
one_screen: Regulators require calibrating VaR/ES on a 12-month historically stressed period (e.g. 250 trading days) representative of serious market stress. Under FRTB, capital is based on stressed ES on such a period.
bodyText: To capture potential losses under adverse conditions, banks must compute a *Stressed VaR* (Basel 2.5) or *Stressed ES* (FRTB) using a past period of high volatility. Each bank selects a recent 250-business-day window of significant market stress that is relevant to its portfolio. For example, a U.S. dealer might choose the 2008 crisis or a 2011 euro debt stress. The chosen period’s data are fed into the VaR or ES model instead of a normal period. Under Basel 2.5, capital was 10-day VaR (99%) plus 10-day Stressed VaR (99%) from a stress window. FRTB instead uses 10-day ES at 97.5% on the stress window for capital. The rules ensure banks hold capital that reflects losses in a realistic stress scenario. Always use a continuous one-year period of actual stress for calibrating Stressed VaR/ES. Selecting a stress period that is not relevant to current portfolio risks, or forgetting to update the stress window periodically. **Historical VaR** — VaR from recent normal market data; **Stressed VaR** — VaR from a past stress period. **No delta.** The concept of calibrating to a stressed period is applied globally in advanced regimes.

title: FRTB rationale (pre-crisis failures)
one_screen: The pre-2008 market risk rules failed to capture tail events and credit concentration. Trading losses in 2008–09 revealed these gaps, prompting Basel 2.5 and then FRTB reforms.
bodyText: Before the crisis, banks often relied on VaR-based models and porous TB/BB boundaries. During 2007–08, widespread trading losses (e.g. on structured credit) showed models underestimated risks. For instance, losses from Lehman and AIG’s trading books were far worse than their VaR predicted. This led to Basel 2.5 (2009) which increased capital on trading products (higher charges on securitisations, addition of stressed VaR). FRTB (Basel 3.1) was developed to fix the “major fault lines” in the old framework. It enforces stricter TB/BB boundary (preventing regulatory arbitrage), uses ES instead of VaR (better tail capture), and adds charges for default risk (DRC) and unmodellable risks (NMRFs). These changes aim to ensure capital better reflects true market risk. Capital frameworks must account for severe but plausible market moves (stress scenarios) and not rely solely on benign historical periods. Relying only on high-confidence VaR and ignoring stress episodes. **Basel II.5** — interim 2009 amendments (added stressed VaR and CVA capital) vs **Basel 3.1 (FRTB)** — comprehensive 2019 reforms with ES, risk sensitivities, etc. **No delta.** All major jurisdictions have recognized the pre-crisis framework’s shortcomings.

title: Trading book boundary (FRTB)
one_screen: FRTB enforces a stricter trading/banking book boundary with clear criteria. Positions held to hedge trading risk go in TB; others belong in BB. The rules aim to prevent arbitrage through misclassification.
bodyText: Prior to FRTB, banks had wide discretion to classify positions, often moving illiquid bonds into the banking book to reduce capital. FRTB closes these gaps by requiring documented intent and specific criteria for trading book inclusion. For example, a position must be held with intent to trade (or hedge another trading position) to go in the trading book. Otherwise it must stay in the banking book. This “marked-to-market requirement” ensures capital reflects actual risk. The revised rules (Basel RBC25) replaced the previous “principles-based” boundary with prescriptive rules and governance requirements. Banks must justify each trading book position with approvals and documentation. This reduces risk-shifting between books and promotes consistency. Any position not held with a trading intent or as a hedge of trading risk must be classified as banking book. Designating long-term or illiquid instruments as trading positions simply to use potentially lower market risk capital. **Trading book** — positions held for short-term resale or hedging trading exposures; **Banking book** — held for earning interest or fulfilling contractual relationships (not for active trading). **No delta.** All regimes that implement FRTB impose stricter boundaries (UK/EU via RBC, US via OCC guidelines, etc).

title: Standardised Approach (sensitivities-based, SA)
one_screen: The FRTB Standardised Approach (SA) computes capital by mapping sensitivities (delta, vega, curvature) to fixed risk weights in buckets, aggregating within each risk class and across two correlation scenarios.
bodyText: Under SA, each risk factor (e.g. interest rate, FX, equity) has pre-set weight tables. A bank computes portfolio delta, vega and curvature sensitivities for each risk factor. Those sensitivities are multiplied by risk weights and summed according to prescribed buckets (e.g. grouping interest rate tenors into zones, currency pairs into FX buckets). Buckets allow intra- and inter-bucket correlations: SA defines two scenarios (medium and low correlation) for combining risk, and takes the larger capital requirement from those. After summing delta, vega, and curvature charges for all classes under the worst-case scenario, SA also adds two extra charges: the **Default Risk Charge** (DRC) for jump-to-default credit risk and the **Residual Risk Add-On** (RRAO) for exotic/basis exposures. These components ensure known market and credit risks are covered even without an internal model. +-----------------------------+ | Sensitivities (Δ, vega, κ) | +-------------+---------------+ | +-------------v---------------+ | Apply risk weights & buckets| +-------------+---------------+ | +-------------v---------------+ | Compute capital in 2 scenarios| |(med/low corr) | +-------------+---------------+ | +-------------v---------------+ | Take larger capital | +-------------+---------------+ | +-------------v---------------+ | Add Default Risk Charge | | + Residual Risk Add-On | +-------------+---------------+ | +-------------v---------------+ | Total SA Capital Charge | +-----------------------------+ SA capital = max(scenario capital) + DRC + RRAO. Forgetting to apply the correct correlation scenario (always take the higher) or omitting the RRAO for exotic positions. **Delta risk** (linear sensitivity) vs **Vega risk** (volatility sensitivity) — both are treated separately in SA and not interchangeable. **No delta.** The SA framework is a standardized Basel formula applied globally (though local regulators may adjust some risk weights).

title: Default Risk Charge (DRC) and Residual Risk Add-On (RRAO)
one_screen: Under FRTB SA, the Default Risk Charge (DRC) is an add-on capital for jump-to-default events on credit instruments.  The Residual Risk Add-On (RRAO) covers positions not captured by the standard sensitivities (e.g. exotic or basis risks).
bodyText: The DRC addresses the gap that credit spread shocks (in the sensitivities method) do not capture actual default. For instruments like bonds or CDS in the trading book, banks must calculate an additional capital charge representing a sudden default loss. The specifics follow a default table of risk weights. The RRAO is for “any instruments bearing residual risk” beyond delta/vega/curvature. Typical examples: exotic options whose risk isn’t well represented by the buckets, correlation-trading positions, or multi-underlying products. FRTB requires a fixed charge or stress scenario calculation for these. Together, SA capital = SB method (sensitivities) OR (DRC+RRAO), whichever is higher. Always add DRC for credit default risk and RRAO for remaining exposures to the sensitivities-based capital. Treating the sensitivities formula as sufficient and ignoring DRC or RRAO, which can underestimate capital for credit and exotic positions. **Default Risk Charge** — covers jump-to-default credit losses; **Residual Risk Add-On** — covers other risks not in SBM (like exotic instrument exposures). **No delta.** Both DRC and RRAO are defined by Basel and apply universally in SA.

title: Internal Models Approach (IMA: ES and liquidity horizons)
one_screen: Under FRTB IMA, banks compute expected shortfall (97.5% conf., 10-day base) on a desk basis, adjusting for liquidity horizons by scaling risk factors to 10, 20, 40, 60, or 120 days as specified.
bodyText: Each trading desk that uses IMA must calculate a daily ES measure. The modeler computes 10-day ES at 97.5% for each desk. Crucially, risk factors have assigned *liquidity horizons* (LH) reflecting how long it takes to exit or hedge. ES is initially computed for a 10-day base then scaled: e.g. a factor with a 20-day LH has its 10-day ES multiplied by √(20/10) to obtain a 20-day ES. Table 1 of MAR33 defines five LH categories: 10, 20, 40, 60, 120 days (higher LH for less liquid products). IMA capital equals the sum of these liquidity-adjusted ES contributions across risk factors in the desk. Desks must have regulators’ approval to use IMA. Each desk must also pass backtesting and P&L attribution (next atom). IMA-based capital is the liquidity-adjusted 97.5% ES at desk level. Using VaR in place of ES, or omitting the liquidity horizon adjustment (treating all factors as 10-day). **Expected Shortfall (ES)** in IMA vs **VaR** (older metric): IMA requires ES at 97.5%, not VaR. **No delta.** The use of ES and liquidity horizons is mandated by the Basel FRTB standard for IMA globally (subject to local implementation delays).

title: P&L attribution (PLA) test
one_screen: To use IMA, each trading desk must pass a daily P&L attribution test comparing model P&L to revalued P&L. Desks that fail must use SA.
bodyText: The PLA test evaluates how well a desk’s risk model explains actual P&L. **Risk-theoretical P&L** is the model’s forecast of one-day P&L using the desk’s risk factors. **Hypothetical P&L** is the P&L from revaluing yesterday’s positions with today’s prices. Basel requires these to be highly correlated over time. A desk must satisfy PLA on an ongoing basis to retain IMA status. Many desks fail PLA because models omit risk factors or simplify valuation. For example, a desk trading exotic options may not include volatility surface shifts or correlation terms in its model, so the hypothetical P&L (which captures actual instrument repricing) diverges from the model’s P&L. Common issues include illiquid instruments with no observable prices, or mis-specified static factors. Failing PLA means the desk’s capital must be calculated using the less favorable standardised approach. Desks using IMA must continuously satisfy PLA (compare model vs revalued P&L). Assuming a desk passes PLA based on backtesting alone; neglecting PLA discrepancies can invalidate the IMA. **Risk-theoretical P&L** — desk’s model-predicted P&L; **Hypothetical P&L** — P&L from revaluing held positions at new market prices. **No delta.** PLA requirements are part of the international FRTB IMA criteria.

title: Risk factor eligibility test and non-modellable factors (NMRFs)
one_screen: IMA is only allowed for risk factors with sufficient market data.  A risk factor passes the Risk Factor Eligibility Test (RFET) if it has enough observable prices.  If it fails, it is a Non-Modellable Risk Factor (NMRF) and incurs a separate stress charge.
bodyText: Under RFET, each risk factor in a modelled desk must have a minimum number of real price observations over the past year (e.g. ~200–300) and data coverage across time. Factors without enough data (e.g. illiquid bonds, bespoke swaps) cannot be modelled as continuous variables. These are designated NMRFs. Banks must then hold capital for NMRFs by assuming a stressed loss scenario (typically a 97.5% loss on those positions in a chosen stress period). This prevents arbitrage of risk factors simply by calling them non-modellable. In practice, NMRFs often force banks to charge for a large fraction of trading positions (especially in fixed income). Managing NMRFs is a major challenge: banks sometimes widen buckets or accept higher capital rather than model each factor. Only use IMA on factors that pass the eligibility test; treat others as NMRFs with separate capital. Labeling too many factors as “modellable” with insufficient data to reduce capital. **Modellable risk factor** — passes RFET (enough price observations); **Non-Modellable Risk Factor (NMRF)** — fails RFET and requires extra capital. **No delta.** The RFET and NMRF treatment are specified by Basel and applied universally in advanced jurisdictions.

title: SA vs IMA: banks' choice
one_screen: Many banks are opting for the Standardised Approach under FRTB because the Internal Models Approach entails onerous requirements.  Surveys show roughly 40% of current model users plan to switch to SA.
bodyText: Deploying IMA under FRTB is operationally complex. PLA failures and NMRF capital often make IMA yield higher capital than SA for certain desks. The extensive data, modeling and approval hurdles prompt many institutions to prefer SA (simpler formulaic approach) unless IMA provides a clear advantage. For example, an ICMA survey found ~40% of banks already using IMA intend to seek IMA approval under FRTB, while another ~40% plan to shift to SA. In other words, SA may become more common despite offering less risk sensitivity, due to practical considerations. Banks can choose SA or IMA at the desk level; they will compare resulting capital and compliance costs. Assuming that using internal models will automatically yield lower capital. In some cases, SA can produce lower capital if IMA requirements force heavy add-ons. **IMA (Internal Models)** — bank-specific models using ES, LH, etc; **SA (Standardised Approach)** — regulator-set sensitivities framework. **No delta.** Surveys on approach choice apply broadly; specifics of adoption vary by jurisdiction but the dilemma is universal.

title: Prudent valuation and XVAs
one_screen: Prudent valuation requires banks to apply Additional Valuation Adjustments (AVAs) to trading positions’ fair values, reflecting valuation uncertainty (bid-ask spreads, model error, etc.). These AVAs are deducted from capital to be conservative.
bodyText: Regulators mandate that fair-valued trading assets must be marked down conservatively. For example, the EU’s CRR/CRD rules (via RTS on prudent valuation) require AVAs to cover risks like market price uncertainty and model risk. Banks quantify AVAs (often at a 90% confidence level) for items such as bid-ask spreads, close-out costs, and other uncertainties. The total AVA reduces Tier-1 capital. Separately, XVAs (e.g. CVA for counterparty credit, FVA for funding) adjust valuation for trading derivatives. These are usually calculated under accounting standards or supervisory frameworks. While CVA (Counterparty Value Adjustment) was specifically addressed in Basel III/CRR2, other XVA components (DVA, FVA) reflect economic value adjustments. Overall, prudent valuation and XVA policies ensure the bank’s book reflect worst-case or “fiduciary” values, protecting capital. Always include regulatory valuation adjustments (AVAs) on marked-to-market positions to account for uncertainty. Relying solely on model or mid-market prices for capital without AVAs, understating risk. **Fair value** — market-based exit price; **Prudent value** — lower value after applying AVAs (90% CI). AVAs include factors like bid-ask and model risk. **No delta.** Prudent valuation standards (including AVA requirements) are embedded in CRR/CRD in EU and similarly in other advanced frameworks.

title: Valuation control and independent price verification
one_screen: Banks must have robust valuation controls: independent price verification (IPV) and hierarchical fair value procedures.  Instruments are categorized by input observability (Level 1,2,3), with Level 3 valuations (no market prices) subject to stringent review.
bodyText: A strong valuation control environment is vital. Banks establish independent valuation committees to review model inputs and outputs. **Independent Price Verification (IPV)** means having separate systems or personnel to compare book prices against external sources (vendors or brokers) daily. Significant discrepancies trigger investigation and adjustments. Regulators (via accounting standards IFRS13/ASC820 and risk rules) define a fair value hierarchy: - *Level 1:* quoted market prices in active markets (highest reliability). - *Level 2:* observable inputs (e.g. dealer quotes, similar instruments). - *Level 3:* unobservable inputs (derived from models). Level 3 instruments (illiquid or complex) carry the highest valuation uncertainty and often the largest AVAs (see MRK-19). Banks must document assumptions for Level 3 models, regularly backtest them against any transaction prices, and escalate issues. In essence, valuation models fall under model risk management (MRM) frameworks, requiring validation and governance. All significant mark-to-market positions must be independently priced or verified each day. Any Level 3 (non-observable) inputs require extensive model validation. Using stale or self-generated prices without challenge, especially for illiquid positions. **Independent Price Verification (IPV)** — reconciling book prices with third-party data; **Model output** — output of a valuation model (which may feed Level 3 valuation). **No delta.** These valuation controls and hierarchy concepts derive from accounting standards and are universally expected in sound practice.

title: Model risk in valuation models
one_screen: Valuation models themselves carry model risk.  Banks must manage model risk for pricing models just as they do for risk models (see MRM pack).  This means independent model validation, backtesting, and capital add-ons for model uncertainty.
bodyText: Any model that produces trade valuations (e.g. Black-Scholes for options, simulation for exotic rates) is subject to model risk. That risk arises from potential errors in model structure, parameters, or missing risk factors. For example, a swap valuation using a one-factor curve model may misprice when rates move non-parallel (model risk). Banks mitigate this through model validation teams, sensitivity analyses, and including AVAs for model risk (see MRK-19). Regulators expect firms to track model performance: for instance, comparing model values to actual trade P&L movements or to prices from alternative models/vendors. Persistent model deficiencies should be captured in governance (e.g. increased capital buffers or additional AVA). In summary, valuation model risk is a subset of overall model risk management (MRM), applying the same principles of validation, documentation and controls. Treat valuation models under the bank’s MRM governance: validate them periodically, and adjust capital or AVAs for significant model errors. Assuming a model is “correct” because it is industry-standard; ignoring its limitations in a stressed scenario. **Model risk** — errors from model inaccuracies; **Market risk** — losses from actual market moves. Valuation models can create market risk if mispriced. **No delta.** Model risk management requirements are consistent across jurisdictions (BCBS Principles for effective model risk management).

title: Jurisdiction: UK, EU, India, US FRTB implementation
one_screen: Jurisdictions vary on FRTB adoption. The UK will implement SA (Basel 3.1) from Jan 1, 2027 and delay IMA to Jan 1, 2028. The EU has postponed its FRTB to Jan 1, 2027. India’s banks currently use RBI’s older VaR or duration-based rules (e.g. 99% VaR at 15 days) and RBI has not adopted FRTB; IFRS 9 (Ind AS 109) is deferred for banks. In the US, FRTB has not been finalized: regulators published Basel III proposals (Dec 2021 and re-proposed Mar 2026), but advanced US banks still use the pre-FRTB market risk rule (99% VaR and stressed VaR).
bodyText: Track local regulatory effective dates for FRTB implementation by jurisdiction (UK 2027/2028, EU 2027, US pending, India Basel 2.5). Assuming FRTB rules apply globally on a single date; implementation timelines diverge significantly across UK, EU, US, and India. **FRTB (Basel 3.1)** — New global market risk capital standard (Sensitivities-Based SA and Desk-Level ES IMA). --- **Legacy Market Risk (Basel 2.5)** — Older VaR and Stressed VaR market risk framework still used in US and India. — Indian banks follow RBI market-risk norms (historically 99% VaR at 15 days with multiplier, or a standardized duration approach). RBI has deferred adoption of IFRS/IndAS 109 for banks, so credit provisions and market risk remain under RBI prudential rules. There is no FRTB implementation timeline from RBI; banks continue on Basel 2.5-style frameworks. — The PRA (FSMA) adopted Basel 3.1: the Standardized Approach takes effect 1 Jan 2027, but the Internal Models Approach (desk-based ES) is delayed until 1 Jan 2028. — CRR3 (Basel 3.1) implementation of the FRTB was deferred by delegated regulation: the FRTB own-funds requirements will apply from 1 Jan 2027, aligning with global delays. (Other Basel III output floor rules took effect 2025.) — US agencies have not implemented the final FRTB. In Dec 2021, Fed/OCC proposed new capital rules including market risk; they re-proposed in Mar 2026. No final rule date exists. Until then, US GSIBs with ≥$1bn trading assets calculate market risk capital under the 1996 rule (99% VaR and stressed VaR as per Basel II.5) and US banks do not have an FRTB-style requirement.

title: What is a Model
one_screen: A model is a quantitative system that processes input data using statistical, economic or financial theory to produce an output.  This definition determines which tools fall under model risk controls.  Not all decision-support tools are “models” in every regime – for example, U.S. guidance explicitly excludes simple spreadsheets or rule-based calculators from the model category, whereas UK and Indian frameworks use broader definitions that include any system with material impact on decisions.
bodyText: Bank regulators emphasize clear model definitions to set scope. For example, the U.S. Federal Reserve’s 2026 guidance defines a model as “a complex quantitative method… that applies statistical, economic, or financial theories to process input data,” and explicitly excludes “simple arithmetic calculations, such as those found within spreadsheets, as well as deterministic rule-based processes”. In contrast, the UK PRA’s supervisory statement (SS1/23) defines a model as “a quantitative method, system or approach that applies statistical, economic, financial or mathematical theories… to process input data into output”. India’s draft model-risk guidance similarly defines a model very broadly to include algorithms, analytics, decision rules, and even spreadsheets if they materially affect decisions. A “spreadsheet-based calculator” might be treated as a basic tool by itself, but if it feeds lending rates or risk scores that drive decisions, RBI says it must be treated as a model. This definitional boundary matters because it determines oversight: what must be inventoried, validated, and controlled. For instance, a bank might use a simple Excel pricing sheet. Under Fed/OCC rules, that might not be a “model” at all, but under PRA or RBI rules it could be classified as a model if it affects credit pricing. Mis-classifying a tool as “not a model” can leave significant risk unmanaged. Conversely, over-classifying every trivial calculation as a model can waste effort. In practice, firms adopt the regulator’s definition in their policies so that model inventories and risk frameworks are consistent across lines of business. +-----------------+ | Model | +-----------------+ | - Uses theory | | - Processes data| | - Predicts outcome | +-----------------+ /_\ | v +---------------------+ | Decision impact | | (e.g. pricing, | | credit approval) | +---------------------+ A “model” always applies a formal quantitative method (with assumptions) to data. Simple tools with no underlying statistical/economic theory are generally not models under regulatory definitions. Treating any tool in Excel as outside model risk. For example, **mistakenly ignoring a spreadsheet that sets loan pricing** because “it’s just a calculator” – when that tool uses inputs and formulas that affect lending decisions. **Spreadsheet/Calculator** — an arithmetic, rule‐based tool (no statistical theory). Often excluded as a “model” in U.S. regs. --- **Statistical Model** — a quantitative method using statistical/economic assumptions to produce predictions. It may be developed in code or a spreadsheet, and is subject to model validation. — RBI’s draft MRM guidance defines a model broadly as any system (including AI/ML) using theoretical or statistical techniques to process inputs into outputs, **including** algorithms, analytics or even decision-rule spreadsheets that materially affect decisions. — The PRA expects firms to define models as “quantitative methods… applying statistical, economic, financial or mathematical theories… to process input data into output”. (Deterministic rules with material impact may still be subject to MRM controls.) — The interagency guidance uses a narrower definition: a “complex quantitative method” that applies statistical/economic theory, **excluding** simple spreadsheets or rule-based tools. (Those tools still need controls, but they aren’t labeled “models” under SR 26-2.) — EBA/ECB internal-model frameworks for IRB capital imply a similar broad notion (any statistical or econometric method), but no single EU-wide MRM definition. In practice, EU regulators follow Basel principles: any quantitative risk model (credit/market/counterparty) must meet validation requirements.

title: Model Risk versus Other Risks
one_screen: Model risk is the potential for adverse outcomes from using a model (e.g. losses or bad decisions), not a type of financial risk like credit or market risk.  It arises from model errors and misuses.  By contrast, credit risk refers to borrower default, and market risk to price moves.  Model risk can exist even if credit and market risk are unchanged.
bodyText: Model risk is fundamentally different from credit or market risk. Model risk refers to losses or misstatements resulting from flaws in the model itself – such as bad data, wrong assumptions, coding bugs or misuse – rather than from the underlying exposures. As the Fed guidance explains, “model risk… can lead to financial loss, errors in financial statements and reporting, and flawed financial and risk management decisions”. In other words, even if a loan portfolio’s creditworthiness is unchanged, faulty credit-risk models can cause bad credit decisions (model risk). By contrast, credit risk is the inherent risk of borrower default or LGD, and market risk is the risk of losses from market movements. Those are separate dimensions: a portfolio with zero credit risk still has model risk if its models are wrong. Because models often measure credit or market risk, practitioners sometimes conflate them. For example, one might say “our credit risk is low,” when in fact the models estimating that risk may be unreliable (model risk). Regulators emphasize treating model risk as a distinct discipline.
