For instance, RBI’s 2024 model-risk principles note that models “are based on assumptions which may not manifest in envisaged ways” and that this “potentially exposes REs to model risk, which has implications on prudential aspects of credit risk management”. In practice, model risk is managed under operational risk/Pillar 2 frameworks or specific model-risk policies, even though it affects credit and market outcomes. +-----------------+ | Loan defaults |--+ +-----------------+ | v +-------------------------+ | Credit Risk Model | | (predicts defaults) | +-------------------------+ | v +-------------------------+ | Wrong assumptions/ | | errors cause bad | | lending decisions | +-------------------------+ Model risk always exists whenever models are used. It must be managed independently of, though it may interact with, other risks like credit or market risk. Treating model errors as “just credit risk.” For example, **believing that a high loss rate is purely credit risk** rather than checking if the credit model itself was faulty. **Model risk** — risk from the use of a flawed model (inaccurate outputs). --- **Credit risk** — risk of loss due to borrower default. They get mixed up because credit models produce credit-risk estimates, but a bad estimate is model risk, not a new kind of credit risk. **No delta.** All regulatory regimes distinguish model risk as the risk of using an incorrect or misapplied model, separate from the underlying credit or market risk the model may measure. (For example, RBI calls out “model risk… which has implications on… credit risk management”; PRA SS1/23 likewise treats MRM as its own discipline.)

title: Sources of Model Risk
one_screen: Model risk arises from many causes: bad input data, flawed methodology or assumptions, coding/implementation errors, and model misuse or misinterpretation.  Any part of a model’s lifecycle can introduce risk – for example, if training data are biased, if key variables are omitted, or if the model is used in a way the developers didn’t intend.
bodyText: Any step in building or using a model can introduce errors (model risk). Common sources include: - **Data issues:** Erroneous, incomplete, outdated or biased inputs. For instance, using stale or unrepresentative data can skew predictions. (If the data have systemic bias, an AI model may perpetuate that bias.) - **Assumption or parameter errors:** Omitting a key variable, using unreasonable assumptions, or calibrating parameters inappropriately. A housing-price model ignoring new market trends might be severely off. Likewise, statistical models rely on assumptions (e.g. linearity, independence) that may not hold. If those are wrong, the model fails. . - **Methodology or design flaws:** Choosing an inappropriate model form or algorithm for the problem. For example, using a linear model for highly nonlinear data can produce poor results. Complex ML methods can themselves be misconfigured (e.g. overfit, wrong architecture). - **Implementation errors:** Programming bugs, calculation mistakes, or software issues. A mis-indexed data array in code could shift inputs, or a wrong formula may be used. Even “human error” in a spreadsheet (e.g. a wrong cell reference) can create huge errors (the famous $6B JPMorgan error was a spreadsheet bug).. - **Usage and interpretation:** Applying a model outside its intended scope, or misunderstanding its output. For instance, using a model built for retail loans to price corporate loans, or misinterpreting probabilities as certainties. Practitioner guides list these clearly. For example, IBM notes that model risk “can stem from various causes: Data (e.g. bias or inaccuracy); Assumptions (unrealistic or omitted variables); Methodology (inherent errors in chosen techniques); Implementation (coding or calculation errors); Interpretation (misreading results); and Usage (using a model inappropriately)”. Regulators expect firms to identify such sources in their risk frameworks. The RBI’s draft guidance on credit models explicitly requires validation to include reviewing data accuracy and underlying assumptions. In practice, a sound validation process scrutinizes each of these sources: checking data quality, testing assumptions, reviewing code, and assessing model use in business processes. Common Sources of Model Risk: +---------------+ +------------------------+ +------------------+ | Data issues | | Flawed methodology/ | | Implementation | | (e.g. bias, | | assumptions (e.g. wrong | | errors (bugs, | | missing values)|--| variables, unrealistic |--| formula mistakes)| +---------------+ | assumptions) | +------------------+ +------------------------+ \ v +--------------------+ | Model misuse or | | misinterpretation | | (outside scope) | +--------------------+ Model risk can come from anywhere in the model’s development or use: data, design, code, or deployment. Every model must be checked end-to-end for these sources of error. Focusing only on one source of risk. For example, **checking a model’s math but ignoring biased input data**. All sources (data, assumptions, code, usage) must be considered. **Coding error** — a bug or mistake in the model’s implementation (e.g. wrong formula or mis-indexing data). --- **Model assumption** — a conceptual choice about how the model works (e.g. assuming linearity). These both cause wrong output but arise in different ways. (Confusing them can lead one to fix code when the real issue is a bad assumption.) **No delta.** The types of model risk sources are similar across jurisdictions. Regulators everywhere expect institutions to address data quality, logical assumptions, technical implementation and model usage in their validation and controls.

title: Deterministic Tools versus Models
one_screen: Regulators distinguish “models” from simpler rule-based tools.  A deterministic tool (e.g. a spreadsheet calculator or rules engine with fixed logic) is not considered a model if it has no underlying statistical or theoretical basis.  U.S. guidance explicitly excludes pure arithmetic spreadsheets from the model definition.  However, if such tools have “material bearing on decisions,” firms often still apply model risk controls to them.
bodyText: In practice, there is a boundary between quantitative models and simpler tools. U.S. SR 26-2 says it excludes “simple arithmetic calculations, such as those found within spreadsheets, as well as deterministic rule-based processes” from the definition of a model. This means a spreadsheet that just adds up values or applies fixed formulas (with no statistical algorithm) is not a “model” under Fed/OCC guidance. By contrast, the UK PRA says that even deterministic methods may need controls if they are complex and impact decisions. RBI’s draft guidance goes further: it says any tool (including decision rules in software) that has a material impact on decision-making should be treated as a model. (For example, a loan-pricing spreadsheet might be just a “basic tool,” but if it factors in risk-adjusted spreads to set rates, RBI says it must be treated as a model.) The key distinction is whether the method relies on a statistical/economic theory or not. **If there is no statistical model underlying it, it is formally a “tool,”** but regulators still expect robust controls. The PRA advises firms to document and control deterministic rules just as they would a model. In short, ***deterministic tools*** are fixed-logic processes (e.g. credit-policy rules coded into a system) whereas ***statistical models*** use probabilistic or econometric methods. Firms should not ignore the risk of a rule-based tool just because it’s not labeled a model. In many cases, best practice is to apply parts of the model risk framework (validation, review) to critical tools. +----------------------+ | Model | +----------+-----------+ | v +----------------------+ |Statistical method | |(theory-driven) | +----------------------+ | v +----------------------+ | Output affecting | | decisions (scores, | | rates, etc.) | +----------------------+ ^ | +----------+-----------+ | Tool (non-model) | +----------------------+ | - Fixed rules/formula| | - No underlying stat | +----------------------+ Tools with complex business impact should be governed even if not classified as “models.” Always clarify in policy which calculations are covered by MRM. Assuming “not a model = no risk.” For example, ignoring validation of a spreadsheet pricing tool because it’s deemed a “non-model.” (In reality, a faulty spreadsheet can cause major errors.) **Deterministic tool** — a fixed‐logic calculator or rules engine (no statistical basis). It may be excluded from the model definition but still needs oversight. --- **Statistical model** — uses statistical/economic theory and assumptions to produce predictions (subject to full MRM). They differ: one is theory-driven (model), the other is rule-based (tool). — RBI’s draft treats even deterministic tools as models if they impact decisions. E.g., a spreadsheet deciding loan rates is a model if it drives pricing. — PRA excludes simple calculators from “model” definition but says complex decision rules may still be subject to MRM controls. — SR 26-2 explicitly **excludes** basic spreadsheets or rule-based software from the model definition, although sound governance requires controls on high-impact tools. — Like the UK, EU supervisors focus on any business-critical method; a simple tool might not be called a model, but it must be validated if it functions like one. (ECB’s internal-model guide treats any algorithm with “material impact” similarly.)

title: Model Inventory and Materiality Tiering
one_screen: Firms must catalogue all models in an inventory and classify them by materiality or “tier.”  This ensures that validation and controls are focused on the most critical models.  Materiality (e.g. impact on capital or decisions) typically determines whether a model is High-, Medium- or Low-tier. Regulators explicitly require a complete model inventory and risk-based tiering.
bodyText: A comprehensive model inventory is a foundation of MRM. Regulators expect banks to maintain a **complete, firm-wide list of all models** – those in use, in development, or even recently retired – with key attributes (purpose, owner, validation status, etc.). The purpose is to “enable firms to identify the sources of model risk” and prioritize controls. RBI’s credit-model circular similarly mandates that banks “maintain a Model Inventory of approved models, insourced or outsourced, with critical information on it”. In practice, each line of business may track its own models, but the firm must compile a consolidated list for oversight and reporting. Once inventoried, models are usually tiered by risk. Regulators say this tiering should be **risk-based**, reflecting each model’s materiality. Factors include financial exposure (e.g. how much money or capital depends on the model) and model purpose (e.g. credit approval vs internal analysis). For example, the Fed guidance introduces a “materiality-based framework” where “model purpose and model exposure” determine materiality. UK SS1/23 Principle 1 requires risk-based tiering so that “validation activities and other risk controls” focus on critical models. RBI draft also requires risk-tiering and annual review of tier levels. A typical approach is to label models Tier 1 (most critical), Tier 2, Tier 3, etc. High-tier models trigger the strictest governance (e.g. board approvals, more frequent reviews), while lower-tier models have scaled-back oversight. +---------------+ | Model Tiers | +-------+-------+ | Tier 1 (High) | +-------+-------+ | Tier 2 (Med) | +-------+-------+ | Tier 3 (Low) | +---------------+ Tiering helps allocate resources. For instance, a retail-credit scorecard impacting $1B loans (Tier 1) would get priority validation and senior oversight. A small-scope risk indicator (Tier 3) might be reviewed less often. Regardless, regulators expect that **no model is left untracked**. The PRA says even decommissioned models should remain in the inventory for historical lessons. Maintain an up-to-date model inventory and use a risk-tiering scheme. This is non-negotiable in MRM policies. Thinking only big regulatory models matter. Banks often miss models used for analytics or financial reporting that still drive decisions. The rule is: **all** models must be inventoried, not just credit/market capital models. **Model inventory** — the list of all models, with details (owner, status, etc.). --- **Asset inventory** — list of financial assets (loans, etc.). They serve different purposes: one tracks models, the other tracks financial exposures. — RBI’s 2024/2026 guidelines require a model inventory of all credit models (including third-party), with board oversight. Tiering by risk is required by draft Guidance (RBI). — PRA SS1/23 Principle 1 mandates a formal model inventory and risk-based tiering to focus validation on material models. — The April 2026 guidance emphasizes a “materiality-based” approach: firms should define material models by purpose and exposure. It does not prescribe fixed tiers, but many banks adopt a tiering scheme to implement the risk-based approach. — EBA/ECB expect banks to inventory all models used for IRB capital or risk management and to apply risk-based oversight. ECB’s internal models guide similarly uses materiality concepts. (No fundamental conflict with other jurisdictions on this point.)

title: Model Lifecycle
one_screen: A model’s lifecycle consists of development, independent validation, approval, deployment/use, ongoing monitoring, updates (recalibration/redevelopment), and eventually retirement.  Each stage has specific risk controls.  Regulators expect firms to manage model risk across the entire lifecycle, not just at inception.
bodyText: Banks treat models much like products: from conception to retirement. The high-level stages are: **Development → Validation → Approval → Deployment/Use → Monitoring & Maintenance → Change/Update → Retirement**. In development, the model’s objectives, data, methodology and documentation are created. Before any model can be used in decisions, it must be **validated** by an independent reviewer (second line) to check design and accuracy (see MRM-08). Then the model must be formally **approved** by management or a governance committee (see MRM-09). Once deployed, the model is used in real operations. Thereafter, the bank must **monitor** model performance and environment continuously (backtesting, stability checks, etc.). If model performance drifts or business needs change, the model is **updated** by recalibrating parameters or redeveloping. Finally, a model may be **retired (decommissioned)** when no longer needed or when replaced by a better model. This end-to-end view is emphasized by regulators. The 2026 interagency guidance and OCC bulletin explicitly outline these stages in their high-level framework, covering development, validation, governance, and monitoring. RBI’s draft guidance similarly lists selection/development, validation, approval, deployment, ongoing oversight, change management, and decommissioning as key lifecycle elements. The Fed/OCC calls for robust controls “throughout the model lifecycle” (implicitly in each phase). Having such a lifecycle framework helps ensure nothing is skipped. For example, a model should never be used before validation and approval; nor should monitoring cease once the model is live. +--------------+ +--------------+ +----------+ +--------------+ | Development | --> | Validation | --> | Approval | --> | Deployment/ | | (purpose, | | (independent | | (senior | | Use | | data, method)| | review) | | sign-off) | | | +--------------+ +--------------+ +----------+ +--------------+ | | v | +-------------+ | Monitoring &| | Maintenance | +-------------+ | v +-------------+ | Updates/ | | Recalibration | +-------------+ | v +-------------+ | Retirement | +-------------+ Governments require oversight at every stage: development, validation, approval, deployment, monitoring, changes, and retirement. Skipping any step undermines model safety. Using a model as soon as it’s built, before validation or formal approval. Validation must precede use, and monitoring must continue until retirement. **Recalibration** — adjusting model parameters to current data. --- **Redevelopment** — building a new model from scratch. Both involve change, but recalibration tweaks an existing model; redevelopment replaces it entirely. **No delta.** All major frameworks envision the same lifecycle stages. The specific terminologies may differ (e.g. RBI separates “selection” and “development”), but all regimes require development, independent validation, governance sign-off, deployment, monitoring, updates, and decommissioning of models.

title: Model Development
one_screen: During development, the model’s purpose, data, and method are defined and documented.  Firms must clearly state the model’s objectives, select appropriate data and variables, choose a methodology suited to the problem, and record all assumptions and design choices.  Good documentation ensures transparency for later review.
bodyText: Model development starts with **problem definition**: what decision the model will support. For example, a credit model might predict default probability for new loan applications. The developer then assembles relevant data. Input data should be adequate and of high quality (see MRM-13). Next is choosing or building the mathematical/statistical method (e.g. logistic regression, decision tree, machine learning). The methodology must fit the purpose (e.g. lifetime PD modeling requires a survival model, not simple linear regression). All key **assumptions** and variables must be explicitly specified. Regulators stress clear objectives and documentation. RBI’s credit model principles, for instance, require “the objectives of the model” to be clearly defined, and that “inputs and assumptions… ensure adequate robustness”. RBI also mandates detailed documentation including sensitivity of outputs to assumptions. Likewise, firms should document model logic, training process, and expected limitations. This documentation is crucial for later validation and audit. PRA Principle 3 expects firms to have development standards and documentation (the PRA SS notes that firms should have model development and use governed under policies, with documentation). Practically, development often involves statistical analysis and iterative testing. Developers calibrate parameters on historical data, check intuitive plausibility (face validity), and may back-test on hold-out data before finalizing the model. The key is to embed sound practice: clear target outcomes, robust data pipelines, explainable methodology, and retrievable code/documents. Once development is done, no use is allowed until the model passes independent validation. A model must have a defined use case, appropriate data, and complete documentation from the start. Never proceed to validation or use without thorough development records. Creating a “black box” with no written spec. Skipping documentation or ignoring model purpose can lead to validation failure. (For example, training a model without stating its decision criteria or target population leaves validation teams clueless.) **Model purpose** — the business decision or metric the model is meant to support (e.g. predicting 1-year PD). --- **Model exposure** — the financial amount or scope to which the model applies. They are different: purpose is “what” the model does; exposure is “how big” its impact is. **No delta.** Development standards are similar worldwide. RBI’s guidance explicitly lists development principles (clear objectives, robust inputs, documentation). PRA and Fed guidance likewise stress that models should be developed in line with policy and in-house standards, though neither prescribes a specific development process beyond these principles.

title: Independent Model Validation
one_screen: Independent validation is a formal review of a model by someone outside the development team.  It checks data, assumptions, methodology, and output accuracy.  True independence (no conflicts with the model developer) is required to ensure objectivity.
bodyText: Model validation is a crucial second-line control. Its purpose is to give management confidence that the model is “fit for purpose.” Validation should start by reviewing the model’s design (the conceptual soundness) and then testing performance. Typical steps include checking whether inputs meet quality standards, verifying calculations, re-running parts of the model in a fresh environment (code review/backtest), and assessing outputs against outcomes. The validator also reviews documentation and ensures compliance with policy. **Independence is key.** The reviewer must not be the same person (or team) who built the model. Regulators insist on unbiased, competent validators. For example, the U.S. Revised Guidance says effective challenge should be done by individuals “with sufficient independence to maintain objectivity”. RBI requires each model be validated by a process “independent of model development”. The validator typically reports to senior management or a separate risk committee. Internal audit (third line) does not perform the day-to-day validation but will later audit the process. Validation should occur before a model goes live and then periodically (e.g. annually or when triggered by events). The Fed/OCC guidance now recommends a risk-based frequency rather than a fixed schedule. RBI’s draft explicitly says each model must be validated before deployment and after any material change or annually. In practice, validators produce a formal report summarizing findings and recommendations. If issues are found, the model must be remediated before use. Independent validation is non-negotiable: an unvalidated model should never enter production. The model validator must be independent of development (a separate person or team) and must rigorously test the model’s integrity before use. Letting the developer self-validate. This destroys objectivity. An independent validator is required by design, not merely someone “reviewing for mistakes.” **Independent validation** — a thorough check of the model by a second line (model risk or quant team). --- **Internal audit** — a separate (third line) review of the framework/process, not a substitute for the validation itself. — RBI requires independent vetting/validation of each model before deployment and at least annually. All models (internal or third-party) must be independently validated. — PRA SS1/23 Principle 4 mandates ongoing, independent and effective challenge of every model. The SS explicitly calls for a validation process separate from development. — SR 26-2 emphasizes objectivity but does not dictate a specific validator role; it simply requires “effective challenge by individuals with sufficient independence”. It allows flexibility in how firms organize independence (e.g. separate team or robust governance). — EBA and ECB Pillar 2 frameworks require internal model validation by an independent function. ECB’s internal-model guide and the EBA IRB Validation Handbook both assume separate validator teams. The concept of independent review is universal.

title: Approval, Governance, and Use
one_screen: Before a validated model can be used, it must be formally approved by senior management or the board (or a delegated committee).  The model’s intended use must align with business needs and policy.  Governance roles (board oversight, risk committees, internal audit) apply: boards must approve MRM policies and receive reports on model issues.
bodyText: Model approval is the gate after validation. Typically, a model is presented to a **model governance committee** or **senior management** (often the Board’s Risk Management Committee) with documentation and validation results. They evaluate whether the model is sound and fit for its intended use. Only then is it authorized for production use. Regulators historically required the board or its delegate to approve model risk policies and significant models. For example, RBI’s circular mandates that new credit models (and material changes) be approved by the bank’s Risk Management Committee of the Board. PRA SS1/23 requires that firms “allocate responsibility” for model governance to senior management, with clear accountability for model policies (principles) – implying top-level sign-off. Once approved, **use test** considerations apply: regulators in risk frameworks often require that the model actually be used in day-to-day decisions. A common regulatory expectation (especially in IRB models) is that models cannot just exist on paper – they must be integrated into decision processes. (Though not explicitly in SS1/23 or SR 26-2, “use test” is a familiar concept from Basel/IRB validation.) Practically, firms should document how a model’s output is used operationally (e.g. credit officers follow the scorecard outputs). Ongoing governance ties in here. The Board is responsible for overall MRM framework oversight and must be informed of material model issues. Regulators expect internal audit (third line) to review the MRM framework and report any findings. For example, the U.S. original guidance stated that “[f]indings from internal audit related to models should be…reported to the board”. Model risk appetite – the firm’s tolerance for model-related errors – should also be approved at the board level. No model may enter production without final sign-off by the appropriate governance authority (Board or delegated committee). The model’s use must match its approved scope. Using a model before board approval or outside its intended use. For example, **rolling out a credit-scoring model without documented Board approval and policies** violates governance norms. **Model approval** — formal authorization by management/board to use a model. --- **Model validation** — the technical check of model accuracy. Approval is a governance step *after* validation; some people mistake a successful validation report for “approval,” but the board’s sign-off is a separate requirement. — RBI’s guidance says deployment (and any changes) of credit models requires prior approval by the Board or its Risk Committee. The Board must also approve the MRM framework and model risk appetite, and internal audit findings must go to the Board. — PRA SS1/23 expects firms to assign overall MRM responsibility to senior management (SMFs) and for boards to oversee MRM policies. High-tier models must be signed off by senior committees. Internal audit is the third line (firm should ensure audit reviews MRM). — SR 26-2 does not prescribe exact boards’ actions, but emphasizes clear roles and accountability in MRM. The prior SR 11-7 (and S&C memo) note that findings from audit should be reported to the board, and that boards should approve MRM policies. — ECB guidance on internal models similarly requires board or management body sign-off of key models and policies (e.g. in IRB models board approval of rating systems). The three-lines framework is expected (first line model owner, second line risk group, third line audit).

title: Ongoing Monitoring and Performance
one_screen: After a model is in use, the firm must continuously monitor its performance and environment.  This includes tracking key metrics (stability indexes, backtests, outcomes) and ensuring the model remains accurate.  Oversight bodies should set thresholds for action and require periodic performance reports, with escalations if issues are detected.
bodyText: Models are dynamic; their performance can drift over time as data or conditions change. Banks therefore establish an **ongoing monitoring program**. This typically involves: - **Performance tracking:** comparing model predictions to actual results (backtesting). For example, periodically compare predicted default rates to realized defaults. - **Data drift checks:** computing stability metrics (PSI/CSI) on input variables or score distributions (see MRM-16). Significant shifts in data distributions may signal model drift. - **Thresholds:** setting quantitative thresholds (e.g. maximum allowable PSI) that, if exceeded, trigger investigation or revalidation. Common practice is PSI<0.10 (little change), 0.10–0.25 moderate, >0.25 significant. - **Periodic reviews:** formal re-validation cycles or ad-hoc reviews when performance degrades. Regulators discourage fixed cadences; instead, use a risk-based approach to determine review frequency. Regulators support strong monitoring. PRA SS1/23 Principle 5 expects firms to have “model risk mitigants” including performance monitoring and expert overrides. The PRA details standards for monitoring model performance (criteria, thresholds, back-testing). RBI’s draft also requires “ongoing performance testing using backward-looking and forward-looking approaches”. In the US, SR 26-2 lists monitoring as a governance activity (OCC noted monitoring and outcome analysis as sound practice in vendor models). Senior management should review model performance at least annually or more often for top-tier models. Reports summarizing key metrics and any breaches of thresholds should be provided to risk committees. Any persistent performance shortfall must be remediated (perhaps via recalibration or new model). Always monitor a model in production. A model’s validity is not one-time; it requires continuous checking. Assuming a validated model will stay valid forever. For example, **ignoring a rising PSI that indicates data shift**, which could make the model obsolete. **Monitoring** — ongoing checks of model output/data (e.g. backtests, stability indices). --- **Validation** — formal, periodic re-assessment of the whole model. They are related but different stages. Monitoring is continuous; validation is periodic/developer review (see MRM-08). — RBI’s draft requires continuous oversight. It even calls for backward/forward performance testing and benchmarking in monitoring. Excessive model risk must be reported to the Board. — The PRA expects firms to monitor model performance and use expert judgment or overrides as needed (SS1/23 Principle 5). Monitoring standards should include criteria and thresholds. — Fed/OCC guidance includes “ongoing monitoring and outcome analysis” as key practices (especially for vendor models). The revised guidance emphasizes risk-based monitoring but is principles-based. — ECB supervisors require regular monitoring of internal models and use of backtesting (as in TRIM/ICAAP reviews). EBA Pillar 2 practices include ongoing performance tracking. 0.25 indicate?" a="A “significant change” in the data distribution, requiring investigation." />

title: Change Management and Recalibration
one_screen: If a model’s performance deteriorates or business conditions change, banks must update the model.  This can be done by **recalibration** (adjusting parameters) or full **redevelopment** (building a new model).  Any changes must follow the same validation and approval process as the original model.
bodyText: Models rarely remain static. Firms implement a formal change-management process. When should a change occur? Common triggers include: backtest failures, PSI breaches, new regulatory requirements, or material shifts in portfolio mix. The key is to identify whether the existing model can be fixed by recalibration or needs replacement: - **Recalibration** means re-estimating the model’s parameters (e.g. refitting a regression with new data) or updating assumptions. It is appropriate when the model form is still valid but its coefficients are stale (e.g. updating PD estimates for current economic conditions). - **Redevelopment** means constructing a new model (possibly using different variables or methodology). This is needed if the old model’s structure is fundamentally wrong or its performance cannot be recovered by tweaking. Regulators expect any material change to undergo re-validation. RBI’s draft guidance explicitly states that any amendments (due to material events) trigger a new validation “before deployment” and at least annually. The PRA also requires that changes follow the firm’s defined governance. The PRA’s standards (see [52]) mention that firms should have clear processes to determine when recalibration vs redevelopment is needed (threshold breaches, root cause analysis). For major changes, the updated model must be re-submitted for independent validation and re-approval. The Fed/OCC guidance no longer mandates fixed review intervals (“no required cadence”), but strongly advocates a risk-based approach: high-risk models may need more frequent updates. In summary, change management is part of the lifecycle: monitor, then decide. Recalibrations are typically quicker fixes, while redevelopments are full projects. Firms must document the rationale for either choice and ensure that the updated model is validated as if new. Every material model change is subject to the same controls as a new model (validation, approval). No tweaks in production without oversight. “Band-aiding” a flawed model without validation. For example, **adjusting a model’s output by adding a fudge factor** to pass performance tests, but not re-validating the underlying logic. **Recalibration** — updating an existing model’s parameters. --- **Redevelopment** — creating a new model (new form or variables). Both are “model change,” but recalibration tweaks the old model, while redevelopment replaces it. — RBI requires validating every amended model; specifically “before deployment” for changes and at least annual reviews. — PRA SS1/23’s MRM framework demands clear procedures for model change (Principle 2 mentions managing “model change, including clear roles for approval”). In practice, firms set criteria based on risk tier and triggers. — The new guidance endorses risk-based timing. It replaced old fixed schedules with a principle that firms should determine frequency and scope of review by materiality. (No formal calibration interval is mandated.) — Internal models under ECB supervision must be recalibrated or redeveloped at least annually and whenever significant changes occur. The ECB’s internal-model guide (and CRR regulations) require model updates to be approved by supervisors and re-validated.

title: Conceptual Soundness and Data Quality
one_screen: **Conceptual soundness** ensures the model’s design and assumptions are valid for its purpose.  Validators check that the model structure (type, variables, functional form) is appropriate.  **Data quality** ensures inputs are accurate and representative.  Validations review data sourcing, completeness, and relevance.  Both steps catch errors before performance testing.
bodyText: In practice, conceptual review and data review are key initial steps in validation. A **conceptual soundness review** looks at the model’s logic: does the methodology fit the problem? Are the right variables included? Are assumptions (e.g. linearity, stability) realistic? For example, a default-probability model would fail conceptual validation if it omitted a key economic variable or used an inappropriate distribution. The review also ensures that the model’s objectives and boundaries are clear. This step guards against fundamental flaws that no amount of testing can fix. Immediately after, **data quality checks** are done. Validators verify that the data used in development accurately reflect the intended population. They check for errors (typos, duplicate records), missing or inconsistent values, and sample bias. For instance, if a credit scoring model was trained on a poor-quality dataset, its predictions will be off. RBI’s guidance explicitly requires validation to “verify the accuracy of data used in the model and reliability of data sources”. This means confirming data fields make sense (e.g. no negative loan amounts) and ensuring no systematic distortions. Validators also ensure that development data cover a representative range of situations; if not, they may recommend additional adjustments or overlays. Together, conceptual and data reviews set the stage for performance testing. A model with sound concept but bad data will still fail, and vice versa. By treating both rigorously, firms ensure that models are fundamentally sensible before examining metrics like AUC or H-L. Always start validation by scrutinizing the model’s design and data. No model should proceed if either the conceptual framework or the input data is suspect. Skipping data checks because “it’s just the same raw inputs.” Even minor data errors (wrong scale, outdated values) can corrupt outputs. Likewise, not questioning assumptions leads to blind faith in a wrong model. **Data bias** — systematic error in inputs (e.g. non-representative sample). --- **Model misspecification** — a flaw in the model’s form or assumptions. They both hurt model results, but one is in the data, the other in the model logic. — RBI validation guidance explicitly includes “verification of data accuracy and reliability of sources”, and checking assumptions. — PRA expects models to use accurate, reliable data and correctly specified methods (explicit guidance on development and validation covers data quality). — SR 26-2 lists data and methodology review as core validation steps. (The OCC press release highlights ongoing monitoring of vendor model data quality.) — EBA/ECB Pillar 2 requires robust data management for internal models. ECB’s validation handbook also focuses on data completeness and consistency.

title: Discrimination Metrics (AUC, Gini, KS)
one_screen: Discrimination measures how well a model ranks outcomes.  Common metrics are **ROC-AUC** (area under the receiver operating curve), **Gini coefficient** and **KS statistic**.  AUC (0.5–1) and Gini (0–1) quantify the model’s overall ranking power, while KS is the maximum difference between cumulative distributions of outcomes.  Higher values mean better separation of groups (e.g. defaulters vs non-defaulters).
bodyText: In credit models (and many risk models), validators assess ranking performance. The ROC curve plots true positive rate vs false positive rate; the area under that curve (AUC) is a popular measure (1.0 = perfect, 0.5 = random). The **Gini** index is closely related: Gini = 2*AUC–1 (so Gini ranges 0–1). For example, a Gini of 0.6 corresponds to AUC 0.8. These metrics summarize the model’s ability to order cases by risk. The **KS statistic** is another measure – it finds the point where the difference between the cumulative default vs non-default curves is greatest; a larger KS indicates better lift. However, none of these metrics tell the whole story. They only measure discrimination (ranking), not calibration. A model might have high AUC yet systematically under- or over-predict probabilities. Therefore, regulators expect both discrimination and calibration checks in validation. Typical thresholds vary by context, but as a rule of thumb (from industry practice): an AUC of 0.7–0.8 is moderate, >0.8 is strong. (Regulators do not set fixed benchmarks but may question models with unusually low discrimination.) Discrimination metrics must be reported for every predictive model. High discrimination is necessary but not sufficient for model quality. Focusing only on one metric. For instance, a model with high AUC but very poor calibration can still misprice risk. Always assess multiple performance aspects. **AUC (Area Under the ROC)** — overall probability that the model ranks a randomly chosen positive higher than a negative. --- **Gini coefficient** — derived from AUC (Gini=2*AUC–1). They are different scales of the same information (Gini ~ 2×AUC minus 1), so they often get used interchangeably. **No delta.** Discrimination metrics are standard in all regimes. Regulators (PRA, Fed, RBI, ECB) expect banks to use them in validating predictive models (especially PD/LGD models).

title: Calibration and Goodness-of-Fit
one_screen: Calibration measures how well predicted probabilities match observed outcomes.  A common tool is the Hosmer–Lemeshow (H-L) test: it groups data (e.g. deciles) and compares predicted vs actual frequencies using a chi-square statistic.  Good calibration means predicted and actual rates align.  However, large sample sizes can cause H-L to reject even small, practically unimportant differences.  Validation should also include graphical plots of predicted vs actual rates as a sanity check.
bodyText: Calibration is distinct from discrimination. For example, two models with the same AUC could have different calibration. In logistic regression models, analysts often use the Hosmer–Lemeshow test to quantify calibration. If the H-L p-value is high, the model is said to fit well; a low p-value suggests poor fit. But practitioners caution that with large test samples, the H-L test is too sensitive: trivial misalignments will become “statistically significant.” In other words, a very large dataset may make almost any model fail H-L even if calibration is acceptable in business terms. Therefore, one should inspect calibration plots (e.g. predicted vs actual by bucket) alongside or instead of relying solely on H-L statistics. Banks typically expect models to be reasonably well-calibrated. For example, EBA Pillar 2 guidance on IRB models requires checking that observed default rates closely match predicted PDs. If not, the model may need adjustment (calibration). If H-L rejects a model, analysts should judge if the deviation is economically material. In summary, calibration assessment involves statistical tests and also human judgement on the materiality of any miscalibration. Always check calibration in addition to discrimination. A model that ranks well (high AUC) but systematically underestimates risk can still be dangerous. Blindly trusting p-values in large samples. A trivial discrepancy with millions of observations can yield a significant H-L test, leading to overreaction. Instead, focus on practical significance (e.g. a small percentage point error in probabilities is often tolerable). **Calibration (Goodness-of-fit)** — how closely the model’s predicted probabilities match actual outcomes (tested by H-L, calibration plots). --- **Discrimination (AUC/Gini)** — how well the model orders outcomes (tested by AUC/KS). They address different qualities. A model can discriminate well but still be mis-calibrated. **No delta.** Calibration is universally required. Both PRA and Fed expect models to be well-calibrated for their intended use. RBI’s draft and IFRS9 guidance (for applicable NBFCs) also emphasize aligned predicted/actual losses.

title: Stability Metrics (PSI and CSI)
one_screen: Population Stability Index (PSI) and Characteristic Stability Index (CSI) measure changes in distributions over time.  PSI compares a variable’s or model-score distribution between the development period and current period.  CSI is similar but often used for categorical variables (e.g. rating grades).  In credit risk, PSI/CSI thresholds (e.g. >0.25) are used as a rule-of-thumb to signal a “significant change” that may require model review.
bodyText: PSI is calculated as Σ (actual - expected)*ln(actual/expected) over bins of the distribution. It quantifies how much the data have shifted. A common practice (from industry “rules of thumb”) is: **PSI <0.10** = little change, **0.10–0.25** = moderate change, **>0.25** = significant change requiring investigation. For example, if the score distribution has more high-risk borrowers now than at development, PSI will rise. CSI is a variant used when variables are categorical (like rating transitions). Banks use these metrics in monitoring (MRM-10). If PSI breaches its threshold, it often triggers a model review or recalibration. Regulators expect banks to track such stability measures for key variables and scores. (EBA/ECB Pillar 2 expectations and TRIM reviews included similar migration/stability checks.) It is important not to treat PSI/CSI breaches as automatic model failure. They are signals that something changed – perhaps the portfolio mix or economy – and model performance must be reassessed. A sudden PSI increase could also come from a one-time data issue. Nonetheless, including PSI/CSI in validation reports is good practice. Monitor variable and score shifts with PSI/CSI. Significant drift (e.g. PSI >0.25) should always prompt model review or action. Relying on fixed PSI thresholds without context. A PSI just above 0.25 in a benign economic situation may not be as urgent as the same PSI during a crisis. Also, using too many bins can artificially inflate PSI; ensure bins are consistent. **Population Stability Index (PSI)** — measures shift in the model *score* or numeric input distribution between time periods. --- **Characteristic Stability Index (CSI)** — measures shift in a *categorical* characteristic distribution (e.g. rating classes). Both flag distribution shifts, but PSI is for continuous scores/inputs, CSI for discrete categories. **No delta.** PSI/CSI are industry-standard techniques. Supervisors generally expect banks to check stability of model inputs and outputs over time. ECB’s internal-model audits (TRIM) and Pillar 2 guidance include similar stability monitoring.

title: Benchmarking and Challenger Models
one_screen: A **benchmark** (or reference) model is an alternate model used as a comparison.  A **challenger model** is a competing model built to test the primary model’s performance.  Banks may use simpler or differently-specified challenger models to sanity-check the primary model.  If the challenger outperforms, it signals the primary model may need improvement.
bodyText: Challenger and benchmark models serve to guard against model errors. For example, a bank’s existing PD model (the “incumbent”) might be compared to a newly-developed simpler model or an industry benchmark. This comparison can be part of validation or periodic review. The challenger might use a subset of the data or a different algorithm. The goal is not necessarily to replace the primary model, but to ensure the primary model is still competitive. Regulators encourage such comparisons. The PCA pillar 2 common terminology refers to “benchmarking” as a supervisory tool. While SR 26-2 does not mandate challengers, it lists ongoing monitoring and outcome analysis as good practices. RBI’s draft also mentions “benchmarking” in its requirements. In practice, a challenger model can help identify when a model has become stale. If performance metrics of the challenger are significantly better on hold-out data, this may trigger a model review or redevelopment. Benchmarking can also refer to comparing to industry models or historical performance. The key is to not rely blindly on one model. Banks should have a process to re-run or update challengers periodically for major models. (Note: having challengers is not a universal requirement; smaller banks may simply revalidate the main model more often.) Maintain at least one independent benchmark (or challenger) for each material model to verify it still performs well. Treating the primary model’s validation in isolation. Example: **believing a long-used model is fine without testing a new approach**. A challenger might reveal weaknesses not caught by routine checks. **Benchmark model** — an external or internally developed reference used for comparison. --- **Primary model** — the model in actual use. They get mixed up when a benchmark is incorrectly used for decisions; remember the primary is the one governing business. **No delta.** Challenger/benchmark practice is recommended by regulators worldwide as part of model governance. (ECB’s internal model guidelines mention the use of simpler collateral models, for example.)

title: Backtesting, Use Test, and Overrides
one_screen: **Backtesting** compares a model’s historical forecasts to actual results (e.g. predicted vs realized losses).  It’s a formal test of predictive accuracy over time.  The **use test** checks that the model is being applied in practice as intended (not just in name).  Banks must also track **overrides** (manual deviations) to ensure that business judgment does not mask model errors.
bodyText: Backtesting is often part of monitoring (see MRM-10). For example, a Value-at-Risk model would be backtested by counting how often actual losses exceed the VaR estimates. In credit PD models, backtesting might look at how forecast default rates compare to observed defaults in each grade. Regulators use backtesting to validate risk models: e.g. Basel committees prescribe backtesting rules for market VaR. In a broader sense, backtesting any model ensures it worked as advertised. The use test (a term from regulatory literature on internal ratings or IFRS9) ensures the model’s output influences decisions. For example, an internal rating model satisfies the use test if credit officers actually use it for approvals. If a model fails the use test (e.g. it was built but never integrated into processes), regulators may question why it was developed at all. Firms should maintain evidence of model usage (audit trails, workflow integration). **Overrides** occur when human experts override a model’s result (e.g. credit underwriters adjusting a score). Some level of overrides is expected (no model is perfect), but they must be tracked. Regulators view systematic overrides as potential model risk. For instance, RBI’s credit model guidance says that subjective overrides must be documented and justifiable. Banks should monitor override frequency and reason codes. An unusually high override rate may indicate the model is not trusted or is mis-calibrated, prompting review. Ongoing monitoring of overrides (and requiring board-level reporting if excessive) is part of robust MRM. Always measure model performance on historical data (backtest) and ensure the model’s output is actually used. Track any manual overrides closely. Ignoring overrides. For example, assuming the model is wrong because many underwriters ignore it, without investigating why. (Frequent overrides themselves are a sign the model may be problematic.) **Backtesting** — evaluating model accuracy by comparing predictions to actual outcomes over time. --- **Use test** — verifying that model outputs are actively used in decision-making. The former is statistical validation; the latter is governance of model usage. **No delta.** All regimes recognize backtesting as a model validation tool (especially for VaR/market models). The use test is a concept from Basel risk-weighted models and IFRS9, applicable in all advanced-model frameworks (incl. RBI’s IFRS9 NBFCs, PRA’s internal use requirement).

title: AI and Machine Learning Models
one_screen: Models using AI/ML must be interpretable and transparent.  Regulators expect that even non-linear models can be explained sufficiently to satisfy risk controls.  New guidelines explicitly stress interpretability (e.g. “explainability” requirements) and governance of AI.  Supervisory expectations for AI in finance are still evolving (often marked as “developing”) but lean toward strong oversight.
bodyText: AI and ML introduce additional complexity in model risk. Unlike linear regressions, many ML models (neural nets, ensemble trees) are “black boxes” by default. Yet regulators require that models be understood by the bank. For example, the ECB’s 2025 guide to internal models adds a section on machine learning, specifying that ML models must be “adequately explainable” and that their performance must justify the added complexity. Similarly, RBI’s draft guidance explicitly lists AI/ML models in scope and requires explainability, bias checks, and human oversight. The new U.S. guidance acknowledges AI/ML as model risk (although it currently excludes “generative AI” from scope), and the OCC has signaled forthcoming guidance on AI. In short, banks cannot claim “it’s just AI” to avoid validation – they must apply model risk principles to AI models too. However, validating AI models is challenging. Common practices include using SHAP values or LIME to explain predictions, simplifying models via surrogate linearizations, or requiring that final decisions be interpretable. Backtesting, discrimination and calibration concepts still apply, but new tests (e.g. for concept drift) may be needed. Given the complexity, the industry relies on “explainable AI” tools and rigorous documentation of how the model learns. Regulators are actively developing expectations for AI. The PRA already includes AI risk in SS1/23 sub-principles. In the U.S., OCC’s 2026 press release noted agencies will solicit input on AI use in banking. RBI’s draft explicitly covers AI: it requires a Board-approved AI governance framework, human-in-the-loop, and the ability to “kill” or decommission high-risk AI models. These emerging rules suggest strong scrutiny on AI: consider them “developing” expectations. Treat AI/ML models as you would any model, with the added requirement that their logic must be interpretable to decision-makers and auditors. Regulatory agencies now often require explainability as a must-have. Tolerating a black box just because it performs well. Ignoring regulations by calling a model “proprietary.” For example, **simply citing vendor secrecy to avoid explaining an AI model** is unacceptable. **Interpretability** — the ability to explain how a model arrives at a result. --- **Predictive accuracy** — how well the model predicts outcomes. A model can be accurate but uninterpretable; regulators require both (accuracy and some level of interpretability). — RBI’s draft explicitly includes AI/ML models. It requires explainability and bias/fairness controls. The draft even suggests specialized oversight (e.g. AI governance board-level) for complex ML models. — The PRA notes that model risk framework should cover AI/Machine Learning where applicable. Firms should ensure all models are well documented; the European Union is working on AI regulations (e.g. the EU AI Act) that will affect bank models. — SR 26-2 excludes “generative AI” for now, but FCA/OCC guidance is forthcoming. U.S. banking supervisors emphasize that ML models, like any models, must be validated and understandable. OCC has announced future guidance addressing banks’ use of AI. — ECB’s updated internal-model guide (2025) explicitly adds explainability for ML. The EU is also developing AI-specific regulations (e.g. the AI Act) that will impact financial institutions.

title: Operational Risk Definition
one_screen: Loss resulting from inadequate or failed internal processes, people, and systems or from external events; this definition explicitly includes legal risk but excludes strategic and reputational risk.
bodyText: Operational risk is one of the core categories of banking risk. Under Basel definitions, it is “the risk of loss resulting from inadequate or failed internal processes, people, and systems, or from external events. It includes legal risk, but excludes strategic and reputational risk”. In practice this means that any operational failure – from a system outage to a fraud loss – is treated as an operational risk event. Banks must categorize losses from things like data breaches, fraud, system downtime, or human error as operational losses. “Legal risk” (e.g. fines or litigation) is counted here too, but strategy mistakes or general PR damage are not part of operational risk. India follows this principle as well: RBI prudential rules in banks treat losses from internal failures or external shocks as operational risk, separate from strategic or reputation issues. (NB India’s banks use RBI norms rather than IFRS 9, so the definition is applied for prudential risk management, not via accounting rules.) Internal jargon: sometimes analysts call these “process risk” or “ops risk”. Everyone should remember the Basel boundary: **legal risk (like litigation)** is included, but **reputational or strategic risk** are separate categories (handled under governance or business risk frameworks). +--------------------+ | Operational Risk | | categories include:| | - Process failures | | - People errors | | - System outages | | - External events | | - Legal failures | +--------------------+ If it’s a loss caused by something going wrong in the bank’s operations or from an outside shock, it’s operational risk. Always capture these losses in your ORM (operational risk management) framework, including any legal or compliance fines as part of operational risk. Do **not** assume strategic mis-steps or brand damage count here – they do not. A common mistake is trying to manage reputational or strategic issues with the operational risk model. They are handled elsewhere (e.g. under strategic risk or conduct frameworks) and should not be lumped under “operational loss data.” **Operational Risk** — loss from failed processes, people, systems or external events (Basel definition). --- **Reputational Risk** — risk that negative perception harms the bank. (Not part of “operational” category.) **No delta.** The basic definition of operational risk comes from Basel and is used globally; all regulators require banks to manage loss risk from failures as outlined above.

title: Basel Operational Risk Event Categories
one_screen: Basel II mandates seven event type categories for operational loss events: internal fraud; external fraud; employment practices and workplace safety; clients, products and business practices; damage to physical assets; execution, delivery and process management; and business disruption & system failures.
bodyText: To ensure banks capture all operational losses, the Basel framework defines seven event-type categories. Every loss should be classified under one of them: - **Internal Fraud** (e.g. employee theft, unauthorized trading) - **External Fraud** (e.g. robbery, cyberattacks by outsiders) - **Employment Practices & Workplace Safety** (e.g. discrimination, health/safety breaches) - **Clients, Products & Business Practices** (e.g. product mis-selling, fiduciary breaches) - **Damage to Physical Assets** (fires, natural disasters) - **Execution, Delivery & Process Management** (errors in transaction processing, failed execution) - **Business Disruption & System Failures** (IT outages, power loss, pandemic-related closures). Banks use these categories to tag and aggregate losses so they can report to supervisors. For example, a trading loss due to a systems bug might be a “process management” event; a hurricane damage to a data center is “physical asset”; a lawsuit from a customer suit is “clients/products”. This taxonomy helps risk managers ensure no area is overlooked. [Risk Category] -> [Event Type Example] +-------------------------+ | Internal Fraud | Employee embezzles funds | External Fraud | Hackers steal customer data | Employment Practices | A discrimination lawsuit | Clients/Business Prac. | Mis-selling products to clients | Physical Assets | Fire destroys a branch | Execution & Process | Trade execution error | Disruption & Systems | Data center outage +-------------------------+ Classify all operational losses under one of Basel’s seven categories. This is mandatory for risk data consistency. Don’t neglect the “clients/products” and “employment practices” categories because they sound vague. For instance, a suit from a client over bad advice goes under “clients/products”, not another category. **Internal Fraud** — loss due to dishonest acts by staff (theft, unauthorized trading). --- **External Fraud** — similar fraud by outsiders (ATM robbery, hacking by non-employees). **No delta.** All Basel-aligned regimes use these same seven event types for operational risk reporting.

title: Modelling Challenges: Fat Tails and Sparse Data
one_screen: Operational loss data are “fat-tailed” (rare extreme losses dominate) and sparse, making capital modelling very difficult.  The loss distribution has infrequent but very large events and little data in the tail.
bodyText: Unlike credit or market risk, operational risk is hard to quantify with statistical models. The main issue is the loss distribution: it tends to be *fat-tailed*, meaning a handful of enormous losses (think $100m+ fines or frauds) dominate the worst-case quantiles. Most of the time losses are small or zero, so the tail is driven by outliers. This irregular, heavy-tail pattern means that conventional models (which assume “normal” or thin-tailed losses) understate risk. You often see statements like “99.9% VaR is dominated by just a few big events”. Another challenge is **sparse data**. Firms may have only a few decades of internal loss history and any particular risk type (e.g. cyber fraud) might have zero or very few data points. Basel’s AMA recognized this by requiring scenario analysis and external data supplements, but regulators later noted that these inputs can be subjective. In practice, even global consortia like ORX (for external loss data) still yield few non-zero data because severe events are rare. These factors create capital volatility and uncertainty. For example, risk experts have shown that a small change in a tail parameter can double the capital estimate. This instability was a key reason Basel ditched advanced models. In summary, operational loss modelling requires special care with tail-fitting, often relying on conservative, simple approaches (or on SMA) to avoid underestimation. Always model operational losses as heavy-tailed. Focus on tail estimation (e.g. extreme quantiles) and acknowledge data scarcity. Use all available data (internal + external + scenario inputs) to capture possible large losses. Do not assume a normal or light-tailed loss distribution. Underestimating tail risk or over-relying on few data points (or ignoring large single events) can lead to severe capital undercoverage. **Tail of distribution** vs **bulk data**. The bulk (small losses) should not be mistaken for the tail. Operational risk capital depends on the tail. **No delta.** Heavy tails and sparse data are universal challenges. All banks must use conservative modeling (or the standardized multiplier approach) to account for them.

title: Risk and Control Self-Assessment (RCSA)
one_screen: RCSA is a structured process where business units (first line) identify and assess their operational risks and controls.  It is typically run by the first line, with second line (operational risk) support.
bodyText: Risk and Control Self-Assessment (RCSA) is a core risk management process. In an RCSA, each business unit workshops its processes, risks, and controls. Teams identify “what can go wrong” (risk scenarios) and evaluate whether existing controls are adequate. The result is a self-assessed risk rating and list of control gaps, all owned by the first-line managers. The second line (Operational Risk or Risk Management functions) facilitates the methodology, reviews results, and consolidates findings across the bank. RCSA ensures that risks are identified close to the business activity and that managers own their residual risks. It helps populate the risk register and guides where to improve controls. However, to be effective, RCSA must be more than a checklist: it needs rigorous facilitation, calibration (e.g. via benchmarking or past loss data), and challenge. Business Unit X First Line (1LOD) | | Risk workshops---reports--> Operational Risk (2LOD) | | Controls identified Review & challenge | Action plans Perform RCSAs regularly (at least annually) and for all material processes. Assign clear ownership: 1st line owns the process and control design, 2nd line owns the RCSA framework and validation. Do not treat RCSA as a tick-box audit. A common mistake is letting units fill out forms without truly analyzing controls or linking to loss data. Ensure RCSA drives real risk improvement. **RCSA** — a proactive self-review by the business of its own risks and controls. --- **Internal Audit** — an independent audit function that tests processes after the fact. RCSA is done by the process owner; internal audit is 3rd-line assurance. **No delta.** The RCSA concept is a best-practice standard worldwide. Banks everywhere use first-line self-assessment to uncover op risk.

title: Key Risk Indicators (KRI) vs Key Performance Indicators (KPI)
one_screen: KRIs are forward-looking metrics signaling risk exposure, whereas KPIs track business performance.  A KRI warns of rising risk (like number of control breaches), while a KPI measures output (like sales volume).
bodyText: Key Risk Indicators (KRIs) and Key Performance Indicators (KPIs) often confuse people but serve different purposes. A **KRI** is a risk-focused measure, intended to alert the bank to increasing risk before losses occur. For example, a KRI might be the percentage of exceptions in a control process, or days since the last system patch (longer time = higher risk). KRIs usually have warning thresholds: if exceeded, management investigates potential failures. A **KPI** is a metric of business performance (e.g. profit margin, new accounts opened). A KRI gives an early warning of possible risk events, while a KPI tells you if you met your targets. In short: “KRIs measure exposure to risk; KPIs measure progress toward goals”. For instance, falling customer satisfaction could be a KRI for conduct risk; growth in assets under management is a KPI for business success. Always align KRIs to actual risk scenarios identified (e.g. RCSA or loss data). And distinguish them clearly from KPIs so risk and business metrics are not mixed. Define KRIs with clear thresholds and action triggers. Link each KRI to a specific risk scenario, and review them regularly. KRIs should be meaningful and measurable (e.g. error rates, incident counts). A frequent mistake is tracking a KPI and calling it a KRI (or vice versa). For example, using branch transaction volume (a KPI) to measure processing risk is misleading. Always double-check if a metric is truly risk-related (KRI) or just performance (KPI). **KRI** — a risk exposure metric that should rise *before* losses (e.g. late detections). --- **KPI** — a performance metric of outcomes (e.g. revenue growth). **No delta.** The concept of KRIs vs KPIs is consistent across banking regulations. All risk frameworks emphasize forward-looking indicators.

title: Internal Loss Data Collection
one_screen: Banks must record all operational losses above a defined threshold. Basel III’s new SMA sets a €20k minimum collection threshold (banks often collect losses of €1k or more internally).
bodyText: An internal loss data collection process ensures the bank tracks each actual loss event. Banks maintain a database of all operational losses by category (see OPR-02) – including fraud losses, fines, system repair costs, etc. Typically there is a **loss event threshold**: events below this amount aren’t individually logged to avoid noise. For example, Basel’s SMA requires data on losses above €20,000. In practice many banks set lower internal thresholds (e.g. $1k) so they also capture frequency patterns. The collected data feed multiple uses: management reporting, trend analysis, scenario calibration, and capital. Under SMA, the “Loss Component” is defined as 15× the 10-year average annual losses recorded (gross, before recoveries). Losses must be **gross of insurance** – a common error is logging net values. Good practice also separates recoveries to analyze control effectiveness. Note: if an operational failure caused a loan loss, classification can be tricky – banks usually classify by legal cause (so a system error that led to a trading loss still counts as operational loss). High-quality data is crucial: even one missing large loss can distort capital greatly. Losss should be captured promptly and reconciled (e.g. accounting vs op-risk logs). The internal loss database is typically owned by the 2nd line (Operational Risk) but populated by 1st line or an incident intake system. Record every material operational loss (gross amount) in the internal loss database. Use the predefined threshold and update it with regulator guidance (e.g. SMA €20k floor). Do not undercount losses by using net-of-insurance amounts. The regulatory capital formula (and risk view) assumes gross losses. Also avoid high thresholds that miss important events – recall a loss just below threshold may lead to serious underestimation of tail risk. **Gross loss** — the total loss amount before any recoveries. --- **Net loss** — the loss after deducting insurance or recoveries. (Banks must record *gross* loss for risk capital.) **No delta.** All Basel-aligned capital frameworks use gross operational losses. Basel’s SMA specifies €20k min threshold (banks can report more granular). For reference, UK regulators also expect banks’ internal loss databases to follow Basel rules for materiality.

title: External Loss Data and Scenario Analysis
one_screen: Banks supplement internal data with external loss data (e.g. industry databases like ORX) and scenario analysis workshops.  External data is limited (often anonymized), while scenario analysis uses expert judgment to estimate severe loss frequency/severity.
bodyText: Because internal loss data is limited, banks use **external data** and **scenario analysis**. External sources include news databases, vendor feeds, and consortium pools (e.g. ORX). However, regulators note such data are sparse and biased toward big publicized events. For example, ORX’s anonymized dataset helps gauge extreme losses, but cannot be directly scaled without judgment. **Scenario analysis** is a forward-looking process: risk experts and business leaders hold workshops to identify plausible “severe but plausible” events and estimate their frequency and impact. For instance, a scenario might be “critical IT system hack causing $50m losses”. Participants use past incidents, market knowledge, and judgment to quantify impact. (Note: scenarios are subjective, so controls are needed to mitigate optimism bias.) Under Basel’s old AMA these elements were required, but guidance emphasized not to **lower** capital estimates via optimistic scenarios. Even though AMA is gone, banks still use scenarios to stress-test resilience and in Pillar 2 reviews. Scenario analysis is especially useful for emerging risks with little history (e.g. cloud failure, cyber events). Use external data and scenario outputs only as supplements to internal loss data. They should capture tail risks that internal records miss. Always document assumptions in scenarios and avoid letting them reduce conservatism. Don’t over-rely on scenarios to justify lowering capital. Supervisors warn that banks often underestimate scenario losses to reduce capital. Also, treat external loss data carefully — small banks shouldn’t blindly import the industry’s largest losses without proper scaling. **Scenario analysis** — expert-driven estimation of tail loss frequency/severity. --- **Stress testing** — systematic shock to risk factor values (more common in market/credit risk). (Both are forward-looking but scenarios use narrative events while stress tests use factor jumps.) **No delta.** Basel guidelines for operational risk encouraged use of external data and scenario inputs (formerly under AMA). Current frameworks (SMA/Pillar 2) still expect firms to consider severe-event scenarios in risk management.

title: Issue and Action Management
one_screen: Issue management tracks identified risk/control weaknesses through to remediation. An “issue” is a control/process gap that could lead to risk materialisation, requiring action plans.
bodyText: Issue (or finding) management is the process of ensuring that problems identified in the risk framework are fixed. An “issue” typically means a **weakness or deficiency** in a control or process; if unaddressed it may let a risk materialise. For example, an audit report might flag that a reconciliations process is missing a key review – that is logged as an “issue.” The bank then assigns a responsible owner, sets deadlines and action plans to correct the gap (e.g. implement a new check), and tracks it to closure. Good issue management involves: clear logging (unique IDs, description of root cause), categorization (risk type, severity), timely escalation to management, and periodic status reporting. Many banks use dedicated software to track issues (some link them to risk indicators). The key is follow-through: every issue should be resolved or formally accepted by senior management if not mitigated. Unresolved issues accumulate “residual risk.” Audit/Incident -> Issue logged | Risk Office tracks and categorizes -> Action plan assigned | Reports to Management and Board until closed All identified issues (e.g. audit findings, RCSA gaps, loss root causes) must be logged and tracked. Assign a clear deadline and owner. Regularly review outstanding issues with senior risk committees to ensure remediation. Avoid letting issues stall. A frequent mistake is opening many low-priority issues and losing track of them. Focus resources on resolving issues that pose the greatest risk. Also, don’t close an issue prematurely: require evidence of a fix (e.g. retest of control) before marking it done. **Issue** — a control/process gap or weakness found, awaiting remediation. --- **Incident (loss)** — an actual event where a risk materialised (the loss itself). (Incidents are root causes for issues; issues may exist before any loss.) **No delta.** Effective issue management is universally required by regulators as part of internal controls and operational risk frameworks. (For example, Basel’s SRP guidelines expect banks to fix risk model weaknesses found in validation/audit.)

title: Control Design vs Control Operating Effectiveness
one_screen: Control design refers to whether a control is appropriately conceived to mitigate a risk; operating effectiveness refers to whether the control actually works in practice at all times. Both must be evaluated independently.
bodyText: Two aspects of a control must be tested: its design and its operating effectiveness. **Design effectiveness** asks, “Is this control logically sufficient to address the risk?” For example, a password policy (design) aims to prevent unauthorized access; it is well-designed if it covers all critical systems. **Operating effectiveness** asks, “Does the control actually work consistently?” Even a well-designed control fails if people ignore it or it’s poorly executed (e.g. employees sharing passwords). In practice, auditors or risk managers often test design by inspection (is the rule documented? covers all cases?) and test operation by sampling actual instances (did staff follow it every time in the sample?). For robust risk management, both must be in place. A common failure is to assume that having a written policy implies complete coverage. In reality, lack of operating effectiveness means the risk is uncontrolled. Test each control along two dimensions. First ensure the control’s design is appropriate for the risk. Then test that the control operates effectively (e.g. performs correctly and consistently). Use samples, walkthroughs, and reconciliations to evidence operation. Never assume a strong design implies it’s working. A classic mistake is having a good procedure on paper but failing to enforce it. For example, a fraud-check process might look solid, but if staff skip steps under pressure, the control is ineffective. **Control Design** — the theory and setup of the control (e.g. policy, procedure). --- **Operating Effectiveness** — the actual execution of the control. **No delta.** This distinction is part of basic internal control frameworks everywhere (Basel/SSOX/SOX). Regulatory guidance (e.g. Basel and audit standards) explicitly require both aspects to be tested.

title: Pillar I: Basic Indicator and Standardised Approaches
one_screen: **Basic Indicator Approach (BIA):** Capital = 15% of average annual gross income (last 3 years).  **Standardised Approach (TSA/ASA):** Divide bank activities into 8 business lines; apply fixed beta factors to each line’s gross income; then average the sum over 3 years.
bodyText: Under Basel II (and prior Basel I transitional norms), simple pillar 1 methods existed before SMA. **BIA** is the simplest: it sets the operational risk capital charge equal to *α* × (average annual gross income), with α=15%. For example, if a bank’s average gross income was €100m, BIA charge = 0.15×100m = €15m. (Years with negative or zero income are dropped.) **Standardised Approach (TSA)** refines this by business line. Basel defined 8 lines (e.g. retail, corporate finance, trading, etc.). Each line’s gross income is multiplied by a line-specific factor (β) – typically 12%-18% depending on line. For example, corporate finance β=18%, retail banking β=12%. The capital charge = average over 3 years of sum(β_i × GI_i). Each negative income can offset positive in the same year. These approaches were “standardised” because any bank could calculate them from simple P&L data. They were retired by 2022 under Basel 3.1, but some regimes still use BIA/TSA for domestic banks or under-transition. +------------------------+ | Basic Indicator (BIA) | | Charge = 15% × avg GI | +------------------------+ vs +-------------------------------+ | Standardised (TSA/ASA) | | Split into 8 lines with betas | | Charge = avg over 3y of Σ(β_i×GI_i) | +-------------------------------+ If using TSA, the 8 business lines and associated beta factors (12–18%) must be applied. National regulators may specify these in detail (EBA or local law). Board approval and risk framework standards are required even under TSA. Do not assume these approaches reflect current risk (they were proxies). Under TSA, a bank with complex products might hold too little capital. Also, don’t confuse “Standardised” with the newer “SMA” – they are completely different. **Basic Indicator (BIA)** — capital = α×(bank’s gross income). --- **Standardised (TSA)** — capital = weighted sum of each business line’s GI (β factors). **No delta.** These formulas were global under Basel II. However, note: - **UK/EU (pre-Basel3.1):** SMEs or retail banks often used TSA with same factors. - **India:** RBI followed Basel II on paper; BIA (15%) and TSA lines were defined in Master Directions. - **US:** US banking regulators allowed these approaches earlier but also introduced standardized (ASA) that resembled TSA.

title: Advanced Measurement Approach (AMA) and Its Abandonment
one_screen: **AMA:** Banks modelled op-risk at 99.9% VaR using internal loss distribution (with scenarios, etc.). AMA was abandoned because it produced unstable, non-comparable capital requirements – a small change in tail estimation could double the capital.
bodyText: Basel II allowed a most sophisticated option, the **Advanced Measurement Approach (AMA)**, for large banks. Under AMA, each bank built internal models (often loss distribution approach) using its own loss data, scenarios, external data and BEICFs. They targeted a 99.9% VaR for operational loss. AMA banks required heavy internal modeling and sophisticated risk frameworks. However, the financial crisis exposed problems with AMA. In practice AMA outputs varied wildly between banks, making the capital numbers non-comparable. The extreme tail of the loss distribution is highly sensitive to inputs: risk modelers found that a ~9% change in a severity parameter could double the capital charge. This instability (and complexity/supervisory burden) led regulators to scrap AMA in Basel 3.1. As a result, AMA ceased being an approved Pillar 1 method globally after 2021.
