When AMA was in use, regulators required it to be conservative. Now banks base Pillar 1 capital on SMA instead. (Many banks still use AMA-like internal models for economic capital or Pillar 2 stress tests.) Don’t rely on unvalidated internal models for regulatory capital. Overfitting to your own data, or using only small-sample scenarios, gave illusion of precision and was a key flaw of AMA. **AMA (old Basel)** vs **Standardised Measurement Approach (SMA)**. AMA = internal models; SMA = formulaic Basel 3.1 approach. They are completely different regimes. **No delta.** All Basel-member regulators moved away from AMA. For example, the EU and UK have implemented SMA; the US agencies have signaled support for Basel’s new approach but have not finalized it.

title: Standardised Measurement Approach (SMA)
one_screen: Basel 3.1’s SMA formula is: **OR capital = BIC × ILM**, where *BIC* (Business Indicator Component) is a scaled bank size metric, and *ILM* (Internal Loss Multiplier) reflects loss history. Specifically, ILM = ln(e–1 + (LC/BIC)^0.8).
bodyText: The **Standardised Measurement Approach (SMA)**, effective from 2022, applies to all large banks. It combines current size with past losses. The **Business Indicator (BI)** is calculated from selected financials (Interest/Lease/Dividend, Services, Financial components of P&L). The BI is bucketed with marginal coefficients (12%, 15%, 18%) to produce the **Business Indicator Component (BIC)**. This BIC roughly scales with bank size. The **Internal Loss Multiplier (ILM)** is then calculated using the bank’s internal Loss Component (LC = 15× the 10-year avg annual loss) relative to BIC. Mathematically: *ILM = ln(e – 1 + (LC/BIC)^0.8)*. The final Pillar 1 capital = BIC × ILM. If a bank had no losses, ILM approaches 1 and capital≈BIC. If losses are high, ILM >1 and capital increases. (Notably, when LC=BIC, ILM=1 exactly, so capital=BIC.) **Example:** Suppose BIC = €1.5bn and LC (15× avg loss) = €1.2bn. Then ILM = ln(e–1 + (0.8)^0.8)≈0.94, so capital ≈ €1.5bn×0.94. If LC rises to €2.25bn, ILM≈1.13 and capital ≈€1.70bn. Compute BI from financials -> Apply α -> BIC (size-based) LC = 15×(10-yr avg loss) ILM = ln(e–1 + (LC/BIC)^0.8) OR Capital = BIC × ILM Use gross losses in LC. The regulator-provided ILM formula must be used exactly. Note: the UK (PRA) has elected to set ILM=1 for all firms (making capital = BIC only). A big mistake is mixing up **BI** with **BIC**. BI is raw aggregated income; BIC multiplies BI by α coefficients for each bucket. Also, don’t miscalculate ILM by using net losses or wrong averages. **BI (Business Indicator)** — the raw income-based metric (sum of income components). --- **BIC (Business Indicator Component)** — the size component used for capital, after applying the Basel α-coefficients. — The PRA has prescribed ILM=1, so capital = BIC. **EU & Others** — Will follow Basel’s formula (BIC×ILM). **IN** — RBI has not adopted SMA for banks (India is behind on Basel 3.1). — No SMA implemented yet; agencies are discussing Basel alignment.

title: Impact of ILM and Bank Differences
one_screen: Even with identical BI/BIC, banks can have very different op-risk capital because ILM captures loss history.  A bank with higher average losses (LC) gets a higher ILM, boosting capital.  Conversely, Basel 3.1 allows a supervisor to neutralize ILM; for example, the UK chooses ILM=1 for all firms.
bodyText: Two banks with the same size (BI/BIC) might hold different operational risk capital if their loss histories differ. Under SMA, capital = BIC×ILM. If Bank A had higher losses over the last 10 years, its LC/BIC ratio is bigger, yielding a larger ILM (and thus capital) than Bank B. For instance, riskhub showed that raising average loss from €80m to €150m with the same BIC increased ILM from 0.94 to 1.13, raising capital by 21%. Thus, historical operational performance influences capital. Critically, jurisdictions can blunt this disparity: Basel lets national regulators set ILM=1 if desired. The UK PRA decided to neutralize ILM entirely. As a result, two UK banks of equal size will hold identical capital regardless of their loss experience. But in regimes that keep ILM active (or in Pillar 2), differences persist. So, a big US bank still using an AMA-like model or a European bank implementing Basel SMA with ILM could end up with capital quite different from a UK peer. Same BIC -> Bank A LC high -> ILM>1 -> Higher ORC Bank B LC low -> ILM<1 -> Lower ORC Always check the local rule on ILM. If ILM=1 is mandated (as in UK), capital is just BIC. Otherwise, ensure the ILM (and LC calculation) is correctly applied. The mistake is to assume size alone dictates capital. Even small banks (low BI) with a bad loss track record can have high capital under SMA. And believing UK banks hold higher capital when actually PRA’s ILM=1 means only BI matters. **BIC (size-based capital)** vs **LC (loss component)**. Two banks could have identical BIC, but if one has LC much bigger, its ILM will be higher, leading to higher final capital. — sets ILM=1 so capital = BIC (loss history ignored). — expected to use ILM formula (like Basel). — Indian banks still on older rules (mostly Basic/Std approaches), so NA. — large banks still under AMA (no SMA yet); the ILM concept isn’t applied.

title: Third-Party and Outsourcing Risk
one_screen: Outsourcing critical functions to vendors creates operational risk.  Concentration risk arises when a single provider dominates (e.g. all banks using one cloud service).  OSFI defines “institution-specific” concentration as overreliance on a single third party for one bank, and “systemic” concentration when many banks depend on the same provider.
bodyText: **Third-party risk** (also called vendor risk) occurs when banks rely on external service providers (for IT, payments, data centers, etc). Key aspects include due diligence, contract management, and exit planning. Even if a task is outsourced, the bank’s 1LOD retains accountability for that risk (supervisors emphasize that rule). **Concentration risk** is a special concern: if many banks use the same vendor, a single vendor failure can hit the entire sector. The Canadian OSFI guideline defines: - *Institution-specific concentration:* loss to one bank from reliance on a single vendor. - *Systemic concentration:* loss across many banks when one third-party provider (or location) fails. A current example is cloud services – if almost all banks use AWS or Azure, an outage there is a systemic threat. Banks must identify critical vendor relationships and manage them (multiple suppliers, safeguards, exit plans). Many regulators now require approval and oversight of critical third parties. The Basel Committee also published sound third-party management principles. Poor outsourcing control can lead to large operational losses (e.g. data breach at a provider, failure of a payment processor). Assess and document the criticality of all outsourced services. Maintain contingency and exit plans. Ensure concentration (especially in cloud) is monitored – e.g. do not let any single third-party failure threaten business continuity. Do not assume risk disappears because a function is outsourced. The bank always remains responsible. Also, beware of relying too heavily on one vendor. A classic error is assuming that utilizing a reputable vendor eliminates risk. Even top vendors can fail (as seen with global outages). **Outsourcing** — contracting services to a third party under a formal agreement. --- **Offshoring** — relocating business processes (could still be in-house or offshore branch). (Outsourcing and offshoring can overlap but are not the same.) **UK/EU** — Regulators (PRA/SRBD/FCA) require firms to have robust outsourcing frameworks (e.g. FCA’s SYSC 8 and DORA regulations on ICT third-party management). — RBI’s Master Directions mandate banks’ risk management of outsourcing (including to cloud and data centers). — OCC and Fed guidance (e.g. OCC Bulletin 2013-29) emphasize vendor management and concentration risk.

title: Operational Resilience (Business Services, Impact Tolerances)
one_screen: Operational resilience is the firm’s ability to avoid intolerable harm to consumers or market integrity from service disruptions. It requires identifying **Important Business Services (IBS)** and setting maximum tolerable disruption (impact tolerances), then testing against severe plausible scenarios.
bodyText: Operational resilience goes beyond traditional op risk. It focuses on ensuring that critical services (e.g. payments, trading systems, ATM networks) continue or quickly recover during major disruptions. Regulators in the UK define it as avoiding “intolerable harm to consumers and threats to market integrity when services are disrupted”. The cornerstone is mapping **Important Business Services (IBS)** – those that if disrupted would harm customers or the market. For each IBS, the bank sets an **impact tolerance** (e.g. max downtime or data loss beyond which harm becomes intolerable). Firms must map all people, processes, technology, and third parties that support each IBS. Then they run severe-but-plausible scenario tests (e.g. cyberattack, data center fire, supplier outage) to see if they can stay within tolerances. For instance, recent examples like AWS and Azure outages are exactly the kind of severe scenarios firms must prepare for. Meeting impact tolerances might involve backup sites, rapid failover, or manual workarounds. Operational resilience is about systemic continuity planning and is a regulatory requirement (especially in UK’s PRA/FCA regime and under EU’s DORA) – it is a distinct discipline from day-to-day op risk management. Identify and document each Important Business Service. For each, define a clear impact tolerance (not just time, but level of harm). Test resilience with scenario exercises at least annually, adjusting plans as needed. Don’t confuse resilience with mere disaster recovery. Resilience is holistic (including customer harm assessment). A common error is to plan only IT backups (DR) without considering how long customers can be without the service or what customer harm might occur. **Operational Resilience** — maintaining essential services during major events (focus on continuity/impact). --- **Operational Risk** — managing losses from failures (focus on losses incurred). — PRA/FCA rules (PS21/3) mandate mapping IBS and setting impact tolerances. — The Digital Operational Resilience Act (DORA) covers ICT resilience, requiring testing of critical functions. — RBI issued Operational Resilience guidelines and mandated core business continuity requirements. — Regulators (Fed/OCC/SEC) encourage resilience planning (e.g. emergency preparedness rules) but no unified regime yet.

title: Business Continuity & Disaster Recovery
one_screen: A **Business Continuity Plan (BCP)** addresses how an institution will continue providing critical products/services after a disruption. A **Disaster Recovery Plan (DRP)** focuses on restoring IT systems and data to resume normal operations.
bodyText: Business continuity (BCP) and disaster recovery (DRP) are key elements of resilience. A **BCP** is a high-level strategy covering all aspects of the business: it identifies essential functions and minimum acceptable service levels, and outlines procedures (e.g. relocation, manual processes) to maintain those functions. A BCP will include communication plans, alternate work sites, and human resource arrangements to cope with events like natural disasters or pandemics. A **DRP** is a subset of BCP that deals specifically with IT recovery. It defines how to recover systems, networks, and data (e.g. via backups, failover to secondary data centers) after an outage. For instance, after a cyberattack, the DRP would guide restoring customer databases and applications. Both plans require regular testing (drills, simulations) to ensure readiness. For example, a bank might simulate a data center blackout and try to operate from the backup site. Regulatory expectations (e.g. RBI’s BCM guidelines, FFIEC in US) mandate routine tests and board oversight of these plans. Maintain up-to-date BCP and DRP, and test them at least annually (or when significant changes occur). Ensure all staff know their roles. Back up critical data offsite and verify restore capability. Do not prepare a plan and forget it. Plans must evolve with the business. A common mistake is outdated contact lists or assuming the “test was enough.” Also, don’t rely solely on IT solutions – people and process continuity must be addressed. **Business Continuity Plan (BCP)** — ensures business operations continue (includes people, processes, systems). --- **Disaster Recovery Plan (DRP)** — detailed IT recovery procedures after an incident. **No delta.** All banking regulators require both BCP and DRP. For example, RBI mandates annual BCM tests; Fed/OCC have similar guidance.

title: Cyber Risk (Governance Level)
one_screen: Cyber risk is the threat of digital attacks or IT failures harming the bank. Governance means the board and senior management overseeing cybersecurity strategy, policies, and incident response, rather than technical implementation.
bodyText: Cyber risk (often called information/cybersecurity risk) involves potential losses from attacks like hacking, malware, or ransomware. At the governance level, it means ensuring the bank has proper oversight over this risk. This includes: appointing a Chief Information Security Officer (CISO), having a board committee for cyber, setting a risk appetite for cyber breaches, enforcing policies (access controls, encryption standards), and running incident response drills. For example, regulators expect boards to understand major cyber threats and ensure management addresses them (e.g. Sarbanes-Oxley and Fed guidance highlight board responsibility for cybersecurity). Organizations increasingly treat cybersecurity as a business-risk issue, not just IT’s job. Recent high-profile outages (AWS, Azure) and cyberattacks underscore this point. Firms must integrate cyber defense into risk management (e.g. cross-functional risk committees, regular audit of cyber controls). Ultimately, effective cyber risk governance means embedding cyber into the risk culture – emphasising that a human or process failure (e.g. poor patching, phishing success) is as much an operational risk as a market shock. Board and executive management must have clear oversight of cyber security. Risk committees should review cyber metrics (KRI) and ensure incident plans exist. All major system changes or third-party integrations need cyber risk assessment. Technology teams should not be left as isolated silos for cyber. A common error is delegating all responsibility to the IT department. Instead, cyber risk must be owned at the enterprise level. **Cybersecurity (tech focus)** vs **Cyber risk governance (management focus)**. Cybersecurity involves tools and processes (firewalls, encryption). Cyber risk governance means leadership sets strategy and ensures controls are in place. — RBI’s Cyber Security Framework for banks requires boards to approve cyber strategies. **UK/EU** — Regulatory requirements (e.g. NIS regulations, DORA) push firms to enhance cyber resilience. — SEC, OCC and FFIEC expect robust cyber governance (board-level oversight).

title: Conduct Risk and Culture
one_screen: Conduct risk is the risk that employee or firm behavior causes harm to customers or markets.  It is a subset of operational risk related to governance and culture. A weak risk culture (incentives, oversight, tone) often underlies conduct failures.
bodyText: **Conduct risk** stems from staff behaviors and culture that lead to poor customer outcomes or market abuse. Unlike pure “financial” risks, conduct events (mis-selling, fraud, negligence) may not cause an immediate loss to the bank but can cause reputational and regulatory costs. Regulators stress that conduct risk is fundamentally about **culture and incentives**. The Basel Committee notes that mis-selling, compliance breaches, and control failures all fall under operational risk, driven by poor conduct. Banks must therefore embed “tone from the top”: fair treatment of customers, clear values, and aligned incentive schemes. For example, incentive plans that reward volume over quality are red flags. Boards are expected to understand if compensation, sales practices, or product design could create conduct risk. In practice, strong conduct risk management means close oversight by compliance and risk units, review of customer outcomes, and control functions that test for unethical behavior (e.g. forced sales). Supervisors may intervene if conduct culture is lacking (e.g. FCA’s “consumer duty”). Embed conduct risk management into the risk framework. This includes board accountability, clear ethical standards, and monitoring of behaviors that might harm customers. Treat compliance breaches and misconduct as operational risk incidents. Focusing only on rule compliance misses the point. The trap is to assume “if there’s no explicit rule violation, behavior is okay.” Conduct risk is broader – it can arise from aggressive sales pressures or conflicts of interest even before any rule is broken. **Conduct Risk** — the risk that unethical or improper behavior by firm or staff causes customer/market harm. --- **Compliance Risk** — the risk of failing to meet regulatory requirements. (Conduct encompasses compliance but also relates to culture and customer fairness.) — FCA and PRA explicitly require firms to manage conduct risk (e.g. Principles for Business, Financial Services Act 2021). — EBA consumer protection rules, MiFID II/IDD sales rules address conduct; EBA has guidelines on culture. — RBI’s Fair Practice Codes and recent Financial Sector reforms emphasize customer interests (e.g. embedding fair treatment). — CFPB, FINRA, etc. handle conduct at retail level; Fed/OCC enforce risk culture via SCB (Supervisory Complexity and Culture) reviews.

title: Change Management Risk
one_screen: Change management risk is the risk that implementing a change (e.g. new system, process revamp) itself causes failures or losses. Major changes must be managed carefully to avoid unintended disruptions.
bodyText: Organizations undertake major change programs (new core banking system, mergers, or regulatory projects). Each such change carries its own risk of introducing errors or disruption. Change management risk includes schedule overruns, technical glitches, data errors, or poor training leading to failures once the change is live. For example, a system upgrade might inadvertently disable a payment batch. Banks thus need rigorous change-control processes: testing in a risk-free environment, phased rollout, fallback plans, and impact assessment. Change risk is operational, not strategic: it arises during the execution of projects. It is often managed under project management and IT risk frameworks, but should be integrated with ops risk (e.g. scenario thinking about “failed change” events). Apply strict change controls: use version control, testing, sign-off at each stage, and rollback procedures. Involve the risk function in major changes and log any near-misses or incidents during implementation. Don’t treat project issues as only project risk. Ignoring a change failure can lead to large operational loss later. Also, avoid “big bang” rollouts without pilot testing – history shows those often go wrong. **Change management risk** — risk of problems due to the change process itself. --- **Project Risk** — risks around delivering the project objectives (time/cost). (There’s overlap, but change risk focuses on aftermath after deployment.) **No delta.** Good change management is a universal best practice (mentioned in Basel principles, IT governance guidelines, etc.). Some regulators (e.g. RBI on IT governance) specifically require robust change controls.

title: Data Privacy Obligations (GDPR, DPDP)
one_screen: Banks must comply with data privacy laws governing personal data.  EU/UK GDPR impose strict controls (e.g. lawful basis, subject rights) with fines up to 4% of turnover.  India’s DPDP Act (2023) requires consent and security, with penalties up to ₹250 Crore.
bodyText: Personal data (customer information) is heavily regulated. Rules like the EU’s GDPR (and UK GDPR) require banks to collect data lawfully (usually with customer consent or legitimate interest), use it only for specified purposes, protect it securely, and honor customer rights (access, correction, erasure). Infringements (e.g. data breaches, misuse) incur steep penalties – up to €20M or 4% of global turnover. Similarly, India’s new DPDP Act (effective 2023) enforces data fiduciary principles: consent, minimization, data security, and data subject rights. Violations can lead to heavy fines (up to ₹250 crores, ~$30M). Banks must therefore govern privacy at an enterprise level: assigning a Data Protection Officer (DPO), maintaining privacy notices, and integrating “privacy by design” into processes. While technical (encryption, access controls) is critical, oversight and policies are also key. For example, GDPR requires breach notification within 72 hours. Compliance failures can lead to both regulatory fines and reputational/legal losses. Handle personal data only as allowed by law: get valid consent or legal basis, limit access, and implement strong security (encryption, etc.). Always comply with notification rules for breaches. Don’t assume data security (e.g. encryption) alone solves privacy. Privacy obligations also demand proper data usage (transparency to customers, data minimization). Ignoring the “legal basis” or consent aspect is a frequent oversight. **Data Privacy** — legal rights and rules about how personal data is used (e.g. GDPR consent). --- **Cybersecurity** — technical measures to protect data (e.g. firewalls, anti-malware). **EU/UK** — GDPR (and UK DPA 2018) require strict data protection principles and enforce through DPIAs and high fines. — The Digital Personal Data Protection Act, 2023 (DPDP) applies broadly; banks must follow its consent, notice, and security norms. Penalties in DPDP Act: up to ₹250 Crore. — No unified federal banking privacy law (GLBA exists for financial privacy, HIPAA for health, etc.), but some states (e.g. California) have robust laws.

title: Population vs Sample in Credit Data
one_screen: A *population* is the entire set of items of interest (e.g. all borrowers), while a *sample* is the subset of that population used for analysis. In credit data, sample bias can mislead risk estimates if the sampled loans systematically differ from the full loan portfolio.
bodyText: Banks rarely have data on every possible borrower (the population). Instead, models use samples such as past borrowers or current customers. If the sample is unrepresentative, estimates of default rates or other risk measures will be biased. For instance, a credit bureau dataset may omit loans that did not originate (an *application bias*), or a portfolio dataset might lack information on people who were denied credit (a *selection bias*). Regulatory guidance emphasizes that models should be validated on a sample representative of current and future portfolios. In practice, analysts must check if the training sample covers all customer segments and time periods. For example, if only performing clients are sampled, average default probability will be under-estimated. Oversampling defaulters can correct imbalance but must be done carefully to avoid altering the underlying distribution. As a rule, increasing sample size will not fix a biased sample – adding more biased data only tightens confidence around the wrong value. The *permanent rule* is: ensure your training data frame covers the same population characteristics as the real credit book. +------------+ +-------------+ | Population | | Sample | | (All loans)| | (Historic, | | | | current data)| +------+-----+ +------+------+ | | v v Model input Model training A larger sample cannot correct a sampling bias; validate models on data representative of the true credit population. Assuming a large sample size eliminates bias. In fact, if the sampling frame is skewed (e.g. excludes declined applicants or past defaulters), even millions of records will give a precisely wrong answer. **Sampling bias** — distortion from how the sample is drawn. --- **Non-response bias** — when sampled applicants fail to provide data (e.g. survey participants differ from non-respondents). Both distort representativeness, but sampling bias is in frame selection, while non-response occurs post-selection. **No delta.** The concept of population vs sample is a statistical fact, not subject to regulatory variation.

title: Key Distributions in Credit Risk
one_screen: In credit risk analytics, certain probability distributions recur: *normal* (e.g. for rescaled aggregate losses), *lognormal* (e.g. for asset values), *binomial* (for default counts), and *Poisson* (for rare-event counts). Understanding their shapes and uses is crucial for modeling credit losses and borrower behavior.
bodyText: **Normal distribution:** Symmetric bell-curve, defined by mean (μ) and variance (σ²). In credit risk, many aggregated quantities (e.g. average credit score across many independent borrowers) tend toward normal by the Central Limit Theorem (CLT) (see QNT-03). Internal models like the Vasicek IRB model assume a normal latent variable for asset returns. **Lognormal distribution:** A variable is lognormal if its logarithm is normal. It is right-skewed (long tail on right). Credit risk example: firm asset values or portfolio losses are often modeled as lognormal. The Vasicek/Merton framework assumes firm asset value follows lognormal growth, so log(asset) is normal. Many individual loss severities (e.g. loss given default) are positive and skewed, fitting a lognormal shape. **Binomial distribution:** Models the number of defaults in *n* independent loans with default probability *p*. If defaults are independent, defaults ~ Binomial(n,p). Its mean np and variance np(1-p). A single loan’s annual loss (either full loss or none) is Bernoulli (a 0-1 loss), so a portfolio loss is the sum of Bernoullis, a binomial. FRM notes: “the probability distribution for the loss from the ith loan is... binomial”. Binomial is key for small portfolio loss estimation or mapping small default events. **Poisson distribution:** Models count of rare independent events over fixed exposure. If the chance of default is small (p ≪ 1) and number of loans large, Binomial(n,p) ≈ Poisson(λ=np). For portfolios with many small exposures and low default rate, default counts ≈ Poisson. Poisson also arises for counting loan prepayments or rare credit events. It has one parameter λ (mean=variance). Using the correct distribution is crucial for risk metrics: e.g. mis-specifying default count as normal (when events are rare) underestimates tail risk. Each distribution’s parameters should be estimated from data or expert priors, and used consistently in simulations or VaR calculations. Loan defaults: aggregate risk: +---------+ +---------+ |Bernoulli| | Binomial| | (0 or 1)| ---> |(n,p) | +---------+ +---------+ | | v v Defaults count ~ Binomial (rare defaults, large n) ≈ Poisson Each distribution’s assumptions must match the credit context (e.g. non-negative, skewed, independent events). Using a normal model for highly skewed or discrete data leads to wrong estimates. Treating an inherently skewed quantity (like loan loss amounts) as normally distributed can underestimate extreme losses. For example, assuming symmetric losses when actual losses (e.g. severe defaults) follow a long-tailed lognormal can understate required provisions. **Binomial distribution** — count of successes (e.g. defaults) in a fixed number of trials (loans) with success probability *p*. --- **Poisson distribution** — count of independent events (e.g. defaults) over fixed exposure/time when events are rare. Poisson can approximate binomial for large *n* and small *p* (np=λ). **No delta.** Probability distributions and their shapes are mathematical truths. Specific regulatory models (e.g. Basel IRB) may use these distributions (e.g. Vasicek’s normal-based model), but the underlying math is universal.

title: Central Limit Theorem (CLT) and Credit Risk
one_screen: The CLT states that the sum (or average) of many independent, identically distributed random variables approaches a normal distribution, regardless of the original distribution. In credit, it justifies using normal approximations for aggregated risks (like portfolio losses) when individual variations are small.
bodyText: If a bank has a large, diversified loan portfolio, each loan’s default or loss contributes a little to total risk. By the CLT, the distribution of total loss approximates normal, even if individual loan losses are skewed. For example, if many similar small loans each have random loss, their average or sum will be near normal. This helps in risk capital models (e.g. using normal quantiles to set capital). However, the CLT has conditions: loans should be *independent* (or only weakly correlated) and none *too large* (“fine-grained” portfolio). Credit portfolios often violate CLT ideal assumptions. Defaults can be correlated through economic cycles (violating independence), and large exposures (“lumpiness”) also break the identical small-size assumption. Basel’s IRB capital formula assumes infinite, independent loans (the “asymptotically fine-grained” condition). In reality, correlated defaults (systematic risk) mean aggregate losses can have fat tails. Thus, CLT only licenses normal approximations under strong diversification. **In practice:** one uses CLT as a guide but tests its validity. Risk managers might apply normal approximations to portfolio VaR only after verifying no extreme concentration. If not, alternative distributions (e.g. Vasicek distribution for correlated losses) are used. The *permanent rule*: use CLT for large, well-diversified groups, but check for correlation or large-exposure breaks. Individual loan losses ~ any dist. (skewed) + many independent exposures | v (CLT: n large, similar loans) Total portfolio loss ≈ Normal dist. (mean=nμ, var=nσ²) Large, independent loan portfolios produce approximately normal aggregate losses, but only if no single loan dominates and correlations are low. If not, explicitly model tail risk instead of relying on CLT. Assuming CLT holds when loans are correlated or a few loans are huge. E.g. a bank with a $1B loan and many $1k loans is not “fine-grained” – CLT fails. Basel notes that violating these assumptions (lumpiness or multiple risk factors) “would result in an incorrect assessment of portfolio risk”. **Normal approximation (CLT)** — valid when summing many i.i.d. variables (small loans, independent). --- **Exact distribution** — e.g. Vasicek’s model or empirical simulation; needed if defaults correlate or portfolio is not fine-grained. CLT’s normal result is a special-case approximation, not always applicable. **No delta.** CLT is a mathematical theorem. Regulatory models like Basel’s IRB build on CLT assumptions, but if portfolio deviates, banks must adjust (e.g. use RWA add-ons).

title: Hypothesis Testing and p-values
one_screen: Hypothesis testing assesses if observed data significantly differ from a specified model (null hypothesis). A *p-value* measures the probability of observing data as extreme as ours if the null hypothesis were true. It is **not** the probability the hypothesis is true.
bodyText: In credit analysis, one might test if a new scorecard has a higher default rate than historical average. The null hypothesis (H₀) could be "new model’s default rate = old rate." After collecting data, compute a test statistic (e.g. difference of proportions) and derive a p-value: the probability of seeing such a difference (or more extreme) by chance if H₀ holds. If p is below a chosen significance level (e.g. 5%), H₀ is rejected, suggesting a real difference. **Common misinterpretation:** p < 0.05 does *not* mean there’s only 5% chance H₀ is true. Instead, it means that if H₀ were true, only 5% of repeated experiments would yield data at least this extreme. StatPearls clarifies: “The p-value is not the probability of the null hypothesis itself. It is the probability that, if the study were repeated infinitely, one would get results at least as extreme as observed.” Thus, p informs us about data extreme-ness under H₀, not the truth of H₀. For example, testing “portfolio default rate > 2%” with sample data: suppose sample default was 2.5%, p = 0.03. This means there’s a 3% chance of seeing ≥2.5% defaults if true rate =2%. We might then conclude rate >2%. But if sample size is small, p can be misleading; also p=0.03 doesn’t prove a big effect, just that result is unlikely by chance. Practically, credit risk model validators use hypothesis tests (often z-tests or chi-square) for things like comparing PDs across time or segments. The permanent rule: set significance (alpha) before testing; treat p-value < alpha as evidence against H₀, but don’t over-interpret it. Statistical significance ≠ business significance: a tiny difference may be statistically significant with large data but irrelevant. Always interpret in context. Use p-values as a measure of data incompatibility with the null, not as proof of hypothesis truth. Treat p<α as grounds to examine assumptions, but also check effect size and practical importance. Believing p=0.03 means “there’s 97% chance this model is superior.” Actually, p=0.03 means “if there were no real difference, only 3% of experiments yield this result”. Don’t confuse p-value with certainty about hypotheses. **p-value** — probability of observing data (or more extreme) under the null hypothesis. --- **Confidence level** — (1–α), e.g. 95% CI means 5% significance; but CI is about parameter range (QNT-05), not the probability that H₀ is false. **No delta.** The logic of hypothesis testing and p-values is the same universally (frequentist inference). Regulatory models may stress statistical rigor (e.g. IRB model validations), but the math doesn’t change by locale. 0.05?" a="No. Failing to reject H₀ (p>0.05) is not proof that the null is true; it just means insufficient evidence against H₀ given sample size." />

title: Confidence Intervals
one_screen: A confidence interval (CI) gives a range of values for an unknown parameter (e.g. portfolio PD) such that, in repeated sampling, a specified percentage (e.g. 95%) of such intervals will contain the true parameter. It quantifies sampling uncertainty around an estimate.
bodyText: After estimating a parameter, say the default rate of a loan grade, we compute a CI. A 95% CI from 1.8% to 2.4% means if we repeated the borrower selection many times, about 95% of those intervals would include the true default rate. Importantly, it doesn’t mean “95% chance the true rate lies in this specific interval.” The true rate is fixed (unknown); the CI’s endpoints are random from sample variance. In credit risk, CIs are crucial. For example, IRB models often use confidence bounds on PDs or LGDs to ensure conservatism. When validating a new PD model, a regulator might require that observed default rates fall within the model’s forecast CI. If 2% forecast with ±0.2% margin, and observed is 2.3%, the interval check helps assess if deviation is within sampling noise or indicates miscalibration. **Calculation:** For large samples, a CI can be approximate normal: estimate ± z*SE, where SE is the standard error of the estimate. For proportion PD, SE = sqrt(p*(1-p)/n). For small samples or rare events, use exact (binomial) or bootstrap CIs. Also, always report confidence level (e.g. 95%) and sample size context. In summary, CI expresses estimation uncertainty: wider if data are sparse or variable, narrower with more/larger data. The permanent rule: always pair point estimates (like PD) with a CI to show reliability. Regulators often look at these intervals when backtesting models. Sample PD = 2.0% (50 defaults/2500 loans) SE = sqrt(0.02*0.98/2500) ≈ 0.009 95% CI ≈ 2.0% ± 1.96*0.9% = [0.22%, 3.78%] Report estimates with their confidence intervals. The interval indicates how much estimation error might exist due to finite data. Misinterpreting CI as probability of parameter. E.g. “We’re 95% sure true PD is between 1.8–2.4%” is wrong. Actually, if we repeated data collection, 95% of such intervals would contain the true PD. **95% confidence interval** — range capturing the true parameter in 95% of repeated samples. --- **Credible interval (Bayesian)** — range where the parameter has 95% probability given the data (Bayesian concept). CI’s guarantee is about the method, not the single interval’s probability. **No delta.** Statistical confidence intervals are universal. Financial regulations (e.g. RBI or ECB validation) may stipulate certain confidence levels, but methodology is the same.

title: Correlation vs Causation; Confounding
one_screen: Correlation means two variables move together; causation means one variable directly influences another. A *confounder* is a hidden common cause that creates a spurious correlation. In credit data, misidentifying causation can lead to wrong risk decisions.
bodyText: For example, a bank might observe that customers with many cellphone lines have higher default rates. This is a correlation. But is having multiple lines causing defaults? Likely not. A confounder like income or employment stability might cause both more phone lines and more default. If we ignorantly treat the phone lines variable as causal, we could erroneously deny credit to people with many phones, which is a mistake. Statistics: we often measure correlation by Pearson’s r (for continuous), or contingency tables for categorical. But high correlation doesn’t prove one causes the other. Another example: when credit scores rose during a boom, did positive sentiment cause better credit history, or did third factors (like unemployment falling) cause both? Without random experimentation, we cannot be sure. **Confounding** is common in observational credit data. Suppose a score model finds married customers default less. Marriage isn’t causing lower defaults per se; perhaps married people are older with steadier jobs (confounders). To claim causation, one needs to control for confounders or use techniques like propensity scoring. Practically, risk analysts should: ask if a predictive factor makes economic sense as a cause, and check if unobserved factors could be driving both. If unsure, treat correlated predictors with caution. For example, IGNORED: days-with-current-employer might correlate with income; controlling for both avoids blaming employer tenure incorrectly. In actual data, observation shows: YearsEmployed ↑ -> DefaultRate ↓ But: YearsEmployed and Income are correlated (r=0.6). Confounder: Income Always question causality claims in credit models. Use domain knowledge and control for confounders to avoid spurious attributions. No matter how strong a correlation, it may be caused by hidden variables. Automatically assuming that a correlated predictor is causal. E.g., “Since region correlates with default, region causes default.” In reality, region may proxy economic conditions (the real cause). Mis-specifying this can lead to misdirected interventions. **Correlation** — statistical association between two variables’ values (e.g. high debt ratio and defaults). --- **Causation** — one variable directly influences the other. They are not the same: correlation is necessary but not sufficient for causation. Always consider other variables that might explain the link. **No delta.** The principle that correlation is not causation is fundamental to statistics. However, regulatory scrutiny may vary: e.g. fair lending laws (in US/EU) demand checking that models do not inadvertently use proxies for protected attributes (a form of confounding fairness).

title: Sampling Biases in Lending
one_screen: In lending analytics, *sampling bias* occurs when collected data systematically exclude certain outcomes. Common biases: **survivorship bias** (ignoring lost/terminated loans) and **selection bias** (e.g. analyzing only accepted applications). These distort estimates like default rates.
bodyText: **Sampling bias:** A sample differs from the true population by design. In credit, a notorious case is “only current customers”: if a bank studies default rates using only customers who renewed their credit cards, it misses those who defaulted or left, underestimating risk. CASRAI warns that bias doesn’t shrink with more data – it leads precisely wrong estimates. **Selection bias:** When the sample is chosen by outcome. For example, analyzing PD using only approved loans ignores applicants who were denied (who might be higher risk). This underestimates risk because we selected out lower-scoring individuals. Another example: surveying customers about repaying loans will naturally exclude those already delinquent or defaulted – giving an overly rosy repayment picture. **Survivorship bias:** A type of sampling bias where only “survivors” are seen. For instance, if a study of corporate bond defaults only includes companies still listed, it misses those that defaulted or delisted. In retail credit: if we only analyze auto loans that have not been repossessed, we ignore those lost deals, again biasing PD down. CASRAI’s classic example: looking only at airplanes that returned (survivors) misleads reinforcement strategy. Similarly, analyzing only ongoing loans ignores those that “didn’t survive” to be included. **Avoidance:** Always define a clear population: e.g. “all loans originated in 2018, tracking until 2021, including those closed by default, pay-off, or charge-off.” Use full origination data, not just current books. If data is truncated (e.g. only current borrowers), acknowledge bias and adjust (maybe via weight or external default statistics). Regulators (e.g. RBI IRB) expect PD models to account for these biases in historical data. Loan Origination cohort 2018 +--------------------+ | All customers | +------+-------------+ | +-> Approved -> Observed loans (used for modeling) | +-> Declined -> (no performance data) <-- selection bias | +-> Never applied Always include all relevant cases in your sample, especially failures. Missing defaulters or rejects biases any risk estimate. Double-check that your data frame contains both “survivors” and “non-survivors” from a cohort. Using only successfully repaid loans to model performance. This creates survivorship bias: only the “winners” are analyzed, making the portfolio look safer than it is. **Survivorship bias** — only survivors of a process are seen (e.g. only extant accounts). --- **Selection bias** — systematic inclusion/exclusion during data collection (e.g. excluding denied applicants). **No delta.** Data representativeness is a universal modeling principle. However, some jurisdictions explicitly emphasize these biases: e.g. the ECB’s IRB guidelines caution against using internal data that exclude defaulted obligors.

title: Linear Regression for Credit Scoring
one_screen: Linear regression models a continuous outcome (like credit line utilization or loss amount) as a weighted sum of predictors. Key assumptions include linearity, independent errors, and homoscedasticity. Coefficients indicate the average change in outcome per unit change in predictor, holding others constant.
bodyText: In regression, we fit a model `y = β₀ + β₁x₁ + ... + βₖxₖ + ε`. For credit analytics, `y` might be a continuous risk measure (e.g. loss given default, log of balance, etc.), and `x` variables could be borrower attributes. The fitting (ordinary least squares) finds β’s minimizing squared residuals. **Assumptions:** (1) Linear relationship: each predictor adds/subtracts constant effect on mean `y`; (2) Independent errors: each loan’s deviation from model is not autocorrelated; (3) Homoscedasticity: error variance constant across `x` values; (4) Errors ~ Normal (for inference). In practice, check residual plots to validate these. If heteroscedastic, use robust SE or transform y (e.g. log). **Interpretation:** A coefficient β indicates that a one-unit increase in that predictor multiplies the outcome by β on the original scale (if y is raw), or adds β to log(y) if log-linear model. E.g., if modelling log-default-loss, `exp(β₁)` approximates multiplicative effect. Always contextualize: e.g. if `x` is credit score, β negative means higher score → lower loss on average. **Example:** Suppose modeling log(outstanding balance) = α + β*(age) + γ*(income) + ε. If β=0.01, each additional year of age raises balance by ~1% (on average). This could be plausible if older borrowers tend to have larger mortgages. **Use in scoring:** Linear regression is less common for binary outcomes (default/no default) – that is logistic (QNT-10). However, linear models help in predicting continuous risks (like loss given default or exposure). They are also a building block for scorecards (though credit scorecards often use logistic or point systems). **Validation:** Check R² (fit quality) but more importantly check predictions vs holdout data. For credit risk, regulators expect residual errors to be uncorrelated with key factors (no omitted variables with pattern). Age Income ... | | +------+------+ | | | v v v Regression model: log(Loss) = β0 + β1*Age + β2*Income + ε Always verify regression assumptions. In credit context, it’s common to transform skewed variables (e.g. take log of balances) so that residuals are more normal/homoscedastic. Interpreting linear model as implying causality. E.g., saying “higher X causes higher risk” just from regression correlation is incorrect without domain insight (see QNT-06). Also, forgetting to check residuals: a high R² does not guarantee unbiased estimates if assumptions fail. **Slope coefficient (β)** — change in the response per unit x, ceteris paribus. --- **Correlation coefficient (r)** — measures linear association between two variables, but is not a regression parameter. High `r` does not directly tell you the slope; regression gives β that predicts y from x. **No delta.** Regression math is universal. However, regulators (like RBI guidelines) may require special considerations (e.g. using macro variables for IFRS9 forecasting models), but that’s about inputs, not the regression method itself.

title: Multicollinearity and VIF
one_screen: *Multicollinearity* occurs when predictors in a regression are highly correlated, inflating coefficient variances and making individual effects hard to separate. The **Variance Inflation Factor (VIF)** quantifies multicollinearity: VIF=(1−R²_j)^(-1) for regressing predictor *j* on others. A VIF>5 (or 10) signals problematic collinearity.
bodyText: In credit models, multicollinearity often arises when using overlapping information: e.g. two credit bureau scores, or income and loan amount. Such redundancy doesn’t harm overall prediction accuracy much, but it makes coefficient estimates unstable. For instance, if income and loan size correlate strongly, including both may lead to neither coefficient being precisely estimated (large SE). To calculate VIF for predictor X_j: regress X_j against all other X’s and get R²_j. Then VIF_j = 1/(1−R²_j). Example: if a predictor has R²=0.9 when regressed on others, VIF=10. This indicates its variance estimate is 10 times what it would be if uncorrelated with others. High VIF means small changes in data can flip the sign or magnitude of β_j. This is dangerous when regulators or stakeholders expect stable interpretability. Remedies: drop or combine correlated variables (e.g. use principal components), or regularization (see QNT-12). But dropping variables may lose predictive info, so trade-off is needed. **VIF interpretation:** - VIF≈1: no correlation with other X’s. - VIF>5: moderate collinearity. - VIF>10: serious collinearity. Often one simplifies by ensuring predictors have pairwise correlations <0.8 or VIFs <5. Check VIFs during regression. If any predictor’s VIF is high (≥10), address it by removal or transformation. Credit-score industry best practice is to avoid multicollinearity so that variable effects are interpretable and stable. Leaving collinear variables in, thinking “it doesn’t matter since model fit is okay.” It *does* matter: if collinearity is ignored, the model can behave erratically on new data or give misleading coefficient signs, which is unacceptable for risk models. **Variance Inflation Factor (VIF)** — measures how much the variance of a coefficient is increased due to collinearity. --- **Standard Error (SE)** — the uncertainty of a coefficient. VIF tells why SE might be high: because variables overlap. VIF is not a direct measure of predictor importance (that’s given by coefficient/SE or other metrics). **No delta.** Multicollinearity is a numerical issue, not jurisdiction-dependent. However, some IRB model validators may scrutinize models for collinearity to ensure stability.

title: Logistic Regression and Credit Scoring
one_screen: Logistic regression is the workhorse for credit scoring (binary default prediction). It models the log-odds of default as a linear function of predictors. Coefficients translate into *odds ratios*, telling how predictors change the odds of default.
bodyText: For binary outcome *Y* (default=1, non-default=0), logistic regression assumes: Here p = P(default|x). Solving gives p = exp(linear)/(1+exp(linear)). This keeps p between 0 and 1. In credit scoring, predictors x are often applicant attributes (income, delinquencies, etc.). **Interpretation:** β_j is the change in log-odds per unit increase in x_j. Exponentiating gives the *odds ratio* (OR): exp(β_j) is how many times the odds multiply when x_j increases by 1. For example, if β_income = -0.2, then OR=exp(-0.2)=0.82, meaning each extra $10k of income (if x_j scaled per 10k) multiplies odds of default by 0.82 (18% reduction). In scorecards, such coefficients are often translated to points. Logistic regression doesn’t assume normal residuals, but assumes linear logit and independent observations. It handles multicollinearity same as linear (high VIF is a problem). Sample size should be adequate: rule of thumb ~10 events per predictor. **Why it’s workhorse:** Because the output is a probability, intuitively meaningful. Regulators and credit officers can interpret “Probability of Default” directly. Also, logistic outputs are monotonic and unbounded in either direction (unlike linear which could predict <0 or >1). Many scorecards use logistic or simplified versions of it. **Industry bins & WOE:** Often continuous predictors are binned and converted to Weight-of-Evidence (WOE) to ensure monotonic relationships. WOE transforms category’s default rates into log-odds, aligning with logistic assumptions. Then a logistic on WOE-encoded features is linear in log-odds, making the model easier to interpret in PD terms. Always express logistic coefficients in odds ratios for interpretation: OR = exp(β). For example, OR<1 means higher x reduces default odds; OR>1 means increases. Double-check that no predicted p<0 or >1 (should never happen in logistic). Misreading coefficients: thinking β itself is the percentage point change in probability. It is not. Only the odds (exp(β)) have the multiplicative effect. E.g. β= -0.1 doesn’t mean 10% drop in PD; it means ~10% drop in odds (OR≈0.90). **Odds** — ratio p/(1-p) of default vs non-default probability. --- **Probability** — p itself (0 to 1). Logistic uses odds in its link. People often mistakenly add β to p directly; the linearity is in log-odds, not in probability. **No delta.** Logistic regression is standard in all jurisdictions for credit scoring. Some regulators (e.g. RBI) allow logistic scorecards for retail IRB models, given interpretability needs. All use the same math.

title: Weight of Evidence (WOE) and Information Value (IV)
one_screen: **Weight of Evidence (WOE):** A transformation of categorical/binned variables for use in logistic models. For each bin/category, WOE = ln(%goods / %bads). It encodes the risk difference of each bin relative to the overall data. **Information Value (IV):** A summary measure of a variable’s predictive power, computed as Σ(bad rate - good rate) * WOE. Credit scoring often bins continuous features into monotonic risk groups, computes WOE and then fits a logistic on those WOE values.
bodyText: Banks commonly use WOE because it yields linear relationships in log-odds space and deals well with missing values. Example: Suppose credit score binned: - Score 1-300: 10% defaults (bads), 90% good => WOE = ln(0.90/0.10)=2.2. - Score 301-600: 5% defaults, 95% good => WOE = ln(0.95/0.05)=2.94. Higher WOE means a bin has relatively more goods (lower default risk). The logistic regression will use these WOE values to model default odds linearly. **IV** is used to rank variable strength: higher IV implies stronger separation between goods/bads. Rough guide: IV<0.02 not useful; 0.1-0.3 medium; >0.5 extremely predictive. It sums the “divergence” of distribution. It’s not regulatory but common industry practice for feature selection. **Why binning:** Continuous variables may have non-linear PD relationships. Binning (e.g. by quantile) and computing WOE enforces piecewise-constant relationship, simplifying model. It also handles missing by treating missing as a separate bin. A caveat: bins should have enough data to avoid volatility. When using WOE, ensure monotonicity: bins should be sorted so that WOE moves consistently (e.g. increasing WOE with score). This avoids non-monotonic risk segments which can cause logistic coefficients to be unstable or non-intuitive. Creating too many bins or bins with small counts. This inflates IV artificially and causes overfitting. Also, forgetting to check monotonic trend: if WOE jumps up then down across bins, it suggests your model may overfit bin boundaries rather than true risk. **WOE** — numeric encoding of bins: ln(%goods/%bads). --- **IV** — aggregate measure of how well a variable’s distribution separates goods/bads. High IV implies big differences in rates across bins. Unlike WOE, IV is a single number per variable. **No delta.** WOE and IV are industry conventions, not mandated by regulators. All jurisdictions use similar methods. However, if under IRB, RBI expects documented binning rationale. IFRS 9 does not specify this detail.

title: Regularisation: Ridge and Lasso
one_screen: *Regularisation* adds a penalty to regression coefficients to prevent overfitting, especially when many predictors or multicollinearity exist. **Ridge (L2)** adds sum of squared coefficients to loss, shrinking them towards zero. **Lasso (L1)** adds sum of absolute values, shrinking and possibly zeroing some coefficients. Which to use depends on goals: ridge keeps all features (shrunk), lasso selects a subset (drives some to zero).
bodyText: In credit modeling, regularisation can improve out-of-sample PD predictions. Ridge (L2) is preferred when many correlated predictors exist (it stabilizes coefficients). Lasso (L1) is useful when you suspect only a few variables matter; it effectively does variable selection by zeroing weaker ones. Often, a hybrid Elastic Net (combination of L1+L2) is used if there’s grouping of correlated features. For example, in a model with dozens of socioeconomic variables (many correlated), ridge would shrink all, reducing variance. If you have hundreds of transactional features (most irrelevant), lasso would pick a smaller subset for simplicity. **Interpretation:** With ridge, coefficients are biased smaller but all remain in model. With lasso, coefficients above threshold become zero (variable dropped). In credit, we must be cautious: lasso’s dropping may run into regulatory issues if dropping variables changes model logic. Usually, final modeler inspects which features lasso kept. **Implementation:** Choose λ (penalty weight) by cross-validation. Larger λ = stronger penalty (smaller coefficients). Compare performance on validation: if too high, model underfits. The permanent rule: regularise to combat overfitting, but always re-express final model in original terms. For some models, especially under IRB, explicit variable reduction might require re-approval. Ridge (L2) for many small signals or multicollinearity; Lasso (L1) when you want feature selection (fewer predictors). Always cross-validate to pick the penalty strength. Blindly using lasso and trusting it removed only noise. It may drop a variable important in reality but slightly less statistically strong. Likewise, too much regularisation (large λ) biases coefficients heavily, harming all predictions. Always check business sense of retained features. **Ridge (L2)** — penalizes square of coefficients; shrinks but keeps variables. --- **Lasso (L1)** — penalizes absolute values; can set some coefficients to zero (feature selection). Both add a term λ∑β² or λ∑|β| respectively to loss. **No delta.** Regularisation is a mathematical technique, not regulated differently. However, some regulatory models may ban black-box tech; explicitly mention if lasso removes key explanatory variables, the resulting model still needs justification of omitted factors.

title: Decision Tree
one_screen: A decision tree recursively splits data by feature thresholds to predict an outcome. It is intuitive and easy to visualise, but a single deep tree often overfits the training data, capturing noise rather than true patterns. Pruning, setting a max depth, or limiting leaf size controls complexity and improves generalisation.
bodyText: A decision tree is a flowchart-like predictive model. Internal nodes test feature values (e.g. “income > ₹50,000?”), branches follow outcomes (Yes/No), and leaves give a prediction (class label or regression value). For example, a credit model might first split borrowers by income, then by past defaults, assigning high default risk to those meeting certain conditions. By partitioning the dataset into homogeneous subsets, a tree fits flexible, non-linear relationships without requiring feature scaling or dummy coding. In credit scoring, trees can capture interactions (e.g. low income * poor history). However, if grown unconstrained, a tree can split until each leaf has few samples, fitting noise and idiosyncrasies. A fully grown tree has low bias but very high variance: it may classify every training case correctly but fail on new data. To mitigate over-complex trees, practitioners use **pruning** (removing branches that add little predictive power) or stop splitting when few samples remain. Cross-validation can determine optimal tree size. Trees are inherently “white-box” models: one can trace the path for a given prediction, e.g. “Income was low collateral insufficient decline loan.” This makes them interpretable, a desirable property in credit risk. +------------------+ | Income > 50k? | +----+------+------+ / \ Yes No | | +-----------+ +-----------+ | Defaulted? | | Collat. > | +-----------+ | 5k? | / \ +-----+-----+ Yes No / \ | | Yes No [Decline] [Approve] [Approve] [Decline] Each split partitions data to increase purity (e.g. reduce variance or Gini impurity). Every split is a simple rule on one feature, building a decision path to a final prediction. Assuming a deeper or more complex tree always improves results. In fact, very deep trees usually overfit: training accuracy rises while test accuracy falls. **Decision tree** — a single model with branches of feature-threshold tests leading to predictions, easy to interpret. --- **Random forest** — an ensemble of many trees (each on a random sample), where the final prediction is an aggregate (majority vote or average). A random forest is not one big tree, but many small trees combined to reduce variance. **No delta.** The concept of a decision tree is mathematical and independent of regulation.

title: Random Forest
one_screen: A random forest constructs an ensemble of decision trees on bootstrapped samples of the data and averages (or votes on) their predictions. This “bagging” approach greatly reduces a single tree’s variance, making the model more stable and accurate, especially on noisy credit data.
bodyText: Random forests apply the bootstrap-aggregation (bagging) technique to decision trees. We draw \(m\) random samples (with replacement) from the training data, train a separate tree on each sample, then combine the results. In classification (e.g. default/no default) the forest takes a majority vote; in regression (e.g. loss given default) it averages outputs. Additionally, at each split, a random forest only considers a random subset of features (e.g. \(\sqrt{p}\) of \(p\) total) to decide the split. This feature subsampling de-correlates the trees, further reducing variance. The ensemble is thus robust: even if some trees overfit their sample, the majority smooths out idiosyncrasies. The model requires minimal preprocessing: features of different scales or missing values are handled inherently by trees. In a credit scoring example, we might build 100 trees on different bootstrap samples of loan records. Each tree might split on various borrower attributes. The forest’s predicted probability of default is the average of all trees’ PD outputs. This typically outperforms one tree, as shown in practice: adding more trees (up to a point) usually lowers test error. Importantly, random forests can provide a measure of *out-of-bag* error (error on samples not included in each bootstrap), which serves as an internal validation. +------------------+ | Training Data | +---------+--------+ | +-----------------+-----------------+ | | | +-------+ +-------+ +-------+ |Sample1| |Sample2| ... |SampleM| +---+---+ +---+---+ +---+---+ | | | v v v +-------+ +-------+ +-------+ |Tree 1 | |Tree 2 | ... |Tree M | +-------+ +-------+ +-------+ | | | v v v Pred1 Pred2 PredM \ ... / ... / \ / / +------------------------+ | Aggregate (avg or vote)| +------------------------+ | Final Prediction A random forest uses *all* trees at inference, so the final prediction is an average (regression) or majority vote (classification) of many decorrelated trees. This ensemble effect dramatically lowers variance versus one tree. Assuming a random forest cannot overfit. In practice, if trees are too deep or features too many, forests can still overfit noise. Also, forests reduce variance but do little to correct bias: if no tree can capture an effect, the ensemble won’t either. **Random forest** — an ensemble that builds many trees on random samples (bagging) and aggregates their outputs for robustness. --- **Gradient boosting** — an ensemble built sequentially, where each tree is trained to correct the residuals of the prior ensemble. Unlike a random forest’s parallel bagging, boosting trains trees one after another. **No delta.** Random forests are a universal statistical technique with no jurisdiction-specific differences.

title: Gradient Boosting
one_screen: Gradient boosting builds a strong predictive model by sequentially adding trees that each fit the residual errors of the ensemble so far. The final model is a weighted sum of many simple trees, tuned by a learning rate. This approach often achieves high accuracy on tabular risk data, which explains why it is a dominant method in credit modeling.
bodyText: In gradient boosting, we start with a simple model (often predicting the mean outcome). Then we iteratively train new decision trees on the *residuals* (errors) of the current model. Each tree’s predictions are scaled by a learning rate (shrinkage) and added to the ensemble. Formally, the algorithm minimizes a loss function (e.g. squared error or logistic loss) via gradient descent: each new tree targets the negative gradient of loss with respect to the model’s predictions. Popular implementations like XGBoost or LightGBM use shallow trees (e.g. max depth 3–5) to keep each tree weak and prevent overfitting. For example, to predict loan default probability, we might start with a base prediction of 0.1. The first tree learns where this is underestimating defaults and pushes those cases higher. The next tree then corrects remaining errors, and so on. After 100 trees, the model might be much more accurate than logistic regression, especially capturing non-linear and interaction effects. Gradient boosted trees excel on credit data because they handle mixed variable types and missing values easily, and can learn complex patterns that linear models miss. +----------------------------+ | Initialize model output | | (e.g. mean of target) | +-------------+--------------+ | Repeat for t = 1..T: +-------------v--------------+ | Compute residuals = | | (target - current model) | +-------------+--------------+ | +-------------v--------------+ | Fit new tree to residuals | +-------------+--------------+ | +-------------v--------------+ | Update model: | | add scaled predictions | | (old model + lr * tree) | +-------------+--------------+ | +----------------------------+ | Updated ensemble model | +----------------------------+ Each new tree in boosting improves the model by focusing on what previous trees missed. The trees are combined additively: final prediction = initial + shrinkage×tree1 + shrinkage×tree2 + … (often in log-odds for classification). Ignoring the learning rate or early stopping. A very small learning rate requires many trees (long training), while a large rate or too many trees can easily overfit. Always validate the number of trees and shrinkage on hold-out data. **Gradient boosting** — an ensemble that fits trees sequentially to residuals, adding them to the model in a stagewise fashion. --- **AdaBoost** — another boosting method that reweights misclassified samples instead of fitting residuals; it focuses on misclassified points and uses weighted voting, rather than explicit gradients. **No delta.** Gradient boosting’s mathematics is universal; no regulator prescribes or forbids its use.

title: Feature Importance vs Explanation
one_screen: Feature importance scores rank variables by their overall influence on model predictions, but they do not explain individual decisions. In contrast, local explanation methods (like SHAP values) allocate credit to features for a specific prediction. Feature importance is a global summary metric; it does not show how a change in a feature value will move the prediction for a particular loan.
bodyText: Global feature importance (e.g. total gain or split frequency in a tree, or magnitude of coefficients in a linear model) measures each feature’s average effect on model performance. For instance, a credit score might have the highest importance in predicting default rates on average across all borrowers. However, this does not explain why any one borrower was classified as default or not. Importance reflects correlation with the target, not causation or individual impact. Moreover, importance can be misleading if features are correlated: one might appear unimportant simply because another correlated feature “soaked up” its effect. Local explanations, by contrast, break down a single prediction. For example, a SHAP (Shapley) value tells us how much a borrower’s income and history contribute to that borrower’s predicted default probability. Feature importance might list “Income: 0.4, Balance: 0.3, Age: 0.1”, meaning on average income was most influential. But it won’t reveal that in one case a high income actually lowered that borrower’s risk by 5%. Feature importance is useful for feature selection or understanding model trends; explanations are necessary for interpreting individual credit decisions (often a regulatory requirement). Global model perspective: Model training on full dataset | Compute feature importances (e.g. total gain per feature) | Importance ranking Local prediction perspective: Single borrower data -> Model prediction | Explain prediction (SHAP values, etc.) | Contribution of each feature to this instance Feature importance scores are an aggregate, global measure. They tell *which features matter most overall*, but not *how* they influence a given prediction. Assuming a high importance feature always increases predictions or that it explains individual cases. For example, “LoanAmount” might be important globally, but the importance metric alone cannot say if a particular high loan amount raises or lowers risk for a specific applicant. **Feature importance** — global ranking of features by average contribution to the model’s performance. It is an aggregate statistic, not an explanation of any single outcome. --- **SHAP (Shapley) values** — local explanation values that decompose a specific prediction into contributions from each feature. They explain individual decisions, unlike global importance. **No delta.** The distinction between global importance and local explanation is mathematical and does not vary by jurisdiction. Regulators universally want model explanations for individual decisions, even if different names are used.

title: SHAP (Shapley Additive Explanations)
one_screen: SHAP assigns each feature a “contribution” value for a specific prediction, based on cooperative game-theoretic Shapley values. These values guarantee local accuracy (they sum to the model output minus a baseline) and consistency (features that change a prediction more get higher attribution). SHAP provides interpretable, additive explanations for individual credit scores.
bodyText: SHAP (SHapley Additive exPlanations) treats each feature as a “player” in a game whose payout is the model’s prediction. The SHAP value of a feature for one observation is the average change in prediction when adding that feature, across all combinations of features. Practically, tree-based models (random forest, boosting) can use TreeExplainer to compute SHAP exactly in polynomial time. The result is that for a given borrower, we get a breakdown: e.g. “+0.05 default probability from low credit score, –0.02 from high income, …, totaling the predicted PD of 0.12.” Plotting SHAP values across many loans gives a global view, while individual SHAP explanations show why each decision was made. Crucially, SHAP values satisfy properties of fairness: efficiency (contributions sum to output), and consistency (if one model increases a feature’s effect, its SHAP value won’t decrease). This makes them theoretically attractive for interpretability. In credit risk, regulators expect that each driver of a decision can be explained. SHAP is one way to meet this interpretability requirement without sacrificing the accuracy of complex ensembles. It allows both global insight (feature importance as average absolute SHAP) and local explanations. SHAP values for one prediction sum to the difference between the model’s output and a baseline. This ensures the explanation is exact (local accuracy). Each feature’s SHAP indicates how much it pushed the score up or down. Treating SHAP as proving causality. SHAP distributes contributions *given the model*, not necessarily reflecting causal effects. Also, using a too-narrow background dataset can bias SHAP values. **SHAP value** — a local explanation: the contribution of a feature to one specific prediction. It is computed under the model’s logic. --- **Feature importance** — a global metric summarizing a model. Unlike SHAP, it does not decompose individual predictions and may miss interactions. **No delta.** SHAP is a mathematical construct; regulatory emphasis on explainability is common (e.g. Fed SR11-7, PRA SS3/16) but does not alter SHAP’s definition.

title: Stationarity
one_screen: A time series is *stationary* if its statistical properties (mean, variance, autocorrelations) do not change over time. Stationarity is required for many modeling techniques (e.g. ARIMA), because these assume the series has no trend or changing volatility. If a credit-related series (like default rate) exhibits trends or evolving variance, it must be transformed (differenced, detrended) before such methods apply.
bodyText: In a stationary series, the average and variability remain roughly constant. There is no long-term upward or downward drift (no trend) and no changing seasonality. For example, a stationary default rate might oscillate around 2% with similar magnitude fluctuations each period. If instead default rates are rising in a credit cycle, the series is non-stationary. Non-stationarity can lead to spurious or unreliable forecasts: for instance, ARIMA models assume consistent autocorrelations over time. To test stationarity, analysts use plots (constant mean/variance visually) and tests like Augmented Dickey-Fuller. If non-stationary, one may *difference* the data (subtract each value from its predecessor) or remove a deterministic trend to achieve stationarity. A stationary transformed series is then suitable for ARMA/ARIMA modeling. +----------------+ | Original series| (may have trend/seasonality) +--------+-------+ | Check stationarity: | +-----+-----+ | | Non-stationary Stationary | | | v | +---------------+ | | Model directly | | +---------------+ | v Transform (difference, detrend) | v +----------------+ | Transformed TS | |(now approx stationary)| +----------------+ | +--------------+ | Fit ARIMA | +--------------+ Stationarity means “no trend, constant mean and variance over time.” In practice, if the mean or variance changes (e.g. rising loan volumes or volatility), remove these effects before modeling. Treating a visibly trending or seasonal series as stationary. Running ARIMA without differencing when data have trend will yield misleading parameters. Always test a series (plot it and use unit-root tests) before assuming stationarity. **Stationarity** — a property of a time series (constant statistical properties over time). --- **White noise** — a special stationary series where each value is random with zero autocorrelation. All white noise series are stationary, but not all stationary series are white noise (white noise has no structure to exploit). **No delta.** Stationarity is a mathematical property. Regulatory models (like CIRB) don’t change this: all quantitative models assume stationarity or explicitly handle non-stationarity.

title: Trend and Seasonality (Decomposition)
one_screen: A time series often contains a *trend* (long-term increase/decrease) and *seasonality* (regular periodic fluctuations). Decomposing the series separates these components plus a residual. For example, credit losses might rise over years (trend) but have higher losses in certain months (seasonal). Identifying and removing trend/seasonality yields a stationary residual suitable for modeling.
bodyText: The **trend** is the smooth, non-random movement over time (upward or downward). Seasonality is a pattern that repeats every fixed period (e.g. every 12 months or every quarter). Decomposition methods (additive or multiplicative) express the series as `Observed = Trend + Seasonality + Residual` (or multiplied if percentage effects). In practice, one might use moving averages or STL (seasonal-trend decomposition) to estimate these. For instance, a bank’s monthly default rate may show a small upward trend due to economic slowdown, plus spikes every year-end (seasonality). By isolating the trend, forecasters can model the remaining (stationary) part more easily. Original Series | v +-----------------+ | Decompose into: | | - Trend | | - Seasonality | | - Remainder | +--------+--------+ | +----+----+ | | Trend Season + Residual Seasonality can be additive (constant amount) or multiplicative (proportional). When modeling, seasonal series may require seasonal differencing (e.g. subtract value from same month last year) or inclusion of seasonal ARIMA terms. Credit data with seasonal effects (e.g. holiday spending) must handle these patterns explicitly. Trend is a long-term direction in the data; seasonality is a repeated cycle of fixed length. Always remove or model these before applying models that assume stationarity. Confusing a slowly changing trend for seasonality (or vice versa). For example, attributing a monotonically rising credit loss rate to seasonality can mislead forecasts. Always inspect plots at multiple time scales. **Trend** — a general upward or downward movement over time. --- **Seasonality** — a periodic pattern repeating at fixed intervals (like higher purchases every Dec). Trend affects the baseline over time, seasonality oscillates around that baseline. **No delta.** The concepts of trend and seasonality are mathematical. Forecasters in any jurisdiction must address them identically.

title: Autocorrelation and Partial Autocorrelation
one_screen: The autocorrelation function (ACF) measures how correlated a time series is with itself at various lags. The partial autocorrelation function (PACF) measures correlation at a lag after removing the effects of shorter lags. Analysts use ACF/PACF plots to identify ARIMA model orders: an AR(p) process has a PACF that cuts off after lag p, while an MA(q) process has an ACF that cuts off after lag q.
bodyText: Specifically, the ACF at lag \(k\) is the Pearson correlation between the series and itself shifted \(k\) periods. A slow decay in the ACF suggests strong autocorrelation (often indicating non-stationarity or an AR component). The PACF at lag \(k\) adjusts for all lags 1..\(k-1\), isolating the direct effect of lag \(k\). In practice, one plots ACF and PACF with confidence bands. For example, if credit default counts show correlation at 1 and 2 month lags but drop to near zero at higher lags, the ACF would have spikes at 1 and 2 then fall off. The PACF might spike at lag 1 and cut off, indicating an AR(1). Time series data --[compute correlations]--> ACF/PACF values at lags 1,2,... (ACF considers all lag interactions, PACF filters out shorter ones) Interpreting these plots guides model choice. A sharp cutoff (near zero correlation beyond lag \(p\)) in PACF suggests an AR(\(p\)); a cutoff in ACF suggests an MA(\(q\)). In seasonal data, repeated ACF spikes can indicate periodicity (e.g. monthly cycle). ACF shows how past values influence future values cumulatively, while PACF shows only the direct lagged influence. Use ACF/PACF to help choose ARIMA orders: e.g. AR(p) if PACF cuts off at p. Reading random noise or one-off spikes as significant. Autocorrelation estimates can be noisy, especially with small samples or a trend. Always check significance bands and consider transformations if needed. **Autocorrelation (ACF)** — correlation of the series with itself at lag k, including indirect effects of shorter lags. --- **Partial autocorrelation (PACF)** — the autocorrelation at lag k after removing contributions from all intermediate lags (1 to k-1). **No delta.** ACF/PACF are statistical tools independent of regulatory context. Their interpretation in model selection is the same everywhere.

title: ARIMA and SARIMA
one_screen: An ARIMA(\(p,d,q\)) model combines autoregressive terms (AR), integration (I – differencing), and moving average terms (MA) to model a time series. The series is differenced \(d\) times to remove non-stationarity, then an ARMA(\(p,q\)) model fits the result. SARIMA extends this by adding seasonal AR, I, MA terms with seasonal period \(m\), allowing modeling of both trend and seasonal dependencies.
bodyText: ARIMA stands for AutoRegressive Integrated Moving Average. In an ARIMA model, \(p\) is the number of AR terms (lags of the dependent variable), \(d\) is the number of differences to make the series stationary, and \(q\) is the number of MA terms (lags of the forecast error).
