For example, ARIMA(1,1,1) on default rates means first difference the series (to remove trend), then fit one AR and one MA component on the differenced series. SARIMA (Seasonal ARIMA) adds seasonal orders \((P,D,Q)_m\): \(P\) seasonal AR lags, \(D\) seasonal differences, and \(Q\) seasonal MA lags, with period \(m\) (e.g. 12 for monthly data). For instance, SARIMA(0,1,1)\(\times\)(0,1,1)\(_{12}\) is a common model for monthly data: it differences once to remove trend and once seasonally (lag 12), with one AR and one MA at lag 12. The forecasting equation is linear in the lagged differenced series and lagged errors. If defaults show both a trend and an annual cycle, SARIMA can capture both. Model orders are typically chosen using ACF/PACF plots and information criteria (AIC/BIC). Original series Y_t (possibly non-stationary) | (difference d times) v Differenced series Δ^d Y_t | (if seasonal, difference every m) v Stationary series | v Fit ARMA(p,q) (plus seasonal ARMA if SARIMA) | v Forecasts (by extrapolating lags of series and errors) ARIMA(p,d,q) = difference \(d\) times to stationarize, then fit ARMA(p,q). Seasonal ARIMA adds seasonal differences and terms for period \(m\). Always difference non-stationary series before modeling. Forgetting to difference a non-stationary series (taking \(d=0\) when a trend exists) or neglecting seasonality. This leads to poor model fit and biased forecasts. Always test for unit roots and seasonal cycles. **ARIMA** — an ARIMA model always includes an integration (I) component; if \(d=0\), it reduces to ARMA. --- **ARMA** — a special case of ARIMA with \(d=0\). ARMA assumes the series is already stationary (no differencing). **No delta.** The ARIMA framework is a mathematical model. Regulatory constraints (e.g. IRB validation) do not change its formulation, although practitioners may prefer simpler models if interpretability is required.

title: Forecast Backtesting (Rolling-Origin, MAPE/RMSE, Baseline)
one_screen: Forecast backtesting evaluates a model’s predictions on hold-out future data using time-aware cross-validation. Rolling-origin (a.k.a. walk-forward) splits move the training end forward in time and test on the next period. Performance is measured by metrics like Mean Absolute Percentage Error (MAPE) and Root Mean Square Error (RMSE). Results must always be compared against a naive baseline (e.g. last-period carry-forward) to gauge real improvement.
bodyText: In rolling-origin evaluation, we simulate real forecasting: train on an initial window, predict the next \(h\) steps, record the error, then expand (or slide) the window forward and repeat. This avoids peeking into the future (random k-fold cross-validation would leak information). For example, use loans data from 2015–2018 to predict 2019 losses, then re-train on 2015–2019 to predict 2020 losses, etc. Errors from each fold are aggregated to assess model stability. Common metrics include RMSE (root mean square error) and MAPE (mean absolute percentage error). RMSE = \(\sqrt{\frac{1}{n}\sum (forecast - actual)^2}\) penalises large errors more heavily. MAPE = \(\frac{100\%}{n}\sum |\frac{forecast - actual}{actual}|\) scales error by actual values; it is easy to interpret but blows up when actuals near zero. Always be aware of the failure modes: MAPE is undefined for zero actuals and may be skewed by small denominators. Crucially, compare the model’s scores to a simple benchmark. A typical naive baseline for time series is “no change” (e.g. forecast \(Y_{t+1} = Y_t\)) or “seasonal naive” (forecast equals last year’s value for seasonal data). If a model’s MAPE or RMSE is not substantially better than the baseline, it may not be useful. For instance, if credit volume declines by 1% each month, a model should beat the baseline forecast of “same as last month.” Time Axis: [Train (t=1..T)] => Forecast [T+1 .. T+h] => Evaluate error then Expand window to T+h, repeat Always reserve future time for testing. Use a sequential backtesting (rolling-origin) that mimics real deployment. Compute forecast errors and compare to a naive model’s error. Metrics alone are meaningless without a baseline. Performing standard k-fold validation (random splits) on time series. This lets future information leak into training folds, giving overly optimistic error estimates. Always use time-ordered splits instead. **MAPE** — Mean Absolute Percentage Error: measures relative error (%). Can exaggerate errors when actual values are small. --- **RMSE** — Root Mean Squared Error: measures absolute error magnitude. Penalises large deviations more. **No delta.** Forecast evaluation is a general statistical procedure. Regulatory guidelines (e.g. IFRS 9 forecast validation) endorse testing forecasts against actuals and baselines, but the methods (rolling backtest, RMSE/MAPE) are the same everywhere.

title: Train / Validation / Test / Out-of-Time Samples
one_screen: Credit models must be evaluated on data that mimic real use. We split data into training (for fitting), validation (for tuning), and test (for performance). Crucially, one should hold out an **out-of-time** (future) sample that the model never sees, to measure true predictive power. In credit, using only random splits risks leakage across economic cycles, so time-based splitting is preferred.
bodyText: A **training** set is used to estimate model parameters. A **validation** set (or multiple cross-validation folds) is used to tune hyperparameters (e.g. depth, regularisation). A final **test** set (or sets) gives unbiased performance on data not used in fitting or tuning. An **out-of-time (OOT)** sample is a test set from a later period (e.g. loans originated in a later year) that simulates the model in production. For example, train on 2015–2017 loans, validate on 2018 loans, and test/OOT on 2019 loans. This ensures the model is evaluated on truly unseen, forward-looking data. Because credit risk often varies over time (economic up/downturns), it is misleading to randomly shuffle all data. Instead, split chronologically: use earlier periods for training/validation and later periods as test. This avoids look-ahead: the model never “knows” future conditions during training. Regulators expect performance on an OOT sample; it reveals if the model generalises across vintage shifts (e.g. a model trained in growth must still score well in recession). Time-line: [Train: 2015-2017] [Validate: 2018] [Test/OOT: 2019] build model choose model evaluate model Reserve the latest data (out-of-time) as the primary test. Use only past data for development and validation to mimic deployment. Using future information in training. For example, randomly splitting data across years can mix up season/economy effects. Always ensure that validation and test sets occur later in time than training data. **Validation set** — used during model development (e.g. hyperparameter tuning). --- **Test (evaluation) set** — held out until final model is chosen, used for final performance. Out-of-time is one type of test set (a test period in the future). **No delta.** The principle of time-based splitting is universal. Banking regulators in all jurisdictions (e.g. Fed, RBI) emphasize out-of-time testing, as future prediction is the model’s true purpose.

title: Data Leakage
one_screen: Data leakage happens when a model’s training data inadvertently includes information that would not be available in practice at the time of prediction. This gives misleadingly good performance on training and validation, but fails in production. In credit, a common mistake is using future borrower information (like a snapshot of end-of-year balance) to predict a loan’s early default – this leaks the outcome into features.
bodyText: There are two main leakage types: *target leakage*, where predictors include the outcome itself (or its proxies), and *train-test contamination*, where observations in the test period influence training (e.g. shuffling time series). For example, if we include “*ever defaulted*” status (logged after six months) as an input to predict one-year default, the model essentially sees part of the answer. Another example: mixing borrowers from 2019 (test year) into 2018 training can let the model indirectly learn future trends. To avoid leakage, ensure each feature is computable from information available at model decision time. In credit scoring, use only origination attributes or lagged variables. Rigorously align time: treat all data as of a cutoff date. For instance, if predicting default within a year, use only features known at loan issuance. Data pipelines should separate historical features from label construction. Finally, always evaluate on truly unseen data (see QNT-23) – a sharp drop from training to test performance is a red flag for leakage or overfitting. +--------------+ +---------------+ | Raw Dataset | | Good Practice | +------+-------+ +-------+-------+ | | Select features (no future info) Train/test split by time | | v v +--------------+ +---------------+ | Model Build | | Prediction | +--------------+ +---------------+ Never include any variable that cannot be known at scoring time. Ask, “Would this feature be available in real-time?” If not, omit or shift it. Including any proxy of the target. For example, “balance after 1 year” to predict default in that year looks innocent but is label leakage. Also beware of merging data incorrectly (e.g. including post-default loan closure status). **Data leakage** — model sees future or target-related information in training, giving overly optimistic accuracy. --- **Overfitting** — model is too complex for the signal in training data (but without artificial leaks). Both can cause test drop-offs, but leakage violates causality. **No delta.** All jurisdictions expect no data leakage in model development. Regulatory model validation (e.g. AIRB guidance) specifically checks that feature timing is correct.

title: Overfitting vs Underfitting
one_screen: **Overfitting** occurs when a model learns noise or spurious details in the training data, capturing patterns that do not generalise. **Underfitting** is when a model is too simple to capture the underlying signal, leaving systematic errors. The goal is a model of balanced complexity: low bias (good fit) without excessive variance (over-precision).
bodyText: Overfitting often appears with very flexible models on limited data. For instance, a deep decision tree or a high-degree polynomial might perfectly classify every sample by carving the feature space finely, but will perform poorly on new data. Symptoms of overfitting include much higher accuracy (or lower error) on training data than on validation/test. Underfitting happens with overly simple models: e.g. linear regression on a clearly nonlinear relationship yields poor fit both on train and test, with high bias. Bias-variance tradeoff underlies this: simple models have high bias and low variance (stable but inaccurate), complex models have low bias and high variance (accurate on train, erratic on new). In credit modeling, overfit models may pick up on quirks of one portfolio and fail on another vintage. Underfit models (like a too-simple PD formula) might miss obvious risk factors entirely. Cross-validation on time-based splits (QNT-22/QNT-23) helps detect both: if training error is low but test error is high, that’s likely overfitting. Model complexity --> Underfit (high bias) ---> Just right ---> Overfit (high variance) Regularisation (limiting complexity, pruning trees, L1/L2 penalties) and sufficient data are key to avoiding overfitting. Underfitting is remedied by adding relevant features or increasing model flexibility. Seek the simplest model that achieves acceptable performance. Every model has a bias-variance tradeoff: increasing complexity reduces bias but increases variance, and vice versa. Chasing a perfect training score (e.g. 100% accuracy) at the expense of generalization. Removing regularisation or adding unnecessary features in hopes of squeezing out a bit more fit often causes worse real-world performance. **Overfitting** — model has captured random noise or idiosyncrasies in training data (high variance). --- **Underfitting** — model is too simple, missing important patterns in the data (high bias). **No delta.** The bias-variance concept is universal. In regulatory terms, an overfit internal model fails validation; an underfit model might under-predict capital needs. All regulators emphasize balance via validation.

title: Documentation Standards for Models
one_screen: Thorough documentation is mandatory: it records the model’s purpose, data sources, methodology, assumptions, performance, and usage. Regulators (Fed, PRA, RBI, EBA) all require clear documentation so that the model can be validated and reproduced. Good documentation ensures continuity, accountability, and transparency in model risk management.
bodyText: Model documentation should include a description of the model’s objective (e.g. “estimate 1-year PD for mortgage portfolio”), data inputs (definition, source, period), transformations, algorithms, and parameter choices. It must detail development decisions (feature engineering, binning, regularisation), performance metrics on development/validation/OOT sets, and limitations. Assumptions (e.g. stability of economic conditions) should be explicit. The documentation also outlines how the model is used (deployment, decision thresholds) and maintenance plan. Regulators expect enough detail to reproduce results: for example, Fed guidance says an effective process “begins with a clear statement of purpose” and that model development involves explicit assumptions. The PRA similarly requires detailed documentation (even from vendors) “sufficient to validate the model’s use”. In practice, documentation may be a written report and annotated code. It should evolve with the model (version control) and be reviewed periodically. Incomplete documentation is a frequent model validation finding. Banks should follow templates (e.g. internal model policy or SS11/13 guidelines) ensuring all sections are covered. Thorough documentation is not just bureaucracy: it captures the business context and justification for each model choice, preventing the “black box” problem. Document *everything*: purpose, data, methodology, parameters, results, assumptions, validation, and intended use. This should be in a permanent model report and supported by traceable code. Assuming code comments or an informal narrative suffice. Documentation must be formal and comprehensive. A common mistake is to omit rationales (“why this feature?”) or validation results. Regulators will flag missing sections. **Model documentation** — a detailed report created by developers (data descriptions, logic, results). --- **Validation report** — an independent assessment by a separate party. It is not a substitute for documentation but relies on it. Developers must still document the model fully. **No delta.** Principles are consistent globally. The Fed’s SR11-7, the PRA’s model guidance, RBI’s risk model norms and IFRS9 guidance all emphasize documentation. For instance, the PRA’s recent policy explicitly aligns IRB documentation requirements with model risk principles.

title: Relational Model & Table Keys
one_screen: The relational model organizes data into structured tables (relations) with rows and columns, using keys to connect data across tables. Each table represents an entity (e.g. **Loan**, **Customer**), rows are records, and columns are fields. A **primary key** is a unique identifier for each row (cannot be NULL). A **foreign key** in one table references a primary key in another to link related data (e.g. an *Account* table has a CustomerID referencing the *Customer* table). This design avoids redundancy (no repeated customer details in every loan row) and enforces data integrity through relationships.
bodyText: The *Loan Book* in banking is not a single table: loans have borrowers, products, schedules, etc. Each aspect lives in its own table with keys linking them. For example, a *Facility* table may link to multiple *Account* rows (one-to-many), and accounts link to *Exposure* or *Transaction* tables. Keys ensure SQL queries join these tables reliably. +-----------+ +----------+ +-------------+ | Facility | | Account | | Transaction | +-----------+ +----------+ +-------------+ | FacilityID| 1 M | AccountID| 1 M | TransID | | ... |-------| FacID FK |-------| AccountID FK| +-----------+ +----------+ +-------------+ Every table should define a **primary key** column(s) that uniquely identifies each row. Putting unrelated data in one wide table (no keys) or not enforcing uniqueness can lead to corruption (e.g. duplicate loan records). **Primary Key** — uniquely identifies a row in its table (no duplicates, no NULLs). --- **Foreign Key** — references a primary key in another table, establishing a link.

title: SELECT, WHERE, and ORDER BY Basics
one_screen: In SQL, `SELECT` chooses columns (fields) to return, `WHERE` filters rows based on conditions, and `ORDER BY` sorts the output.
bodyText: For example, on an *Exposure* table, one might retrieve loan amounts and borrower IDs for high-risk loans: Here `SELECT LoanID, Principal, BorrowerID` picks columns, `WHERE RiskRating = 'High'` filters rows to high-risk ones, and `ORDER BY Principal DESC` sorts the resulting loans by size (largest first). The `WHERE` clause applies conditions (e.g. numerical comparisons, string matches) to each row; only rows meeting all conditions appear in the result. After filtering, `ORDER BY` arranges the rows by one or more columns. Without `ORDER BY`, SQL does not guarantee any specific row order. If a specific ordering is needed, always include an `ORDER BY` clause. By default, results are unordered. Omitting a `WHERE` filter can return huge result sets. Ensure conditions are correct; unintended broad filters (e.g. `WHERE 1=1`) can slow the query and return irrelevant data. **WHERE** — filters rows before grouping or sorting (applies to individual rows). --- **ORDER BY** — sorts the final result rows (after filtering). **No delta.** The semantics of `SELECT`, `WHERE`, and `ORDER BY` are standard SQL across jurisdictions.

title: Aggregation with GROUP BY and HAVING
one_screen: The `GROUP BY` clause groups rows by column values for aggregate calculations, and the `HAVING` clause filters those groups.
bodyText: For instance, to summarize a loan portfolio, one might compute total outstanding by product: This splits the data by each `ProductType` (group), then `SUM` is applied per group. Often combined with `COUNT`, `AVG`, etc. To filter on aggregate values (e.g. only products with large totals), use `HAVING`: This returns only products where the summed balance exceeds a threshold. Note `HAVING` comes after grouping, unlike `WHERE` which filters rows before grouping. All non-aggregated columns in the `SELECT` list must appear in `GROUP BY`. Omitting required `GROUP BY` columns (or aggregating every column) causes SQL errors. Also, forgetting `HAVING` conditions when needed means large groups won’t be filtered. **WHERE** — filters individual rows before grouping. --- **HAVING** — filters entire groups after aggregation. **No delta.** Aggregation with `GROUP BY`/`HAVING` is consistent across SQL dialects. [threshold]`." />

title: SQL Joins (inner, left, right, full)
one_screen: SQL `JOIN` combines rows from two tables based on matching column values. An *INNER JOIN* yields only rows with matches in both tables, while *LEFT/RIGHT/OUTER JOIN* include all rows from one side (and NULLs for the other).
bodyText: For example, joining a *Facility* table to its *Account* table: each facility (one side) may link to multiple accounts (many side). An inner join lists only facilities that have accounts, whereas a left join lists all facilities with matching accounts (NULL account fields if none). Beware of **fan-out**: joining a 1:M relationship will duplicate the "one" side row for each "many" side row, potentially inflating counts. Always ensure join keys are correct and understand cardinality. +---------+ +---------+ | Table A | | Table B | +---------+ +---------+ \ / \ JOIN / \ / +-----------+ | Result | +-----------+ Always specify an `ON` condition (join key) to match rows. For example: `ON Facilities.FacID = Accounts.FacID`. Forgetting the join condition (or typo) leads to a Cartesian product (every A with every B). Also, joining on the wrong key can cause hidden duplicates (fan-out). **INNER JOIN** — returns only rows where keys match in both tables. --- **CROSS JOIN** — returns Cartesian product (every row of A with every row of B), no key condition. **No delta.** JOIN semantics (INNER, LEFT, RIGHT, FULL) are standard SQL.

title: Set Operations (UNION, INTERSECT, EXCEPT)
one_screen: SQL set operators combine result sets like mathematical sets. `UNION` stacks rows from two queries (duplicates removed by default). `UNION ALL` includes duplicates. `INTERSECT` returns only rows present in both queries. `EXCEPT` (or `MINUS`) returns rows in the first query that are not in the second.
bodyText: Example: to list all unique borrower IDs from two legacy loan tables: This yields each ID once. To find IDs present in both tables: All SELECTs combined by UNION/INTERSECT/EXCEPT must have the same number of columns and compatible types. Forgetting that `UNION` removes duplicates; use `UNION ALL` if you need to preserve them. Also ensure column order and types match. **UNION** — appends rows from queries into one result (distinct by default). --- **JOIN** — combines columns from tables based on a key. **No delta.** Set operations behave the same in standard SQL for all jurisdictions.

title: Subqueries vs. CTEs (Common Table Expressions)
one_screen: A *subquery* (nested query) is an inline SELECT within another query, whereas a *CTE* (WITH clause) defines a named temporary result set you can reference in the main query. CTEs improve readability for complex logic and can be referenced multiple times.
bodyText: For example, instead of nesting multiple subqueries, use a CTE: This defines `RecentLoans` once, then queries it. A subquery approach would nest the SELECT inside another SELECT. WITH cte_table AS ( +------------------+ | (complex query) | +------------------+ ) SELECT * FROM cte_table; SELECT * FROM ( +------------------+ | (complex query) | +------------------+ ) AS sub; A CTE must be immediately followed by a SELECT (or INSERT/UPDATE/DELETE) that references it. A CTE’s scope is limited to one statement; it cannot be reused outside. Also, avoid overly deep nesting – break logic into multiple CTEs if needed. **Subquery** — an unnamed SELECT inside another query (inline, not reusable). --- **CTE (WITH)** — a named temporary table defined for one query (improves clarity and reuse). **No delta.** CTEs and subqueries are standard SQL features everywhere.

title: Window Functions (ROW_NUMBER, RANK, LAG, LEAD, running totals)
one_screen: SQL window functions perform calculations across rows related to the current row without collapsing groups. For example, `ROW_NUMBER()` assigns a sequential number to rows in a partition, while `RANK()` assigns equal numbers to tied values. `LAG(col,1) OVER(...)` gets the previous row’s value, and `LEAD` gets the next row’s. You must include an `OVER(PARTITION BY ... ORDER BY ...)` clause. Window functions are ideal for credit roll-forwards: e.g. computing a loan delinquency at each period and comparing to the prior period using `LAG` or cumulative sums.
bodyText: Example: to assign row numbers within each product line: Here `ROW_NUMBER` restarts count for each `ProductType` group. `RANK()` would give the same sequence number to ties. Always specify an `ORDER BY` inside the window if using `LAG`, `LEAD`, or ranking; otherwise the result order is arbitrary. Forgetting `PARTITION BY` leads to global ranking instead of per-group. Also, not knowing `RANK()` vs `ROW_NUMBER()` can miscount ties. **ROW_NUMBER()** — assigns unique sequential numbers (1,2,3...). --- **RANK()** — assigns the same rank to ties (1,2,2,4...). **No delta.** Window function syntax is SQL-standard (though exact function names may vary slightly by dialect).

title: CASE Statements for Conditional Bucketing
one_screen: The SQL `CASE WHEN` expression assigns values based on conditions. It’s often used to bucket or categorize data. For instance, creating delinquency buckets:
bodyText: Each `WHEN` tests a condition and returns the corresponding label. An `ELSE` provides a default (for any values not matched). The result of `CASE` is a single column value. Always include an `ELSE` clause in `CASE` unless you intentionally want NULL for unmatched cases. Omitting `ELSE` yields NULL for rows that meet none of the `WHEN` conditions. Also, `CASE` is evaluated in order – once a condition matches, later ones are skipped. **CASE** — standard SQL conditional expression (multi-branch). --- **DECODE** (Oracle) — an older function only in Oracle SQL, similar to a simple `CASE`. Prefer `CASE` for portability. **No delta.** `CASE WHEN` is ANSI SQL standard everywhere. = 90 THEN 'High' WHEN score >= 50 THEN 'Medium' ELSE 'Low' END`." />

title: NULL Handling and Three-Valued Logic
one_screen: In SQL, `NULL` represents missing or unknown data. Comparisons with `NULL` yield *UNKNOWN*, not true or false. SQL employs three-valued logic (TRUE, FALSE, UNKNOWN). For example, `NULL = NULL` is UNKNOWN, so a `WHERE` filter excludes those rows. To test for missing data use `IS NULL` or `IS NOT NULL`.
bodyText: For instance, to find accounts without an open date: Regular operators (`=`, `<`, etc.) cannot be used with NULL. Use `ISNULL()` or `COALESCE()` functions to substitute defaults when needed. Always use `IS NULL` or `IS NOT NULL` to check for NULL values. Treating NULL as a value in conditions (e.g. `WHERE Balance != 0` won’t catch NULL balances). Also, when using `JOIN`, NULLs can cause unmatched rows. **NULL** — absence/unknown value (three-valued logic). --- **0** — numeric zero, a definite number (not NULL). **No delta.** SQL’s handling of NULLs is universal.

title: Date Handling and Reporting Periods
one_screen: SQL provides date/time functions to manipulate and extract parts of dates. Common functions include `YEAR(date)`, `MONTH(date)`, or `DATEPART` to group or filter by time units. For example, to group loan originations by year: ```sql SELECT YEAR(OriginationDate) AS Year, COUNT(*) FROM Loans GROUP BY YEAR(OriginationDate); ``` This uses `YEAR()` to extract the year component. One can similarly use `MONTH()`, or perform arithmetic (e.g. adding intervals). Reporting often requires custom periods (e.g. fiscal year or quarters) — these can be calculated with date functions or by joining a calendar table.
bodyText: Dates can also be compared or ranged: e.g. `WHERE SaleDate BETWEEN '2025-01-01' AND '2025-12-31'` for a calendar year. Convert strings to actual `DATE` or `DATETIME` types (using `STR_TO_DATE` or client-side parsing) to leverage date functions. Do not treat dates as plain text. Ignoring the time component can yield unexpected results (e.g. missing same-day records). Always truncate times or use date boundaries. **DATE** — stores year-month-day (no time). --- **DATETIME/TIMESTAMP** — includes time (hours-min-sec). Make sure to use the correct type for dates versus full timestamps. **No delta.** Date arithmetic and functions follow SQL standards universally.

title: Query Performance Basics (Indexes, Table Scans, Execution Plans)
one_screen: Indexes speed up queries by allowing the database to quickly locate rows on indexed columns. A full table scan reads every row and is efficient only if a large fraction of rows qualify. For example, if querying a small subset (e.g. 1% of rows) on an indexed column, the database will use the index; if ~10% or more of rows match, a sequential scan may be faster.
bodyText: Use `EXPLAIN` (or equivalent) to view the execution plan of a query. This shows which indexes (if any) are used and the estimated cost. The plan also shows join methods (nested loop, hash join, etc.) and whether tables are scanned. A query running slowly often indicates missing indexes, inefficient joins, or large scans on big tables. Put indexes on columns used frequently in `WHERE`, `JOIN`, or `ORDER BY` clauses (primary keys are automatically indexed). Assuming an index will always be used: if statistics are outdated or the query doesn’t use the indexed column properly (e.g. function on column), the optimizer might do a full scan. **Index Scan** — uses an index to retrieve specific rows. --- **Sequential (Table) Scan** — reads every row of the table. **No delta.** Index usage and execution plan analysis are general across RDBMS; the concept of cost-based optimization is universal. 10%)." />

title: Writing a Reconciliation Query
one_screen: Data reconciliation means comparing two sources to ensure consistency. In SQL, this often involves joining or aggregating data from two tables/reports and highlighting mismatches. For instance, reconciling a daily loan balance extract against the general ledger might involve summing balances by loan and comparing. One approach is a full outer join on key columns to find rows missing on either side. Alternatively, compare aggregates: ```sql SELECT A.LoanID, A.Balance AS Balance_A, B.Balance AS Balance_B FROM LoansTable A FULL OUTER JOIN GL_Loans B ON A.LoanID = B.LoanID WHERE A.Balance <> B.Balance OR A.LoanID IS NULL OR B.LoanID IS NULL; ``` This returns loans where balances differ or exist only in one source. Another common pattern is comparing totals by category: sum balances in each source and `JOIN` or `UNION` to compare totals.
bodyText: TableA Full Join TableB = Discrepancies (NULLs for missing) Always match on a clear key (e.g. LoanID) and include all data sources needed. Use aggregates (sums, counts) to verify totals align as a quick check. Mismatched keys or joins hide differences. For example, an inner join drops unmatched rows, missing a discrepancy. To catch all differences, use a full outer join or compare aggregates. **INNER JOIN** — only matching rows (not useful alone for recon). --- **FULL OUTER JOIN** — includes mismatches from both sides (needed to find missing records). **No delta.** Reconciliation logic is generic SQL.

title: Data Quality Checks (Completeness, Duplicates, Referential Integrity)
one_screen: Common SQL data quality checks ensure tables have no missing (NULL) values in mandatory fields, no unexpected duplicates, and maintain referential integrity. For **completeness**, verify required columns have no NULLs: `SELECT COUNT(*) FROM Loans WHERE AccountID IS NULL;`. For **duplicates**, check for duplicate keys (e.g. `SELECT LoanID, COUNT(*) FROM Loans GROUP BY LoanID HAVING COUNT(*)>1;`). For **referential integrity**, ensure every foreign key matches a primary key: `SELECT fk.col FROM ChildTable fk LEFT JOIN ParentTable pk ON fk.col=pk.col WHERE pk.col IS NULL;` (rows returned have broken links).
bodyText: Ensure primary/unique keys have no duplicates (they enforce uniqueness) and foreign keys match existing parent rows. Mistaking legitimate multiple entries (e.g. multiple payments per loan) for duplicates. Always confirm the correct key: a *primary key* versus a *natural unique*. **PRIMARY KEY** — key defined in schema, cannot have duplicates. --- **UNIQUE constraint/index** — also enforces uniqueness, but (unlike primary key) usually allows one NULL. **No delta.** Data quality principles (completeness, duplicates, referential checks) are universal.

title: Data Mart Design: Fact and Dimension Tables
one_screen: In a data warehouse or risk data mart, tables are designed as *fact* or *dimension*. A **fact table** contains measures (numeric data) and foreign keys to dimensions. A **dimension table** contains descriptive attributes (e.g. borrower name, product category) and a primary key. Dimension tables (one side) are small and static (e.g. Time dimension, Product dimension). Fact tables (many side) are large and growing, storing transactions or snapshots (e.g. exposures, losses) with keys to link each record to its dimensions.
bodyText: For example, a *Loan_Fact* table might have columns `(LoanKey, CustomerKey, ProductKey, Balance, InterestRate)`, where `CustomerKey` points to a *Customer_Dim* table with `(CustomerKey, Name, Segment, RiskRating)`, and `ProductKey` points to a *Product_Dim* table. This star schema lets analysts slice facts by any dimension attribute. +-------------+ | Loan_Fact | +-------------+ | CustomerKey |--> +-----------+ | ProductKey |--> |Customer_Dim| | Balance | +-----------+ +-------------+ | ... | +-----------+ Fact tables should contain only keys (foreign keys) and measure columns. All descriptive attributes belong in dimensions, not the fact. Placing text or descriptive fields in the fact table (denormalization) is discouraged. It bloats the fact and complicates queries. **Fact Table** — contains numeric measurements and foreign keys linking to dimensions. --- **Dimension Table** — contains attributes (descriptions) and a primary key. **No delta.** The star schema concept of fact vs dimension is standard in DW design.

title: Why Use Python (Not Excel) for Large Data
one_screen: Python can handle much larger datasets and reproducible workflows than Excel. Excel is limited to about one million rows and often crashes on complex models, whereas Python (pandas, numpy) can process “Big Data” in code. Python code is also text-based and version-controllable, reducing manual errors inherent in spreadsheets. In risk work, large loan tapes, exposure tables, or simulation outputs often exceed Excel’s capacity. Python scripts (using pandas) can load SQL extracts or CSV files into DataFrames and manipulate millions of rows efficiently.
bodyText: For example, summarising a 5-million-row loan file by segment is trivial in Python (`df.groupby('Segment').sum()`), whereas in Excel it would require slow pivot operations or manual aggregations. Python’s libraries (pandas, NumPy, sklearn) also support advanced analytics and are open-source, making code sharable and auditable. For datasets much larger than a few hundred thousand rows, use Python (or similar) instead of Excel. Code-based analysis ensures reproducibility and auditability. Trying to do complex analytics by dragging/clicking in Excel invites errors (wrong formula ranges, copy-paste mistakes). Don’t rely on untested spreadsheets for critical risk numbers. **Excel Workbook** — a spreadsheet with cells and formulas, suitable for small-scale, ad-hoc tasks. --- **Python Script** — text-based code (pandas/numpy) for large-scale or repeatable analysis. **No delta.** The limitations of Excel and advantages of code apply universally.

title: Pandas Series and DataFrame (Mental Model)
one_screen: In pandas, a **Series** is a 1D labeled array of data (similar to a column), and a **DataFrame** is a 2D table of data with labeled axes. You can think of a DataFrame as equivalent to a spreadsheet or SQL table: each column in a DataFrame is a Series, and all Series share the same index (row labels).
bodyText: For example, creating a loan DataFrame: This yields a table with 3 rows and 3 columns. Under the hood, each column (LoanID, Balance, Status) is a pandas Series, and they all align on their index (0,1,2). You can access a column as `df['Balance']` (a Series) or a single value as `df.loc[1, 'Status']`. +--------+-----------+ | LoanID | Balance | ... +--------+-----------+ | 101 | 50000 | | 102 | 75000 | | 103 | 100000 | +--------+-----------+ All columns in a DataFrame must have the same length (same index). A DataFrame cannot contain “ragged” columns of different lengths. Passing a dict of lists of different lengths to `DataFrame()` will error. Always ensure input data dimensions align. **Series** — a one-dimensional labeled array (single column). --- **DataFrame** — a two-dimensional table, essentially a dict of Series, like a spreadsheet or SQL table. **No delta.** These pandas concepts do not vary by region.

title: Reading and Writing Data (CSV, SQL, etc.)
one_screen: Pandas provides I/O functions to read/write various formats. To load CSV: `pd.read_csv('file.csv')` returns a DataFrame. To read from SQL: use `pd.read_sql(query, connection)` which executes a SQL query or table and returns a DataFrame. For example: ```python import pandas as pd import sqlite3 conn = sqlite3.connect('db.db') df_sql = pd.read_sql("SELECT * FROM exposures", conn) df_csv = pd.read_csv("loans.csv") ``` To save a DataFrame: `df.to_csv('out.csv', index=False)` or `df.to_sql('table_name', conn, if_exists='replace')`.
bodyText: When loading, specify parsing options for dates (`parse_dates`), encodings, or chunk size for large files. Always close database connections or use context managers. Explicitly set parameters when reading data: e.g. `parse_dates=['date_col']` for dates, or `index_col=` if needed. This ensures correct dtypes. Loading very large files without chunksize can exhaust memory. Similarly, calling `to_sql` on millions of rows may time out or lock the DB; consider batch inserts. **read_csv** — reads a delimited text file into a DataFrame. --- **to_sql** — writes a DataFrame to a SQL database table. **No delta.** Pandas I/O functions work the same regardless of jurisdiction.

title: Selection and Filtering in pandas (`loc` vs `iloc`)
one_screen: In pandas, `.loc` and `.iloc` index/select data differently. `.loc` uses labels (row index or column names), whereas `.iloc` uses integer positions. For example, `df.loc['C345']` selects the row with index `'C345'`, while `df.iloc[5]` selects the 6th row by position. For conditional filtering, use boolean indexing: `df.loc[df['Balance'] > 100000]` returns rows where Balance exceeds 100k. Both `.loc` and `.iloc` accept row and column indexers: `df.loc[row_labels, col_labels]` and `df.iloc[row_nums, col_nums]`.
bodyText: Key difference: `.loc` includes the ending label in slicing (`df.loc['A':'D']` includes 'D'), whereas `.iloc` excludes the endpoint (`df.iloc[0:3]` returns positions 0,1,2). Always ensure you pass the correct type of index (label vs integer) or you’ll get a KeyError/IndexError. Use `.loc` when indexing by row/column name, and `.iloc` for numerical positions. Using `.iloc` on an index that’s not a RangeIndex can return unexpected rows. For instance, if the DataFrame index is strings, `.iloc[0]` still returns the first row, not row with label 0. **`.loc`** — label-based indexing (select by row/column names). --- **`.iloc`** — positional indexing (select by row/column integer location). **No delta.** These pandas behaviors are the same everywhere.

title: GroupBy and Aggregation (Split–Apply–Combine)
one_screen: In pandas, use `groupby` to perform SQL-style GROUP BY operations. The process is “split-apply-combine”: split the DataFrame into groups by some key, apply an aggregate or transformation to each group, then combine the results. For example, to sum balances by product: `df.groupby('ProductType')['Balance'].sum()`. This yields a Series (index=ProductType, values=Sum).
bodyText: After grouping, common aggregates include `.sum()`, `.count()`, `.mean()`, `.min()`, `.max()`. Pandas also has `.agg()` to apply multiple functions or custom ones. The result keys become the index by default (similar to GROUP BY making the group columns the new index). This produces a MultiIndex Series with each (ProductType, Vintage) combination’s total balance. Use `reset_index()` if you want the keys as columns again. By default, grouped keys become the index of the result. Use `as_index=False` in `groupby()` or `reset_index()` afterward to turn them back into columns. Forgetting to aggregate: `df.groupby('X')` alone does not compute anything. Also, using `apply(lambda x: ...)` is often much slower than using built-in aggregates. **groupby** — aggregates data by keys (like SQL `GROUP BY`). --- **pivot** — reshapes (reorients) data without aggregating (or with separate logic). Pivot tables convert grouped results to a wide format, which is a distinct operation. **No delta.** The split-apply-combine paradigm is language-agnostic; pandas follows it consistently.

title: pandas Merge/Join vs SQL Join
one_screen: Pandas `merge` function performs SQL-like joins. For example, `pd.merge(df1, df2, on='key', how='inner')` is analogous to `SELECT * FROM df1 JOIN df2 ON df1.key=df2.key`. The `how` parameter can be `'inner'`, `'left'`, `'right'`, or `'outer'`, just like SQL joins. When merging, common columns (keys) must match on name or be specified via `left_on`/`right_on`. After merge, index labels are reset unless you preserve them.
bodyText: Example: This yields rows where `CustID` matches `ID`. A left join (`how='left'`) would keep all loans, adding customer info or NaN if missing. Explicitly specify `how` and `on` parameters to avoid ambiguity. By default, `how='inner'` and pandas attempts to join on any common column names. If two DataFrames share column names besides the key, `merge` may join on all of them unintentionally. Rename or use `suffixes=` to disambiguate. **merge** (pandas) — database-style join on keys (columns or index). --- **concat** (pandas) — stacks DataFrames (like SQL `UNION`), not a join on keys. **No delta.** Pandas merge behavior is consistent across environments.

title: Handling Missing Data in pandas
one_screen: Pandas represents missing data as `NaN` (for floats) or `NaT` (for datetimes) or `None` in object columns. Use `df.isna()` (or `isnull()`) to detect missing values, returning a boolean mask. You can drop rows or columns with missing data via `df.dropna()`, or fill values with `df.fillna(value)`. For example, `df['Balance'].fillna(0, inplace=True)` replaces missing balances with 0.
bodyText: Always be careful: operations skip `NaN` by default (e.g. `sum()` treats `NaN` as zero, but `mean()` ignores it). Deciding to drop or fill depends on context. For instance, missing credit score might be imputed or flagged. Detect missing explicitly with `isna()`. Always decide on a strategy: either drop records or fill them (imputation). Mixing `None` and `NaN`: some pandas methods distinguish them, but generally `isna()` catches both. Beware that `df['col'] == np.nan` does not work (use `isna`). **NaN** — pandas float “Not a Number” for missing. --- **Empty string** — a valid string, not missing. `isna()` returns False for `''`. **No delta.** pandas missing-value handling is the same everywhere.

title: Dates and Time Series Indexing in pandas
one_screen: Pandas has robust datetime support. Convert columns to datetime with `pd.to_datetime()`, then you can use date methods. To generate regular time sequences, `pd.date_range(start, end, freq='M')` creates a monthly-end index. You can then align or reindex data by time, and use `df.resample('M').sum()` to aggregate by month.

Also, you can use `.dt` accessor: `df['Date'].dt.month` to get month, etc. Always convert date columns to `datetime64` dtype (using `to_datetime`) before analysis. This allows use of datetime methods and indexing. Forgetting `set_index` with a `DatetimeIndex` means you can’t use `.resample()`. Also, be mindful of time zones if mixing data from different regions. **Timestamp** — a single datetime (e.g. 2026-08-01 00:00). --- **Period** — a span (e.g. Aug 2026); use pandas `Period` if needed. **No delta.** pandas date utilities are standard regardless of locale. = '2025-01-01') & (df['Date']

title: NumPy Vectorization and Portfolio Summary
one_screen: Python loops over DataFrame rows (or Python lists) are slow for large tables. Instead, use NumPy/pandas vectorized operations, which run in optimized C. For example, summing balances grouped by condition: ```python # slow (loop): total = 0 for bal in df['Balance']: total += bal

Even custom functions can often be expressed as vectorized NumPy functions or pandas aggregations. In short: treat DataFrames like in-memory tables and use built-in operations. This is akin to using `SUM` in SQL vs iterating rows in application code. Always prefer pandas/NumPy vectorized methods (`.sum()`, `.mean()`, etc.) over manual Python loops for column-wise operations. title: Code Quality: Reproducibility, Testing, Version Control
one_screen: Treat analytical scripts like software. Use virtual environments (`venv`/`conda`) and a `requirements.txt` to pin library versions, ensuring others can reproduce the environment. For example, `pip freeze > requirements.txt` captures exact package versions. Use clear folder structure and document data sources in code comments.
bodyText: Testing is essential: write unit tests or assertions to verify code correctness. For example, test that a summary statistic matches a known result or that two different methods yield the same total. A single risk number untested is a hidden model risk. Frameworks like `pytest` can automate tests. Finally, use version control (e.g. Git). Commit code regularly with meaningful messages. This allows rollback, review (code audit), and collaboration. Store scripts in a repository (internal or GitHub Enterprise). Each change to analysis code should be tracked like financial model changes. Pin and document dependencies, and always run tests after making changes. Copying code around or running analyses manually without scripts. Avoid “lone excel-like” scripts with no version history or tests. **Unit Test** — automated check of a small code piece against expected output. --- **Version Control Commit** — a snapshot of code changes saved in a repository. **No delta.** These software best practices apply to analysts worldwide.

title: What a bank treasury actually does
one_screen: Bank treasury is the balance-sheet control centre that converts customer activity into managed funding, liquidity, interest-rate and market positions. Unlike a corporate treasury, it does not merely finance an operating business: maturity transformation and financial intermediation are themselves part of the bank’s business model.
bodyText: A corporate treasury primarily raises funding, manages surplus cash, foreign-exchange exposures and financing risks created by a non-financial operating business. A bank treasury sits inside a financial intermediary whose assets and liabilities are largely financial claims. Deposits arrive with one pattern of tenor, optionality and repricing; loans and securities create another. Treasury must make the aggregate balance sheet fundable and liquid while controlling the resulting risks. The exact organisational split differs, but four functions recur. **Funding** obtains wholesale or internal funding and manages the liability structure. **Liquidity management** ensures cash obligations can be met, maintains liquid-asset buffers and manages collateral. **Asset-liability management (ALM)** measures structural mismatches in maturity and interest-rate repricing. **Markets activity** executes transactions used to invest liquidity, raise funding or hedge exposures. Basel liquidity principles explicitly require banks to identify the full range of liquidity risks, maintain a liquid-asset cushion and allocate liquidity costs, benefits and risks to significant business activities. Treasury therefore sees customer businesses differently from the customer-facing unit. A lending desk sees an asset earning a customer rate. Treasury sees a stream of cash flows requiring funding for a particular behavioural tenor, consuming liquidity under stress and potentially creating interest-rate risk. A deposit business sees a product margin. Treasury sees a funding source whose stability, repricing behaviour and withdrawal risk must be estimated. Treasury normally acts within limits rather than trying to eliminate every mismatch. Some maturity transformation is intrinsic to banking. The objective is to decide which risks the bank is willing and able to retain, which should be transferred internally through funds transfer pricing, and which should be hedged or funded externally. +------------------+ | Customer assets | | loans, securities| +------------------+ | v +------------------+ | Bank treasury / | | ALM centre | +------------------+ | | | v v v +------+ +------+ +------+ |Fund- | |Liquid| |IRR / | |ing | |ity | |hedge | +------+ +------+ +------+ ^ | +------------------+ | Customer funding | | deposits, debt | +------------------+ A bank treasury manages the consequences of the whole balance sheet, not merely a portfolio of securities. Treating treasury profit as the objective and forgetting that treasury is also the bank’s central allocator and controller of funding and liquidity risk. **Bank treasury** — the function managing structural funding, liquidity, balance-sheet risk and related market execution. --- **Corporate treasury** — the function financing and managing financial risks of a primarily non-financial operating business. **No delta.** Organisational charts vary, but the economic role arises from banking intermediation rather than jurisdiction-specific mathematics.

title: Banking book versus trading book
one_screen: The banking-book/trading-book boundary is not shorthand for “held long term” versus “traded frequently”; it is a regulatory classification determining which risk framework applies. Moving an exposure across that boundary can change valuation, capital treatment, risk measurement, governance and permissible hedging recognition.
bodyText: The **trading book** contains positions assigned to the regulatory trading perimeter under applicable capital rules. The **banking book** is the non-trading portion of the balance sheet. The distinction matters because market risk in the trading book and interest-rate risk in the banking book are governed through different prudential machinery. A fixed-rate bond illustrates the point. Economically, its value changes when interest rates change regardless of where it is booked. If it is a trading-book position, that risk is generally captured through the market-risk capital framework. If it sits in the banking book, the structural interest-rate exposure enters IRRBB measures such as economic value of equity and net interest income. The economic sensitivity exists before regulation; the boundary determines how that sensitivity is classified and supervised. Basel defines IRRBB as risk to capital and earnings from adverse interest-rate movements affecting banking-book positions. This prevents a common conceptual error: accounting classification and prudential-book classification are related operationally but are not synonyms. A position's accounting measurement basis does not, by itself, answer which prudential risk framework applies. Nor can a bank freely relabel positions merely because one treatment appears more favourable; the boundary is governed by regulatory assignment criteria and controls. For ALM, the consequence is practical. Structural customer loans, deposits, non-maturity balances, term funding and relevant off-balance-sheet positions feed the banking-book risk system. Treasury must identify which cash flows belong there, how they reprice and which embedded options affect them. RBI’s 2025 forthcoming IRRBB Directions similarly define IRRBB around banking-book positions and require measurement of both ΔEVE and ΔNII. +----------------------+ | Bank positions | +----------------------+ | v +----------------------+ | Regulatory boundary | +----------------------+ | | v v +-----------+ +-----------+ | Trading | | Banking | | book | | book | +-----------+ +-----------+ | | v v +-----------+ +-----------+ | Market- | | IRRBB / | | risk | | ALM | | framework | | framework | +-----------+ +-----------+ Book classification determines the applicable prudential risk framework; economic interest-rate sensitivity exists irrespective of the label. Using “banking book” to mean “held to maturity” or assuming an accounting category automatically determines the prudential book. **Prudential book classification** — regulatory allocation between trading and banking books for risk and capital purposes. --- **Accounting classification** — the financial-reporting basis used to recognise and measure an instrument. — RBI’s forthcoming 2025 IRRBB Directions measure banking-book interest-rate risk through ΔEVE and ΔNII; implementation date remains to be communicated. [RBI, Commercial Banks – Forthcoming Instructions Directions, 2025] — UK prudential rules retain a regulatory distinction between traded market risk and banking-book interest-rate risk; precise booking criteria must be verified against the current PRA Rulebook and UK capital framework. — CRR prudential rules and EBA IRRBB standards distinguish trading/non-trading activities; EBA/GL/2022/14 addresses IRRBB and CSRBB arising from non-trading book activities. [EBA/GL/2022/14] — US capital and supervisory frameworks separately address trading-market risk and structural interest-rate risk; precise trading-book assignment must be verified against the current US capital rule.

title: The balance sheet as a set of mismatches
one_screen: ALM begins by discarding accounting labels and viewing the balance sheet as dated cash flows and repricing events. Risk appears because the timing, rate basis, optionality and liquidity characteristics of assets do not line up perfectly with those of liabilities.
bodyText: A bank can be balanced in the accounting sense—assets equal liabilities plus equity—while remaining heavily mismatched economically. A long fixed-rate loan funded by a deposit that can reprice tomorrow creates no accounting imbalance, but it creates **repricing risk**. A five-year asset funded by three-month wholesale debt creates a **maturity mismatch** because the funding must be renewed before the asset returns cash. Four clocks matter. **Contractual maturity** is when principal is legally due. **Behavioural maturity** is when cash is realistically expected to leave or return after considering customer behaviour. **Repricing maturity** is when the interest rate can next reset. **Liquidity horizon** asks when cash must actually be available under stress. These dates can differ sharply for the same product. Consider a nominally overnight deposit. Contractually it can leave immediately. Behaviourally, a stable portion may remain for years. Its administered rate may reprice only gradually when market rates move. For liquidity stress, however, some portion may run off within days. One liability therefore occupies different positions in contractual, behavioural, interest-rate and liquidity analyses. ALM maps these dimensions across the balance sheet, then asks which mismatches the institution wants to retain. Basel notes that maturity transformation—funding longer-term assets with shorter-term liabilities—is fundamental to banking and makes banks inherently exposed to liquidity risk. The same transformation also creates interest-rate sensitivity where repricing dates differ. This is why a single “average maturity” cannot describe a bank’s balance sheet. The useful representation is a collection of cash flows, reset dates and options allocated across time buckets, currencies and rate bases. From that map emerge gap analysis, duration, EVE, NII, liquidity stress testing and FTP. +---------------------+ | Balance-sheet item | +---------------------+ | v +---------------------+ | Decompose cash flows| +---------------------+ | | | | v v v v +------+ +------+ +------+ +------+ |Legal | |Behav.| |Rate | |Cash | |matur.| |matur.| |reset | |need | +------+ +------+ +------+ +------+ \ | | / \ | | / v v v v +-------------------------+ | ALM mismatch profile | +-------------------------+ Accounting balance does not imply economic matching. Using contractual maturity as the universal time axis for deposits, prepayable loans and other products whose behavioural or repricing dates differ. **Maturity mismatch** — assets and liabilities return principal on different effective horizons. --- **Repricing mismatch** — asset and liability interest rates reset at different times, even if principal maturities match. **No delta.** The cash-flow logic is economic; supervisors may prescribe different measurement assumptions, but the underlying mismatch does not change.

title: Where IRRBB comes from
one_screen: IRRBB is not one risk but four interacting mechanisms: repricing gap, yield-curve shape, basis and optionality. A balance sheet can appear matched against one mechanism and remain materially exposed to another.
bodyText: **Repricing risk** arises when assets and liabilities reset at different times. A fixed-rate asset funded by a frequently repricing liability is the simplest example. **Yield-curve risk** arises because rates at different maturities do not necessarily move in parallel: the short end can rise while long rates barely move, or the curve can steepen, flatten or invert. **Basis risk** appears where two rates have similar tenor but reference different pricing indices or otherwise move imperfectly together. A floating-rate asset and floating-rate liability therefore do not constitute a perfect hedge merely because both reset every three months. RBI’s forthcoming framework defines basis risk as the effect of changes in rates for instruments of similar tenor priced from different interest-rate indices. **Optionality risk** comes from rights that change cash-flow timing when rates change. Borrowers may prepay fixed-rate loans; depositors may redeem term deposits; customers may leave non-maturity deposits in place or withdraw them; contractual caps and floors alter instrument sensitivity. Options can be explicit in contracts or behavioural in customer actions. Their defining feature is non-linearity: the cash-flow profile itself changes with the rate scenario. These mechanisms can offset or reinforce one another. A bank may close its simple repricing gap with a derivative but retain basis risk if the hedge references a different index. It may match contractual maturities yet remain exposed because customers prepay assets when rates fall. A parallel-rate hedge can still lose under a curve twist. Basel’s IRRBB framework therefore expects identification of gap, basis and option risks and uses multiple standardised shock shapes rather than a single parallel rate shock. RBI’s forthcoming framework likewise requires scenarios capturing parallel and non-parallel gap risks and consideration of basis and embedded-option behaviour. +------------------+ | Banking book | +------------------+ | v +------------------+ | IRRBB sources | +------------------+ | | | | v v v v +------+ +------+ +------+ +------+ |Re- | |Curve | |Basis | |Option| |price | |shape | |risk | |ality | +------+ +------+ +------+ +------+ \ | / \ | / v v v +------------------+ | EVE and NII risk | +------------------+ Matching reset dates eliminates only part of IRRBB; basis, curve and option risks can remain. Declaring a floating-rate asset “hedged” because its funding is also floating-rate without checking whether the indices, reset conventions and embedded options match. **Repricing risk** — sensitivity created by different reset timing. --- **Basis risk** — sensitivity created by imperfect co-movement of different reference rates even when reset timing is similar. **No delta.** Basel and major national frameworks recognise the same fundamental economic sources, although prescribed scenario calibrations can differ.

title: Economic value of equity versus net interest income
one_screen: EVE asks how interest-rate shocks change the present value of the banking book; NII asks how they change near-term interest earnings and expense. Neither dominates the other because they expose different parts of the same balance-sheet risk.
bodyText: **Economic value of equity (EVE)** is an economic-value perspective. Conceptually, expected interest-rate-sensitive asset cash flows are discounted to present value, expected liability cash flows are deducted, and relevant off-balance-sheet cash flows are incorporated. **ΔEVE** compares that value under a rate shock with the base value. Long-dated fixed-rate exposures can create large EVE sensitivity even when next year’s accounting earnings move little. **Net interest income (NII)** is an earnings measure: interest income minus interest expense over a defined projection horizon. **ΔNII** compares projected NII under a rate scenario with a base projection. It is particularly sensitive to which assets and liabilities reprice during that horizon, how deposit rates are assumed to respond and what replacement-business assumptions are used. The distinction is easiest through a long fixed-rate asset funded by a short-reset liability. A rate rise can increase funding expense quickly, reducing NII. It also increases discount rates applied to the fixed asset’s distant cash flows, reducing its economic value. Both perspectives identify risk, but they measure different manifestations and time horizons. Conversely, exposures can look benign in one metric. A position with favourable one-year NII after a rate rise can still lose substantial economic value beyond the projection horizon. Optimising exclusively to EVE can also produce an earnings profile management finds unacceptable. Basel therefore treats both economic-value and earnings perspectives as important to IRRBB management. RBI’s forthcoming directions require ΔEVE and ΔNII and specify, for disclosure, a run-off balance sheet for EVE and a rolling twelve-month constant-balance-sheet projection for NII. The practical discipline is not to reconcile the two metrics into one number. Their disagreement is information: it reveals which horizon, cash-flow assumption or exposure is driving the risk. +------------------+ | Rate scenario | +------------------+ | | v v +----------+ +----------+ | Present- | | Earnings | | value | | horizon | | effect | | effect | +----------+ +----------+ | | v v +----------+ +----------+ | Delta | | Delta | | EVE | | NII | +----------+ +----------+ \ / \ / v v +------------------+ | Full IRRBB view | +------------------+ EVE is a value perspective and NII is an earnings perspective; a sound IRRBB framework needs both. Choosing whichever metric shows the smaller risk and treating the other as redundant. **ΔEVE** — change in the present economic value of rate-sensitive banking-book cash flows under a shock. --- **ΔNII** — change in projected net interest earnings over a specified horizon under a scenario. **No delta.** The two-perspective mental model is common; regulators differ in prescribed shock, horizon and modelling details.

title: Duration and its limits
one_screen: Duration compresses a stream of cash flows into an approximate first-order sensitivity to interest rates. It is powerful for intuition and dangerous when treated as a complete model of a bank balance sheet.
bodyText: **Macaulay duration** is a present-value-weighted average time to cash flow. **Modified duration** converts that timing concept into approximate price sensitivity. For a small yield change, the familiar approximation is: `ΔP / P ≈ −Dmod × Δy` where `P` is value, `Dmod` is modified duration and `Δy` is the change in yield. A position with modified duration five therefore loses approximately 5% for a one-percentage-point rise in yield, before allowing for curvature. A bank can compare the rate sensitivity of assets and liabilities using duration concepts. If the economic value and duration of assets are much greater than those of liabilities, rising rates can reduce asset value more than liability value and therefore reduce economic equity. The approximation has strict limits. First, duration is local: it is most accurate for small changes around the current curve. **Convexity** captures second-order curvature ignored by the linear approximation. Second, a single duration often assumes a parallel movement in rates, whereas yield curves twist. Third, cash flows may not be fixed. Loan prepayments, deposit withdrawals, early redemption and embedded caps or floors can change cash flows as rates change, making effective duration scenario-dependent. Fourth, instruments linked to different indices introduce basis risk that one duration number cannot capture. For banks, the most dangerous limitation is behavioural optionality. A non-maturity deposit does not possess an economically useful long duration merely because a modeller assigns one. The duration emerges from assumptions about stability and repricing behaviour, which must be validated and stressed. Basel and RBI IRRBB frameworks therefore require richer scenario analysis and behavioural assumptions rather than relying only on a duration-gap statistic. +------------------+ | Cash flows | +------------------+ | v +------------------+ | Present-value | | weighting | +------------------+ | v +------------------+ | Duration | +------------------+ | v +------------------+ | Approx. rate | | sensitivity | +------------------+ | v +------------------+ | Add curve, basis,| | options, convexity| +------------------+ Duration is a sensitivity approximation, not a complete description of IRRBB. Interpreting a low aggregate duration gap as proof that the balance sheet is hedged without testing non-parallel shocks and behavioural options. **Duration** — first-order sensitivity derived from the timing and present value of cash flows. --- **Maturity** — the date principal is contractually or behaviourally expected to return; it does not directly measure value sensitivity. **No delta.** Duration mathematics does not change across jurisdictions.

title: Gap analysis and repricing buckets
one_screen: Repricing gap analysis places rate-sensitive assets and liabilities into the periods when they next reprice, then compares the two sides. It is a map of timing mismatch, not a complete forecast of earnings or value.
bodyText: A **repricing bucket** is a time interval such as overnight, one month, three months, one year or longer. A rate-sensitive asset is placed into the bucket containing its next effective repricing date; a rate-sensitive liability is treated the same way. The simple bucket gap is: `Gap = rate-sensitive assets − rate-sensitive liabilities` A positive gap means more assets than liabilities reprice in that bucket. Under a simplified parallel-rate assumption, rising rates can increase income faster than expense. A negative gap suggests the reverse. A **cumulative gap** sums bucket gaps up to a selected horizon. The method is valuable because it makes concentration visible. Two banks can have the same total assets and liabilities while one has a large one-month liability reset against five-year fixed assets and the other is closely matched across buckets. Yet the sign of a bucket gap is not an earnings forecast. Assets and liabilities may reprice by different amounts; deposit rates may respond only partially or with delay; yield-curve points may move differently; options may alter expected cash flows; new business can replace maturities. A bucket also loses information because every cash flow inside the interval is treated as though its timing were equivalent. Gap analysis is therefore best treated as a diagnostic layer. It identifies where timing mismatches reside and supports limit setting and scenario design. More sophisticated NII and EVE models then apply scenario-specific curves, behavioural assumptions, cash-flow timing and basis relationships. RBI’s forthcoming IRRBB directions explicitly recognise gap, basis and option risks and require both internally selected and prescribed stress scenarios. +-------------------+ | Assets/liabilities| +-------------------+ | v +-------------------+ | Next repricing | | date | +-------------------+ | v +-------------------+ | Time buckets | +-------------------+ | v +-------------------+ | RSA - RSL | | by bucket | +-------------------+ | v +-------------------+ | Gaps -> scenarios | | -> NII / EVE | +-------------------+ Repricing gaps locate timing mismatches; they do not by themselves capture basis, curve or option risk. Multiplying each bucket gap by one assumed rate shock and calling the result a complete IRRBB measure. **Repricing gap** — difference between assets and liabilities scheduled to reset in a time bucket. --- **Liquidity gap** — difference between cash inflows and cash outflows over time; an item can reprice without producing cash. **No delta.** Bucket definitions and regulatory templates may differ, but the analytical mechanism is universal.

title: Behavioural modelling of non-maturity deposits
one_screen: A non-maturity deposit has an overnight contractual withdrawal right but may behave like multi-year funding. ALM therefore models both how long balances remain and how their administered rates respond to market rates; those assumptions can dominate measured IRRBB.
bodyText: A **non-maturity deposit (NMD)** has no fixed contractual maturity at which the entire balance must be repaid. Transaction and savings balances are typical economic forms. Contractually, customers may be able to withdraw quickly. Behaviourally, a portion of an aggregate portfolio can remain persistent. Two models are required. The **balance model** estimates how much funding is stable and for how long. The **repricing model** estimates how the administered deposit rate responds when market rates change. A useful concept is deposit **beta**: the proportion of a market-rate change eventually passed through to the customer rate. **Lag** describes how quickly that pass-through occurs. Suppose market rates rise 100 basis points and a deposit rate historically rises only 40 basis points after a delay. Treating the deposit as instantly repricing by 100 basis points overstates funding-cost sensitivity. Treating the entire balance as fixed for five years can make the opposite error. Stability and repricing must be estimated separately. Segmentation matters. Operational transaction balances can behave differently from rate-sensitive surplus balances; retail behaviour can differ from wholesale behaviour. Models therefore group accounts with sufficiently similar economic characteristics, estimate decay or stability and test behaviour under changing rate environments. The danger is false precision. Historical stability observed during calm periods may not survive intense competition, digital withdrawals or customer concentration. Behavioural assumptions must therefore be governed, validated and stressed rather than treated as contractual facts. Basel IRRBB standards specifically recognise NMD optionality. RBI’s forthcoming framework prescribes behavioural treatment and, for its standardised methodology, caps core-deposit proportions and average maturities by category. +------------------+ | NMD balances | +------------------+ | v +------------------+ | Segment | +------------------+ | | v v +---------+ +---------+ | Balance | | Deposit | | stability| | repricing| +---------+ +---------+ | | v v +---------+ +---------+ |Behav. | |Beta / | |tenor | |lag | +---------+ +---------+ \ / v v +------------------+ | EVE / NII profile| +------------------+ An NMD’s contractual overnight maturity is not its behavioural ALM tenor. Using a single “average life” for NMDs without separately modelling rate beta, lag and stressed balance decay. **Core deposit assumption** — the estimated stable portion of an NMD portfolio used for behavioural modelling. --- **Contractual maturity** — the legal withdrawal horizon, which for an NMD may be immediate despite behavioural stability. — RBI’s forthcoming 2025 IRRBB framework specifies NMD modelling constraints in its standardised methodology, including category-specific caps on core proportions and average maturity; implementation date remains to be notified. [RBI 2025, Chapter V] — PRA-supervised firms are expected to manage structural liquidity and interest-rate assumptions within their prudential risk frameworks; exact NMD model constraints should be verified against current PRA requirements. — EBA/GL/2022/14 and related technical standards prescribe detailed IRRBB behavioural treatment, including NMD assumptions. [EBA/GL/2022/14] — supervisory IRR guidance emphasises supportable assumptions for deposit behaviour; institution-specific modelling remains central. [Federal Reserve interagency IRR guidance]

title: Prepayment, early redemption and pipeline risk
one_screen: Customer and business options make future banking-book cash flows conditional rather than fixed. Prepayments shorten assets, early withdrawals shorten liabilities, and pipeline commitments can create exposure before an instrument has even reached the balance sheet.
bodyText: A fixed-rate loan may permit a borrower to repay principal early. When market rates fall, refinancing becomes attractive, so prepayments may accelerate precisely when the bank would prefer to retain the higher-yielding asset. The bank receives cash back sooner and may have to reinvest it at lower rates. This is **prepayment risk**. A term deposit can contain the opposite option. If market rates rise and early withdrawal is permitted at an acceptable penalty, the customer may redeem the old deposit and seek a higher rate. The bank loses funding earlier than the contractual maturity assumed in a static schedule. This is **early-redemption risk**. **Pipeline risk** arises before expected business is fully booked. A bank can commit to lend at a fixed rate while the customer retains a period in which to draw or complete the transaction. If market rates change before funding or hedging is finalised, the economic value of the commitment changes. Forecast origination volumes can also fail to materialise, leaving anticipatory hedges larger than the eventual exposure. These are forms of optionality because the amount or timing of future cash flows changes with rates or customer choices. Modelling requires an exercise function: how prepayment, withdrawal or drawdown probability changes under different scenarios. Purely historical averages are insufficient when current incentives differ from the historical sample. The practitioner must also distinguish **automatic options**, whose contractual payoff follows a formula, from **behavioural options**, whose exercise depends on human decisions and operational frictions. Basel and RBI IRRBB frameworks explicitly require embedded options and behavioural assumptions to be captured and stressed. RBI’s forthcoming framework addresses loan prepayments, term-deposit redemption and option-sensitive cash flows. +------------------+ | Rate movement | +------------------+ | v +------------------+ | Customer/business| | incentive changes| +------------------+ | | | v v v +------+ +------+ +------+ |Loan | |Deposit| |Pipe- | |prepay| |redeem | |line | +------+ +------+ +------+ | | | v v v +------------------+ | Cash-flow timing | | changes | +------------------+ | v +------------------+ | EVE / NII changes| +------------------+ Where exercise behaviour depends on interest rates, cash-flow timing must be scenario-dependent. Projecting prepayments or deposit redemptions from a single historical average and holding that rate constant across all interest-rate scenarios. **Prepayment risk** — an existing asset returns principal earlier than expected. --- **Pipeline risk** — expected or committed future business changes exposure before final booking or funding. **No delta.** Option exercise economics are universal; prescribed regulatory modelling parameters can vary.

title: IRRBB stress tests and supervisory outliers
one_screen: An IRRBB stress test asks whether the balance sheet remains tolerable under severe rate paths and stressed customer behaviour; a supervisory outlier test is a regulatory screening device, not the bank’s complete risk appetite. Passing the outlier test does not prove IRRBB is safe.
bodyText: A robust test begins with a base cash-flow and behavioural model, then applies multiple shocks. A **parallel up** or **parallel down** scenario shifts the curve broadly in one direction. **Steepener** and **flattener** scenarios change the relationship between short and long rates. **Short-rate shocks** isolate the front of the curve. Basis and option stresses should be layered where material. Each scenario is translated into ΔEVE and, where relevant, ΔNII. Behaviour should not automatically remain at the base case: deposit stability, deposit beta, loan prepayments and term-deposit redemption may change under stress. Reverse stress testing asks a different question: what combination of rate and behavioural assumptions would breach a critical risk or capital limit? Basel’s supervisory outlier test uses six prescribed interest-rate shock scenarios for EVE and identifies banks with a maximum EVE decline exceeding a supervisory threshold calibrated at 15% of Tier 1 capital. The threshold is a supervisory trigger for attention rather than a statement that exposure immediately below 15% is acceptable. RBI’s November 2025 forthcoming framework adopts a six-shock EVE structure and identifies a bank as an outlier if ΔEVE decline exceeds 15% of Tier 1 capital in any prescribed scenario. It places IRRBB capital assessment in ICAAP under Pillar 2 and permits supervisory responses including additional capital, hedging, exposure reduction, parameter constraints or risk-management improvements. Its implementation date, however, remains to be communicated; the Directions explicitly describe interim preparedness and reporting. +------------------+ | Base IRRBB model | +------------------+ | v +------------------+ | Rate + behaviour | | stress scenarios | +------------------+ | v +------------------+ | Delta EVE / NII | +------------------+ | v +------------------+ | Internal limits | | + outlier tests | +------------------+ | v +------------------+ | Capital / hedge /| | risk response | +------------------+ A supervisory outlier threshold is a screening threshold, not a target risk appetite. Managing ΔEVE to sit just below the regulatory outlier threshold while ignoring NII, basis risk, optionality and internal stress scenarios. **Stress test** — a broad internal or supervisory assessment under severe scenarios and assumptions. --- **Supervisory outlier test** — a prescribed screen used to identify unusually high exposure under standardised shocks. — RBI’s November 2025 forthcoming framework places IRRBB in Pillar 2/ICAAP and uses a 15% of Tier 1 ΔEVE outlier threshold; implementation date remains to be notified. [RBI 2025, Chapter V] — IRRBB is addressed through supervisory/Pillar 2 assessment rather than a universal Pillar 1 IRRBB capital charge; current PRA-specific calibration should be checked against applicable rules. [Bank of England, 2025 capital assessment discussion] — EBA standards implement supervisory outlier testing for IRRBB, including the 15% Tier 1 EVE threshold architecture and EBA/GL/2022/14 governance. [EBA IRRBB RTS; EBA/GL/2022/14] — US supervisory guidance requires sound IRR measurement and stress analysis but does not use the EU-style ILAAP/IRRBB rule package as its naming architecture. [Federal Reserve interagency IRR guidance]

title: Hedging IRRBB and hedge accounting
one_screen: An economic hedge changes the bank’s risk; hedge accounting changes how qualifying hedge effects appear in financial statements. A hedge can be economically effective without receiving hedge-accounting treatment, and accounting treatment must never determine whether the underlying risk is actually controlled.
bodyText: IRRBB can be hedged by changing the balance sheet or adding derivatives. Treasury may raise longer-term fixed funding against fixed-rate assets, issue floating funding where asset income floats, alter securities holdings or use interest-rate swaps and other derivatives.
