The objective is to change the cash-flow or value sensitivity of the consolidated banking book. Suppose a bank holds long fixed-rate assets and is exposed to rising rates. In a stylised swap hedge, it may receive floating and pay fixed. As market rates rise, the floating receipts increase and offset part of the asset/funding mismatch. The useful hedge quantity is therefore not derivative notional alone but the sensitivity offset: tenor, curve point, index, optionality and cash-flow profile must line up sufficiently with the exposure. **Hedge effectiveness** is economic: does the hedge offset the intended risk under relevant scenarios? **Hedge accounting** is an accounting mechanism governing when and how gains and losses from a qualifying hedge relationship are recognised. It exists partly because the accounting timing or measurement of the hedging instrument and hedged item can otherwise differ. ALM must therefore run two conversations simultaneously. Risk management asks whether EVE, NII, basis and option exposures are reduced. Finance asks whether designation, documentation and accounting eligibility are met. Optimising the second while worsening the first is not sound hedging. There is a critical Indian accounting constraint. RBI deferred Ind AS implementation for scheduled commercial banks until further notice in March 2019. Therefore, Indian scheduled commercial banks must not be described as applying Ind AS 109 merely because IRRBB or hedge accounting is being discussed. RBI has separately issued Ind AS implementation guidance relevant to applicable NBFCs. +------------------+ | IRRBB exposure | +------------------+ | v +------------------+ | Economic hedge | | design | +------------------+ | v +------------------+ | EVE / NII offset | +------------------+ | +----------------+ | | v v +----------------+ +----------------+ | Risk outcome | | Accounting | | effectiveness | | eligibility | +----------------+ +----------------+ Economic hedge effectiveness and hedge-accounting qualification are separate tests. Rejecting a sound economic hedge because its accounting presentation is inconvenient, or accepting a poor risk hedge because it produces desirable accounting treatment. **Economic hedge** — a position designed to offset financial risk. --- **Hedge accounting** — accounting treatment for a qualifying designated hedge relationship; it does not itself reduce risk. — RBI deferred Ind AS implementation for scheduled commercial banks until further notice; do not equate Indian bank hedge accounting with Ind AS 109. Relevant Ind AS NBFCs are a different population. [RBI/2018-2019/146; RBI NBFC Ind AS guidance] — hedge-accounting treatment depends on the applicable UK accounting framework; specific designation rules should be verified against current accounting standards. — hedge-accounting treatment depends on the EU-adopted accounting framework applicable to the institution; specific designation rules should be verified against current standards. — US GAAP hedge-accounting requirements differ from IFRS-based frameworks; specific qualification and presentation rules should be verified against current US accounting standards.

title: Funding liquidity risk versus market liquidity risk
one_screen: Funding liquidity risk is the risk that the bank cannot obtain cash when obligations fall due without unacceptable loss; market liquidity risk is the risk that an asset cannot be sold or financed quickly near its expected value. One can trigger the other, but they are not the same risk.
bodyText: A bank has **funding liquidity** when it can meet payment obligations as they come due. Failure can occur because deposits leave, wholesale funding does not roll, collateral calls rise, committed credit lines are drawn or other cash needs exceed available resources. Basel defines bank liquidity as the ability to fund asset increases and meet obligations when due without unacceptable losses. **Market liquidity** describes the ease with which an asset can be sold or monetised. An asset may be economically sound but difficult to sell quickly except at a steep discount. Bid-ask spreads can widen, market depth can disappear, secured lenders can increase haircuts and transactions large relative to market capacity can move prices. The risks interact. A funding outflow forces the bank to raise cash. If external borrowing is unavailable, it may sell securities. Forced selling into an illiquid market produces losses. Those losses can weaken confidence, trigger more funding withdrawals or reduce collateral capacity, creating a feedback loop. The distinction also explains why “assets exceed liabilities” does not settle a liquidity question. Solvency is principally about whether asset value is sufficient relative to obligations and capital. Liquidity is about whether cash can be produced at the required time. A bank can own valuable long-term assets and still be unable to convert them to immediate settlement cash without severe loss. Treasury therefore manages both sources of cash and the monetisability of assets. A liquidity buffer must not merely look valuable on a normal-day balance sheet: assets need sufficient market depth, credit quality, operational availability and lack of encumbrance to generate cash in stress. Basel’s HQLA and liquidity principles are built around this distinction. +------------------+ | Cash obligation | +------------------+ | v +------------------+ | Funding available?| +------------------+ | yes | no v v +---------+ +----------------+ | Pay | | Monetise assets| +---------+ +----------------+ | v +----------------+ | Market liquid? | +----------------+ | yes | no v v +------+ +--------+ |Cash | |Loss / | |raised| |delay | +------+ +--------+ Funding liquidity concerns obtaining cash on time; market liquidity concerns converting positions into cash at tolerable value. Calling a security “liquid” solely because it has a quoted market price in normal conditions. **Funding liquidity risk** — inability to meet cash obligations when due without unacceptable loss. --- **Market liquidity risk** — inability to transact or monetise an asset quickly at a price close to its expected value. **No delta.** The economic distinction is universal.

title: High-quality liquid assets
one_screen: HQLA are not simply “safe securities”; they are assets that the liquidity framework recognises as capable of generating cash rapidly under stress with little loss. Eligibility, operational availability, encumbrance, haircut and portfolio composition all matter.
bodyText: The Liquidity Coverage Ratio requires a stock of **high-quality liquid assets (HQLA)** against stressed net cash outflows. Basel describes HQLA as assets that can be easily and immediately converted into cash at little or no loss of value. Three questions therefore precede the label. First, is the asset intrinsically liquid enough under the regulatory eligibility criteria? Second, is it **unencumbered**, meaning it is not already pledged or otherwise unavailable for monetisation? Third, can the bank operationally sell or repo it when needed? A qualifying security trapped in the wrong legal entity, pledged elsewhere or operationally inaccessible is not equivalent to immediately usable liquidity. Basel distinguishes levels of HQLA because assets have different liquidity characteristics. Level 1 assets receive the most favourable treatment; lower HQLA levels are subject to haircuts and composition caps. A **haircut** reduces the amount of liquidity value recognised relative to the asset’s market value. Its purpose is to allow for value uncertainty and monetisation risk. HQLA management therefore involves more than holding a target nominal amount. Treasury monitors market value, regulatory value after haircuts, encumbrance, currency, legal-entity location, settlement access and concentration. The buffer must also remain usable in stress: a liquidity regime that requires assets never to decline would defeat the purpose of a stress buffer. India adds a distinctive interaction because qualifying government securities held for statutory liquidity purposes can, within RBI-defined MSF and FALLCR carve-outs, also be recognised as Level 1 HQLA for LCR purposes. The overlap is governed rather than automatic. RBI also revised valuation of Level 1 government securities for LCR purposes from 1 April 2026 to incorporate applicable LAF/MSF haircuts. +------------------+ | Asset | +------------------+ | v +------------------+ | HQLA eligible? | +------------------+ | v +------------------+ | Unencumbered and | | operationally | | monetisable? | +------------------+ | v +------------------+ | Apply haircut / | | composition rules| +------------------+ | v +------------------+ | Recognised HQLA | | value | +------------------+ HQLA status is based on stressed monetisability under regulatory conditions, not merely credit quality. Using the market value of an eligible security as its LCR value without checking encumbrance, haircut and composition treatment. **HQLA** — assets meeting prudential liquidity eligibility and operational requirements. --- **Liquid asset in ordinary language** — any asset thought readily saleable; it may not qualify as regulatory HQLA. — RBI allows specified government securities within mandatory SLR to count as Level 1 HQLA through MSF/FALLCR carve-outs; revised Level 1 government-security haircut treatment is effective from 1 April 2026. [RBI/2022-23/25; RBI/2025-26/27] — the PRA liquidity regime applies UK prudential HQLA requirements; precise eligibility and haircut rules should be checked against the current PRA Rulebook. [PRA SS24/15] — EU LCR requirements are contained in CRR Part Six and Delegated Regulation (EU) 2015/61. [CRR/Delegated Regulation 2015/61] — US LCR rules use regulatory HQLA categories and apply the LCR according to the tailoring framework rather than uniformly to all banks. [OCC Bulletin 2019-52]

title: The Liquidity Coverage Ratio
one_screen: LCR asks whether a bank has enough recognised HQLA to withstand modelled net cash outflows over a severe 30-calendar-day stress period. It is a standardised short-horizon resilience test, not a forecast of the bank’s actual next 30 days.
bodyText: Conceptually: `LCR = stock of HQLA / total net cash outflows over 30 days` Under the Basel architecture, the ratio is calibrated around a 30-calendar-day stress horizon and a 100% minimum in ordinary conditions. Net outflows are not simply contractual maturities. Liability and off-balance-sheet categories receive regulatory **run-off rates** representing assumed stressed withdrawals or draws, while eligible inflows receive prescribed recognition subject to limits. The question is therefore: after applying the rulebook’s stress assumptions, can the recognised liquid-asset stock cover the resulting net cash requirement for 30 days? A stable retail deposit may receive a lower assumed run-off than a less stable or certain wholesale balance because their stressed behaviour is assumed to differ. An undrawn commitment can generate a contingent outflow even though no cash is owed today. Contractual receivables can generate inflows, but the framework prevents a bank from treating unlimited expected inflows as a substitute for a liquidity buffer. LCR is intentionally stylised. An actual crisis can last longer than 30 days, run-off rates can exceed regulatory assumptions, liquidity can be trapped by currency or legal entity and intraday settlement demands can arise even when the end-of-day LCR looks comfortable. Basel explicitly treats intraday liquidity separately from the original LCR calibration. India’s current framework follows the Basel architecture but has local calibrations. RBI’s April 2025 amendments, effective 1 April 2026, add 2.5 percentage points to run-off rates for internet/mobile-enabled retail deposits, producing 7.5% for qualifying stable balances and 12.5% for less-stable balances, and revise government-security HQLA valuation. +----------------------+ | 30-day stress inputs | +----------------------+ | | v v +-----------+ +-----------+ | Stressed | | Eligible | | outflows | | inflows | +-----------+ +-----------+ \ / v v +----------------------+ | Net cash outflows | +----------------------+ ^ | +----------------------+ | Recognised HQLA | +----------------------+ | v +----------------------+ | LCR = HQLA / net | | stressed outflows | +----------------------+ LCR measures standardised 30-day stressed liquidity coverage, not long-term funding stability. Reading a 110% LCR as “the bank can survive exactly 33 days”; the ratio is based on prescribed stress assumptions, not a linear survival clock. **LCR** — HQLA relative to standardised net stressed cash outflows over 30 days. --- **Survival horizon** — the modelled time until available liquidity is exhausted under a particular internal stress scenario. — RBI uses the Basel LCR architecture with Indian calibrations and SLR/FALLCR interaction; revised digital-deposit run-offs and government-security haircut rules are effective 1 April 2026. [RBI/2025-26/27] — PRA-supervised firms operate under the UK liquidity framework, with LCR embedded alongside broader liquidity supervision and ILAAP. [PRA SS24/15] — LCR is a binding CRR liquidity requirement supplemented by Delegated Regulation (EU) 2015/61. [CRR Part Six, Title I] — LCR applicability is category-based rather than universal: the tailoring framework applies full, reduced or no LCR depending on firm category and specified risk indicators. [OCC Bulletin 2019-52]

title: The Net Stable Funding Ratio
one_screen: NSFR asks whether the bank’s longer-term assets and activities are supported by sufficiently stable funding over a one-year structural horizon. Where LCR is a short-term stress-buffer test, NSFR is a balance-sheet funding-structure test.
bodyText: Conceptually: `NSFR = Available Stable Funding / Required Stable Funding` **Available Stable Funding (ASF)** assigns greater value to liabilities and capital expected to remain available over the relevant horizon. Long-term debt, capital and stable deposit categories generally provide more ASF than very short or unstable wholesale funding. **Required Stable Funding (RSF)** reflects how much stable funding the bank’s assets and certain off-balance-sheet exposures are judged to require. Cash and highly liquid short-term assets require relatively little stable funding; longer-dated or less-liquid assets require more. The Basel standard requires NSFR of at least 100%, meaning ASF must be no less than RSF. The structural question is different from LCR. A bank could carry enough HQLA to pass a 30-day LCR while financing a large portfolio of long-dated assets with funding that matures shortly after that horizon. NSFR constrains that reliance on unstable maturity transformation. Conversely, a bank can have strong long-term funding and still face a severe immediate run that threatens its LCR. NSFR is also not the same as contractual one-year matching. ASF and RSF are weighted prudential constructs. A liability maturing inside a year can still receive some stable-funding recognition, while an asset’s RSF depends on more than contractual maturity. India’s final NSFR rules were issued earlier but implementation was deferred during the pandemic; RBI made them effective from 1 October 2021 for covered commercial banks. The US final rule became effective 1 July 2021 and applies on a tailored basis to large banking organisations. +------------------+ | Liabilities + | | capital | +------------------+ | v +------------------+ | ASF factors | +------------------+ | v +------------------+ | Available Stable | | Funding | +------------------+ | v +------------------+ | ASF / RSF >= 100%| +------------------+ ^ | +------------------+ | Required Stable | | Funding from | | assets/OBS | +------------------+ LCR addresses short-term liquidity stress; NSFR addresses structural funding stability. Calling NSFR a “one-year LCR”; its numerator and denominator are stable-funding weights, not one-year cash inflows and outflows. **ASF** — regulatory measure of funding expected to be sufficiently stable. --- **RSF** — regulatory measure of the stable funding required by assets and specified exposures. — RBI NSFR guidelines for covered commercial banks have applied since 1 October 2021. [RBI/2020-21/95] — the UK prudential framework implements stable-funding requirements alongside PRA liquidity supervision; current scope must be checked against the PRA Rulebook. [PRA SS24/15] — CRR contains the NSFR in Part Six, including Articles 413 and 428b. [Regulation (EU) No 575/2013, as amended] — the interagency NSFR rule is tailored to large banking organisations, has a one-year structural focus and became effective 1 July 2021. [Federal Reserve final rule, 2020]

title: Intraday liquidity
one_screen: A bank can end the day liquid and still fail during the day if payments arrive before offsetting receipts. Intraday liquidity is the capacity to meet payment and settlement obligations at the required time, not merely by the reporting cut-off.
bodyText: Bank cash flows are not synchronised. A large payment may need to settle at 10:00 while the cash inflow expected to fund it arrives at 15:00. The bank therefore needs intraday sources of liquidity: opening cash, central-bank balances, incoming payments, intraday credit, collateralised facilities or other immediately available resources. The key metric is not simply net daily cash flow but the **timing profile** within the day. A bank can receive 100 and pay 100 during the same day yet need substantial liquidity if most payments occur before receipts. The maximum cumulative net outflow is therefore a useful conceptual measure of the day’s peak funding requirement. Settlement systems make this operationally critical. Failure to settle can delay counterparties’ receipts, which can in turn impair their ability to make payments. Intraday liquidity risk can therefore propagate through payment and settlement networks even when institutions appear solvent on an end-of-day basis. Collateral management is inseparable from intraday liquidity. Securities may need to be pre-positioned before they can support central-bank or secured intraday credit. An asset technically eligible but not operationally positioned may be useless at the moment a payment queue builds. The Basel Committee developed seven quantitative intraday monitoring tools and explicitly stated that intraday liquidity management is a key element of overall liquidity risk management. It also noted that intraday liquidity was not included in the calibration of the original LCR. This means a healthy LCR cannot be treated as proof that settlement liquidity is adequate. Start of day | v +------------------+ | Opening liquidity| +------------------+ | v +------------------+ | Payments - | | receipts by time | +------------------+ | v +------------------+ | Cumulative net | | position | +------------------+ | v +------------------+ | Peak intraday | | liquidity need | +------------------+ | v End of day Intraday liquidity is about having cash at the required settlement time, not merely sufficient cash by day-end. Using daily net cash flow or LCR as a proxy for peak intraday funding needs. **Intraday liquidity** — resources needed to settle obligations during the business day. --- **End-of-day liquidity** — the closing cash position after that day’s receipts and payments have occurred. **No delta.** Payment-system structures and reporting details differ, but the timing mechanism is universal.

title: Survival horizon and liquidity stress testing
one_screen: Liquidity stress testing converts a scenario into daily cash needs and monetisable resources; survival horizon is the time until the bank can no longer meet obligations under that scenario without prohibited or extraordinary assumptions. Unlike LCR, it is institution-specific and can span multiple phases of stress.
bodyText: The exercise begins with **contractual cash flows** and then replaces normal assumptions with stressed behaviour. Retail deposits may run faster, wholesale funding may cease to roll, committed facilities may be drawn, secured-funding haircuts may rise, derivatives may require collateral, asset sales may incur discounts and some contingent funding sources may disappear. Scenarios should separate **idiosyncratic stress**, where confidence in the bank deteriorates; **market-wide stress**, where funding and asset markets are disrupted generally; and a **combined stress**, where both happen together. Basel liquidity principles expressly call for severe stress scenarios and contingency funding plans linked to the resulting liquidity needs. For each day or time band, treasury calculates stressed inflows, outflows and available liquidity. Cumulative net outflow is compared with the liquidity buffer and other credible counterbalancing capacity. The **survival horizon** is the point at which available resources cease to cover cumulative needs under the assumptions. The word “credible” matters. A funding source should not be counted merely because it exists in normal markets. Monetisation capacity must consider haircuts, settlement timing, operational readiness, legal-entity location and whether several actions compete for the same collateral. Management actions can be incorporated only where they are sufficiently executable within the stress horizon. Stress testing is therefore more informative than a single ratio. It shows the path to failure: which day, currency, entity or funding source causes the breach. It can also expose cliffs—a stable profile for ten days followed by a large wholesale maturity on day eleven. +------------------+ | Stress scenario | +------------------+ | v +------------------+ | Stressed inflows | | and outflows | +------------------+ | v +------------------+ | Counterbalancing | | liquidity | +------------------+ | v +------------------+ | Cumulative cash | | position by day | +------------------+ | v +------------------+ | First shortfall | | = survival limit | +------------------+ Survival horizon is scenario-dependent; there is no meaningful survival-horizon number without stated assumptions. Counting an asset sale, secured borrowing and central-bank borrowing simultaneously when all three rely on the same collateral. **LCR horizon** — a standardised 30-calendar-day regulatory stress window. --- **Survival horizon** — the institution-specific time until liquidity resources are exhausted in a defined stress. **No delta.** Supervisory specifications vary, but institution-specific cash-flow stress and survival analysis are common liquidity-risk tools.

title: Contingency funding plans
one_screen: A contingency funding plan converts liquidity stress analysis into an executable crisis playbook: triggers, decision rights, funding actions, collateral, communications and escalation. A list of theoretical funding sources is not a CFP unless those sources can actually be mobilised under stress.
bodyText: A **contingency funding plan (CFP)** begins before the crisis. It defines early-warning indicators such as deposit outflows, widening funding spreads, falling unencumbered collateral, unusual drawdowns, reduced market access or rapid deterioration in liquidity metrics. Thresholds escalate the issue to named decision-makers rather than relying on ad hoc judgement. The plan then maps actions to stress severity. Early actions might shorten asset deployment or increase secured funding. More severe stages may involve monetising liquidity buffers, raising term funding where markets remain open, mobilising collateral, reducing new commitments or using available central-bank facilities subject to eligibility and internal governance. Each funding source needs an operational dossier: amount, currency, haircut, settlement time, legal entity, pre-positioning requirement, documentation, counterparty capacity and any constraint created by using it. The same asset cannot support two independent actions simultaneously. Governance is as important as funding capacity. A usable CFP identifies who can invoke it, who executes transactions, who communicates with supervisors and counterparties and how information is produced during fast-moving stress. Periodic testing should verify that access channels, collateral movements and communication trees work in practice. Basel’s sound liquidity principles call for robust, operational contingency funding plans tied to stress-test results. In the US, Regulation YY requires covered bank holding companies to maintain a CFP addressing identified stress events, available and alternative funding sources, invocation triggers, a liquidity-event management process, communication, early-warning monitoring and periodic operational testing. +------------------+ | Early-warning | | indicators | +------------------+ | v +------------------+ | Trigger breached | +------------------+ | v +------------------+ | Crisis governance| | invoked | +------------------+ | v +------------------+ | Funding / buffer | | actions | +------------------+ | v +------------------+ | Monitor + escalate| +------------------+ A contingency funding source is useful only to the extent it can be operationally accessed in the stress in which it is being counted. Listing “sell securities” or “raise secured funding” without identifying haircuts, settlement time, collateral availability and responsible execution teams. **CFP** — the executable response plan for liquidity stress. --- **Liquidity stress test** — the analytical scenario that quantifies the liquidity problem the CFP must address. — RBI liquidity-risk requirements use contingency funding and stress-management principles; precise current commercial-bank requirements should be verified against applicable RBI consolidated directions. — CFP capability forms part of the broader PRA liquidity and ILAAP supervisory framework. [PRA SS24/15] — contingency planning sits within the EU liquidity-risk and ILAAP supervisory architecture; detailed requirements should be verified against current CRR/CRD and EBA guidance. — Regulation YY expressly requires covered firms to maintain, update and periodically test contingency funding plans with triggers, action plans and alternative funding sources. [12 CFR 252.34(f)]

title: ILAAP and the naming trap
one_screen: ILAAP is the formal internal liquidity adequacy assessment terminology used in UK and EU supervisory architecture; it is not the universal global name for bank liquidity assessment. India and the US require liquidity-risk governance, stress testing and contingency planning through their own frameworks without universally relabelling that architecture “ILAAP”.
bodyText: The **Internal Liquidity Adequacy Assessment Process (ILAAP)** is a structured assessment of whether an institution has adequate liquidity and funding resources relative to its risks. A credible assessment integrates risk appetite, cash-flow mismatch analysis, stress tests, liquid-asset capacity, funding concentrations, intraday risk, contingency planning and governance. It is broader than proving compliance with LCR and NSFR. The key practitioner point is linguistic as much as technical. In UK prudential supervision, ILAAP is an explicit formal term. The PRA’s current SS24/15 states that its liquidity and funding supervisory approach covers the Internal Liquidity Adequacy Assessment Process and the Liquidity Supervisory Review and Evaluation Process. The version confirmed final in January 2026 took effect on 20 January 2026. The term is also embedded in EU supervisory vocabulary; EBA has issued guidance specifically concerning ICAAP and ILAAP information. That does **not** mean every jurisdiction calls its internal liquidity assessment an ILAAP. Indian banks are subject to RBI liquidity standards, ALM, LCR, NSFR and supervisory risk-management requirements, but practitioners should not import a UK/EU label into an RBI rule unless the RBI text itself uses it. Likewise, the US uses formal liquidity-risk-management, stress-testing, liquidity-buffer and contingency-funding constructs. Regulation YY, for example, prescribes liquidity-risk management and CFP requirements without framing them as an EU-style ILAAP. For cross-border roles, the right translation is functional rather than lexical: ask which local process performs internal liquidity adequacy assessment, not whether every regulator uses the same acronym. +----------------------+ | Internal liquidity | | adequacy assessment | +----------------------+ | v +----------------------+ | Risk + stress + | | buffer + funding + | | CFP + governance | +----------------------+ | | v v +------------+ +-------------+ | UK / EU | | IN / US | | "ILAAP" | | local terms | +------------+ +-------------+ ILAAP describes a formal UK/EU supervisory construct; internal liquidity adequacy is a universal problem, but the acronym is not a universal regulatory label. Writing “the bank submits its ILAAP” in an India or US procedure merely because that is what the equivalent process is called in a UK or EU entity. **ILAAP** — the formal Internal Liquidity Adequacy Assessment Process terminology used in UK/EU prudential supervision. --- **Liquidity-risk framework** — the broader universal set of risk governance, stress, buffers and contingency processes, whatever the local regulator calls it. — RBI has LCR, NSFR, ALM, liquidity stress and related prudential requirements, but “ILAAP” should not be assumed to be RBI’s universal formal naming convention. [RBI LCR/NSFR framework] — ILAAP is an explicit PRA supervisory construct under SS24/15 and the Internal Liquidity Adequacy Assessment part of the PRA framework. [PRA SS24/15, January 2026] — ILAAP is established supervisory terminology and is addressed in EBA guidance on ICAAP/ILAAP information. [EBA ILAAP guidance] — US rules use liquidity-risk management, stress-testing, buffer and CFP constructs rather than an EU-style universal “ILAAP” label. [12 CFR 252.34]

title: What funds transfer pricing solves
one_screen: FTP gives each business an internal price for the funding and liquidity consequences it creates, separating customer-product performance from centrally managed balance-sheet risk. Without FTP, business profitability can look strongest precisely where the bank is taking the most hidden maturity and liquidity risk.
bodyText: Suppose a business originates a five-year fixed-rate loan at 8%. Calling 8% its revenue ignores the fact that somebody must fund the loan for five years or bear refinancing risk. Conversely, a stable deposit business creates funding value that should not disappear inside a central treasury result. **Funds transfer pricing (FTP)** solves this allocation problem. Treasury or another central function applies an internal transfer charge to funding-consuming assets and an internal transfer credit to funding-providing liabilities. The business then sees a margin after recognising the balance-sheet resources it consumes or supplies. For a simplified loan: `Customer yield − FTP charge = business spread before other costs` For a deposit: `FTP credit − customer deposit rate = business funding spread before other costs` The transfer price is internal; it is not an external cash transaction with a customer. Its purpose is managerial economics and risk allocation. Good FTP transfers centrally manageable funding and liquidity risks away from the originating unit while leaving that unit accountable for the risks it controls, such as customer pricing or credit decisions. Treasury can then aggregate mismatches, hedge them centrally and observe the bank-wide funding position. The Federal Reserve’s interagency FTP guidance defines FTP as a central process allocating the costs and benefits associated with funding and contingent liquidity risks to business lines, products and activities. It states that FTP influences new-business volumes and terms and can align risk-taking incentives with the institution’s risk appetite. Basel liquidity principles similarly require allocation of liquidity costs, benefits and risks to significant business activities. +------------------+ | Customer business| +------------------+ | asset | deposit v v +--------+ +--------+ | FTP | | FTP | | charge | | credit | +--------+ +--------+ \ / v v +------------------+ | Central treasury | +------------------+ | v +------------------+ | Aggregate funding| | + liquidity risk | +------------------+ FTP should make the originating business economically accountable for the funding and liquidity consequences it creates. Judging product profitability from customer rate minus direct operating cost while leaving funding tenor and contingent liquidity cost in treasury. **FTP rate** — an internal transfer price used to allocate funding/liquidity economics. --- **Customer rate** — the contractual interest rate charged to or paid to the external customer. **No delta.** FTP methodology is an internal-management mechanism; supervisory expectations vary in detail, but its economic allocation problem is universal.

title: Matched-maturity FTP
one_screen: Matched-maturity FTP prices each asset or liability against internal funding of a comparable effective tenor rather than against one pooled average funding rate. It removes the accidental subsidy that otherwise makes long-dated assets look as cheap to fund as short-dated ones.
bodyText: Assume treasury can raise three-month funds at one internal cost and five-year funds at a higher cost. A flat FTP rate would charge both a three-month asset and a five-year asset the same amount, despite the longer asset creating substantially more refinancing and liquidity exposure. Under **matched-maturity FTP**, the internal rate is selected from the FTP curve at the product’s effective funding tenor. A five-year bullet loan is therefore charged an internal five-year transfer rate; a shorter exposure receives a shorter rate. Amortising assets can be decomposed into cash-flow strips or assigned a blended rate reflecting their repayment profile. On the liability side, a stable source of funding receives a credit related to the tenor of funding value it provides. A long-term issued liability can therefore earn a higher transfer credit than unstable overnight funding if the term structure and liquidity economics warrant it. The critical word is **effective**. Contractual maturity is appropriate only when contractual cash flows reasonably represent economic behaviour. Prepayable loans require expected prepayment assumptions. Non-maturity deposits require behavioural tenor. Revolving commitments require contingent rather than simply funded treatment. The FSI’s liquidity transfer-pricing work identifies matched-maturity marginal funding costs as better practice and notes that amortising and non-maturing products require blended marginal rates. It specifically criticises one-average-rate approaches because they fail to penalise longer-term funding commitments or reward longer-term funding benefits. Matched-maturity FTP does not mean treasury actually issues an external bond matching every customer transaction. The transfer is a pricing construct: it allocates the economic cost of the tenor while treasury centrally optimises the actual funding portfolio. +------------------+ | Product cash | | flows | +------------------+ | v +------------------+ | Effective tenor | +------------------+ | v +------------------+ | FTP curve point /| | blended strip | +------------------+ | v +------------------+ | Transfer charge | | or credit | +------------------+ | v +------------------+ | Business margin | +------------------+ Funding cost should follow the effective tenor of the exposure, not the accounting period in which profitability is reported. Charging every asset the current overnight funding rate because treasury happens to be funding the bank overnight today. **Matched-maturity FTP** — internal pricing against funding economics of comparable effective tenor. --- **Matched external funding** — actually issuing external funding that mirrors an individual asset’s cash flows. **No delta.** Matched-maturity pricing is an economic allocation principle rather than a jurisdiction-specific formula.

title: The FTP curve and its components
one_screen: An FTP curve converts tenor into the bank’s internal marginal value or cost of funding; it normally combines a reference-rate component with institution-specific term-liquidity economics, while contingent liquidity costs are allocated to exposures that can create stressed funding needs. The components must remain interpretable or business behaviour cannot be controlled.
bodyText: A useful conceptual starting point is: `FTP tenor rate ≈ base/reference rate + funding-liquidity premium` with a separate or embedded: `contingent liquidity charge` The **base rate** represents the time value and benchmark interest-rate component appropriate to the relevant currency and tenor. The **liquidity or funding premium** represents the additional marginal cost associated with obtaining term funding for the bank rather than simply observing a benchmark risk-free curve. This premium can vary substantially by tenor and market condition. The **contingent liquidity charge** addresses exposures that may require cash in stress even though they are not fully funded today. Undrawn commitments, potential collateral calls and other contingent demands can force the bank to hold standby liquidity. The Federal Reserve’s FTP guidance explicitly describes contingent liquidity risk as the cost of holding standby unencumbered highly liquid assets and expects that cost to be allocated to the businesses creating the contingent funding need. The curve should be marginal rather than merely an average of historic funding costs. Average cost answers what past liabilities cost; marginal cost is closer to what incremental balance-sheet usage economically requires now. The FSI identifies marginal matched-maturity funding cost as better practice. Care is required when combining components. Credit spread, liquidity premium, interest-rate risk and contingent charges can overlap if definitions are vague. A well-governed FTP framework states exactly what each component transfers and prevents the same risk from being charged twice. +------------------+ | Base/reference | | term curve | +------------------+ | v +------------------+ | + Funding / | | liquidity premium| +------------------+ | v +------------------+ | Matched-maturity | | FTP curve | +------------------+ | v +------------------+ | + contingent | | liquidity charge | | where relevant | +------------------+ Every FTP component should correspond to a distinct economic cost or benefit and have a defined risk owner. Adding a “liquidity spread”, “term premium” and “contingency premium” without checking whether two components charge the same underlying risk. **Funding-liquidity premium** — internal compensation for the marginal cost/value of term funding. --- **Contingent liquidity charge** — allocation for potential stressed cash needs that may arise from currently unfunded or conditional exposures. **No delta.** Curve construction is institution-specific; the economic components do not depend on jurisdictional naming.

title: Charging liquidity to the business that consumes it
one_screen: Liquidity cost belongs with the activity that creates the need to fund or hold a buffer, even when treasury centrally executes the funding. Central execution without decentralised pricing hides the risk from the business decision that created it.
bodyText: An asset consumes funding because cash leaves when the asset is originated and returns over time. The longer or less liquid the exposure, the greater the funding commitment it can impose. A committed but undrawn facility creates a different cost: there may be no cash outflow today, but stress can trigger a draw exactly when market funding is least available. FTP should therefore trace each material funding or contingent-liquidity requirement back to its originating activity. The transfer charge then enters product pricing, profitability metrics, limits and new-product approval. Federal Reserve guidance explicitly expects FTP costs and benefits to be allocated based on funding risk and contingent liquidity risk and incorporated into product pricing and business metrics. A useful sequence is: identify the cash-flow or contingent exposure; determine effective tenor and stressed liquidity behaviour; select the matched FTP rate; add the contingent-liquidity component where appropriate; then measure the customer business margin after those charges. This attribution creates the correct question for a product manager. The question is no longer “does the customer yield exceed the coupon on deposits?” It becomes “does the customer return compensate for credit risk, operating cost, capital, matched funding and liquidity consumption?” Risks allocated elsewhere under the bank’s framework should not be double-counted, but none should disappear. Central treasury remains responsible for aggregation because a bank has natural offsets. One business can produce stable deposits while another originates loans. Central funding lets treasury recognise those offsets. FTP ensures that the economic benefit of the funding source and cost of the consuming asset are visible to the appropriate businesses even though no external borrowing is matched transaction by transaction. +------------------+ | Business activity| +------------------+ | v +------------------+ | Funding / stress | | liquidity need | +------------------+ | v +------------------+ | FTP allocation | +------------------+ | v +------------------+ | Product pricing | | and profitability| +------------------+ | v +------------------+ | Behaviour changes| +------------------+ The central location of treasury execution does not justify centralising the economic cost away from the business that creates it. Charging funded loan balances for liquidity while giving undrawn commitments zero charge because they have not yet produced a cash outflow. **Risk execution owner** — the central function that funds or hedges aggregate exposure. --- **Risk-originating business** — the activity whose product decision created the funding or contingent-liquidity need. **No delta.** Allocation design is institution-specific; the economic incentive principle is universal.

title: FTP for non-maturity deposits
one_screen: NMD FTP is difficult because the product has no contractual term from which to select a transfer rate. The transfer credit must be built from a governed behavioural replication of stable balances and repricing behaviour, not from either overnight maturity or an arbitrary long-term tenor.
bodyText: A non-maturity deposit can be withdrawn quickly but may provide persistent aggregate funding. Crediting it purely at an overnight FTP rate ignores that stable funding value. Crediting the entire balance at a long-term rate assumes stability the bank may not actually possess. A common conceptual approach begins by segmenting the portfolio and separating a **volatile** component from a **core or stable** component. The volatile portion receives short-tenor treatment. The stable portion is assigned to a ladder or **replicating portfolio** of maturities based on estimated balance persistence and repricing behaviour. Its FTP credit becomes a weighted blend of transfer rates across those maturities. The model must distinguish balance stability from deposit-rate behaviour. A balance can remain in the bank for years but reprice rapidly when market rates change. Such a deposit supplies stable funding but less interest-rate benefit than one whose administered rate moves slowly. Combining the two assumptions into one “duration” obscures the economics. This methodology also links FTP to IRRBB. If the NMD desk is credited with a five-year funding value, treasury effectively accepts the corresponding behavioural position and must manage the resulting interest-rate exposure. The NMD model used for FTP, ALM and risk should therefore be reconcilable even when the exact purposes require different conservative overlays. FSI better-practice work states that non-maturing products require blended marginal transfer rates rather than a single average funding rate. The modelling challenge is not to find one objectively “correct” maturity; it is to establish a stable, validated and stressable representation of how the portfolio actually behaves. +------------------+ | NMD portfolio | +------------------+ | v +------------------+ | Segment balances | +------------------+ | | v v +---------+ +---------+ | Volatile| | Stable | | portion | | portion | +---------+ +---------+ | | v v +---------+ +---------+ |Short FTP| |Replicate| |tenor | |maturity | +---------+ +---------+ \ / v v +------------------+ | Blended FTP | | credit | +------------------+ NMD transfer value must come from behavioural assumptions that are explicit, governed and consistent with the risk transferred to treasury. Rewarding a deposit franchise with long-term FTP credit while ALM independently models the same deposits as short-lived, creating profits from inconsistent assumptions. **Behavioural tenor** — modelled persistence used to represent how long funding effectively remains. --- **Contractual tenor** — legal maturity; for an NMD it may provide almost no information about aggregate funding persistence. **No delta.** Regulatory behavioural constraints may influence model boundaries, but the FTP problem itself is universal.

title: How bad FTP distorts behaviour
one_screen: FTP is a behavioural control disguised as an internal price. Set it wrongly and rational business lines will optimise the wrong objective—creating excessive maturity transformation, unstable funding, cheap commitments or artificial deposit growth while reported product profitability still looks attractive.
bodyText: Consider a flat FTP curve. A five-year loan and a three-month loan receive the same funding charge. The longer asset earns more customer spread without paying for its extra funding commitment, so the business is incentivised to originate long-duration assets. The balance sheet accumulates structural mismatch even if every individual transaction passes its profitability hurdle. Now suppose all deposits receive the same FTP credit. A highly rate-sensitive deposit that disappears quickly in stress can look as valuable as a stable operating balance. The business is then rewarded for volume rather than funding quality. A third distortion appears when undrawn commitments receive no contingent liquidity charge. The business earns fees while treasury bears the cost of liquidity needed if customers draw during stress. Rational behaviour is to create more commitments than the bank would choose if their liquidity cost were visible. FTP can also distort behaviour through stale curves. If market funding costs rise sharply but FTP updates slowly, businesses continue originating assets at yesterday’s internal cost. The reported margin becomes an accounting artefact. Federal Reserve guidance specifically warns that failure to apply FTP effectively can misalign business incentives and lead to excessive on-balance-sheet asset growth or off-balance-sheet commitments because funding and contingent liquidity are mispriced. FSI research similarly found that average-rate transfer pricing failed to penalise longer-term asset commitments, failed to reward longer-term funding and encouraged risky maturity transformation. The diagnostic question is therefore not merely whether the FTP calculation is mathematically correct. It is: **what transaction would a rational business produce more of because of this price?** If that behaviour is inconsistent with the bank’s risk appetite, the FTP design is wrong or incomplete. +------------------+ | FTP signal | +------------------+ | v +------------------+ | Product economics| | seen by business | +------------------+ | v +------------------+ | Origination / | | deposit behaviour| +------------------+ | v +------------------+ | Balance-sheet | | composition | +------------------+ | v +------------------+ | Actual liquidity | | and funding risk | +------------------+ The quality of FTP should be judged partly by the behaviour it incentivises, not only by the elegance of its calculation. Treating an FTP model as a finance-allocation exercise and failing to test which products become artificially profitable under its assumptions. **FTP accuracy** — economic faithfulness of the internal funding and liquidity signal. --- **Accounting allocation accuracy** — whether internal revenue and cost mechanically reconcile; reconciliation alone cannot prove incentives are correct. **No delta.** Incentive distortion from mispricing is an economic mechanism independent of jurisdiction.

title: Why a solvent bank can fail
one_screen: Solvency is about whether assets ultimately cover liabilities with adequate capital; liquidity is about whether cash is available when payment is due. A bank can possess positive economic net worth yet fail if it cannot monetise assets or obtain funding fast enough to settle immediate obligations.
bodyText: Imagine a bank with long-term assets worth 110 in an orderly valuation and liabilities of 100. Economically it has positive net worth of 10. If 30 of liabilities must be repaid today but the bank has only 10 of immediate cash, it needs to raise another 20. If markets will lend against the assets, or the assets can be sold near their orderly value, the timing mismatch can be bridged. If funding markets close and buyers demand a severe fire-sale discount, the bank may be unable to raise 20 without crystallising large losses. A liquidity problem has now become a solvency problem. Banks are particularly exposed because maturity transformation is central to intermediation: shorter or withdrawable funding supports assets that often return cash over longer horizons. Basel’s liquidity principles explicitly recognise this structural vulnerability. Capital does not mechanically solve the timing problem. Equity absorbs losses and protects creditors from asset-value deterioration, but it is not a pile of settlement cash. A well-capitalised bank still needs immediately usable liquidity, collateral and access to payment systems. Conversely, holding liquidity does not cure true negative net worth: cash can postpone but not erase losses exceeding capital. This distinction explains why bank resilience requires both capital and liquidity frameworks. Capital absorbs unexpected losses; liquidity buffers and funding arrangements bridge cash-flow timing under stress. Treasury and ALM must therefore ask both questions whenever stress appears: **what is the value loss?** and **when is cash needed?** +------------------+ | Assets > debts | | economically | +------------------+ | v +------------------+ | Cash due now | +------------------+ | v +------------------+ | Immediate cash | | sufficient? | +------------------+ | yes | no v v +------+ +----------------+ |Pay | | Borrow / sell | +------+ +----------------+ | v +----------------+ | Market access? | +----------------+ | yes | no v v +------+ +--------+ |Bridge| | Failure| +------+ +--------+ Positive net worth cannot substitute for cash at the moment an obligation must settle. Answering a liquidity challenge by pointing to a strong capital ratio without demonstrating how the next cash obligation will actually be paid. **Solvency** — adequacy of asset value and loss-absorbing resources relative to liabilities. --- **Liquidity** — ability to obtain cash in time to meet obligations without unacceptable loss. **No delta.** The distinction follows balance-sheet economics, not jurisdiction.

title: The credit-liquidity feedback loop
one_screen: Credit deterioration can create liquidity stress, and liquidity stress can create additional credit losses; the loop runs through collateral, funding confidence, asset sales and customer drawdowns. Stress models that shock credit and liquidity independently can therefore miss the mechanism that makes combined crises severe.
bodyText: Begin with declining credit quality. Expected losses rise and the market value of affected assets can fall. Securities or loans used as collateral may attract larger haircuts, reducing secured borrowing capacity. At the same time, creditors and depositors can become less willing to fund the bank, increasing withdrawals or shortening available funding tenor. Liquidity stress then forces actions that can worsen credit and capital. Selling less-liquid assets rapidly may crystallise losses. Cutting new lending can weaken borrowers that were relying on refinancing. Drawing on committed credit lines can increase precisely when customers themselves are under stress, creating new funded exposures while the bank is trying to preserve cash. Derivatives and secured funding can add another channel. Falling asset values or ratings can generate collateral demands. More collateral becomes encumbered, leaving fewer unpledged assets available for alternative funding. A funding problem therefore reduces balance-sheet flexibility. This is a **feedback loop** because each round changes the starting point for the next. Credit loss weakens funding confidence; weaker funding forces asset monetisation; monetisation crystallises losses; losses further weaken confidence. Basel’s liquidity principles require banks to consider institution-specific and market-wide stress, contingent obligations and the possibility that funding sources close during severe conditions. The Federal Reserve’s liquidity-risk framework similarly requires stress cash-flow projections and CFP assessment of alternative funding sources rather than assuming normal-market access. The ALM implication is that a combined stress cannot be built by simply adding a credit loss number to a liquidity outflow number. Assumptions must interact: haircuts, funding availability, drawdowns, collateral requirements and asset-sale discounts should respond to the deteriorating state of the institution. +------------------+ | Credit quality | | deteriorates | +------------------+ | v +------------------+ | Losses / lower | | collateral value | +------------------+ | v +------------------+ | Funding confidence| | weakens | +------------------+ | v +------------------+ | Outflows / forced| | asset sales | +------------------+ | v +------------------+ | More losses and | | weaker credit | +------------------+ | +----------> back to top Credit and liquidity stresses are endogenous to one another once confidence, collateral and forced transactions begin to interact. Running a “combined” stress by adding independently modelled credit and liquidity outputs without changing funding, haircut or drawdown assumptions as credit quality deteriorates. **Credit loss** — loss caused by deterioration or default of an obligor or exposure. --- **Liquidity loss** — cost or failure arising from obtaining cash or monetising assets under stress; it can amplify credit losses without being the same risk. **No delta.** The feedback mechanism is economic and appears across banking systems.

title: India’s SLR, MSF, FALLCR and LCR interaction
one_screen: India’s distinctive feature is that specified government securities held within the mandatory SLR can also receive LCR HQLA recognition through the MSF and FALLCR carve-outs. SLR and LCR are different requirements, but RBI deliberately permits overlap so qualifying statutory holdings can provide recognised stress liquidity.
bodyText: **Statutory Liquidity Ratio (SLR)** is an Indian statutory liquidity requirement based on Net Demand and Time Liabilities (NDTL). **LCR** is the Basel-style ratio of recognised HQLA to 30-day stressed net cash outflows. They answer different questions: SLR requires specified liquid-asset holdings; LCR tests short-term stressed liquidity adequacy. The crucial interaction is HQLA recognition. RBI permits government securities held **above** mandatory SLR to qualify as Level 1 HQLA subject to the rules. It also permits government securities **within** mandatory SLR to be counted as Level 1 HQLA to the extent allowed under the **Marginal Standing Facility (MSF)** and the **Facility to Avail Liquidity for Liquidity Coverage Ratio (FALLCR)**. In April 2022, RBI noted that the MSF component had fallen to 2% of NDTL and increased FALLCR from 15% to 16% of NDTL. The total HQLA carve-out from mandatory SLR therefore became 18% of NDTL: 2% through MSF plus 16% through FALLCR. This does **not** mean “SLR equals LCR”. The denominator, purpose and operational rules remain separate. Nor does it mean every rupee of statutory holdings automatically enters LCR at full value. The asset must satisfy applicable HQLA conditions, and RBI’s April 2025 final amendments—effective 1 April 2026—require Level 1 government securities to be valued for LCR at no more than market value adjusted for applicable LAF/MSF haircuts. The practitioner’s mental model is overlap, not addition: the same qualifying security can help satisfy a statutory holding requirement and, within RBI’s defined accessibility framework, contribute to the LCR numerator. +----------------------+ | Government securities| +----------------------+ | v +----------------------+ | Mandatory SLR stock | +----------------------+ | | v v +----------+ +-----------+ | MSF | | FALLCR | | carve-out| | carve-out | | 2% NDTL | |16% NDTL | +----------+ +-----------+ \ / v v +----------------------+ | Up to 18% NDTL | | HQLA carve-out | +----------------------+ | v +----------------------+ | Apply current LCR | | eligibility/haircut | +----------------------+ SLR and LCR are separate requirements; RBI’s MSF/FALLCR rules determine how specified securities within mandatory SLR can also count as LCR HQLA. Adding “18% SLR liquidity” to the HQLA buffer as though they were separate pools when the same securities have already been counted through the MSF/FALLCR overlap. **SLR** — India’s statutory liquid-asset holding requirement linked to NDTL. --- **FALLCR** — the RBI facility permitting specified securities within mandatory SLR to be reckoned as HQLA for LCR purposes; it is not a second SLR requirement. — RBI permits an 18% of NDTL HQLA carve-out from mandatory SLR through 2% MSF plus 16% FALLCR; government-security LCR valuation is subject to the revised haircut treatment effective 1 April 2026. [RBI/2022-23/25; RBI/2025-26/27] — no SLR/FALLCR construct equivalent to this Indian RBI mechanism; UK firms follow the PRA liquidity/HQLA framework. [PRA SS24/15] — no Indian-style statutory SLR/FALLCR overlay exists in the CRR LCR architecture; EU HQLA treatment follows CRR and Delegated Regulation (EU) 2015/61. [CRR Part Six] — no Indian SLR/FALLCR construct applies; US HQLA and LCR requirements are governed through the US liquidity rules and tailoring framework. [OCC Bulletin 2019-52]

title: Cross-jurisdiction liquidity and IRRBB architecture
one_screen: Basel supplies the common LCR, NSFR and IRRBB architecture, but national implementation is not identical: India has the SLR/FALLCR overlay and a forthcoming 2025 IRRBB regime; the UK embeds liquidity adequacy in PRA ILAAP supervision; the EU combines CRR liquidity ratios with EBA IRRBB/CSRBB standards; the US tailors LCR/NSFR by firm category and uses liquidity-risk/CFP terminology rather than a universal ILAAP label.
bodyText: The common core makes cross-border work look deceptively uniform. LCR asks about 30-day stressed liquidity; NSFR asks about structural stable funding; IRRBB measures banking-book exposure from adverse interest-rate movements. Basel provides the international architecture, but each jurisdiction determines legal scope, local calibration and supervisory process. India implements Basel-style LCR and NSFR but overlays LCR with the statutory SLR and MSF/FALLCR mechanism. NSFR has applied to covered commercial banks since 1 October 2021. RBI’s November 2025 consolidated “forthcoming” Directions place the new IRRBB framework in Pillar 2/ICAAP, require ΔEVE and ΔNII, prescribe stress testing and use the 15% Tier 1 EVE outlier threshold; as of the current Directions, the implementation date is still to be communicated. The UK’s PRA framework explicitly uses ILAAP as a formal supervisory construct. Current SS24/15, effective 20 January 2026, sets out the PRA’s approach to supervising liquidity and funding risks. In the EU, LCR and NSFR sit in CRR Part Six, while EBA/GL/2022/14 addresses IRRBB and **credit spread risk in the banking book (CSRBB)**, with associated technical standards for supervisory outlier tests and standardised approaches. The US adopts LCR and NSFR for covered large organisations through a tailoring framework rather than imposing identical requirements on every bank. US liquidity supervision also uses explicit liquidity-risk management and CFP requirements rather than adopting ILAAP as the universal regulatory label. +--------------------+ | Basel architecture | | LCR / NSFR / IRRBB | +--------------------+ | v +--------------------+ | National adoption | +--------------------+ | | | | v v v v +------+ +------+ +------+ +------+ | IN | | UK | | EU | | US | +------+ +------+ +------+ +------+ |SLR/ | |PRA | |CRR + | |Tailor| |FALL | |ILAAP | |EBA | |scope | |CR | | | |CSRBB | |CFP | +------+ +------+ +------+ +------+ Basel comparability does not eliminate jurisdiction-specific legal scope, calibration or supervisory vocabulary. Copying an EU or UK policy into India or the US by changing the regulator name while leaving ILAAP terminology, scope assumptions and local liquidity mechanics unchanged. **Basel standard** — international prudential architecture produced by the Basel Committee. --- **Local rule** — the legally applicable national or regional implementation, which may tailor scope, calibration and supervisory process. — LCR includes the SLR/MSF/FALLCR interaction; NSFR has applied since 1 October 2021; RBI’s November 2025 IRRBB Directions place the forthcoming regime in Pillar 2/ICAAP but state that implementation date will be communicated separately. [RBI/2020-21/95; RBI/2022-23/25; RBI 2025 Directions] — PRA SS24/15 explicitly supervises liquidity and funding through an ILAAP/LSREP architecture; the current version became effective 20 January 2026. [PRA SS24/15] — CRR Part Six contains LCR/NSFR requirements; EBA/GL/2022/14 addresses IRRBB and CSRBB with related technical standards. [CRR; EBA/GL/2022/14] — LCR/NSFR requirements are tailored by firm risk category rather than uniform across banks; liquidity-risk management and contingency funding are formal supervisory constructs without a universal ILAAP label. [OCC Bulletin 2019-52; Federal Reserve NSFR final rule; 12 CFR 252.34]

title: The integrated ALM decision cycle
one_screen: ALM is the repeated process of converting the balance sheet into risk measures, comparing them with appetite and constraints, changing pricing, funding or hedges, and then measuring again. The decisive skill is understanding that capital, liquidity, IRRBB and FTP are different views of one evolving balance sheet rather than separate regulatory exercises.
bodyText: The cycle starts with positions and behavioural assumptions. Assets, liabilities and off-balance-sheet exposures are mapped by maturity, repricing date, currency, rate basis and option characteristics. Non-maturity deposits, prepayments and contingent draws require models because contractual schedules alone do not describe their economic behaviour. The same balance sheet is then viewed through multiple lenses. **IRRBB** produces EVE and NII sensitivities. **Liquidity analysis** produces cash-flow gaps, LCR, NSFR, intraday requirements and internal stress survival. **Capital analysis** asks how losses and valuation changes interact with available loss-absorbing resources. **FTP** converts those system-level costs and benefits into business-level prices. Management then compares the outputs with risk appetite, regulatory minima, internal limits and strategic objectives. A breach or undesirable trend can be addressed through several levers: change product pricing, alter origination mix, attract a different funding tenor, issue wholesale funding, change liquid-asset holdings, hedge interest-rate exposure, reduce commitments or adjust business limits. The key is to analyse side effects. Raising long-term funding can improve structural liquidity but reduce margin. Selling liquid assets to repay funding can change LCR and market-risk capacity. Extending deposit behavioural tenor may improve one measure only if the assumption is genuinely supportable. A derivative hedge can reduce EVE while altering NII or basis risk. Basel’s liquidity principles require liquidity costs and risks to enter pricing, stress testing and contingency planning, while IRRBB standards require both economic-value and earnings views. Integrated ALM is the governance mechanism that forces these views to reconcile before action is taken. +----------------------+ | Positions + behaviour| +----------------------+ | v +----------------------+ | Measure | | EVE / NII / liquidity| | capital / FTP | +----------------------+ | v +----------------------+ | Compare with | | appetite + limits | +----------------------+ | v +----------------------+ | Choose action | | price/fund/hedge/mix | +----------------------+ | v +----------------------+ | Recalculate effects | +----------------------+ | +-------------> back to measure No ALM action should be judged on a single metric when it materially changes another part of the balance-sheet risk profile. Fixing the metric that appears on the current committee dashboard while shifting the underlying risk into another horizon, legal entity, basis, liquidity bucket or accounting presentation. **ALM optimisation** — choosing a balance-sheet configuration that jointly respects risk appetite, liquidity, capital, earnings and strategic constraints. --- **Single-metric optimisation** — improving one ratio or sensitivity without accounting for the risk transferred elsewhere. **No delta.** Regulatory constraints differ, but the integrated decision logic is universal: measure the same balance sheet from multiple risk perspectives, act, and remeasure.

title: Equities
one_screen: An equity is a residual claim on a company: debt and other senior claims are paid first, and shareholders own what remains. Its price therefore reflects both expected future cash generation and the uncertainty around that residual.
bodyText: Equity represents ownership rather than a contractual promise to repay principal. A common shareholder usually has voting rights, a residual claim on assets after creditors, and potential participation in dividends and capital appreciation. Unlike a bond coupon, a dividend is generally discretionary: the board may reduce or omit it, subject to applicable law and the company’s circumstances. The economic value of an equity can be viewed as the present value of cash flows ultimately available to shareholders. In practice, market prices move because expectations change about revenue, margins, investment, financing, competitive position, interest rates and risk. A company can report rising profits while its share price falls if the market had expected even stronger results or if the discount rate applied to future cash flows rises. Primary and secondary markets serve different functions. In a primary issuance, the company raises capital by selling newly issued shares. In the secondary market, investors trade existing shares with one another; the company normally does not receive the trade proceeds. Market capitalisation equals share price multiplied by shares outstanding, but it is not the same as enterprise value, which also reflects net debt and other claims. Equity risk is multi-dimensional. Market risk moves the whole price; idiosyncratic risk comes from the issuer; liquidity risk affects the ability to transact near observed prices; corporate actions such as dividends, splits, rights issues and buybacks change positions or economics. For a banking professional, the important operational point is that the security identifier, listing venue, currency, settlement cycle, corporate-action treatment and legal owner can all matter independently of the headline share price. Company raises equity | v Primary issuance | v Shares become outstanding | v Secondary-market trading | +--> price discovery +--> liquidity +--> transfer of ownership Equity is a residual claim: higher upside comes with lower contractual seniority than debt. Treating a listed share as if it promises repayment at a fixed date. It does not have a contractual maturity like a plain bond. **Market capitalisation** — share price multiplied by shares outstanding; an equity-value measure. --- **Enterprise value** — a broader value of the operating business that adjusts equity value for debt, cash and other claims. **No delta.**

title: Fixed Income
one_screen: A fixed-income instrument converts financing into contractual cash flows: interest, principal and sometimes embedded options. Its value is driven by the timing and certainty of those cash flows and the discount rates used to value them.
bodyText: A bond is a debt instrument. The issuer receives funding and promises specified payments to investors. A plain fixed-rate bond has a face value or principal, a coupon rate, payment dates and a maturity date when principal is due. Other debt instruments may pay floating rates, no interim coupon, amortising principal or cash flows linked to inflation, credit events or options. The basic valuation rule is simple: a bond’s price is the present value of its future contractual cash flows, discounted at rates appropriate to their timing and risk. Two bonds with identical cash flows can still trade at different yields if they differ in liquidity, tax treatment, collateral, legal ranking or market convention. Credit quality matters because promised cash flows are not guaranteed merely because they are contractual. Seniority determines where an instrument sits in the capital structure. Secured debt has claims over specified collateral; senior unsecured debt ranks ahead of subordinated debt; equity is residual. Maturity describes when principal is contractually due, while duration describes price sensitivity to interest-rate movements. These are related but not interchangeable. Fixed-income analysis separates several risks. Interest-rate risk changes the value of otherwise unchanged cash flows. Credit risk concerns whether the issuer pays in full and on time. Spread risk changes the market compensation demanded for credit and liquidity. Optionality changes the cash-flow pattern itself: a callable bond may be redeemed when refinancing is favourable to the issuer, limiting investor upside. For operations and risk, the instrument definition must include coupon convention, day-count basis, business-day rule, payment calendar, redemption terms, seniority, currency and settlement convention. A one-line label such as “5-year bond” is insufficient to reproduce its economics. Issuer needs funding | v Creates debt instrument | +--> coupon / interest +--> principal +--> maturity +--> optional features | v Investor discounts expected cash flows | v Market price Value the cash-flow contract, not the product label. Using maturity as a synonym for interest-rate risk. A long maturity can have low or high duration depending on coupons and optionality. **Maturity** — the contractual date by which principal is due. --- **Duration** — a measure of a bond price’s sensitivity to changes in yield or interest rates. **No delta.**

title: Clean Price and Dirty Price
one_screen: A bond quote may exclude accrued interest even though settlement does not. Clean price is the quoted price without accrued interest; dirty price is the amount economically paid for the bond before fees: clean price plus accrued interest.
bodyText: Coupon interest accrues economically between payment dates. Suppose a bond pays a coupon every six months. The seller who has held the bond for part of the coupon period has earned part of the next coupon even though the issuer will pay the full coupon to whoever owns the bond on the payment date. Settlement therefore compensates the seller for accrued interest. The standard relationship is: Dirty price = Clean price + Accrued interest The clean price is useful for price comparison because it removes the predictable saw-tooth movement caused purely by coupon accrual. The dirty price, sometimes called the full price, is the value used to determine the cash consideration for settlement, subject to market-specific conventions and transaction charges. Accrued interest depends on the coupon amount and the fraction of the coupon period that has elapsed. That fraction is determined by a day-count convention such as Actual/Actual, 30/360 or Actual/365. Two instruments can therefore accrue differently even when they have the same coupon rate and calendar dates. Around a coupon payment date, the mechanics can look counter-intuitive. Immediately before coupon payment, accrued interest is high. After the coupon is detached and paid, accrued interest resets, while the clean price should not mechanically jump by the same amount merely because time passed. This is why analysts distinguish clean and dirty measures. The distinction also matters in reconciliations. A trader may discuss a clean-price move, the risk system may mark a full price, and the settlement instruction may reflect principal amount plus accrued interest. If systems disagree on the field definition, a correct trade can appear to have a valuation or cash break. Coupon date A ---------------- Coupon date B | | |<------ accrued interest ------->| ^ | trade date clean price + accrued interest = dirty / full price Always identify whether a bond price field is clean or dirty before comparing valuations or settlement amounts. Explaining a dirty-price increase caused by one day of accrual as market P&L. **Clean price** — bond price excluding accrued coupon interest. --- **Dirty price** — clean price plus accrued interest; also called full price. **No delta.**

title: Yield to Maturity and the Price–Yield Relationship
one_screen: Yield to maturity is the single discount rate that equates a bond’s market price with the present value of its promised remaining cash flows. For a plain fixed-rate bond, price and yield move in opposite directions because a higher discount rate lowers present value.
bodyText: Yield to maturity, or YTM, compresses a bond’s price and scheduled cash flows into one annualised rate. It is the discount rate that makes the present value of remaining coupons and principal equal to the observed full economic price under the relevant market convention. It is therefore an internal rate of return on promised cash flows, not a guarantee of realised return. The inverse price–yield relationship follows directly from present-value mathematics. If all promised cash flows are unchanged and the discount rate rises, each future payment is worth less today, so the bond price falls. If the discount rate falls, present values rise and the price increases. A bond trading below par usually has a YTM above its coupon rate; one trading above par usually has a YTM below its coupon rate, assuming a plain fixed-rate bullet bond. YTM has assumptions and limitations. It treats the promised cash-flow schedule as if it occurs, so defaultable bonds can have a quoted YTM that overstates economically expected return. It also embeds a reinvestment assumption for interim coupons if interpreted as a realised compound return. Callable, puttable and otherwise optional bonds may need yield-to-call, yield-to-worst or option-adjusted measures because the maturity cash-flow path is not fixed. A small yield movement does not cause the same percentage price change for every bond. Sensitivity depends mainly on duration and convexity, which are separate concepts. YTM tells where the bond sits on a price–yield curve; duration and convexity describe the local shape of that curve. Operationally, YTM calculations depend on clean/full-price handling, settlement date, coupon schedule, day count, compounding frequency and redemption value. Two systems can produce different yields from the same headline price if conventions differ. Higher required yield | v Future cash flows discounted more heavily | v Lower present value | v Lower bond price Lower required yield -> higher bond price For a plain fixed-cash-flow bond, hold cash flows constant: yield up means price down, and yield down means price up. Calling YTM the investor’s guaranteed return. Default, reinvestment, sale before maturity and optionality can all change realised return. **Coupon rate** — contractual interest rate applied to face value. --- **Yield to maturity** — discount rate implied by current price and promised remaining cash flows. **No delta.**

title: Duration and Convexity
one_screen: Duration is the first-order estimate of how a bond price changes when yield changes; convexity is the second-order correction for the curve in the price–yield relationship. Duration gives the slope, convexity improves the estimate when moves are larger.
bodyText: Duration is both a cash-flow timing concept and a practical risk measure. Macaulay duration is a present-value-weighted average time to receive cash flows. Modified duration converts that concept into approximate percentage price sensitivity to a small parallel change in yield. If modified duration is 5, a 1 percentage-point rise in yield implies roughly a 5% price fall before allowing for convexity. The approximation is: Percentage price change ≈ − Modified duration × yield change The minus sign reflects the inverse price–yield relationship. Duration is local: it is most accurate for small changes and for instruments whose cash flows do not change when rates move. Convexity captures curvature. A plain option-free bond normally has positive convexity, meaning the price gain from a given fall in yield is larger than the price loss from an equal rise in yield. Adding a convexity term improves the approximation: Percentage price change ≈ −D × Δy + ½ × Convexity × (Δy)^2 Embedded options can change the shape materially. A callable bond may exhibit reduced or negative effective convexity when rates fall because the issuer becomes more likely to call it, capping price appreciation. For instruments whose expected cash flows change with rates, effective duration and effective convexity are more useful than measures assuming fixed cash flows. Duration is not maturity. A 10-year high-coupon bond generally has lower duration than a 10-year zero-coupon bond because more value is received earlier. Duration is also not credit spread duration unless the shock being measured is explicitly a spread change. At portfolio level, duration supports hedging and risk aggregation, but parallel-shift duration misses changes in curve shape. Key-rate durations or bucketed sensitivities are needed when different maturities move by different amounts. Yield shock | v First-order effect --------> Duration | +--> curvature correction -> Convexity | v Estimated bond-price change Use duration for local slope and convexity for curvature; neither is a substitute for understanding the cash flows and options. Quoting a single duration number as if it captures every possible yield-curve movement. **Maturity** — time until contractual principal repayment. --- **Duration** — price sensitivity to yield changes, derived from the timing and present value of cash flows. **No delta.**

title: Credit Spreads
